t.gessi bolognesi@44.4,11.4:
Ride south out of Bologna and within ten minutes the city's suburbs give way to something surprising: a range of low hills made of gypsum, a soft, crystalline rock that dissolves in water and forms caves, sinkholes and strange, shiny outcrops. These are the Gessi Bolognesi, a protected regional park between the Savena and Idice valleys, and in 2023 they became part of the UNESCO site for the evaporitic karst and caves of the northern Apennines.

The gypsum glitters in the sun, especially the large mirror-like crystals called selenite, and the hills are riddled with caves. The most famous, the Grotta della Spipola, can be visited on guided tours, and the Buco dei Vinchi and other sinkholes dot the landscape. Prehistoric people used the caves, and the gypsum itself was quarried for centuries; the stone was used in Bologna's buildings. The park also includes the calanchi, badlands of eroded clay, around the Abbadessa area, which look almost lunar in the late afternoon light.

The riding starts immediately. The roads up the Savena valley toward Pianoro and Loiano, and the climbs along the ridges toward Monte Calderaro and San Lazzaro, are full of bends and give views back over the plain toward Bologna. The famous SS65 Futa road, the old route from Bologna to Florence over the Apennines, begins its climb here, and is a classic for motorcyclists, with a long sequence of curves up to the Futa pass. On weekends it is very popular, with bikes everywhere and the occasional police check.

Pianoro, Rastignano and San Lazzaro all have fuel and bars, and Bologna is minutes away. The city's food culture is legendary: tagliatelle with ragù, tortellini in broth, mortadella, and the wines of the Colli Bolognesi, such as Pignoletto. If you are passing through, Bologna's porticoes and towers, especially the leaning pair, deserve an evening walk. Spring and autumn are perfect for riding; summer on the plain is hot and humid, while the hills are a little cooler.
t.vena del gesso romagnola m te mauro@44.2:
Driving through the hills of Romagna, south of Faenza, you notice a long, pale ridge cutting across the valleys like a wall. This is the Vena del Gesso Romagnola, a band of gypsum rock about twenty-five kilometres long, and Monte Mauro is its highest point, rising above the villages of Riolo Terme, Brisighella and Fognano. The ridge is now a regional park and part of the UNESCO site for the evaporitic karst of the northern Apennines.

The gypsum makes for an unusual landscape: cliffs that shine in the sun, sinkholes and caves, and patches of rare plants that love the alkaline soil. The Tanaccia cave near Brisighella and the Re Tiberio cave on the Senio river have long histories of human use, from prehistoric times on. On the summit of Monte Mauro stand the ruins of a medieval castle and a small church, and the views stretch across the hills toward the Adriatic.

Brisighella is the jewel of this area. A medieval village with three hills, each topped by a landmark: the fortress, the clock tower and the sanctuary of Monticino. Its Via degli Asini, the street of the donkeys, is an elevated covered lane where carters once stabled their animals. Riolo Terme has thermal baths, and the whole area is known for olive oil, especially the Brisighella oil, one of the most prized in Italy.

The riding is excellent. The roads that climb from the plain along the valleys of the Lamone, Senio and Santerno, and cross between them over the hills, are twisty and scenic, with good surfaces and moderate traffic. The road from Brisighella toward Marradi and the Tuscan border is a fine ride, as are the routes toward Casola Valsenio and Palazzuolo sul Senio. Imola's Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari is not far, and this part of Romagna is passionate about motorcycles and motor racing.

Castel Bolognese, about twelve kilometres away, is the nearest larger town, but Brisighella and Riolo Terme have fuel and plenty of trattorias. Romagna's food is hearty: piadina flatbread, cappelletti, and the local Sangiovese wine. Autumn brings truffle and chestnut festivals in the hill villages.
t.historic centre of siena@43.3,11.3:
Siena sits on three ridges in the heart of Tuscany, a red-brick medieval city that has hardly changed its shape in seven hundred years. At its centre is the Piazza del Campo, a sloping, shell-shaped square paved in brick and divided into nine sections, a reminder of the Council of Nine that governed the city in its golden age. The Palazzo Pubblico, with the slender Torre del Mangia, stands at the bottom of the square, and inside are frescoes by Ambrogio Lorenzetti showing the effects of good and bad government, painted in the fourteenth century.

Siena was a rich republic and a rival of Florence, and its wealth came from banking and trade along the Via Francigena, the pilgrim road to Rome. The Monte dei Paschi, founded in 1472, is often described as the oldest surviving bank in the world. The city's cathedral, with its striped marble and an extraordinary inlaid floor, was intended to be even bigger, but the plague of 1348 put an end to the plans; the unfinished nave still stands. The historic centre is a World Heritage site.

Twice a year, on 2 July and 16 August, the Campo hosts the Palio, a bareback horse race between the city's contrade, or districts. It lasts about ninety seconds and is preceded by days of ritual, rivalry and celebration. If you are in Siena then, expect huge crowds and closed streets.

The centre is a limited traffic zone, a ZTL, and riding into it without permission brings automatic fines, so leave the bike outside the walls in one of the parking areas and walk. The riding around Siena is classic Tuscany: the SR2, the old Via Cassia, south toward the Val d'Orcia, and the roads through the Crete Senesi, a landscape of bare clay hills, offer gentle curves and huge views. To the north, the Chianti Classico roads toward Castellina and Radda are among the most popular biking roads in Italy.

Siena has fuel outside the walls and plenty of food. Try pici, a thick hand-rolled pasta, and panforte, a dense spiced cake. Spring and autumn are perfect for riding here.
t.vena del gesso romagnola m te penzola@44:
The Santerno valley climbs south from Imola into the Apennines toward Tuscany, and about fifteen kilometres up, the river cuts through a ridge of shining grey-white rock. This is the western end of the Vena del Gesso Romagnola, the gypsum vein that runs across this part of Romagna, and Monte Penzola rises above the village of Borgo Tossignano, with Fontanelice and Casalfiumanese nearby.

Gypsum, a soft mineral that forms in evaporating seas, creates its own kind of landscape: sinkholes, caves, cliffs that glitter with crystals, and a flora adapted to dry, alkaline soils. The Vena del Gesso was laid down about six million years ago, when the Mediterranean partially dried up, and it is now a regional park and part of the UNESCO site for the evaporitic karst of the northern Apennines. Near Borgo Tossignano, the rock has been quarried, and the cliff faces show the layers of crystals clearly. The village of Tossignano, perched on the ridge above the valley, has a fine view.

Imola, down on the plain, is home to the Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari, the racing circuit where Formula One and motorcycle races have long been held. It is also where Ayrton Senna died in 1994, and there is a memorial to him at the Tamburello corner. Romagna is motor-racing country, home to many famous motorcycle racers, and the passion for bikes is palpable.

The riding up the Santerno valley is excellent. The SP610 Montanara road follows the river through Borgo Tossignano and Fontanelice toward Castel del Rio and the Tuscan border, with a good sequence of bends and pleasant views. From Castel del Rio, with its medieval humpback bridge, the roads over the hills toward the Senio and Sillaro valleys are twistier and quieter. Surfaces are generally good, and traffic moderate, with more bikes at weekends.

Castel San Pietro Terme, about thirteen kilometres away, is the nearest town of size, and Borgo Tossignano has fuel and bars. Local food includes the cappelletti and tagliatelle of Romagna and, in autumn, the chestnuts and mushrooms of the Apennines. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; summer can be hot and hazy in the valleys.
t.historic centre of san gimignano@43.5,11:
Seen from the surrounding countryside, San Gimignano looks like a medieval Manhattan: a cluster of stone towers rising from a hilltop above vineyards and olive groves in the Val d'Elsa. In its heyday, in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, the town had dozens of them, built by rival families as symbols of power and wealth. Fourteen survive, enough to make it one of the most recognisable towns in Italy and a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1990.

The town grew rich as a stop on the Via Francigena, the pilgrim route from Canterbury to Rome, and from the trade in saffron, which was grown in the area and sold across Europe. The plague of 1348 and the town's subsequent submission to Florence ended its golden age, and its decline froze it in time. The Collegiata, the main church, is covered inside with frescoes of Old and New Testament scenes, and the Palazzo Comunale and its tower, the Torre Grossa, can be climbed for a view over the rooftops and the hills. San Gimignano is also known for its white wine, Vernaccia di San Gimignano, which was the first Italian wine to receive the DOC designation in 1966. The town's gelato shops have a strong reputation, and the queues to prove it.

The centre is closed to traffic, and the town is crowded with day-trippers in summer, especially around midday. The best time to see it is early in the morning or in the evening, when the tour buses have gone and the towers glow in the low light. Park outside the walls in one of the car parks and walk in.

The riding around San Gimignano is classic Tuscany: winding roads through hills, past vineyards, cypress-lined drives and farmhouses. The roads toward Volterra, about thirty kilometres west, are particularly good, crossing a wilder landscape of rolling hills and clay badlands. To the east, Colle di Val d'Elsa, known for its crystal glass, and the Chianti roads beyond offer more curves.

Poggibonsi, about nine kilometres away, has fuel and every service. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for riding.
t.bassa collina reggiana@44.6,10.6:
The low hills south of Reggio Emilia, where the Po plain starts to ripple up toward the Apennines, hide a strange geology: outcrops of gypsum, the glittering crystalline rock left behind when ancient seas evaporated millions of years ago. Water dissolves gypsum easily, and over time it has carved caves, sinkholes and blind valleys into these hills. The Bassa Collina Reggiana, the low Reggio hill country, is part of the UNESCO site Evaporitic Karst and Caves of Northern Apennines, listed in 2023, and around Borzano, Albinea and Vezzano sul Crostolo you can see the white and grey gypsum cliffs poking through the woods and vineyards.

The caves here are mostly closed to the public and protected for their bats and fragile formations, but walking paths lead past outcrops, sinkholes and viewpoints. One of the best known is the Tana della Mussina near Borzano, a cave where archaeologists found traces of prehistoric burials. The landscape is green and gentle, with oak woods, vineyards producing the sparkling red Lambrusco, and fields where the cows that give milk for Parmigiano Reggiano graze.

The riding is pleasant rather than dramatic, with small roads winding through the hills, linking villages and farms with short climbs, tight bends and views over the plain. Head further south and the roads get more serious: the road up the Crostolo valley toward the Apennine passes, and the route to Canossa, where the ruins of Matilda of Canossa's castle stand on a white rock. It was here in 1077 that Emperor Henry IV stood in the snow for three days to beg forgiveness from Pope Gregory VII, an episode that gave the expression going to Canossa to several languages. Expect traffic near Reggio Emilia and on weekends, and fog on winter mornings in the plain.

Scandiano, about seven kilometres away, is the nearest larger town, with fuel, shops and restaurants, and a fine castle that belonged to the Boiardo family; the poet Matteo Maria Boiardo was born here. Albinea and Vezzano have cafés and trattorias serving local food like erbazzone, a savoury pie with greens and cheese, and cappelletti in broth. A visit to a Parmigiano Reggiano dairy, where you can see the cheese being made at dawn, is a highlight of any trip.
t.cathedral@44.6,10.9:
Modena's cathedral is one of the masterpieces of Romanesque architecture in Europe, and the inscription on its facade still names its makers with pride: the architect Lanfranco and the sculptor Wiligelmo. Work began in 1099 to house the relics of Saint Geminianus, the city's patron, and the result is a building of pale stone, with arcaded galleries, lions supporting the columns of the portal, and carved panels telling the story of Genesis with an expressive power that still surprises. The Ghirlandina, the cathedral's bell tower, leans slightly and rises high above the rooftops, and together with the Piazza Grande they form a UNESCO site.

The city around the cathedral is prosperous, compact and full of arcades, with elegant shops, markets and cafés. Modena is the home of traditional balsamic vinegar, aged for years in barrels in attics, and of tortellini, zampone and other rich dishes. It is also the hometown of Luciano Pavarotti, and the opera tradition runs deep here.

For riders, Modena means one thing: motors. The city lies at the heart of Italy's Motor Valley. Ferrari has its home in Maranello, a short ride south, with a museum and the Fiorano test track, while Maserati was founded in Bologna but has had its headquarters in Modena for decades. The Enzo Ferrari Museum in the city centre is housed in a striking yellow building next to the house where Enzo was born. Ducati in Borgo Panigale near Bologna and Lamborghini in Sant'Agata Bolognese are both within easy reach, so a day of pilgrimage to the temples of engineering is entirely possible.

The city centre has a limited traffic zone, the ZTL, monitored by cameras, and entering it without permission can result in hefty fines, so park outside and walk. Fuel and services are plentiful on the ring road. The roads south into the Apennines, toward Pavullo nel Frignano and the passes of the Modenese hills, are a great escape from the flat plain and the heavy traffic of the Via Emilia. Summer is hot and humid, winter foggy and cold; spring and autumn are the most pleasant seasons for a visit.
t.historic centre of naples@40.9,14.3:
Naples is not a city you ride through so much as one you survive and then fall in love with. The historic centre, a UNESCO site since 1995, sits on the street plan of Neapolis, the Greek new city founded around the sixth century BC, and the three ancient decumani still run straight through it, the most famous being Spaccanapoli, the street that splits Naples in two. Along them, churches, palaces, shrines, workshops and laundry-hung alleys are packed together with an intensity found nowhere else in Europe.

The treasures are endless: the cathedral with the relics of San Gennaro, whose blood is said to liquefy three times a year; the Sansevero chapel with its astonishing veiled Christ in marble; the cloister of Santa Chiara covered in majolica tiles; the underground city of Greek and Roman tunnels and cisterns; and Via San Gregorio Armeno, the street of nativity-scene makers, where figures of saints share shelf space with footballers and politicians. Maradona is everywhere, on murals and altars, a saint of the city in all but name.

Riding in Naples is an extreme sport. Scooters swarm everywhere, often carrying entire families, traffic lights are treated as suggestions, and the streets of the old centre are narrow, cobbled, slippery and crowded with pedestrians. Much of the centre has limited traffic zones, and theft of motorcycles and items left on them is a real risk, so use a secure garage and keep valuables with you. The rewards outside the city are huge: the road up Vesuvius, the coast road to Sorrento and the Amalfi coast, the Phlegraean Fields with their volcanic craters, and the hills of the Campanian interior.

Food is reason enough to come. Naples is the birthplace of pizza, and the pizzerias of Via dei Tribunali serve some of the best in the world, simple margheritas with soft, blistered crusts. Add sfogliatelle pastries, fried street food, espresso drunk standing at the bar, and you will not go hungry. Fuel is available on the main roads outside the centre. Spring and autumn offer pleasant temperatures; summer is hot and crowded, but the evenings, when the city comes alive in the streets, are magical.
t.costiera amalfitana@40.6,14.6:
The Amalfi coast road is the reason many riders first dreamed of Italy, and it lives up to the legend and then some, with a few catches. The SS163 Amalfitana, carved into the cliffs above the sea in the nineteenth century, winds along the southern side of the Sorrento peninsula from Positano to Vietri sul Mare, with hundreds of bends, sheer drops, tunnels, bridges and villages clinging to the rocks. Amalfi itself, a small town of about five thousand people at the mouth of a ravine, was once a powerful maritime republic that rivalled Venice and Genoa in the Middle Ages, and its cathedral, with its striped facade and Arab-Norman cloister, is a reminder of that glory.

The coast was listed by UNESCO in 1997 for its landscape of terraced lemon groves, vineyards and villages, shaped by centuries of human work on impossibly steep slopes. Atrani, just next door, is one of the smallest towns in Italy, a tangle of alleys and stairways. Ravello, high above, has the gardens of Villa Rufolo and Villa Cimbrone, with views that inspired Wagner and countless writers.

Now the honest part. The road is narrow, and in summer it is clogged with tour buses, cars and scooters, so traffic jams can last for hours, and the buses often need the whole road to get around the bends. Local authorities have at times restricted traffic in summer, so check current rules before you go. The best times to ride are early morning, or in spring and autumn, when the road is quieter and the light is soft. Parking in Amalfi and Positano is scarce and expensive, but motorcycles have an advantage over cars.

Maiori, about four kilometres away, is the nearest town over five thousand people, with fuel and more space, and the roads inland over the mountains from Amalfi to Agerola or from Maiori over the Valico di Chiunzi offer spectacular views and less traffic. Food is a highlight: fresh seafood, pasta with lemons, and of course limoncello, the lemon liqueur made from the local sfusato lemons. Treat yourself to a swim from a rocky beach after the ride.
t.via appia regina viarum@41.5,13.0:
South of the Alban Hills, the Via Appia drops onto the Pontine plain and runs dead straight for mile after mile, as if the Roman engineers had laid it with a ruler, which in a sense they did. This was the Regina Viarum, the queen of roads, begun in 312 BC by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus to link Rome with Capua, and later extended to Brindisi. Here, near Sezze Scalo and Latina, the road crossed the Pontine Marshes, a malarial swamp that defeated would-be drainers from the Romans to the popes. Travellers sometimes took a canal boat alongside the road instead, and the poet Horace complained about the mosquitoes and the frogs keeping him awake on that very journey.

The marshes were finally drained in the 1930s under Mussolini, in a huge project that created new farmland and new towns, including Latina, founded in 1932 as Littoria, with its rationalist architecture of squares and straight avenues. The modern SS7 follows the line of the old road across the plain, lined with umbrella pines and eucalyptus, and the whole route of the Appia became a UNESCO site in 2024.

The riding on the plain is fast, flat and straight, and the traffic can be heavy and impatient, so do not expect much fun on the SS7 itself. The real pleasure is in the hills to the east, the Monti Lepini, where Sezze sits on a ridge overlooking the plain. The roads up to Sezze, Bassiano and Sermoneta climb in tight bends through olive groves and forests, with views over the plain to the sea and the Circeo promontory. Sermoneta, with its Caetani castle, is one of the most beautiful medieval villages in Lazio, and the Garden of Ninfa below it, built among the ruins of a medieval town, is famously romantic but open only on certain days.

Sezze, about five kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and is known for its artichokes, celebrated with a festival in spring. Latina and the coast offer more services and beaches. Local food includes buffalo mozzarella, fresh vegetables from the reclaimed land and the hearty cooking of the hill towns. Spring is lovely, with green fields and mild weather.
t.18th century royal palace at caserta wit:
When Charles of Bourbon, king of Naples, decided to build a royal palace to rival Versailles, he did not do things by halves. The Reggia di Caserta, begun in 1752 to a design by Luigi Vanvitelli, is one of the largest royal palaces in the world, with some twelve hundred rooms, four inner courtyards, a theatre and a grand staircase that has appeared in films including Star Wars, where it stood in for the palace of Naboo. Behind it, a park stretches for three kilometres up the hillside, with fountains, statues and a long chain of pools and cascades fed by an aqueduct that Vanvitelli built specially, ending at a great waterfall at the top.

The whole complex, including the aqueduct and the silk-weaving colony of San Leucio, a utopian industrial village founded by Charles's son Ferdinand, is a UNESCO site. The park is so large that many visitors rent bicycles or take a shuttle bus to reach the top; walking all the way up and back takes a couple of hours. The English Garden, at the top on the right, is a romantic landscape with exotic trees, fake ruins and a bath of Venus.

Caserta is a city of about seventy-five thousand people north of Naples, and riding around it means dealing with heavy traffic, impatient drivers and potholes. The good news is that the hills to the northeast, toward Caserta Vecchia, a beautifully preserved medieval village with a Romanesque cathedral, offer winding roads with views over the plain. Further afield, the Matese mountains and the Benevento hills offer quieter, more scenic riding. Summers are very hot, so visit the palace and park in the morning, and ride in the cooler hours.

Caserta has fuel, shops and restaurants, and plenty of cafés around the palace. The region is the home of buffalo mozzarella, and the farms around Caserta and Capua produce some of the best, eaten fresh on the day it is made. Try it in a caprese salad, on a pizza or simply on its own with a drizzle of olive oil. Capua, a short ride away, has a Roman amphitheatre second in size only to the Colosseum.
t.the via appia from sinuessa to the pagus:
The Via Appia, the Queen of Roads, ran from Rome to Brindisi, and in 2024 UNESCO inscribed long stretches of it as a single World Heritage site. Near Mondragone, on the coast of northern Campania, the road passes the site of Sinuessa, a Roman colony that once guarded the route where it reached the sea after crossing the coastal plains from the north. Not a great deal stands above ground today, so this is a place where you read the landscape rather than tour the ruins.

The landscape is worth reading. Behind the coast rises Monte Massico, a limestone ridge whose southern slopes produced Falernian, the most celebrated wine of ancient Rome, praised by poets and drunk at the best tables of the empire. Vines are still grown here, and the modern Falerno del Massico wine is a reasonable way to toast the past. To the north lies the river Garigliano and the ruins of Minturnae, with its theatre and forum, while the plain inland is buffalo country, and the mozzarella made from their milk in this part of Campania is superb.

The coast itself is a mixed experience, and it is fair to say so. Long sandy beaches stretch away, but they are lined with holiday developments, some unfinished, and litter can be a problem along the roadsides. The real pleasure lies in the light over the Tyrrhenian Sea in the evening and in the sense of riding on top of two thousand years of traffic.

On the bike, the main coastal road, the Domitiana, is straight and busy, with trucks and erratic local driving. Much better are the roads climbing over Monte Massico and into the hills towards Sessa Aurunca and the extinct volcano of Roccamonfina, with chestnut woods, tight bends and quiet villages. Watch for potholes and gravel, which are common on minor roads in this part of Italy, and for drivers who treat lane markings as suggestions. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; summer brings heat and beach traffic.

Mondragone, about four kilometres away, is a town of over twenty-five thousand people with fuel, shops and plenty of places to eat. Order fresh mozzarella wherever you see it made, preferably eaten the same morning, and the simple lunch becomes one of the best of the trip.
t.villa de cafaggiolo@44.0,11.3:
In the green bowl of the Mugello, north of Florence, the Medici family kept a house long before they ruled the city. Cafaggiolo was an old family property, and around the middle of the fifteenth century Cosimo the Elder had the architect Michelozzo transform it into a fortified country villa, with battlements, a tower and a moat, a cross between a castle and a farmhouse. Lorenzo the Magnificent spent time here as a boy, and the villa became a favourite retreat for hunting and escaping the plague in the city. It is one of the Medici Villas and Gardens in Tuscany listed by UNESCO, and visits depend on current restoration and opening arrangements, so check before you arrive.

The Mugello valley around it is a broad, fertile basin ringed by the Apennines, with fields, vineyards, chestnut woods and small towns. Scarperia, a few kilometres away, has been making knives for centuries, and its palace is decorated with coats of arms. San Piero a Sieve sits right below the villa, and Borgo San Lorenzo is the main town of the valley.

For riders the Mugello is sacred ground. Just outside Scarperia lies the Mugello circuit, home of the Italian MotoGP race every spring, when the hills fill with fans and the sound of engines echoes across the valley. Even without a race, the roads around are a joy. To the north, the Passo della Futa and the Passo del Giogo cross the Apennines towards Bologna with endless bends, climbs and descents through woods and pastures, and on a fine Sunday they are full of bikes. The Futa road was once part of the Mille Miglia race. Near the top of the Futa stands a vast German war cemetery from the Second World War, a sobering sight.

The roads are well surfaced, but traffic can be heavy on weekends, police controls are common, and tight bends can catch you out. In winter, frost and ice are possible on the passes, and the weather can turn quickly in the mountains.

Fuel is available in San Piero a Sieve, Scarperia and Borgo San Lorenzo. For lunch, look for tortelli di patate, potato-filled pasta typical of the Mugello, served with meat sauce or butter and sage, and a glass of Tuscan red, preferably after the riding is done.
t.gessi di zola predosa@44.5,11.2:
Southwest of Bologna, where the flat Po plain meets the first ripples of the Apennines, the hills around Zola Predosa hide a strange geology. These are gypsum hills, made of evaporite rock formed when an ancient sea dried out millions of years ago, leaving layers of shimmering selenite crystals. Water dissolves gypsum easily, and over time it has carved sinkholes, blind valleys and caves through the rock. In 2023, the Evaporitic Karst and Caves of the Northern Apennines were listed by UNESCO, and the Gessi Bolognesi around here are a key part of that story.

The gypsum has been quarried for centuries, and the crystal blocks were used in Bologna's medieval walls and buildings. Today, the hills are a patchwork of woodland, meadows and vineyards, with a few walking trails leading to the sinkholes and cave entrances. The caves themselves are mostly closed to the public, home to bats and fragile formations, but guided visits are sometimes organised by local caving groups. The wine from these hills, Pignoletto, is a crisp white that pairs perfectly with the region's rich food.

For motorcycle lovers, this is holy ground. The Ducati factory and museum in Borgo Panigale are only a few kilometres away, on the western edge of Bologna, and a factory tour is a pilgrimage many riders make. To the south, the hills rise quickly, and roads climb toward the Apennine passes. The SS65 della Futa and the road over the Raticosa pass to Florence are legendary, with endless bends, fast sections and stunning views. These roads are popular on weekends, so expect plenty of company, and be aware of police checks.

Zola Predosa, with sixteen thousand residents, is a busy town with all the services you need, including fuel and supermarkets. Calderino and Riale are smaller villages nearby. Bologna, just a short ride away, is the capital of Italian food, so make time for tagliatelle al ragù, tortellini in brodo and mortadella. Avoid riding in the city centre, which is restricted to traffic, and instead park on the outskirts and explore on foot.
t.teatro lauro rossi@43.3,13.5:
Macerata is a hill town that takes its culture seriously, and the Teatro Lauro Rossi is the polished little jewel in the middle of it. Built in the second half of the eighteenth century in the heart of the old centre, it is a classic Italian horseshoe theatre with tiers of boxes in cream and gold, and it carries the name of Lauro Rossi, a nineteenth-century composer born in the town. If the doors are open, step in for a look; the room is intimate enough that you can imagine the whole town crammed in for a premiere, gossiping between acts.

The theatre is only half the musical story. A few streets away stands the Sferisterio, a vast neoclassical arena built in the early nineteenth century for a ball game called pallone col bracciale, which now hosts an open-air opera festival every summer. Macerata is also the birthplace of Matteo Ricci, the Jesuit who travelled to China in the sixteenth century, learned Chinese and became a celebrated go-between of cultures; you will see his name on streets and plaques around town. The university here is one of the oldest in Italy, which keeps the bars full of students.

Getting here is a treat. The town sits on a ridge between the Potenza and Chienti valleys in the Marche, with rolling farmland falling away on every side, and to the southwest the high wall of the Sibillini mountains, snow-capped into spring. The roads that climb up from the valley floor are a series of switchbacks and long, flowing bends, often with excellent tarmac. Head west toward the Sibillini for bigger climbs, or east to the Adriatic coast, less than an hour away. Inside the walls, the old centre has restricted traffic zones and steep, narrow lanes, so park outside and walk in.

Macerata has thirty thousand inhabitants and all the services you need, with fuel stations on the main roads below the old town. The local speciality is vincisgrassi, a rich baked pasta related to lasagna, and you should also try ciauscolo, a soft, spreadable salami from the Marche hills. A Verdicchio or a red Rosso Piceno will suit either, though if you are riding on, save it for the evening and settle for an espresso under the arcades.
t.villa de cerreto guidi@43.8,10.9:
Cosimo I de' Medici liked to hunt, and in the 1560s he had a villa built on a hilltop at Cerreto Guidi, on the edge of the marshes and woods west of Florence, where the game was plentiful. From the outside it is austere, a solid block of stone facing a square, but the approach is spectacular: a pair of great brick ramps, known as the Medici bridges, zigzag up to the entrance. The villa is part of the UNESCO listing of the Medici Villas and Gardens in Tuscany, and it holds a dark legend. Cosimo's daughter Isabella died here in 1576, and the story goes that she was murdered by her husband, Paolo Giordano Orsini, for her alleged infidelity. Whether it is true or not, it is told to every visitor.

The villa is surrounded by the Montalbano hills, a long ridge covered in vineyards, olive groves and woods, with stunning views over the Arno valley. Four kilometres away is Vinci, the village where Leonardo was born in 1452, with a museum dedicated to his inventions and the farmhouse at Anchiano where he is said to have been born. The countryside produces Chianti Montalbano wine and excellent olive oil.

The riding is superb. The roads that climb the Montalbano ridge, through villages like Vinci, Lamporecchio and San Baronto, are full of tight bends, steep gradients and panoramic views, and they are popular with cyclists, who use them for training. The surface is generally good, but there can be gravel on the smaller roads. Traffic is light, except on weekends, when Florentines head for the hills. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild weather and glorious colours.

Cerreto Guidi is a small town with cafés and a few restaurants, and Lamporecchio, five kilometres away, and Empoli, a little further, have fuel and supermarkets. Lamporecchio is famous for brigidini, thin, crispy aniseed wafers sold at fairs throughout Tuscany. For a proper meal, try pappardelle with wild boar sauce, ribollita or a steak, grilled over wood, all washed down with a glass of local red if you are done for the day.
t.villa de poggio a caiano@43.8,11.1:
Of all the Medici villas, Poggio a Caiano is the one that changed architecture. Lorenzo the Magnificent commissioned it from Giuliano da Sangallo in the 1480s, and the result was something new: a country house raised on an arcaded platform, with a portico topped by a classical pediment, the first time a temple front had been put on a private villa since antiquity. Palladio would develop the idea in the Veneto decades later. Inside, the great hall is decorated with frescoes by Andrea del Sarto, Pontormo and others, and Pontormo's lunette of Vertumnus and Pomona, with its lazy figures lounging on a wall, is one of the most charming paintings of the Renaissance. The villa is part of the UNESCO listing of the Medici Villas and Gardens in Tuscany.

The villa has its own dark tale. In 1587, Grand Duke Francesco I and his wife Bianca Cappello died here within a day of each other, officially of fever, though rumours of poisoning by his brother Ferdinando have never gone away. Today, the villa also houses a museum of still-life paintings from the Medici collections, and its gardens and park are open to visitors.

The town lies between Florence and Prato, at the foot of the Montalbano hills. The countryside around it produces Carmignano, one of the oldest protected wine areas in the world, its boundaries defined by decree in the early eighteenth century, and a short ride up the hill, the Medici villa of Artimino, known for its many chimneys, looks out over the vineyards. The riding is good once you escape the busy roads of the plain: the lanes climbing through Carmignano and Artimino toward the ridge are narrow and twisty, with views over the Arno valley and Florence, and the surface varies from smooth tarmac to patched and gravelly.

Poggio a Caiano, with nearly eight thousand inhabitants, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Prato, a few kilometres north, is a large textile city with everything. Prato is known for its cantucci, crunchy almond biscuits dipped in Vin Santo, and for mortadella di Prato. Try a plate of pappa al pomodoro, a thick tomato and bread soup, or a bistecca alla fiorentina, if you are hungry enough.
t.the via appia in rome@41.8,12.5:
Rome's regina viarum, the queen of roads, leaves the city through the Porta San Sebastiano and heads south-east toward Capua and eventually Brindisi. It was begun in 312 BC by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, and the first miles out of Rome are now protected within the Parco Regionale dell'Appia Antica. The stretch of the old road is lined with tombs, ruins of villas, catacombs and umbrella pines, and the original paving stones, huge polygonal basalt blocks, still surface parts of it.

Those stones are the first thing a rider needs to know about. They are uneven, slippery when wet and brutal on suspension, and on Sundays and holidays parts of the road are closed to motor traffic anyway. The best way to experience the old road is on foot or by bicycle, which you can hire near the park's visitor centre. Leave the bike parked and walk among the ruins.

The highlights are many. The tomb of Caecilia Metella, a huge drum-shaped mausoleum of the first century BC, was turned into a fortress in the Middle Ages. The catacombs of San Callisto and San Sebastiano are among the largest underground cemeteries of early Christian Rome. The Circus of Maxentius and the Villa dei Quintili are impressive ruins, and the aqueducts in the nearby Parco degli Acquedotti make dramatic silhouettes at sunset.

Riding in Rome is an experience. Traffic is chaotic, scooters weave everywhere, and the historic centre is a limited traffic zone, the ZTL, with cameras that will fine you if you enter without permission. Fuel is easy to find, and so is food: carbonara, cacio e pepe, supplì and artichokes alla giudia in season. South of the city, the Appia continues toward the Alban Hills, where the riding improves with winding roads around the volcanic lakes of Albano and Nemi and the towns of the Castelli Romani, famous for their white wine and porchetta.
t.palais de seravezza@44.0,10.2:
Seravezza is where the Apuan Alps meet the Versilia coast in northern Tuscany. Behind the beaches of Forte dei Marmi, the mountains rise abruptly, white with marble scars, and Seravezza sits at the mouth of a valley where two rivers join. The Palazzo Mediceo, built in the 1560s for Cosimo I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, was a summer residence and a base for overseeing the region's marble quarries and silver mines. It is one of the Medici villas and gardens inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2013, and today it hosts museums and exhibitions.

The marble is everywhere. Michelangelo came to these mountains in the early sixteenth century to open quarries on Monte Altissimo, above Seravezza, at the request of the Medici pope Leo X, and the marble roads he planned are part of local legend. The quarries are still worked, and the landscape is cut by giant white terraces visible from far away. Pietrasanta, nearby, is a town of sculptors and marble workshops.

For riders, the road from Seravezza up through the valley toward Arni and over the Passo del Cipollaio is a superb route, climbing in tight hairpins through chestnut woods and past quarries, with a tunnel through the mountain and a descent into the Garfagnana on the other side. Marble trucks use these roads on weekdays, and the surfaces can be slippery with marble dust, especially when wet. Weekends are quieter, but the coast below is busy in summer.

Seravezza is small, but Querceta, three kilometres away, has fuel and supermarkets. The coast towns of Forte dei Marmi and Viareggio have everything, though prices are high in summer. Try the lardo di Colonnata, cured pork fat aged in marble tubs in the nearby quarry village. Come in spring or autumn, when the coast is calm and the mountains are clear, and the contrast between the white marble and the blue sea is at its most striking.
t.teatro gentile da fabriano@43.3,12.9:
Paper made Fabriano. Since at least the thirteenth century, craftsmen in this inland town of the Marche have made paper, and they are credited with key innovations: the use of animal gelatine to size the sheets and, most famously, the watermark. Fabriano paper is still made here today, and the Museo della Carta e della Filigrana, in a former monastery, shows the old techniques with working demonstrations. Your banknotes may well have been printed on paper from this town.

The Teatro Gentile, the town theatre, takes its name from Gentile da Fabriano, the great painter of the International Gothic style, born here in the fourteenth century, whose Adoration of the Magi in the Uffizi is one of the most sumptuous paintings of its age. The theatre is a nineteenth-century opera house with tiers of boxes, typical of the many small but elegant theatres in the towns of the Marche. The town centre around it has a fine square with a fountain, a medieval palace and an old hospital.

Fabriano sits in a valley in the Apennines, surrounded by hills and mountains, and the riding in all directions is good. To the east, the Gola della Rossa and Frasassi gorges carry the road through narrow limestone canyons, and the Grotte di Frasassi, near Genga, are among the largest show caves in Italy. To the west, roads cross the Apennine ridge into Umbria, towards Gubbio, with winding climbs and fine views. Surfaces are generally good on the main roads, rougher on the minor ones. The area was hit by earthquakes in 1997 and 2016, and some villages still show the damage.

Fabriano has fuel and all services, and its old centre has cafés and restaurants serving the hearty cuisine of the inland Marche. Salame di Fabriano, a fine-grained pork salami, is a local specialty, and truffles appear on menus in season. The mountains around offer cool air in summer, when the coast is hot and crowded. On a quiet evening, walking through the old streets, you can almost hear the sound of the paper mills that once powered the town's prosperity.
t.teatro feronia@43.2,13.2:
San Severino Marche has one of the most unusual town squares in Italy. The Piazza del Popolo is an elongated ellipse, lined with arcades and palaces, and it was originally a market space outside the walls of the medieval town on the hill above. Today it is the heart of a town of eight thousand people in the valley of the Potenza river, in the inland Marche, and the Teatro Feronia stands on it, an elegant nineteenth-century theatre named after an ancient Italic goddess of fertility and freedom.

The town has a long history. The Roman town of Septempeda lay in the valley nearby, and its ruins can be visited. In the Middle Ages, the inhabitants moved up onto the hill of Montenero, where the old castle and the cathedral still stand, and the town later spread down into the valley. San Severino was home to a school of painters in the fifteenth century, the Salimbeni brothers, whose frescoes can be seen in local churches, and the Pinacoteca has works by Pinturicchio and others.

The Potenza valley runs from the Apennines down to the Adriatic, and the road along it is a pleasant ride, with hills on either side covered in fields and woods. From San Severino, roads climb into the mountains to the west, towards the Sibillini range and the high plateaus around Castelluccio, which are famous for their wildflowers in early summer. To the south, Tolentino, nine kilometres away, has the basilica of San Nicola with remarkable frescoes. The minor roads in the hills are winding and quiet, ideal for relaxed riding, though surfaces vary.

San Severino has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the arcades of the Piazza del Popolo are lined with cafés where you can sit and watch the town go by. The local cuisine is rich: vincisgrassi, a baked pasta dish like lasagne, and ciauscolo, a soft spreadable salami from the Marche. The area was affected by the 2016 earthquakes, and some buildings are still under repair. In the evening, when the lights come on in the square and families stroll under the arcades, the town has a warm and welcoming atmosphere.
t.monte raschio@42.2,12.2:
Beech trees usually need altitude and cool weather in central Italy, so it is a surprise to find a beech forest at only about five hundred metres on Monte Raschio, a low volcanic hill near Oriolo Romano, north-west of Rome. The forest survives here thanks to a local microclimate, with humidity from Lake Bracciano and the volcanic soils, and it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe, a site that spans many countries.

The area around Monte Raschio is the land of the Monti Sabatini, the volcanic hills surrounding Lake Bracciano, a large crater lake that supplies water to Rome. Oriolo Romano is a small town laid out in the sixteenth century by the Santacroce family, with a grand palace, the Palazzo Altieri, which contains a gallery of portraits of all the popes. Bracciano, on the lake, has a magnificent castle, the Castello Orsini-Odescalchi, one of the finest Renaissance castles in Italy.

The riding around Lake Bracciano is pleasant. The road around the lake is scenic, with views over the water and the hills, and the roads into the Monti Sabatini and towards Viterbo wind through woods and farmland. Traffic can be heavy on summer weekends, when Romans head to the lake, but weekdays are quieter. Further north, the Monti Cimini and Lake Vico offer more winding roads through beech and chestnut forests. Surfaces vary, and some minor roads are rough.

Oriolo Romano is a small town with basic services, and Manziana and Bracciano, nearby, have fuel, shops and restaurants. The lake is popular for swimming in summer, and motorboats are banned, so the water is clean and quiet. The local food includes lake fish, porchetta and the wines of the area. A walk in the beech forest on Monte Raschio, especially in autumn when the leaves turn gold, is a peaceful escape from the heat and noise, and it is remarkable to think that this forest has survived so close to Rome.
t.ferrara@44.8,11.6:
Ferrara is a city built for walking and cycling, with flat streets, a ring of Renaissance walls nine kilometres long, and so many bicycles that it is called the city of bicycles. In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, under the Este family, it was one of the great courts of Renaissance Italy, and the Estense castle, with its moat and drawbridges, still dominates the centre. The city's Renaissance planning, especially the Herculean Addition, a new quarter laid out in the late fifteenth century, led historians to call it the first modern city in Europe, and UNESCO has inscribed Ferrara and the Po Delta as a World Heritage Site.

The Mille Miglia, the legendary road race from Brescia to Rome and back, passed through Ferrara, and the historic version of the race, for classic cars, still crosses the city every year in May, with crowds lining the streets to watch. The Palazzo dei Diamanti, with its façade of diamond-shaped stones, hosts major art exhibitions, and the cathedral, with its Romanesque façade, stands opposite the castle. The poet Ludovico Ariosto lived here and wrote Orlando Furioso.

The riding around Ferrara is flat, across the Po plain, with long straight roads, canals and fields. It is relaxing rather than exciting, but the Po Delta, to the east, is a fascinating landscape of lagoons, marshes and pine forests, with flamingos, herons and fishing villages, and the roads along the river and the coast are scenic. The plain is hot and humid in summer and often foggy in winter. The city centre has a limited traffic zone, the ZTL, so park outside and walk or rent a bicycle.

Ferrara, a city of ninety thousand, has fuel, shops and restaurants. The local food is distinctive: cappellacci di zucca, pasta filled with pumpkin, salama da sugo, a cured pork sausage served with mashed potatoes, and the coppia ferrarese, a twisted bread with a protected designation. A ride or walk along the walls, with the trees above and the city on one side and the countryside on the other, is the best way to see Ferrara.
t.etruscan necropolises of cerveteri and t:
The Etruscans built their houses of wood and mud brick, which is why so few survive, and they built their tombs of rock, which is why we know them best through their dead. The Banditaccia necropolis at Cerveteri, north-west of Rome, is a city of tombs: great round tumuli covered in grass, cut into the volcanic tufa and laid out along streets, with chambers inside carved to look like houses, with beds, chairs, columns and beams. The necropolis, together with the painted tombs of Tarquinia further north, was listed by UNESCO in 2004, and walking its lanes is one of the most atmospheric experiences in central Italy.

The Tomb of the Reliefs is the most famous, its walls decorated with carved and painted household objects, tools, weapons and animals, as if the family wanted to take their whole home into the next life. The ancient city of Caere, which these tombs served, was one of the most powerful Etruscan cities, trading across the Mediterranean, and the finds from its tombs fill museums in Rome and beyond.

The riding around Cerveteri is a mix of busy coast and quieter hills. The Via Aurelia runs along the coast, fast and busy, while inland roads climb into the Monti della Tolfa, with twisting lanes, oak woods, pastures and views over the sea. Lake Bracciano, a volcanic lake to the east, offers a lovely loop with good roads and fine views. Traffic near Rome can be heavy, and Italian driving styles call for alertness.

The modern town of Cerveteri sits right beside the site, with petrol, bars and trattorias a couple of minutes away. Ladispoli, on the coast, is bigger. The town has a small museum in its medieval castle and a pleasant historic centre, and the local wine, Cerveteri DOC, is a good match for the hearty cooking of northern Lazio: pasta with wild boar, roast meats and grilled vegetables.

April and October are the gentlest months, with fewer school groups among the tombs. Summer can be hot and dry, and the tombs offer welcome shade. Wander among the tumuli in the late afternoon, when the light softens and the cicadas sing, and step down into a tomb carved like a home, where an Etruscan family hoped to spend eternity together.
t.minturnae and the garigliano crossing@41:
Where the Via Appia crossed the River Garigliano, the Romans built a town, and armies have been fighting over the crossing ever since. Minturnae was founded as a Roman colony in the late fourth century BC on the border between Lazio and Campania, and its ruins lie beside the river near the modern town of Minturno: a theatre still used for summer performances, a forum, temples, baths, a stretch of the Via Appia's paving and the arches of an aqueduct striding across the fields. A small museum displays statues and finds from the site.

The crossing has seen some decisive battles. In 915 a Christian alliance defeated a Saracen stronghold near the river mouth, in 1503 Spanish forces under Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba won a crucial victory over the French here, and in 1944 the Garigliano formed part of the German Gustav Line, with fierce fighting as the Allies pushed north toward Rome. War cemeteries in the area are a sober reminder of that last battle.

The riding is varied and rewarding. The Via Appia, now the SS7, runs along the coastal plain, busy with traffic, and the coast road toward Gaeta, Sperlonga and Terracina is beautiful, with cliffs, beaches and old towns perched above the sea. Inland, the Monti Aurunci rise steeply, with twisting roads through olive groves, oak woods and hill villages offering wonderful views. Traffic is heavy in summer, especially at weekends, and road surfaces vary.

Minturno is a town of about sixteen thousand people, with fuel, shops, cafés and restaurants, and the hilltop old town is a pleasant place to wander. Across the river in Campania lies buffalo mozzarella country, and the coast offers fresh fish and seafood. Try a plate of spaghetti with clams, or a fresh mozzarella with tomatoes and basil, and a glass of local wine.

The shoulder seasons suit it best, when the theatre stones are warm rather than scorching and the coach parties have gone home. Summer brings heat and beach crowds. Walk along the old paving of the Via Appia by the river, look at the theatre and the aqueduct, and think of the legions, merchants, pilgrims and armies that have passed this way for more than two thousand years.
t.via appia regina viarum@41.7,12.7:
The Romans called it the queen of roads, and in 2024 UNESCO agreed, listing the Via Appia from Rome to Brindisi as a World Heritage site. Begun in 312 BC by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, it was the first great Roman road, built to move armies south toward Campania and later extended to the port of Brindisi, the gateway to Greece and the East. These coordinates lie in the Alban Hills south-east of Rome, near Lanuvio, Velletri and Genzano, where the road climbed over the volcanic hills before dropping toward the Pontine plain.

The Alban Hills are the Castelli Romani, a cluster of hill towns around two volcanic lakes, Albano and Nemi, where Roman aristocrats, popes and later Roman families came to escape the summer heat. Genzano is famous for its bread and for the Infiorata, when the main street is carpeted with flower petal pictures each June. Ariccia is the home of porchetta, roast pork with herbs, sold in roadside stands, and Nemi is known for wild strawberries. Lanuvio, an ancient town in its own right, has a long history of wine-making.

The riding in the Castelli Romani is a mix of pleasure and frustration. The roads wind through the hills, around the lakes and between the towns, with fine views over the Roman Campagna and toward the sea. But traffic is heavy, especially at weekends, when Romans pour out of the city for lunch, and the roads are narrow, the surfaces patched and the parking chaotic. Ride early in the morning or on a weekday for the best experience.

Fuel, food and coffee are easy to find in every town, and Velletri, a town of nearly fifty thousand, has every service. The local wine is the Castelli Romani white, light and fresh, and the fraschette, informal taverns selling wine, porchetta, bread and cheese, are a local institution.

October has the edge over every other month, with soft light and harvest still in the air. The grape harvest in October brings festivals to many towns. Somewhere on the slopes below Lanuvio the old line is still traceable, and finding it is half the fun. Then do the sensible Roman thing and stop for porchetta and a glass of white in the shade before riding on.
t.punta licosa and the mount stella region:
According to legend, the siren Leucosia threw herself into the sea here after failing to lure Odysseus to his doom, and her body became the little island off Punta Licosa. It is a fine story for a fine place. Punta Licosa is a low, wild headland on the coast of the Cilento, south of Salerno, covered in Mediterranean scrub, pines and holm oaks, with rocky coves and clear water, and it forms part of the Cilento and Vallo di Diano National Park, listed by UNESCO in 1998 as a cultural landscape. Behind it rises Monte Stella, the mountain that gives its name to the surrounding hills, dotted with small villages and terraced olive groves.

The nearby villages of Castellabate, perched on a hill with a medieval castle, Santa Maria di Castellabate by the sea and the small harbour of San Marco are charming and lively in summer. The Cilento is also where the American physiologist Ancel Keys lived for many years in the village of Pioppi, studying the local diet and helping to define what became known as the Mediterranean diet.

The riding is superb. The coast road winds above the sea, with views over the Gulf of Salerno, and the roads that climb into the hills around Monte Stella, through villages like Perdifumo and Pollica, are twisty, narrow and full of character. Surfaces vary from good to rough, and traffic is light outside August, when holidaymakers pour in from Naples and Rome. Watch for gravel, potholes and the occasional goat.

Agropoli, about twelve kilometres north, is the main town, with fuel, shops and a pretty old town on a headland. Santa Maria di Castellabate has small shops and restaurants. Local food is a reason to come in itself: buffalo mozzarella from the plain around Paestum, Cilento white figs, olive oil, anchovies from Pisciotta, fresh fish and pasta with local vegetables.

The headland itself is reached on foot from San Marco, along a path through the scrub, and it is a beautiful walk with chances to swim in quiet coves. Come in late spring or September, when the sea is warm and the crowds have gone. The Greek temples of Paestum lie just to the north, one of the best-preserved groups in the world, a perfect addition to a Cilento day.
t.chaco culture@36.1,-108.0:
Getting to Chaco Canyon is part of the point. The last stretch of road into this remote corner of north-western New Mexico is unpaved, rutted and washboarded, and after rain it turns to slick mud that can make it impassable for any kind of vehicle. Take that seriously: on a road bike it is tough, and on a big touring machine it can be miserable. But the reward is extraordinary. Between roughly 850 and 1150, the Ancestral Puebloan people built monumental great houses here, multi-storey stone buildings with hundreds of rooms, aligned with the sun, moon and cardinal directions, linked by straight roads across the desert. Chaco Culture National Historical Park was listed by UNESCO in 1987.

Pueblo Bonito is the most famous of the great houses, a D-shaped complex of around six hundred rooms and dozens of kivas, the round ceremonial chambers, built over several centuries. Walking through its doorways and courtyards, you see the precision of the masonry and wonder at the organisation needed to build it. On Fajada Butte, a spiral petroglyph marks solstices and equinoxes with daggers of sunlight, though access to it is restricted.

The park is also a certified dark sky park, with spectacular night skies and astronomy programmes. The landscape is high desert, with mesas, canyons and sagebrush, and the light at dawn and dusk turns the stone walls gold and red. Summer is hot, with afternoon thunderstorms, and winter can be cold, with snow.

Bloomfield and Farmington, to the north, have full services, and there are trading posts along the main highway. Carry plenty of water and food, and check road conditions with the park before setting out.

The riding to Chaco, apart from that last stretch, is about long open highways across the Navajo and Puebloan lands of the Four Corners, with vast views, little traffic and the occasional livestock on the road. April to early June and mid-September to October usually bring the kindest temperatures. Walk through Pueblo Bonito in the early morning, when the canyon is quiet and the shadows long, and feel the weight of a civilisation that built something this ambitious in such a hard land.
The Aztecs never came anywhere near Aztec, New Mexico. The ruins here were named by nineteenth-century settlers who assumed, wrongly, that such impressive buildings must have been made by the famous people of central Mexico. In fact, they were built by Ancestral Puebloans between about 1100 and 1300, as part of the great Chacoan world centred on Chaco Canyon, sixty miles to the south, and they are included with Chaco in the UNESCO listing of the Chaco Culture.

The West Ruin is a great house of around four hundred rooms, with original wooden beams still in place in some ceilings, preserved by the dry climate, and walking through its low doorways and dark rooms is an atmospheric experience. The Great Kiva, reconstructed in the 1930s by the archaeologist Earl Morris, gives a vivid idea of what these ceremonial chambers were like when in use, with its roof, benches and central fire box. The site is compact, easy to visit and has a good visitor centre.

The town of Aztec is a small, friendly place on the Animas River, with fuel, food and lodging, and the larger city of Farmington is nearby. North, across the Colorado border, the old mining town of Durango is the starting point of the Million Dollar Highway, one of the great mountain roads of the American West, climbing over high passes through the San Juan Mountains toward Silverton and Ouray. Mesa Verde National Park, with its cliff dwellings, is also within a day's ride.

The riding around Aztec is a mix of open highways across high desert and mesas, river valleys with cottonwoods and farms, and, to the north, the mountains of Colorado. Traffic is light outside the towns, but watch for oil field trucks, livestock and wildlife, especially deer at dawn and dusk. Weather can change quickly, with afternoon thunderstorms in summer and snow in winter.

Local food includes New Mexican dishes with green and red chile, enchiladas, burritos and sopaipillas with honey. Late spring and autumn spare you both the summer furnace and the winter snow. The Great Kiva is cool and dim even on a hot afternoon, and a few minutes sitting on its bench in silence is the best rest stop for a hundred miles.
t.villa la magia@43.9,11.0:
The Medici loved the countryside, especially when it came with hunting grounds, and Villa La Magia at Quarrata was one of their country retreats at the foot of the Montalbano hills, a few kilometres south of Pistoia. Francesco I de' Medici bought it in the sixteenth century to use as a hunting lodge, and it belongs to the World Heritage inscription for the Medici villas and gardens of Tuscany. The villa is a solid rectangular building around a courtyard, more farmhouse than palace, with a park that has become home to contemporary art installations, a rather unexpected touch for a Renaissance hunting lodge.

The Montalbano is a long, low ridge separating the plains of Pistoia and Florence from the lower Arno valley. Its slopes are covered with olive groves, vineyards and woods of oak and chestnut, and its villages perch on spurs with views across the plain. Carmignano, on the other side of the ridge, produces a red wine that was one of the first to have its production area legally defined, by a decree of Cosimo III de' Medici in 1716. Vinci, Leonardo's birthplace, lies on the southern slope, and the drive there over the hills is one of the loveliest in the area.

The riding on the Montalbano is excellent. The road along the ridge, from San Baronto toward Vinci and Carmignano, is twisty and narrow, with olive groves on both sides and sudden views across Tuscany. San Baronto is a meeting point for cyclists and motorcyclists, with a café where people gather at weekends. The surface is generally good, but there are cyclists, farm vehicles and cars driven by locals who know every bend. Summer is hot; spring and autumn are perfect, with soft light over the hills.

Quarrata, a town of about ten thousand, has a filling station and somewhere to eat; Pistoia, a short ride away, has a beautiful medieval centre and a lively market. Tuscan food here means beans, bread soups, grilled meat and olive oil from the Montalbano, which is excellent. The villa's opening times vary, so check before you go. Afterwards, ride up to the ridge, stop at a viewpoint and look down at the plain, with the Apennines to the north and the dome of Florence's cathedral on the horizon on a clear day.
t.the via appia from 83rd mile to formiae@:
The queen of roads, the Romans called it: the Via Appia, begun in 312 BC by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, ran from Rome to Capua and later on to Brindisi, the gateway to Greece and the East. Near Formia, the old road comes down from the hills of Itri to the coast of the Gulf of Gaeta, and a stretch of it, with its paving stones and roadside monuments, survives in the countryside. In 2024, UNESCO listed the Via Appia as a whole, and this section between the eighty-third mile from Rome and the ancient town of Formiae is one of its pieces.

Formia was a favourite resort of the Roman elite, who built villas along the coast. Cicero had one here, and it was near Formia that he was murdered in 43 BC on the orders of Mark Antony. A large tower tomb by the road is traditionally called the Tomb of Cicero, though the attribution is uncertain. The town itself is busy and modern, rebuilt after heavy damage in the Second World War, when the Gustav Line ran close by. Gaeta, across the gulf, has a fine medieval quarter, a fortress, and the Montagna Spaccata, a mountain split by a deep cleft in the rock, with a sanctuary built into it.

The riding here mixes busy and beautiful. The modern Via Appia, the SS7, is a main road with traffic, but the coastal road toward Sperlonga, the Via Flacca, is a delight, with tunnels, cliffs and views of the sea. Inland, the Aurunci mountains rise steeply, and the roads climbing to villages like Maranola and Campodimele are narrow, twisty and nearly empty. Summer brings heat and holiday traffic, especially on weekends; spring and autumn are better. Watch for Italian drivers' enthusiasm for overtaking on bends.

Formia sorts out fuel and lunch, and Gaeta has a lovely old centre. Local food includes Gaeta olives, small and dark, the tiella, a pie filled with octopus or vegetables, and fresh seafood. The village of Itri, inland, is known for olive oil and for the bandit Fra Diavolo, who was born there. Walk a stretch of the ancient road if you can find it, and feel the paving stones under your boots; they carried legions, merchants and poets, and now a motorcyclist taking a break.
Crystals the size of a hand catch the sun along the Vena del Gesso, a ridge of selenite gypsum that runs for some twenty-five kilometres across the hills of Romagna, from the Sillaro valley to the Lamone. The rock formed millions of years ago when the Mediterranean dried up and its salts were deposited, and it has since been carved by water into caves, sinkholes and blind valleys. In 2023, UNESCO listed the evaporite karst and caves of the northern Apennines, and the Vena del Gesso is the heart of it. Monte Casino is one of the peaks on the ridge, near Borgo Tossignano and Casola Valsenio.

The ridge is strikingly beautiful: white cliffs above woods of oak and hornbeam, with caves where prehistoric people lived and medieval quarrymen dug gypsum for plaster. The Rocca di Tossignano, a ruined fortress on the cliff above Borgo Tossignano, has views along the ridge and down the Santerno valley. Casola Valsenio, in the next valley, is known as the village of herbs, with a large garden of aromatic and medicinal plants and a festival in their honour. Riolo Terme, nearby, has spa waters and a castle.

The riding is excellent and varied. The roads running up the Santerno and Senio valleys are smooth and fast, while the minor roads climbing over the ridges between them are narrow, steep and twisty, with spectacular views. Imola, a short ride away, has the Autodromo Enzo e Dino Ferrari, the famous circuit where Formula One and motorcycle races have been held, and you may see riders heading there for track days. The surface on small roads can be broken, and there are cyclists in large numbers at weekends. Summer is hot; spring and autumn are lovely, with the hills green or golden.

Borgo Tossignano and Casalfiumanese have fuel and shops; Imola, about twelve kilometres away, has everything. The cooking of Romagna is famously generous: piadina, the flatbread filled with ham and cheese, tagliatelle with ragù, cappelletti in broth and the local wines, Sangiovese and Albana. A piadina at a roadside kiosk is the perfect quick lunch. If you have time, walk a stretch of the trail along the ridge, where the gypsum crystals glitter underfoot.
t.teatro angelo mariani@43.9,12.2:
Sant'Agata Feltria is a small hill town in the upper Marecchia valley, with a castle on a rock, steep streets and one of the oldest wooden theatres in Italy. The Teatro Angelo Mariani dates from the early seventeenth century and has been rebuilt and restored over the centuries, with tiers of wooden boxes painted in soft colours around a small stage. It is named after Angelo Mariani, a nineteenth-century conductor who was a close collaborator of Verdi. The theatre is intimate, seating a few hundred at most, and it still hosts concerts and plays.

The town is known for another thing: truffles. Every October, on Sunday afternoons, Sant'Agata Feltria holds a white truffle fair, when the streets fill with stalls, the air smells of truffles and roasted chestnuts, and people come from all over the region. The Rocca Fregoso, the castle on its rock above the town, is a striking sight, with a children's museum inside. The surrounding valley, the Valmarecchia, is full of fortified villages: San Leo, on its cliff, where the adventurer Cagliostro died in prison, Pennabilli, home of the poet and screenwriter Tonino Guerra, and Novafeltria, the main town in the valley.

The riding here is superb. The roads climb through the hills of the Montefeltro with endless curves, dropping into valleys and climbing over ridges, with views of fortresses and villages on every peak. The surface can be patchy and narrow, and in places landslides have damaged the road, but traffic is light. The light in autumn is especially beautiful, with the oak woods turning gold and the hills soft and hazy. Summer can be hot in the valleys but cooler on the ridges, and winter brings fog and occasionally snow.

Sant'Agata Feltria has cafés and restaurants, but for fuel, Novafeltria, seven kilometres away, is the reliable choice. Local food includes truffles, of course, along with mushrooms, chestnuts, cheeses aged in pits in the ground, and pasta made by hand. The theatre's opening times vary, so ask locally. Afterwards, ride to San Leo, one of the most dramatic villages in Italy, and watch the sun set over the Montefeltro hills, with San Marino on its mountain in the distance.
t.kin bineola@36.0,-108.1:
Over a thousand years ago, the people of Chaco Canyon built great houses of finely laid sandstone, multi-storey buildings with hundreds of rooms and ceremonial kivas, and connected them with roads that ran straight across the desert. Kin Bineola is one of the outlying great houses, some distance south-west of the canyon, on the Navajo Nation in north-western New Mexico. Its walls still stand in places to several storeys, with the characteristic Chacoan masonry of small stones packed between larger ones. It is one piece of the World Heritage property for the Chaco Culture, together with the canyon and other outliers.

The name is Navajo, often translated as house in which the wind whirls, and the landscape around it is vast, empty and beautiful, with mesas, washes and sagebrush plains under a huge sky. The nearest town is Crownpoint, some thirty-five kilometres away, a Navajo community known for its rug auctions, where weavers sell their work directly. Chaco Canyon itself, with Pueblo Bonito and the other great houses, is a long drive north on dirt roads. The night skies here are among the darkest in the United States, and the stars are extraordinary.

Riding here is an adventure, and not for every bike. The roads to Kin Bineola are dirt, often deeply rutted, washboarded and sandy, and after rain they turn into slick mud that can be impassable. A dual-sport bike or adventure machine is the right tool; a heavy road bike is not. There are no services, no shade and often no phone signal, so carry plenty of water, fuel and tools, and tell someone your route. Summer is hot with afternoon thunderstorms; winter is cold and can bring snow.

For fuel and supplies, Crownpoint has basics, and the towns along Interstate 40, such as Thoreau and Grants, have everything. Food in Navajo country includes fry bread and Navajo tacos, mutton stew and green chile. Remember that you are on Navajo Nation land: respect local rules, stay on established roads, and do not climb on the walls or remove anything from the site. Arrive in the late afternoon if you can, when the low sun turns the stone gold and the wind, true to the name, whirls through the empty rooms.
t.villa adriana@41.9,12.8:
Hadrian never did anything by halves. Below the hill town of Tivoli, on the plain east of Rome, the emperor built himself a retreat that was less a villa than a private city: palaces, baths, libraries, theatres, gardens and long reflecting pools spread over more than a hundred hectares. Villa Adriana was constructed in the early second century AD, and Hadrian, a restless traveller and amateur architect, filled it with references to places he had seen, most famously the Canopus, a long pool lined with columns and statues meant to evoke the Egyptian canal of that name. Walking through the ruins today, among cypresses and olive trees, you get a sense of a man trying to bring the whole empire home.

The villa was plundered for centuries after the fall of Rome, its marble burned for lime and its statues carried off to collections across Europe. Even so, what survives is vast and astonishing: the Maritime Theatre, a circular island villa surrounded by a moat, the great baths with their collapsed vaults, and the Pecile, a huge colonnaded courtyard. The site is listed by UNESCO, as is the Renaissance Villa d'Este up the hill in Tivoli, with its fountains and terraced gardens.

The approach by motorcycle can be a mixed bag. Coming from Rome on the Via Tiburtina, traffic is heavy, the road is busy with lorries, and the suburbs sprawl a long way. But once you are out of the city and approaching Tivoli, the scenery improves, with the town perched on the slopes of the Monti Tiburtini above the plain and the Aniene river tumbling through it. The roads up into the hills behind Tivoli, toward Vicovaro and the Valle dell'Aniene, offer much better riding: winding, climbing and lined with olive groves, with views back over the Campagna.

The modern town of Villa Adriana, around the site, has fuel, cafés and shops, and Tivoli itself, a few minutes uphill, offers restaurants and bars in its old centre. Arrive early to beat the heat and the tour groups, give yourself at least two hours to wander the ruins, and wear something more comfortable than riding boots if you can. Afterward, a plate of pasta and a glass of local wine in Tivoli will round off the visit well.
t.ancient capua@41.1,14.3:
Santa Maria Capua Vetere does not look like much as you ride in, a busy Campanian town of tangled traffic and apartment blocks, but under and around it lies ancient Capua, once one of the richest cities in Italy. The Via Appia passed straight through, and its great amphitheatre, second in size only to the Colosseum, still dominates the edge of town. This was where the gladiator schools trained their fighters, and it was from a school in Capua that Spartacus broke out in 73 BC with a band of fellow slaves, beginning the revolt that shook Rome for two years. The amphitheatre and a small gladiator museum nearby are the obvious stops, and the Mithraeum under the town, with its painted scene of the god slaying a bull, is one of the best preserved in Italy.

The town is part of the stretch of the Via Appia that runs from the plain of Capua down toward the sea at Formia, a section included when the Appian Way was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2024. The ancient road, built from 312 BC onward, linked Rome with the south and eventually the port of Brindisi, and Capua was one of its most important stops. The royal palace of Caserta, a few kilometres away, is the other great monument of the area, built by the Bourbon kings in the eighteenth century to rival Versailles.

As for riding, this is the Campanian plain, flat, fertile and intensely busy. Traffic is chaotic by northern European standards, with scooters, trucks and cars weaving in all directions, and the roads can be rough and badly patched. Keep your wits about you, and do not expect to make good time. The reward comes when you head for the hills: north toward the Monte Maggiore range or the volcanic slopes of Roccamonfina, where quieter roads wind through chestnut woods and olive groves with views back over the plain.

Santa Maria Capua Vetere has all the services you need: fuel, cafés, bakeries and pizzerias. This is mozzarella country, the buffalo mozzarella of Campania, so stop at a local dairy shop and try it fresh, preferably still warm. Park close to the amphitheatre where you can keep an eye on the bike, give yourself an hour for the ruins and the museum, and then decide whether Caserta deserves the afternoon.
t.historic centre of urbino@43.7,12.6:
Urbino is a whole hill turned into an idea. In the fifteenth century Federico da Montefeltro, a professional soldier who earned a fortune leading other people's armies, used it to build one of the most refined courts in Renaissance Italy, and the town that grew around his palace is still almost entirely brick and stone of that age. It was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 1998, and it remains a lively university town rather than a museum.

The Palazzo Ducale is the reason to come. Its façade with the twin towers looking west over the hills is one of the great images of Italian architecture, and inside, the Galleria Nazionale delle Marche holds Piero della Francesca's mysterious Flagellation of Christ and the famous Ideal City panel. Federico's studiolo, a tiny study lined with inlaid wood creating illusions of cupboards, books and instruments, is one of the most perfect rooms anywhere. Raphael was born in Urbino in 1483, and his father's house is open to visitors.

Riding into Urbino is a pleasure, because the hills of the Montefeltro roll in all directions with small roads following the ridges. The SS73bis from Fermignano and the road from Urbania along the Metauro are flowing and scenic, while the ride north-west to San Leo, with its fortress on a sheer rock where the adventurer Cagliostro died a prisoner, is one of the finest short rides in central Italy. Further south, the Furlo gorge carries the ancient Via Flaminia through a narrow limestone cleft and a tunnel the Romans cut in the first century.

Inside the walls the streets are steep, often cobbled or paved with brick, and closed to most traffic. Park at the Borgo Mercatale below the palace and take the lift or the spiral ramp designed by Francesco di Giorgio Martini, which was built so that horses could climb to the palace stables. Summer days are hot; the hills catch a breeze, and the evenings are wonderful.

Fuel is available on the approaches and around Fermignano. For food, try crescia sfogliata, the flaky local flatbread filled with cheese, ham or greens, which students eat by the hundred, and the local truffles and cheeses of the Montefeltro. Urbino is small enough that you can see the essentials in half a day and long enough to make you want to stay the night.
t.val d orcia@43.1,11.6:
Every photograph you have ever seen of Tuscany with a farmhouse on a bare hill, a winding line of cypresses and a soft haze over rolling fields was probably taken somewhere close to here. The Val d'Orcia is the valley of the river Orcia, south of Siena, a farmed landscape that Renaissance landowners deliberately shaped to look like the paintings of their time. UNESCO listed it in 2004 as a landscape designed with an idea in mind, and on a clear morning that idea is very easy to grasp.

The roads are the real joy. The SP146 from San Quirico d'Orcia toward Pienza and Montepulciano curls along the crests with views on both sides, and the old Via Cassia runs through Torrenieri and San Quirico on the line of the medieval Via Francigena, the pilgrim road to Rome.
