Corners are open and readable, the surface is mostly good, and the gradients are gentle enough that you can enjoy the scenery without missing an apex. Many of the most famous viewpoints sit at the end of white gravel roads, the strade bianche, which are fine at walking pace but worth treating with respect after rain.

Ride early. The valley is at its finest in the first hour of sunlight, when mist pools in the hollows and the cypresses throw long shadows. In late spring the fields are green and dotted with poppies; in early summer they turn gold; by autumn they are ploughed to bare grey-brown clay, and the place looks like the surface of a gentler moon. Midsummer middays are hot and hazy, and the roads fill with camper vans.

Montalcino, on its hill to the west, is the home of Brunello, one of Italy's great red wines. Bagno Vignoni, a hamlet near San Quirico, has a large thermal pool where the main piazza ought to be, with steam rising off it on cold mornings; the ancient baths are no longer for bathing, but there are modern spas nearby. Further south the hilltop fortress of Radicofani and the dark bulk of Monte Amiata, an extinct volcano, close the horizon.

Fuel is easiest on the main roads and in the larger towns; Chianciano Terme, about twenty kilometres east, is the nearest town of real size, and it is wise not to run low in the valley itself. Pecorino, crusty bread, a plate of pici with garlic and tomato, and a glass of local red make lunch here a lesson in not hurrying.
t.historic centre of the city of pienza@43:
Pienza is what happens when a pope decides to rebuild the village he was born in. In the fifteenth century the hamlet was called Corsignano, and one of its sons, the humanist Enea Silvio Piccolomini, became Pope Pius II. He commissioned the architect Bernardo Rossellino to turn it into an ideal Renaissance town, and within a few years a cathedral, a papal palace, a bishop's palace and a town hall stood around a single carefully composed square. The village got a new name, after the pope, and became one of the first places where Renaissance ideas of town planning were put into actual stone.

The square, Piazza Pio II, is small and perfectly balanced, a stage set that is also a working town centre. Step into Palazzo Piccolomini and walk through to the loggia at the back, which opens onto a hanging garden and a view straight down over the Val d'Orcia toward Monte Amiata. Pius wanted that view built into his house, and it is easy to see why. The cathedral beside it has a famous flaw: the ground beneath its apse is unstable, and the building has been sinking and cracking almost since the day it was finished.

The town is tiny, barely more than a thousand residents, and its lanes have names that tourists love to photograph, among them Via dell'Amore and Via del Bacio. Walk the path along the southern wall in the late afternoon, when the light rakes across the hills below and the farmhouses glow on their crests.

Pienza's other fame is cheese. Pecorino di Pienza, made from sheep's milk and aged fresh, semi-aged or long, is sold in shops all along the main street, and the smell of it follows you out of town. A wedge in the tank bag is a fine thing to have on a ride.

The road that brought you here is part of the pleasure. The SP146 runs east to Montepulciano and west to San Quirico d'Orcia, a crest road of open bends and constant views, busy with cars and cyclists in summer but magical on a weekday in May. Park outside the walls; the old centre is closed to traffic. For fuel, plan to fill up in Chianciano Terme or another of the larger towns around the valley, as Pienza itself is small.
t.san marino historic centre and mount tit:
San Marino is a whole country balanced on the ridge of a single mountain, and you feel it the moment the road starts to climb out of the coastal plain. Monte Titano rises steeply from the hills behind Rimini, a long limestone crest with sheer cliffs on its eastern side, and the old town of San Marino clings to the top with three towers strung along the ridge like stitches. The first, Guaita, is the oldest and the most photographed; the second, Cesta, sits on the highest point; the third, Montale, is a slender lookout you can only see from outside.

Tradition says the republic was founded in 301 by Marinus, a Christian stonemason from the Dalmatian coast who fled persecution and settled on the mountain. Whatever the precise truth, San Marino claims to be the oldest surviving republic in the world, and it has kept its independence through popes, dukes, Napoleon and the unification of Italy. It is still governed by two Captains Regent who serve six-month terms, a system older than most of Europe's states.

The road up from Rimini runs through the lowland towns of Serravalle and Borgo Maggiore and then begins to switchback, with the Adriatic spreading out behind you and the coastline curving away toward Pesaro. It is a busy road in summer, full of coaches and cars, so pick your time: early in the morning or later in the afternoon you get the climb with fewer people and kinder light. There are car parks around the old town where bikes can be left; from Borgo Maggiore a cable car runs up to the centre.

The views from the top are the reason to come. On one side, the coast and the sea; on the other, the Montefeltro, a wild jumble of hills and rocky outcrops that rolls away toward the Apennines. The roads into that country, toward San Leo with its fortress on a cliff and on to Urbino, are wonderful, twisty and much quieter than the coast, and they are the natural continuation of the ride.

Fuel in San Marino has generally been a little cheaper than in Italy, thanks to different taxation, and stations line the main road through the lowlands; Borgo Maggiore and the other towns have shops and bars too. Up in the old town, try a slice of torta Tre Monti, a layered wafer cake named after the three towers, and enjoy the strange feeling of having crossed a border without noticing.
t.beneventum and the arch of trajan@41.1,1:
Benevento was a Samnite town called Maleventum when the Romans arrived, and they reportedly changed its name to Beneventum, good event instead of bad event, after defeating King Pyrrhus nearby in 275 BC. The city became an important stop on the Via Appia, and later the starting point of the Via Traiana, a shorter route to Brindisi built by the Emperor Trajan. In 114 AD, the city erected a triumphal arch in his honour where the new road began, and it is one of the best preserved Roman arches anywhere, covered with reliefs celebrating Trajan's achievements, from his conquests to his care for the poor. It stands today at the edge of the old town, its marble a soft cream colour, its carvings still sharp.

The city has another treasure. Santa Sofia, a church built by the Lombard Duke Arechis II in the eighth century, with a striking star-shaped plan and an elegant cloister, is part of the UNESCO listing of the Longobards in Italy. The Lombards ruled Benevento as an independent duchy and later principality for centuries, long after the rest of their kingdom had fallen to Charlemagne. There is also a Roman theatre, still used for summer performances.

Benevento has a darker legend. For centuries it was said to be the place where witches from all over Italy gathered under a walnut tree by the river Sabato to celebrate their sabbaths. The legend inspired the name of Strega, the yellow herbal liqueur made in the city since the nineteenth century, and witch motifs are everywhere in local shops.

The surrounding landscape is the hilly interior of Campania, with vineyards, olive groves and wheat fields, and the mountains of the Matese and the Taburno nearby. The roads in the area are a mix of fast expressways and winding country roads. The road up to the Matese massif, to the north, climbs through forests to a high plateau and a lake, and is a favourite with riders from Naples. The Sannio wine region, around Benevento, produces Falanghina and Aglianico, among Campania's best.

Benevento has fuel, garages and plenty of trattorias. Ride the hills in spring, when they are green, or in autumn, during the harvest. Summer is hot, but the mountains offer relief.
t.kin nizhoni@35.4,-107.8:
Navajo speakers call it Kin Nizhoni, which means beautiful house, and the name has outlived the walls. This is one of the Chacoan outliers, a village of stone-and-mud buildings put up about a thousand years ago by Ancestral Puebloan people who were linked to the great centre at Chaco Canyon, some distance to the north. The outliers sit scattered across the high desert of northwestern New Mexico, often connected to Chaco by straight prehistoric roads, and each tells a piece of the story of a society that traded turquoise, pottery and macaw feathers across a very large area.

What you see today is low and quiet, with eroded walls and rubble mounds in sagebrush and juniper country. It rewards a slow look rather than a quick photograph. The landscape here is the Colorado Plateau edge, dry and bright, with Mount Taylor rising to the north, a mountain sacred to the Navajo and several Pueblo peoples, and the black lava flows of El Malpais lying to the south. The air is dry, the sky enormous, and in the evening the sandstone glows orange and red.

Riding in this part of New Mexico is easy and long. Interstate 40 and the old Route 66 run along the corridor, with fast, open roads, strong crosswinds and endless horizons, while the side roads to the outlier are narrower and sometimes unpaved. Monsoon storms between July and September can bring sudden downpours, hail and flash floods in arroyos, and the dirt tracks can become impassable after rain. Spring is windy, summer hot at midday, and autumn is the best season, with crisp air and golden cottonwoods in the valleys. Winter brings snow and ice at this elevation, so check conditions.

Grants, about twenty-five kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel, motels, cafés and a mining museum, and Milan is closer and smaller. Fill up before leaving town, carry water, and be aware that there is little shade at the site. Treat the ruins with respect, stay on marked paths, and take only photographs, because the stones are fragile and sacred to descendants who still live in the region.
The Medici left behind a necklace of villas around Florence, and the group of them listed by UNESCO in 2013 shows how a banking family turned itself into a ruling dynasty with the help of architecture. The hills north of the city, around Fiesole and the Mugnone valley where these coordinates fall, were favoured from the fifteenth century because they were cooler, greener and safely above the plague and the politics of the town below. Humanists, painters and poets were invited to talk and eat in these gardens, which is where some of the Renaissance really happened.

The villas themselves are low, calm buildings, quite plain from the outside, with terraces, cypress alleys, lemon houses and views across the valley to the dome of the cathedral. It is a quieter kind of grandeur than the palaces in the city, designed for conversation instead of display, and many of the gardens are open to visitors, though times vary a lot, so check before you ride up.

The riding here is lovely but small scale. The roads climb out of Florence in tight, narrow turns between stone walls, olive terraces and cypress, with limited visibility and a lot of cyclists and tour minibuses. It is a ride for a slow Sunday morning, not for pushing, and surfaces can be broken by roots and winter frost. Parking in Fiesole is limited, so arrive early. Caldine and Pian di Mugnone are quiet villages without much more than a cafe or two, while Florence, a few kilometres away, has everything, fuel included.

If you want a proper ride after the gardens, follow the Mugnone valley and the old Via Bolognese north over the Futa Pass, which tops out around nine hundred metres in the Apennines. The road has long, flowing bends, beech woods and views that open once you clear the tree line, and it is a classic among Tuscan motorcyclists. Near the top is a large German war cemetery, a sobering reminder that the Gothic Line ran through these hills in 1944. Autumn is excellent, with chestnut leaves turning and mist lying in the valleys at dawn.
t.abruzzo@41.8,13.7:
Abruzzo is the part of Italy that most Italians forget to brag about, which is probably why it is still so wild. These coordinates sit in the high Apennines near Pescasseroli, the main village of the Abruzzo, Lazio and Molise National Park, which was founded in 1923 and is one of the oldest in Italy. It protects one of the last populations of the Marsican brown bear, a distinct subspecies that survives in the low hundreds at best, as well as wolves, chamois and red deer. You are unlikely to see a bear from the saddle, but the signs on the road warning of animal crossings are not decoration.

The beech forests around Villavallelonga are part of the UNESCO listing for the ancient beech forests of Europe, and in autumn they turn copper and gold in a way that makes riders slow down without being asked. Pescasseroli is also the birthplace of Benedetto Croce, the philosopher, in 1866, and the village is pretty without being polished, with stone houses, wood smoke in cold months and a handful of places selling cheese, cured meats and honey.

The riding is excellent, and mostly uncrowded. The roads climb through thick forest, open onto high meadows, drop beside Lake Barrea's turquoise water and wind over passes, with the Forca d'Acero, at around fifteen hundred metres, the best known. Corners are medium and rhythmic, surfaces generally decent, and traffic light outside August, but cold nights and high altitude mean ice is possible early and late in the season, and fog is common. Take layers, because a sunny valley can be near freezing at the pass.

Pescasseroli has about two thousand people, and you should plan fuel before you arrive, using larger towns on the approach like Avezzano or Sora rather than counting on a village pump being open on a Sunday. Cafes and trattorie exist, serving heavy mountain food, with lamb, pecorino, pasta with wild mushrooms and sometimes polenta. Autumn is the star season, but May and June are green and the road is still empty. Keep your speed down in the forest, because deer and the odd bear matter more than your lap time, and respect the quiet.
t.villa du poggio imperiale@43.7,11.2:
Poggio Imperiale announces itself with an avenue, a long, straight, cypress-lined approach running up from Porta Romana in Florence, with statues in niches and the villa waiting at the top like the end of a sentence. It began as a Medici property in the sixteenth century, but its grand form came in the 1620s, when Maria Maddalena of Austria, wife of Cosimo II, enlarged it and gave it the name Imperiale in a nod to her Habsburg origins. The cool neoclassical front you see today was added in the early nineteenth century under Napoleonic rule.

It is still a working school, an old state boarding school for girls, so access is limited and the building sits in a different mood from the villas that are museums. That is part of its charm. You can admire the avenue and the facade from outside, and ask about visits, but do not turn up expecting a ticket office.

Florence itself is a bad place to ride in a hurry. Narrow streets, a huge restricted traffic zone with cameras, and trams make the centre hostile, but the southern edge where Poggio Imperiale sits is a good launching point for the ride toward Siena. Fuel is no problem, since the suburbs of Florence and nearby Grassina have petrol stations on every main road. The old Via Chiantigiana, the SR222, leaves the city through Grassina and climbs into Chianti, one of the loveliest rides in central Italy: rolling hills of vines and olives, stone farmhouses, cypress-lined drives and road signs for Greve and Panzano. The corners are moderate, the surface mostly fine, and the rhythm is relaxed, but weekend traffic includes cyclists, camper vans and slow tourists, so start early.

Siena, the other half of the ride title, is a medieval city built on three ridges, with a shell-shaped main square that hosts the Palio horse race twice each summer. Its centre is closed to most traffic, so park outside and walk. Between the two cities there is no shortage of wine cellars, though riders should decline the tastings politely or share the glass with a passenger. Late April, May and the weeks around the October grape harvest are the loveliest times, when the hills are green or gold and the light does the work.
t.the santa sofia complex@41.1,14.8:
Benevento has been a crossroads for about as long as there has been a road to cross, but the Santa Sofia complex belongs to a particular chapter, the Lombards. In the eighth century the duchy of Benevento was the last Lombard power in southern Italy, and Duke Arechis II built Santa Sofia as his palace church, around the 760s. It is a strange, beautiful building, a hexagon surrounded by a ring of columns and walls, with an odd star-like plan that has puzzled architects ever since. Inside the plain stone are traces of frescoes, and the later Romanesque cloister next door is a lovely quiet square. It is part of the UNESCO listing for the Longobards in Italy, which came in 2011.

Benevento is a city of nearly fifty thousand people, so fuel, food and parking are manageable, with the old centre partly closed to cars. The town is also famous for witches, because legend says they once gathered under a walnut tree near the river, and the local liqueur, Strega, takes its name from the story, bright yellow and sweet. Torrone, the nougat, is the other local treat, and you can buy it everywhere.

Riding in the surrounding area is gentle but varied, with the Sabato and Calore rivers meeting at the city and hills rising on every side. The roads are in decent condition on main routes and rougher on side ones, with sudden potholes after rain and plenty of patched asphalt. Do not expect motorway speeds, and watch for trucks heading to the nearby industrial areas.

A short hop away is Maccoli-Perrillo, a hamlet worth a quiet detour, and the ride list ties this stop to the old Roman road, the Appia Traiana, which makes a neat pairing. The stone of Roman Benevento and the stone of Lombard Benevento are only a few hundred metres apart, and noticing that layering is the pleasure of the place. Visit in spring or autumn, as midsummer heat on the narrow streets can be fierce, and aim for late afternoon when the light turns the church walls warm.
t.villa de la petraia@43.8,11.2:
La Petraia stands on the slope above Castello, on the north-western edge of Florence, and the first thing you notice is its tower, a leftover from the medieval fortress that stood here before the Medici made it a villa. Ferdinando de' Medici bought it in the 1560s and had Buontalenti reshape it, keeping the tower and building around it, so that the house looks like a small castle that learned manners. The garden below is laid out in terraces, with a fountain topped by a Venus wringing out her hair, a famous work by Giambologna.

The most surprising room is the central courtyard, which was roofed in glass in the nineteenth century to become a ballroom. That happened when the villa passed to the House of Savoy, and Victor Emmanuel II, the first king of united Italy, used it with his companion Rosa Vercellana, whom the Florentines called Bela Rosin. The frescoes around the walls show scenes from Medici history and were painted much earlier, which makes the ballroom feel like a time capsule with a skylight.

The ride starts in the suburbs and soon turns pleasant. From Sesto Fiorentino, a town of forty-odd thousand with fuel and cafes, you can climb through olive terraces on narrow roads toward Monte Morello, with views back over the Arno plain. Surfaces are patchy and the lanes are tight, so keep to a slow pace, particularly on weekends when walkers and cyclists use the same roads.

The second half of the ride title is Cerreto Guidi, a village west of Florence where the Medici built a hunting lodge, and the road from here runs along the Arno valley to the hills of Montalbano, Leonardo's country, with Vinci close by. The terrain is soft, with vines, olive groves and cypress, and the road meanders in an unhurried way that suits a late afternoon. Fuel is easy along the main road through Empoli, but pumps in the hills are rare, and many places close on Sundays, so fill up in town.

Go in May, when the garden is fresh, or in October, when the grapes are in and the air is clear. Check opening days, because Florentine villas often close on one weekday each week.
t.teatro giovanni battista pergolesi@43.5,:
The people of Jesi take their opera seriously, and they have a reason. Giovanni Battista Pergolesi was born here in 1710, and by the time he died in 1736, at the age of twenty-six, he had written the Stabat Mater and the comic opera La serva padrona, two works that changed music. The theatre that carries his name was opened in 1798, a neoclassical jewel with tiers of boxes and a good-sized stage, in the heart of the old town on the main square. It still has a season, and a ticket for an evening performance is a treat if you are staying nearby.

Jesi is a walled town of about thirty-seven thousand on the Esino river, in the Marche region, and it has all the services you need, including fuel, food and parking just outside the old walls. Its other claim to fame is Emperor Frederick II, who was born here in 1194, in a tent in the piazza, according to the story, because his mother was travelling and did not want to give birth indoors where doubters could challenge the child's origin. Whether you believe it or not, it is a good tale to take to the bar. Wine drinkers will know the area for Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi, a dry white that goes well with fish and with the local porchetta.

The riding is the real treat of the Marche, because the landscape is a pattern of low ridges running from the Apennines to the Adriatic, like waves frozen in place. West of Jesi the road enters the Gola della Rossa, a limestone gorge with good bends and thin traffic, and further on you reach the Frasassi gorge and its caves, one of the larger cave systems in Italy. The asphalt on provincial roads is mixed, and tight bends hide gravel in places, so keep a bit in reserve.

Monsano is the quiet neighbour next door, where the lanes are narrow and the hills green. Spring and autumn are pleasant, the summers hot and dry, and in winter the higher roads can ice up. Dinner in the old town on a mild evening is the best finish.
t.teatro bramante@43.7,12.5:
Urbania has had three names. It began as Castel delle Ripe, became Casteldurante in the thirteenth century, and was renamed in 1636 when Pope Urban VIII took over the duchy and gave it his own. In the Renaissance it was a pottery town, famous for majolica, the tin-glazed painted earthenware that Duke Guidobaldo and his court sent as gifts around Europe, and the ceramics still sold in the shops carry on that tradition. The theatre that bears the name of Bramante, the great architect who was born in nearby Fermignano, stands in the town centre, a small, intimate house with tiers of boxes in the Italian manner, and the town itself is a small walled place on a bend of the Metauro river, with brick arcades and a handsome ducal palace.

Urbania also has some stranger attractions. In the church of the Dead, a small chapel, a group of naturally mummified bodies, dating from the eighteenth century and found by chance in the nineteenth, sits in glass cases behind the altar, and visitors usually leave quiet. On a happier note, the town claims to be the home of the Befana, the old witch who brings gifts to Italian children on the night of 5 January, and holds a big festival in her honour at Epiphany, when thousands of children fill the streets.

The riding in the Marche hinterland is first class. The valley of the Metauro winds through the Apennine foothills, with roads that climb through oak woods and open ridges, and the landscape is a patchwork of golden fields and clay-coloured villages. The Furlo gorge, a spectacular limestone pass where a Roman road tunnel still survives, lies a short way to the north-east. Surfaces are generally good, with the usual patches and gravel, and the traffic is light outside summer weekends. Spring is lovely, with wildflowers, and autumn brings truffles and mist.

Urbania has about five and a half thousand people, with fuel, bakeries and a supermarket, and Sant'Angelo in Vado, a few kilometres up the valley, is known for its white truffle fair in autumn. For lunch, order a plate of tagliatelle with truffle in season, or crescia, the local flatbread stuffed with ham and cheese. The coffee in the main square is excellent, and the arcades give shade.
t.villa dei papiri@40.8,14.3:
The Villa of the Papyri is mostly still buried. It was a huge seaside villa at Herculaneum, on the slope below Vesuvius, and when the eruption of 79 AD sent a mud and ash flow down on the town, the villa was covered by twenty metres of hard volcanic rock. In the 1750s, the Bourbon engineers who were digging in the area tunnelled down and found marble statues, bronzes of rare quality and a library of around 1,800 papyrus scrolls, charred into black lumps by the heat. The scrolls, many of them works by the Epicurean philosopher Philodemus, have been read in recent years using X-ray imaging and artificial intelligence. The villa may have belonged to Julius Caesar's father-in-law, Piso, though this is a guess. The villa in Malibu that houses the Getty Museum is a copy of it.

Today Herculaneum, now called Ercolano, is a crowded Neapolitan suburb of fifty thousand, and the excavated Roman town lies in a pit at the bottom of its streets. It is smaller than Pompeii but better preserved, with wooden beams, carbonised furniture and painted walls still in place, because the mud sealed everything. The villa is not generally open to visitors, and the site is mostly a place to think about what lies under your wheels.

The ride is a lesson in Neapolitan traffic. The roads are fast, noisy and chaotic, with scooters weaving, lights ignored and the surface patched and cracked. Ride defensively, and park the bike in a secure garage, since theft is a real concern in this area. The best riding is up the volcano. The road through Ercolano climbs by hairpins through pines and lava fields to a car park at about a thousand metres on Vesuvius, and the final stretch is a path to the crater. Weather and closures vary, so check before you go.

Fuel is plentiful around Ercolano, Portici and San Giorgio a Cremano, and Naples is a short ride along the coast. Take a coffee at a bar on the corner and have a sfogliatella, the crisp shell pastry, for breakfast. If you have time, go in spring or autumn, when the air is clear and the view of the bay and Capri is sharp.
t.basilica of st apollinare in classe@44.4:
For centuries the sea reached this field. Classe was the port of Ravenna, a harbour built by Augustus to station the Roman Adriatic fleet, and merchants, sailors and soldiers filled its quays until the river silt choked the channels and the coast crept east. Today the port is farmland, the sea is five kilometres off, and the great church of Sant'Apollinare stands alone among the fields, a tall brick basilica with a round bell tower, rising from the plain like a ship stranded on a sandbank. It was consecrated in 549, in the time of Justinian, and stands over the tomb of the first bishop of Ravenna, Apollinaris, who is said to have been a disciple of Saint Peter. UNESCO listed the early Christian monuments of Ravenna in 1996.

Inside, the apse glows. A great mosaic shows Apollinaris standing among green meadows in prayer, with twelve sheep representing the faithful, and above him the sky is gold, with a cross set among stars. The colours, made of tiny pieces of glass and stone, have lasted for fourteen centuries and look nearly fresh. Light from the windows moves across the surface through the day, and the basilica is best in the morning or late afternoon. The nave is wide and plain, a long procession of marble columns, and it feels very quiet.

The pine forest behind the church, the Pineta di Classe, was already ancient when Dante wrote about it. The poet spent his last years in Ravenna, exiled from Florence, and he died here in 1321. He set the earthly paradise at the top of Purgatory in a divine forest that many readers take to be this one, with birds singing in the pines. Walking among the trees, on sandy paths with the smell of resin, is worth an hour.

The ride is flat and easy, along the straight roads of the Romagna plain, where the main hazard is fog and the second is agricultural traffic. The Apennines rise a short way inland, with good roads climbing through chestnut woods. Ravenna, four kilometres away, has everything: fuel, parking, cafes and a splendid sequence of mosaics in San Vitale and other churches. Piadina, the thin flatbread of Romagna, stuffed with prosciutto and squacquerone cheese, is the proper lunch. Mosquitoes can be fierce in summer near the pinewood, so bring repellent.
t.villa de artimino@43.8,11.0:
The Medici liked to hunt, and Ferdinando I wanted somewhere to do it. In the late sixteenth century the grand duke commissioned the architect Bernardo Buontalenti to build him a hunting lodge on the hill of Artimino, west of Florence, and the result was a large, plain and strangely beautiful villa with a loggia, a terrace and a forest of chimneys. It is nicknamed the villa of the hundred chimneys, though there are fewer than that, and the stacks along the roofline give the building a rhythm that you can recognise from a long way off. It is one of the Medici villas and gardens that UNESCO listed in 2013 for the way they shaped the Italian idea of a country house.

The setting is the Montalbano, a low range of wooded hills covered with olive terraces, vineyards and cypress. The wine here, Carmignano, is one of the oldest named in Italy, and local tradition says that Catherine de' Medici brought Cabernet vines from France, and the red is still blended with that grape. Below the villa lies Comeana, with a big Etruscan tumulus, one of several burial mounds in the area that show that the hills were important long before the Medici. A small Etruscan museum in the village of Artimino adds context.

The riding is gentle and lovely. The lanes climb through olive groves in tight bends, with stone walls, cypress avenues and views down to the plain, and the surface varies from smooth to patched. In spring the hillsides are green and the poppies are out, and in autumn the vines turn red and the olive harvest begins. Traffic is light on the hill roads, though tour buses visit the villa on some days. Mornings are the best time.

Poggio a Caiano, three kilometres away, has another Medici villa, designed for Lorenzo the Magnificent, and enough shops and fuel to be useful, while Florence lies twenty-odd kilometres to the east. For lunch, order a plate of local ham, ribollita bean soup or a steak, and a glass of Carmignano if you are not riding. The walk around the villa terrace, with its view over the plain, is a good way to finish.
t.pompeii@40.8,14.5:
Nobody in Pompeii knew that Vesuvius was a volcano. The town had been shaken by a violent earthquake in 62 AD and was still rebuilding in August 79, when the mountain exploded, burying the streets under a rain of pumice and then a hot flow of ash. About two thousand people died in the town, and the ash preserved bread in ovens, graffiti on walls, ruts in the stone roads and the hollows left by bodies. Excavation began in 1748, and in the 1860s the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli poured plaster into the hollows to produce the figures you see in the museum. UNESCO listed the archaeological areas of Pompeii and Herculaneum in 1997.

The site is huge and takes at least three hours on foot. The long straight Via dell'Abbondanza runs through the middle, lined with shops, bakeries, bars with built-in counters and houses with painted walls. The theatre, the forum and the amphitheatre lie across the town, and the Lupanar, the brothel, is one of the busiest rooms. It is hot and shadeless in summer, so bring a hat, water and good shoes, and go in the first hour after opening or late in the afternoon. Many streets are cobbled with large stepping stones for crossing the road, with wheel ruts in between.

The modern town of Pompei, nearby, is known for its great sanctuary of Our Lady of the Rosary, a pilgrimage church that draws visitors in huge numbers. The roads between the site and the coast are busy, narrow and chaotic, with scooters and buses, and parking is awkward. Use a secure garage and avoid leaving luggage on the bike. Fuel is easy, in Pompei, Boscoreale and Torre Annunziata, all within a few kilometres.

The best riding in the area begins when you leave the plain. The road over the Lattari mountains to the Amalfi Coast climbs through lemon terraces and drops to a narrow cliff road with hairpins, tunnels and tour buses, among the great coastal rides of Europe, though in summer it moves at the speed of the slowest coach. Early spring and autumn are better, and so is a weekday morning. Allow time for a coffee at a cliff-top bar, with the sea far below.
t.villa dei misteri@40.8,14.5:
Outside the walls of Pompeii, a few hundred metres from the Herculaneum Gate, stands a villa that holds one of the strangest paintings in the Roman world. The Villa of the Mysteries was a large country house and wine estate, and in one of its rooms a continuous frieze, nearly life-sized, runs around all four walls against a vivid red background, the famous Pompeian red. The figures include women, a young initiate, a satyr, a winged figure with a whip and the god Dionysus himself, and they seem to show a ritual of initiation into his cult, though nobody has ever been sure of the exact meaning. The paintings date from about the middle of the first century BC, some decades before the eruption.

The villa is a good place to see how the wealthy of Pompeii lived outside the crowded town. It had a terrace facing the bay, rooms for guests, a wine press room with a large wooden press, and a cellar with big storage jars in the ground. The vineyards of the area were famous in antiquity, and some modern growers have replanted Roman varieties on the slopes of Vesuvius nearby. Walking through the villa in the early morning, with sun lighting the faded frescoes and a smell of dust and warm stone, feels like being let into a private house.

For the ride, the route from the main site to the villa is a short, flat one, along roads that are busy and bumpy. Pompei and Boscoreale are both towns of around twenty-five thousand people, so fuel and food are not a problem, and Torre Annunziata and Naples are close. Boscoreale has its own Roman villa, with a wine press and a museum. A coffee in the old centre, with a sweet pastry, is a good start to the day. The summer heat is intense, so go early, and keep your jacket on in traffic.

If you have an afternoon, the road up Vesuvius from Boscoreale or Terzigno is a rewarding climb through pine woods and lava beds, with views of the whole bay. Check the opening hours and weather first, and bring a layer, since it is cooler at the top.
t.mesa verde national park@37.3,-108.5:
On a high sandstone plateau in the south-west corner of Colorado, the Ancestral Puebloan people lived for about seven hundred years, from roughly the sixth century to the end of the thirteenth, and in the last century or so of that time they built their homes in the shelter of the cliffs. Mesa Verde, the Green Table, takes its Spanish name from the pinon and juniper that cover the mesa top. The cliff dwellings, tucked beneath overhanging rock, are among the best preserved in North America, and Cliff Palace, the biggest of them, has around a hundred and fifty rooms and many circular ceremonial chambers called kivas.

The people left around 1300, after a long drought and a time of upheaval, and moved south, and their descendants are among today's Pueblo peoples of New Mexico and Arizona. Cowboys looking for stray cattle found the cliff dwellings in 1888, and the area was made a national park in 1906, the first in the United States set aside to protect the work of human hands. Many of the dwellings can only be seen on ranger-led tours, which involve ladders and narrow passages and need to be booked, and the details, including closures for conservation, change from season to season, so check the park's information before you go.

The approach is part of the experience. Highway 160 runs along the foot of the mesa, and the park road climbs from the entrance through a series of switchbacks, with speed limits set low and long views over the Montezuma Valley. The mesa top is about 2,100 to 2,600 metres high, so the air is thin and temperatures can drop quickly in the evening. Summer thunderstorms bring lightning, and snow in winter can close parts of the park road. Late spring and early autumn are the best times, with fewer visitors than in July and August. Wildlife includes mule deer, wild turkeys and the occasional black bear.

Cortez, thirteen kilometres from the coordinates, is a town of more than eight thousand, with fuel, motels and restaurants, and Mancos, a smaller town to the east, has a few cafes and a friendly feel. Fill up before heading up the mesa, and carry water.
t.certosa@44.5,11.3:
Bologna has a way of making even its dead look sociable. The Certosa, the monumental cemetery just north-west of the old walls, began life as a Carthusian monastery and was turned into a public burial ground at the start of the nineteenth century, when Napoleonic rules said the dead should lie outside the city. The monks' cloisters and chapels were simply adapted, and over the next two centuries families commissioned sculpture on a scale that makes the place feel like an open-air museum. Marble weeping women, family portraits in stone, scenes from daily life, and a lot of whiskered gentlemen in frock coats line long arcades.

The names are a quick tour of Bolognese pride. The poet Giosue Carducci, who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1906, is buried here, as is the painter Giorgio Morandi, who spent his life painting bottles and jugs in the most patient way imaginable. More recent visitors leave flowers for the songwriter Lucio Dalla. It is a quiet, shaded, gently strange place, and the porticoes are the best of it. A long covered arcade links the cemetery with the city, in the same family as the porticoes that make Bologna so walkable in the rain.

Riding in here is straightforward and a little tiresome. You reach the Certosa from the ring roads and the Via Emilia, flat and urban, with endless traffic lights and buses, and you should know that the historic centre is a limited-traffic zone with cameras, so a bike left in the wrong place can bring a fine through the post. Park outside it and walk. The city is at the foot of the Apennines, and if you want proper corners, the hills south of town are where Bolognese riders play, on roads running up towards the passes towards Tuscany. Ducati's home at Borgo Panigale is on the same side of town, and you will see its red bikes everywhere, bought, loved and ridden.

Fuel and coffee are no trouble at all in a city of this size, and nobody will rush you in a bar. Try the mortadella, the tortellini in broth, or a plain tagliatelle with the long-simmered ragu, which is nothing like what is served abroad. Autumn, with fog on the plain and warm light on the brickwork, suits the Certosa better than any other season.
t.universita e accademia@44.5,11.4:
Walk into the courtyard of the Archiginnasio in Bologna and you walk into a gallery of coats of arms. Thousands of them cover the walls and ceilings, painted and carved by students over the centuries, each one a small act of vanity from a young man far from home. This was the main seat of the University of Bologna, which claims to be the oldest university in the world, founded in 1088. Students from all over Europe gathered here to study law, and the city got rich and proud on them. Dante, Petrarch and Copernicus are among the names said to have passed through, and the university's first women professors arrived here long before most of Europe allowed such a thing.

The most unforgettable room is the Anatomical Theatre, carved entirely in spruce wood in the seventeenth century, with a canopy supported by two skinless figures and a dissecting table in the centre. It is ghoulish, beautiful and entirely serious, and a reminder that medicine had to be learned by looking. It was mostly rebuilt after bombing in the Second World War, using the original pieces.

All of this sits on the doorstep of Piazza Maggiore and the churches of San Petronio and Santo Stefano, in a city whose porticoes were added to the UNESCO list in 2021. There are about forty kilometres of covered arcades in Bologna, built because the medieval city needed more room for students and sensibly extended the upper floors over the pavement. Walking from one to the next in a rainstorm is one of the great urban pleasures.

For a motorcyclist, the centre is a puzzle, and a limited-traffic zone with cameras means you should leave the bike outside the old walls, in a paid car park or on the street in the area beyond the ring, and enter on foot. Bologna's hills begin just south, on the road to the Apennine ridge. The Futa and Raticosa passes have been favourites with Italian riders for ages, and the Mille Miglia and Giro d'Italia ran through them. Fuel at petrol stations on the ring.

Eat well here. This is the home of tagliatelle al ragu, tortellini in brodo and mortadella, and the evening aperitivo is a ritual. A late afternoon wander under the arcades, then a long dinner, is the right way to spend the day.
t.marechiaro@40.8,14.2:
There is a song about Marechiaro, and for once the song is not exaggerating. The little fishing hamlet on the Posillipo headland, at the western edge of the Bay of Naples, inspired a poem by Salvatore Di Giacomo in the 1880s about a window and a flower, and Francesco Paolo Tosti set it to music, so that "Marechiare" has been sung in Neapolitan kitchens and concert halls ever since. Locals will point out the so-called Fenestella, a small window on a wall above the sea, as the very one. Whether the poet had it in mind or not is a matter for a pleasant argument over a plate of fried fish.

The name means clear sea, and the water here is genuinely a clean, glassy green over dark rock. Posillipo is a ridge of volcanic tuff, part of the Phlegraean Fields, the caldera country west of Naples where the ground still steams at Solfatara. The Greeks called the hill Pausilypon, meaning a pause from sorrow, and Romans built seaside villas along it. Just along the coast the ruins of the villa of Vedius Pollio, a freedman and friend of Augustus, include a theatre and a tunnel cut through the hill. Close by lies the Gaiola, a marine protected area with two small islets and clear water that is worth a look.

Getting here is an exercise in Neapolitan riding. Via Posillipo winds along the cliffside from Mergellina, with the bay below and Vesuvius floating in the haze across the water, and the views are among the best in southern Italy. The road is narrow, busy, and often lined with parked cars, and the lanes down to Marechiaro itself are steeper and tighter still. Scooters weave, buses squeeze, and everyone drives by negotiation. Go slowly, watch the cobbles and manhole covers, which can be treacherous in the wet, and treat every blind corner as occupied. A weekday morning is easiest. Summer weekends bring crowds to the swimming platforms and restaurants.

Fuel is available in Posillipo and Bagnoli, each with around twenty thousand people, and in the city centre beyond. At Marechiaro itself you get the small harbour, a few rocks to sit on and some simple seafood restaurants. Try spaghetti with clams or a fried fish cone and stay for the light, which turns copper over Capri in the early evening.
t.historic centre of rome@41.9,12.5:
You cannot ride into the heart of Rome with any dignity, but you can arrive in a way that does the city justice. Come in by the Appian Way, the Via Appia Antica, laid down in 312 BC by the censor Appius Claudius and later called the queen of roads, and the approach tells you who built this city and what they wanted from it. The old stone surface, with its basalt blocks, still runs for miles south of the walls, between pines, tombs and lonely arches of aqueduct. Closer to the centre the road joins the real city, with the Colosseum, the Forum and the imperial fora lined up like a geology of power, the Pantheon with its famous open oculus, and then Baroque Rome, with Bernini fountains in squares that seem to appear around every corner.

The historic centre has been inhabited for nearly three thousand years, and the layers show. The Tiber bends around it, the seven hills rise above it, and the Vatican, a state of its own, sits just across the river. Rome is tangled and noisy and beautiful in the way that very old cities are, and the best way to see it is on foot with a good map and no plan.

For a rider, the city is a test of nerve and patience. The centre is a limited-traffic zone with cameras at its gates, so bikes without a permit can be fined if they enter at the wrong time. Locals zigzag past on scooters, buses and taxis share narrow lanes, and the setts, the small square cobbles known as sampietrini, turn greasy in rain and can throw a bike sideways. Park outside, in one of the paid car parks or on the streets beyond the walls, and take a bus, tram or your own two feet. Evenings are better than midday, when the heat and the tourists peak together.

Outside the city the ride picks up. The Alban Hills to the south-east have winding roads through chestnut woods and lakes in old volcanic craters, and the road to Tivoli and Villa d'Este, with its fountains, is an easy morning's run. The ring road is fast and crowded, with petrol stations at regular intervals on the outskirts. Anywhere in the city, you are never far from a decent coffee, a supplì, or a bowl of cacio e pepe.
t.the basilica of san salvatore@42.7,12.7:
Spoleto is a hill town in Umbria with a past much longer than most people expect. It was a Roman colony, then the capital of a Lombard duchy, and the Lombards, who came into Italy in the sixth century, ruled a great swathe of the peninsula from here. The basilica of San Salvatore lies just outside the old centre, below the hill, and few churches in Italy are older, dating from the fourth or fifth century and reshaped in the early Middle Ages. Its pale, plain facade looks classical, with a triple doorway and carved frieze, because its builders reused Roman fragments and copied Roman forms.

Inside the building is spare and quiet, with a high nave, a vaulted ceiling and bare walls, and it feels very old in a way that polished churches do not. The church is part of the group of Lombard sites in Italy inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2011, which recognises how the Lombards blended Roman, Christian and Germanic traditions. It sits next to a cemetery, which adds to the stillness, and the cypresses around it frame the view toward the hills.

Spoleto itself is a joy to ride to. Approaching from the Via Flaminia, the old Roman road that still runs through the town, you pass olive groves, small hill villages and views of the Apennines. The roads south toward Terni and east toward Norcia are good riding country, with smooth asphalt, long curves and little traffic outside holidays, and the Valnerina valley is especially fine. The old town has steep lanes, and traffic restrictions apply in the centre, so park outside the walls and walk.

With nineteen thousand inhabitants Spoleto has petrol stations and trattorias, many serving strangozzi pasta with truffle and local lentils. Choose spring or autumn, with clear air and hills in green or gold, and avoid late June and July if you dislike crowds, because the festival fills the town. The stone steps up to the fortress, the Rocca Albornoziana, and across the great Ponte delle Torri are a good way to work off lunch.
t.archiepiscopal chapel@44.4,12.2:
Ravenna was the capital of the western Roman empire in the fifth century, then of the Ostrogothic kingdom under Theodoric and later of Byzantine Italy, and each of these rulers left a layer of mosaics that glitter in the dark. The Archiepiscopal Chapel, dedicated to Sant'Andrea, was built around the year 500 by Theodoric, who was an Arian Christian, and its vault and walls are covered in gold and white mosaics of birds, flowers, and a Christ dressed as a Roman soldier, trampling a lion and a serpent. It is a tiny space, barely big enough for a small group, but the effect is astonishing.

The great mosaics of San Vitale and Sant'Apollinare Nuovo are close at hand, and the whole group of early Christian monuments is a World Heritage site. Ravenna is also where Dante spent his last years and died in 1321, and his tomb, a small neoclassical shrine, is a short walk from the chapel. The Adriatic once lapped at the city walls, but the sea has retreated, leaving the port of Classe a few kilometres away.

The label tied to this stop mentions the Vena del Gesso Romagnola, and that is a fine reason to ride. This is a ridge of gypsum that runs along the Apennine foothills, white and sharply cut, with caves, sinkholes and woods above the valley of the Santerno and Senio. From Ravenna you cross the flat plain, drained marshland of poplar rows and farms, then climb the hills of Brisighella and Monte Mauro, with their small, winding roads and outcrops of pale rock. The surface is variable, narrow and with tight bends, and the plain is windy and foggy in winter.

Ravenna has eighty thousand people, so petrol, parking and a meal are all easy to find, though the old centre is a traffic-limited zone. Local food is rich, with piadina flatbread, cappelletti pasta and clams from the coast. Bicycles are everywhere, so look carefully at junctions. Go in spring or autumn for gentle weather, and look for the mosaics with a short break from the heat.
Gian Carlo Menotti was an Italian-born composer who made his career in America, and in 1958 he decided that Spoleto, a small hill town in Umbria, would be the right home for a festival that brought together artists from both sides of the Atlantic. That is the origin of the Festival dei Due Mondi, the Festival of Two Worlds, which still fills the town with opera, theatre, dance and music every year in late June and July. The theatre that bears his name, the Teatro Nuovo, was built in the nineteenth century and is the main stage, a handsome horseshoe with gilt boxes and a painted ceiling.

The festival gives Spoleto a summer energy that is unusual for a town of its size. The Piazza del Duomo, a sloping square in front of the cathedral, becomes an open-air auditorium for the closing concert, and every little square seems to have a quartet or an exhibition. The town can be cramped and expensive during the festival, so book ahead, and expect the lanes to be full of people at all hours.

For riders, Spoleto is a base for some of the best roads in central Italy. The Via Flaminia runs through, but the pleasure lies east and south: the road along the Valnerina toward Norcia, the home of cured pork and truffles, follows the river Nera through narrow gorges and woods, with long curves and little traffic. Further on, the high plateau of Castelluccio and the Piano Grande flowers in early summer in a carpet of colour. The Monteluco road, which climbs through ilex woods above the town to an old hermitage, is short and twisty.

The practicalities are easy in Spoleto, with petrol stations on the ring road and trattorias everywhere. Park outside the old town and use the escalators and lifts that carry visitors up the hill. Winter can be cold, with fog in the valleys and snow on the higher roads, and the best seasons are late spring and early autumn.
t.villa medici de fiesole@43.8,11.3:
Fiesole sits on a hill above Florence, and it has looked down on the city for much longer than Florence has existed. The Etruscans founded a settlement here, and the Romans built a theatre, baths and a temple that are still visible. When the Medici came to power in the fifteenth century they chose the slope below Fiesole for a country villa, and Giovanni de' Medici, the younger son of Cosimo, commissioned Michelozzo to design one around 1450. The result, Villa Medici, is built on terraces cut into the hillside, with a loggia that opens out over a sweeping view of the Arno valley and the dome of Florence cathedral.

The villa became a gathering place for scholars, artists and poets, among them Lorenzo the Magnificent's circle and the philosopher Pico della Mirandola. It was a place of conversation and leisure, a deliberate break from the business of banking and politics, and the terraced gardens with their lemon pots and cypress trees were part of the design. The villa is now private and not open to the general public, but its gardens can be glimpsed from the road, and the view from the terrace of the town itself shows much the same scene.

The ride up from Florence is short and charming. The Via Fiesolana and the old Via Vecchia Fiesolana climb in tight bends between stone walls, olive groves and villas, and the road is narrow, with room for only one vehicle at some corners. Buses and tourists make the main road busy, so go early. The surface is mixed and dappled shade can hide patches of damp. Florence itself has a large restricted traffic zone, and cameras fine unauthorised vehicles, so plan your route.

Fiesole is small but has a few cafes and gelaterie around its main square, and fuel stations are on the way up from the city. Florence has everything. Spring and autumn give clear light on the hills, and the early evening, when the city below turns gold.
t.alta valle secchia@44.4,10.4:
The upper valley of the Secchia is the high Apennine country of Reggio Emilia, a landscape of beech woods, bare grassy ridges and deep river valleys, where Emilia gives way to Tuscany. The river rises near the Passo del Cerreto, at about 1,260 metres, and flows north through sparsely populated hills before dropping to the plain and the Po. The region is part of the Tuscan-Emilian Apennine National Park, with wolves, golden eagles and red deer in the high country.

The nearest town is Castelnovo ne' Monti, a lively little place with about ten thousand people in the shadow of the Pietra di Bismantova, a great flat-topped rock that rises out of the hills like a ship's hull. Dante mentions it in the Purgatorio as the image of a difficult climb. The countryside is also the home of Parmigiano-Reggiano, and the cheese dairies, where the wheels are made each morning from the milk of local cows, are open to visitors. Mountain villages have stone houses with slate roofs, and chestnut woods provide flour for sweet cakes.

For riders, these are some of the finest roads in northern Italy. The road up to the Passo del Cerreto climbs through woods and open pasture, with plenty of bends and sweeping views, and further east the Passo di Pradarena rises higher, to about 1,570 metres, with stunning views across the valley. Traffic is light, apart from summer weekends, when motorcyclists arrive from Parma and Modena. The surface is generally good, though frost has damaged parts, and gravel appears after rain. Mist gathers in the valleys in the morning, and thunderstorms build on summer afternoons.

Castelnovo ne' Monti has fuel, shops, restaurants and hotels, and is the best base, while villages higher up have only a bar or a shop. Food here means tortelli, cured ham, mushrooms and chestnut dishes, with cheese and a glass of red from the hills. Winter brings snow to the higher passes, and the best time is from May to October.
t.tarracina and the crossing of the lautul:
The Appian Way runs south from Rome across the Pontine Marshes, and at Terracina it meets a wall of rock. The Romans did not go round it. In the early second century AD the emperor Trajan had a vast cutting made through the cliff, leaving a sheer wall about thirty-five metres high, and carved numbers into the rock face at intervals of ten Roman feet so that the labourers could track their progress. The marks are still visible, and standing at the bottom looking up gives a sense of the scale of Roman road engineering. The place is called Pisco Montano, and the road still runs through it.

Terracina, the Roman Anxur, is a town of thirty-one thousand people on the coast between Rome and Naples, with a long sandy beach below and an old town built on a hillside. On top of the hill stand the remains of a huge temple of Jupiter, built on terraces of arches and arcades in the first century BC, and from there the view takes in the sea, the Circeo promontory and, on a clear day, the islands of Ponza. The cathedral, built into a Roman temple, has a pavement of old stones and a pulpit with mosaics.

Farther inland, at the pass of Lautulae, the Romans fought and lost a battle to the Samnites in 315 BC, one of the early reversals in the long wars for control of central Italy. The ground has changed, but the narrow strip between mountain and marsh still shapes the line of the roads.

The ride here is a good one. The coast road to Sperlonga and Gaeta is a series of bends above the sea, with cliffs, caves and little beaches below. At Sperlonga, the grotto of the emperor Tiberius, where a banquet was held in the first century and the roof collapsed, has a museum of the sculptures found there. Inland, the Monti Ausoni offer quiet roads through olive groves and villages. In summer the coast is crowded, and traffic is heavy at weekends, so go early or come in spring and autumn.

Terracina has fuel and plenty of seafood restaurants. Try spaghetti with clams or a fry of small fish. Late spring is lovely, with warm days and a clear sea.
t.district of villa manzo@40.8,14.2:
Posillipo is the hill that Naples looks at when it wants to feel it lives somewhere grand. It is a long ridge of soft volcanic tuff that runs out into the bay on the western side of the city, with villas, gardens and terraces, and views over the water to Vesuvius and the islands of Capri and Ischia. The Greeks called it Pausilypon, which means a pause from pain, and the Romans agreed: the rich built villas here, and the ruins of one of them, that of Vedius Pollio, can still be visited in a park above the sea. Virgil is said to be buried in the park near Mergellina, though the evidence is slim and the scholars are polite about it.

I cannot tell you exactly what stands at the Villa Manzo mark, but the setting is clear. The road along the ridge, Via Posillipo, winds past high walls and gates, gardens full of lemons and bougainvillea, and hidden stairs that drop to little coves. At Marechiaro, the fishing hamlet made famous by a song, a few restaurants still serve fresh fish on terraces over the water. The Gaiola protected marine area, below the cliff, has clear water and a handful of rocky islets.

On a motorbike the hill is a pleasure and a test. The bends are tight and the road is narrow, with parked cars on both sides and vans stopping where they please. Naples traffic has its own logic, and scooters, buses and pedestrians flow through it in ways that seem chaotic at first and begin to make sense. Surfaces are patched, with cobbles in the old quarters and manhole covers that are treacherous in the wet. Leave nothing on the bike, and park it in a garage if you can, since theft is a real risk. The restricted traffic zones in the centre have their own rules, so check before entering.

Posillipo has about twenty-three thousand people, and fuel is available in Fuorigrotta, the busy district to the north, which has seventy thousand. Pizza is the thing to eat, and the simple Margherita, with tomato, mozzarella and basil, is still the benchmark. A sfogliatella and a coffee in the morning will set you up for the day.

Spring and early autumn have the clearest light, and sunset from the hill, with the bay turning pink, is the reason to be here.
t.abruzzo@41.8,13.9:
Bears are the thing everyone asks about in Abruzzo, and the honest answer is that you probably will not see one. The Marsican brown bear, a small, isolated population, survives in the mountains of the Apennines, and the National Park of Abruzzo, Lazio and Molise, created in 1923, is its stronghold. The park also protects wolves, chamois and deer, and a lot of ancient beech forest, some of which is part of a group of European beech forests listed by UNESCO. Seeing a bear is rare, but a roadside sign and a bear-shaped warning tell you where you are.

Villetta Barrea and Civitella Alfedena are two villages beside the Lago di Barrea, a reservoir that fills a valley under steep wooded slopes. Civitella, with only three hundred inhabitants, has a small museum of the wolf and a good view of the lake. Villetta Barrea has a bit more, with a few shops and bars. Pescasseroli, the park's main village, is a short ride away. All have small hotels, and the food in the area is hearty, with lamb, pecorino, mountain sausages and soups of beans and chestnuts.

The road through the park, the old state road, runs along the valley between steep forested slopes and open meadows, with gentle bends that suit a relaxed pace. The surface is mostly good, but the mountains throw rock and gravel onto the road after rain, and wildlife can step out at dusk. Winters are cold, and snow can close the higher roads. Autumn, when the beeches turn gold and red and the deer are rutting, is the best season, with clear air and quiet roads. Summer weekends are busy with walkers.

Fuel is a problem to plan. The villages have little or none, and the nearest town of any size is Castel di Sangro, about nineteen kilometres away, with nearly six thousand people. Fill the tank there or at Pescasseroli before you go into the park.

This part of Italy is also on the way to the Via Appia, the Roman road that runs from Rome to Brindisi, and the ride joins the two together, ancient and wild.
t.galliera@44.5,11.3:
Bologna is a city of arcades, and the longest ones stretch for miles. The porticoes, built over the centuries to give shelter from sun and rain, and to add room to the upper storeys, run for tens of kilometres through the old centre and out to the sanctuary of San Luca on a hill south of the city. UNESCO listed them in 2021. Via Galliera, the long street leading north from the centre towards Porta Galliera, is a good place to walk under them, with palaces, churches and shops on one side and the shade of the vaults on the other.

The city itself is among the most pleasant in Italy, with brick and terracotta in warm shades, a lively university that is among the oldest in Europe, and a deep love of food. The two leaning towers, the Asinelli and the Garisenda, rise above the old centre, and a climb up the taller offers a view over the roofs. Piazza Maggiore, the great square, is lined with the city hall and the basilica of San Petronio.

Bologna is also a place of pilgrimage for motorcyclists. Ducati has its factory at Borgo Panigale, on the western edge of the city, and the museum there is a joy, with racing machines, classic models and prototypes. The Mugello circuit, home of the Italian MotoGP, lies in the hills to the north of Florence, and the old road over the Futa Pass leads there, with long, flowing bends through chestnut and beech. The roads south of the city are some of the most famous in the country.

In the city itself, the old centre is closed to most traffic, and fines for entering are severe, so leave the bike in a garage or outside the ring road and take a bus or walk. There is plenty of fuel on the edge of the centre, and the city has three hundred and sixty-six thousand people. Eat tortellini in broth, tagliatelle with ragù and a slice of mortadella, and wash it down with a glass of Sangiovese.

Spring and autumn are the best times, with mild weather and clear light. Summer is hot, and the city empties in August.
t.cerveteri@42.0,12.1:
Cerveteri was the Etruscan city of Caere, one of the richest and most powerful in Italy in the seventh and sixth centuries before Christ, and its dead lie in houses. The Banditaccia necropolis, on a ridge outside the modern town, is a city of tombs: round mounds of earth on stone drums, laid out along streets and squares, each containing rooms cut in the soft volcanic rock to look like homes, with beds, benches, columns and carved ceilings. The Tomb of the Reliefs, with stucco images of household objects, shows how the Etruscans pictured the afterlife. UNESCO listed the necropolises of Cerveteri and Tarquinia together in 2004.

Walking among the mounds is an unusual experience. Cypress and pine trees give shade, the paths are clear, and the sounds of the town fade away. The site is open most days, though hours change with the season, and the museum in the town holds finds from the tombs, including painted vases of great beauty. A famous Greek vase, the Euphronios krater, was dug up illegally near Cerveteri in the 1970s, sold to a New York museum and returned to Italy decades later.

The riding is a matter of flat roads and fast traffic. The Via Aurelia runs along the coast, with trucks and cars heading for Rome, and the modern roads are busy. The old centre of Cerveteri has narrow streets, and the road up to the necropolis is a gentle climb. Better riding lies inland, in the hills behind Cerveteri, where the lanes cross volcanic ridges and quiet farmland, with views of Lake Bracciano and the Tolfa Mountains. The surface is fair, the bends are easy, and the country is empty at weekdays.

The town has sixteen thousand people and fuel, bars and trattorias. Marina di Cerveteri, on the coast, is a seaside resort of nearly eight thousand that is quiet in winter and packed in summer. Local white wine, from the Cerveteri denomination, goes well with fish and pasta.

Visit in spring or autumn when the weather is mild. Summer is hot, and the stones of the tombs hold the heat. The Appian Way, on this ride, is a very different monument to Roman power, a long road of paving stones heading south.
t.jardin de boboli@43.8,11.2:
Cosimo I's wife, Eleonora of Toledo, bought a half-finished palace on the south bank of the Arno in 1549 and decided it needed a garden. The Boboli, behind the Pitti Palace, rises up a steep hill in a series of terraces, avenues and lawns, and it became the model for formal gardens across Europe, including Versailles. The design began under the sculptor Tribolo and was carried on by other Medici artists over the next century. A curved amphitheatre of grass behind the palace was used for festivals and plays, and the great grotto designed by Buontalenti has fantastical stone carvings and a Venus bathing in a hidden room.

Walking up through the Boboli is a pleasure. Cypress and ilex shade the avenues, statues emerge from hedges, and fountains play in pools. At the top, a view across the roofs of Florence takes in the dome of the cathedral and the hills of Fiesole. The Isolotto, an oval island with a pond and a ring of statues, is a calm place to sit. A ticket is needed, hours change with the season, and the garden is usually closed on the first and last Monday of the month.

Florence is a hard place for a rider, but a rewarding one. The historic centre is closed to most traffic, with cameras that fine violators, so park outside it and walk or take a bus. Cobbled streets and tram lines add slippery hazards in the rain, and summer crowds make any move slow. Once you get out of the city, the roads are marvellous. The Chiantigiana, the old road between Florence and Siena, winds through vineyards, olive groves and villages, with gentle bends and big views. The roads to the Val d'Orcia, farther south, give a taste of the Tuscan landscape you know from photographs, with cypress-lined lanes and bare green hills.

The city has three hundred and fifty thousand people and fuel at the edges. Scandicci, to the south-west, has forty-five thousand and has stations and shops. Lunch should include a bistecca alla fiorentina, a thick T-bone grilled over charcoal, or a more modest plate of ribollita, a thick vegetable soup.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons. In August the heat is oppressive and many locals leave town.
t.treno della barca@44.5,11.3:
The longest building in Bologna is not a palace or a church. It is a block of flats, curving along the edge of a district called Barca, on the western side of the city, and locals call it the train, il Treno. It was built in the 1960s as social housing, to a design by the architect Giuseppe Vaccaro, and it stretches for hundreds of metres in a single, slightly bent line, with a long row of balconies and a shared walkway. Whatever you think of postwar architecture, it was an ambitious attempt to house thousands of people in a planned community, and it is still a home today.

It is not a monument for admiring so much as a piece of the city you pass through. The district has shops, a park and a library, and cyclists use the paths, with a feel of being outside the historic centre and closer to everyday Bologna. A rider can pull in for a coffee, look at the long facade and get a sense of the city beyond the porticoes.

Just beyond lies Casalecchio di Reno, where the Reno river leaves the Apennines and enters the plain. The weir, the Chiusa di Casalecchio, is a medieval feat of hydraulic engineering that fed the canals of Bologna and drove its silk mills. The town is a lively one, with thirty-four thousand people, and has plenty of fuel and shops. From here the road up the Reno valley leads to the hills, and the old road to Florence, the Porrettana, climbs into the mountains with long bends and views of beech woods.

This is motorcycle country. The Ducati factory is on the other side of the city, and the hills of the Bolognese Apennines are full of bikes at weekends. The roads are twisty, the surfaces mostly good, and the scenery lovely, though speed checks are frequent and the locals ride fast. Take care on the bends where cyclists climb in the middle of the road.

Eat tigelle, small round breads filled with cured pork and cheese, or a plate of tortelloni. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and late summer brings heat and haze. The ride goes on to the gentle foothills of Reggio Emilia, a quiet area of villages and vineyards.
t.san paolo fuori le mura@41.9,12.5:
The name tells the story: Saint Paul outside the walls. According to tradition, Paul was beheaded on the road to Ostia, and a Christian woman buried him in her family's cemetery beside the Via Ostiense, about two kilometres from the old city wall. Constantine built a small church over the grave in the early fourth century, and by the end of that century three emperors had replaced it with a vast basilica, the largest in Rome until the new Saint Peter's. In 1823 a fire destroyed most of the building, and it was rebuilt in the nineteenth century as a faithful copy of the old one, with a forest of eighty granite columns along the nave.

What you notice first is the light. The nave is long and bright, with alabaster windows, a gilded ceiling and a floor of polished marble, and high on the walls runs a frieze of medallion portraits of every pope, from Peter to the present, a row of faces that has been extended over the years. Under the high altar lies the tomb of the apostle, and a stone slab, marked with the name Paulo Apostolo Mart, can be seen through a window. Look for the Byzantine-style mosaic on the triumphal arch, which survived the fire, and for the Gothic cloister next door, a delight of twisted columns and inlaid stone, tucked beside the abbey.

Because it belongs to the Holy See, the basilica has extraterritorial status, like the Vatican, though you will not notice it. Riding to it is a matter of dealing with Rome. The Via Ostiense is a wide, busy road, with trams and buses, and the traffic is the usual mixture of impatience and improvisation. Watch for the cobbles, called sampietrini, which are slippery in rain, and for the limited traffic zones in the centre that fine unauthorised vehicles. The Garbatella district nearby has a quiet, garden-city charm with its low houses and courtyards.

Fuel is no problem in a city of nearly two and a half million, and the area has cafes, pizzerias and trattorias that cater to locals rather than tourists. Testaccio, a short way off, is the place for an authentic plate of cacio e pepe or oxtail stew. Entry to the basilica is free, though the cloister and museum charge a fee, and dress rules require covered shoulders and knees. Come in the morning or late afternoon, and make sure you look up.
t.theatre of herculaneum@40.8,14.3:
Herculaneum is the smaller, better-preserved sister of Pompeii, and the theatre is one of its hidden treasures. When Vesuvius erupted in AD 79, Herculaneum was buried not by falling ash, as Pompeii was, but by a series of pyroclastic surges, which killed the people who had fled to the boathouses on the beach and then entombed the town under about twenty metres of hardened volcanic material. The deep burial protected wooden beams, furniture, food and even the upper floors of houses. The theatre was found in the early eighteenth century by workers digging a well, and for years explorers tunnelled in the dark to reach it, taking away statues for the Bourbon king of Naples.

The theatre had room for about two and a half thousand spectators, with a semicircular auditorium, stage and a stage building decorated with marble. Some of it can be visited today only through the original tunnels, which are cramped and dim, and access is limited, so check ahead whether visits are possible. The modern excavations of the town itself lie in the open air, under a protective roof in places, with fine houses, mosaics and a well-preserved bath building. Anyone who has seen Pompeii should come here, because the intimacy is greater.

The surrounding place is the dense, busy town of Ercolano, built directly on top of the buried one, at the foot of the volcano. Riding here means Naples traffic, with narrow streets, aggressive overtaking and scooters appearing from every side. Park only in a guarded place and do not leave anything on the bike, since theft is a real concern in the area. The road up Vesuvius itself, a series of hairpins through pine and broom, offers dramatic views over the bay, and you can park near the crater rim and walk the last stretch.

Fuel and food are plentiful, since Ercolano and Portici together hold over a hundred thousand people. Eat pizza in the Neapolitan style, a soft, charred disc with tomato and buffalo mozzarella, and drink a coffee at the bar standing, as locals do. The Circumvesuviana railway links the site with Naples in about twenty minutes, and for many visitors a train is easier than a bike. Spring and autumn are best, as summer heat bounces off the stone and the crowds are heavy.
t.san luca@44.5,11.3:
The Sanctuary of the Madonna di San Luca sits on the Colle della Guardia, a green hill above Bologna, and what makes it special is the way you reach it. A covered arcade, nearly four kilometres long and with some six hundred and sixty arches, climbs from the edge of the city to the church, built between 1674 and 1793 so pilgrims could carry an icon of the Virgin down into town and back in the rain. It is the longest portico in the world, and it forms part of the arcades of Bologna that UNESCO listed in 2021. The icon, which tradition says was painted by Luke the Evangelist, is taken in procession to the cathedral each May.

The church itself is an oval baroque building, with a dome that stands out on the skyline and a terrace that looks over the roofs of the city to the plain and, on clear days, the Alps. Cyclists come in great numbers, because this climb is a favourite of Italian racing, a short, steep hill used in the Giro dell'Emilia. The arcade starts at the Arco del Meloncello, an elegant arch at the point where the covered way crosses the road, and from there steps and ramps carry on up through the trees.

You can ride up by road, and the route from Casalecchio di Reno or from the city climbs in easy hairpins, with some bumpy surface and tight corners. It is a short run, but expect cyclists, and the road is narrow, so go gently. Traffic restrictions may apply on feast days and during processions. Beyond the hill, the Apennine foothills open up, and the Bolognese hills have lanes that wind among vineyards and villas, a great place to ride in spring and autumn.

Casalecchio di Reno, just under two and a half kilometres away, has about thirty-four thousand people, and Bologna beyond has everything. In the city, limited traffic zones are strict, so leave the bike outside the centre if you plan a day on foot. Bologna is the home of tortellini in broth, of tagliatelle with ragù and of mortadella, and a plate of any of them at a family trattoria makes the climb worthwhile. The porticoes shelter you from sun and rain, which is why they were built.
t.archaeological areas of pompei@40.8,14.5:
Pompeii is the most famous ruin in the world, and it deserves its fame in a way that is hard to explain until you have walked its streets. In AD 79 Vesuvius erupted for two days, burying the town under about four metres of pumice and ash, and what was left was a Roman provincial city caught mid-sentence, with graffiti on the walls, loaves in an oven and a dog chained in a doorway. The letters of Pliny the Younger describe the eruption from across the bay, and they are the first account of a volcanic event by an eyewitness. Excavations began in 1748, and about two-thirds of the town is now uncovered.

Look for the details: the stepping stones across the streets, worn by cart wheels, the thermopolia, or snack counters, set into the pavement, the painted walls of the Villa of the Mysteries just outside the gate, in a deep red that is still bright, and the plaster casts of people and animals made by pouring plaster into the hollows left in the ash. The amphitheatre, among the oldest in existence, seated about twenty thousand. The UNESCO listing covers also Oplontis and Boscoreale, the villas around the volcano.

The ride into the area is part of the story. From the autostrada the road comes in through the plain of Campania, a flat, fertile land under the cone of Vesuvius, with orchards, greenhouses and the endless urban sprawl of the Naples suburbs. The streets around the ruins are busy and in places rough, and you should take care with parking, since petty theft is a risk. Use a guarded car park near the Porta Marina entrance and take your valuables with you. The summer heat inside the site is intense, and there is almost no shade, so bring a hat and water.

The modern town of Pompei, with about twenty-four thousand people, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the Sanctuary of the Madonna of the Rosary draws pilgrims. Wine from the slopes of Vesuvius, called Lacryma Christi, is worth tasting. Visit in April, May, October or November, and consider entering as soon as the gates open, when the light is low and the tour groups have yet to arrive. If you have time, ride up the volcano road to see the crater and the view over the bay.
t.kakadu national park@-13.0,132.5:
