Kakadu is a vast area in the Top End of the Northern Territory, about twenty thousand square kilometres of floodplains, escarpments, billabongs and savanna woodland, and it is one of the few places in the world that has been given World Heritage status for both its natural and cultural values. The name is said to derive from Gagudju, a language spoken by Aboriginal people in the northern part of the park. Aboriginal people have lived here for tens of thousands of years, and the park is owned by its Aboriginal traditional owners and leased to the national parks service.

The rock art is the cultural treasure. Thousands of paintings are spread across galleries at sites such as Ubirr and Nourlangie, showing animals, spirit beings, hunters and, in some cases, ships and guns of early European and Macassan visitors, so the paintings form a record of an extraordinary span of time. Some places are sacred or restricted, so follow signs, stay on marked paths, and listen to ranger-led talks where they are offered.

Nature is just as strong a draw. The wetlands of Yellow Water teem with birds, including jabirus, magpie geese and sea eagles, and saltwater crocodiles lurk in the water, so keep well back from the edge and never swim in unmarked waters. The seasons are dramatic. The dry season from May to October is hot and clear, with burnt grasslands and good access, while the wet season from November to April brings storms, flooding and closed roads. Mornings and evenings are the best times to see wildlife.

The Arnhem Highway and the Kakadu Highway are sealed and straightforward, and riders can travel them easily in the dry season, though many tracks into the park's attractions are gravel and may be closed in the wet. Heat is intense, and road trains and wandering wildlife demand attention. A park pass is required. Fuel is available at Jabiru and Cooinda, but distances are long and prices high, so carry spare capacity and plenty of water. Book accommodation ahead in the dry season.
t.siena@43.3,11.3:
Siena is the opposite of Florence in nearly every way that matters, and the Sienese would like you to remember it. It sits on three ridges in southern Tuscany, a compact medieval city of brick and stone in warm reddish-brown tones, and at its centre lies the Piazza del Campo, a vast shell-shaped square sloping down to a tall brick tower, the Torre del Mangia, about a hundred metres high. Twice each summer, on the second of July and the sixteenth of August, the square is covered with earth and ten riders from the city's districts, the contrade, race bareback around it in the Palio, a dangerous, chaotic event that lasts about ninety seconds and is felt by the whole city as a matter of honour.

The seventeen contrade, each with its own emblem, colours and fountain, dominate local life, and you will see their flags hanging in the streets. The cathedral, made of striped black and white marble, has a floor of inlaid scenes and a library of painted manuscripts that dazzles. The city was a rival to Florence in the Middle Ages, a banking power and home to its own school of painting, and its bank, Monte dei Paschi, founded in 1472, claims to be the oldest in the world still operating. Local food includes panforte, a dense spiced cake, and ricciarelli, soft almond biscuits.

For riders, Siena is the starting point for a famous scenic ride. South of the city, the roads wind through the Crete Senesi, a landscape of pale clay hills, and then into the Val d'Orcia, a UNESCO site of rolling fields, cypress-lined lanes and hilltop towns such as Pienza and Montalcino. Surfaces are generally good, with gentle curves and wide views, and the white gravel roads, strade bianche, add some adventure for those who like it. Spring, when the fields are green, and late September, when the grapes are ripe, are the best times. July and August are hot, and tourist traffic is heavy.

Be careful in the old city, because much of it is a restricted traffic zone where unauthorised vehicles can be fined by camera, so park outside the walls and walk in. Fuel stations and workshops are on the ring roads, and plenty of cafés and trattorias are in the historic centre. Stay for sunset in the Campo, when the brick turns gold.
t.sorrento@40.6,14.4:
Sorrento sits on top of a cliff, and the whole town is aware of the drop. It lies on the northern side of the peninsula that separates the Bay of Naples from the Gulf of Salerno, about fifty metres above the water, with Vesuvius filling the view across the bay and the island of Capri visible from the headlands. Lemon groves, some of them netted against frost, cover the slopes behind the town, and the lemons are the foundation of limoncello, the sweet yellow liqueur that is sold in every shop. According to myth, this is the coast of the Sirens, who lured sailors onto the rocks with their singing.

The town centre is built around Piazza Tasso, a busy square named for the sixteenth century poet Torquato Tasso, who was born in Sorrento, and the old lanes around it are lined with shops selling inlaid wood, lace and ceramics. Small cloisters, such as the one at San Francesco, offer quiet corners, and the marinas below the cliffs, reached by steep stairways, have small restaurants and ferries to Capri and Naples. A tradition of craft, and a strong tourist trade since the days of the Grand Tour, have shaped the town.

For the rider, Sorrento is the start of the Amalfi Coast road, the SS163, sometimes called the Nastro Azzurro or blue ribbon. It heads over the spine of the peninsula, then twists along a cliff for about fifty kilometres through Positano, Praiano and Amalfi toward Salerno. The road is narrow, hemmed in by walls and rock, with tight hairpins, blind bends and buses that need the whole width of the road at some corners. Scooters and cars weave in and out. Traffic in July and August can be dreadful, and in peak periods local authorities have limited access by number plate on certain days, so check before you go. Leave early in spring or autumn, and the road is far more enjoyable.

Sorrento has fuel stations, workshops and endless places to eat, from pizza to grilled fish. The best views are from the terraces of the old cliffside hotels, and an evening walk along the cliff-top gardens at sunset, with Vesuvius turning purple across the bay, is the best way to end a day.
t.ouray@38.0,-107.7:
Ouray sits at the bottom of a box. Tall red and grey cliffs rise on three sides of the town, leaving only a narrow gap to the north, and the whole place looks like a Swiss village that took a wrong turn into Colorado, which explains why it calls itself the Switzerland of America. About a thousand people live here, in Victorian wooden houses along a main street lined with shops, hotels and a hot springs pool fed by the same geothermal water that bubbles up around the town. An hour in the pool, with the cliffs above, is the standard remedy for stiff shoulders after a long ride.

The town was founded in the 1870s during the silver and gold boom, named after Chief Ouray of the Ute people, who tried to negotiate peace with the settlers, and for years it was a hard-working mining camp. The old mines are still scattered across the hills, and you can see their wooden structures high above the road. A short walk from the main street leads into Box Canyon Falls, where a waterfall roars through a narrow gorge, and on the hillside, jeep roads climb to ghost towns and passes above the tree line.

The road south to Silverton, US 550, is the legendary Million Dollar Highway. It leaves Ouray by cutting along the face of the cliff, in a series of tight curves with long drops on the outside and very little in the way of barriers, then climbs over Red Mountain Pass at 11,018 feet, about 3,360 metres. The surface is generally good, but the bends are tight, the road is narrow in places and snow and ice can appear in any month. Rockfall and fog are other hazards. Early morning is the best time, with less traffic and better light.

Ouray has fuel, along with a good range of cafés, hotels and small restaurants, and in summer it fills up, so book ahead. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in July and August, and the high passes can turn cold quickly. Pack warm layers even on hot days, and keep an eye on the sky. The town's ice cream shops are a pleasant reward before heading out.
t.durango@37.3,-107.9:
Durango owes its existence to a railway, and the railway still runs. In 1881 the Denver and Rio Grande built a narrow-gauge line up the Animas river canyon to the silver mines at Silverton, and the town was laid out to serve it. Today the Durango and Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad still operates a coal-fired steam train over the same route, with black smoke, cinders and a long whistle echoing between the cliffs, and the depot on the edge of the old town is a major attraction. The main street, Main Avenue, with its brick Victorian buildings, saloons and the Strater Hotel, has changed little since the town's early years.

The town sits at about 6,500 feet, in the broad valley of the Animas, with the dark ridges of the San Juan Mountains rising to the north and the dry mesas of the Four Corners country to the south. About eighteen thousand people live here, and the mix of ranchers, students at Fort Lewis College, outdoor enthusiasts and tourists gives it a lively character. Craft breweries and coffee shops are plentiful. Fifty kilometres or so west lies Mesa Verde National Park, where Ancestral Puebloans built cliff dwellings in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and the park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

For riders, Durango is a starting point of the San Juan Skyway, a loop of about 380 kilometres through the mountains. The road north from the town follows the Animas valley up through Hermosa, climbs over Coal Bank Pass, about 10,640 feet, and Molas Pass, about 10,910 feet, then descends into Silverton. The curves are long and sweeping, the surface is smooth and the views of peaks and aspen forests are superb. Summer is the main season, with the high passes snowed over from late autumn to spring, and afternoon storms can bring hail and lightning, so early starts are wise.

Durango has fuel at several stations, repair shops and a good choice of places to eat, with Mexican and New Mexican cuisine featuring green chilli. Prices climb in summer, so reserve a room early. A slow walk along the river trail in the evening is a good way to relax after the saddle.
t.silverton@37.8,-107.7:
Silverton is a mining town that never quite stopped, and the proof is in the muddy streets. It sits at about 9,300 feet in a high basin in the San Juan Mountains, ringed by peaks of more than 13,000 feet, and the single paved main street, Greene Street, is lined with false-fronted wooden buildings from the 1880s, all in good repair. About six hundred people live here year-round, and in winter the town is cut off by snow and avalanches, while in summer it fills with visitors from the train and the road.

Its fortunes came from silver and gold. Prospectors arrived in the 1870s, and the miners worked claims in the surrounding mountains, shipping ore out by wagon and, after 1882, by the narrow-gauge railway from Durango. Blair Street, one block behind the main street, was once a row of saloons and brothels, and its history is part of the town's reputation. The county museum, in the old jail, tells the story, and old mines nearby, such as the Mayflower Mill, offer tours. Ghost towns like Animas Forks, high above Silverton at nearly 11,200 feet, can be reached by jeep road and show how brutally cold and isolated life was.

For riders, Silverton is the middle of the San Juan Skyway. The road south toward Durango climbs Molas Pass and drops down the Animas valley, while the road north, the Million Dollar Highway, climbs to Red Mountain Pass and then descends in tight turns to Ouray. Both are paved and generally in good shape, but the altitude affects engines and riders, and summer storms arrive fast and bring cold rain. Night temperatures fall to near freezing even in July. Keep an eye on the sky, and carry extra layers.

Silverton has a few fuel stations, along with simple cafés and pubs, and a small selection of hotels and bed and breakfasts that fill up on busy weekends. At this altitude it is wise to drink plenty of water and take it easy on arrival. The summer light is brilliant, and the long evening shadows move slowly across the peaks, which is worth waiting for before you head down the road.
t.taos@36.4,-105.6:
Taos is a small town with a big reputation among painters, writers and people who came for a visit and stayed. It lies at about 7,000 feet on a high plateau at the southern end of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains in northern New Mexico, with the dark ridge of the range rising to the east and the dry sagebrush plain dropping to the Rio Grande gorge to the west. The light is extraordinary, clear and golden, and early in the twentieth century it drew a group of artists, the Taos Society of Artists, who painted the landscape and the people. D. H. Lawrence also lived near here for a time in the 1920s, and his ranch can be visited.

Four kilometres north of the plaza, Taos Pueblo has been inhabited for about a thousand years, and its multi-storey adobe buildings, set in front of Taos Mountain, are among the oldest continuously inhabited communities in North America. UNESCO listed it in 1992. Residents still live in the pueblo, and visitors are welcome at certain times, with rules about photography and respect, so check before you go. Taos also has a bridge across the Rio Grande gorge, completed in 1965 and about 650 feet, nearly 200 metres, above the river, which gives dizzying views.

The Enchanted Circle is a loop of about 84 miles that runs from Taos north to Questa, east to Red River, over to Eagle Nest and Angel Fire and back, circling Wheeler Peak, the highest mountain in New Mexico at 13,161 feet. The road is smooth, with long, flowing bends through forests of pine and aspen, high alpine meadows and old mining villages. Summer is the busy season, with cool mountain air and afternoon thunderstorms, and autumn, when the aspens turn gold, is spectacular. Snow can close higher parts of the road in winter.

Fuel stations, repair shops and restaurants are easy to find in Taos, which has about five and a half thousand people. The food is distinctly New Mexican, with green and red chilli on almost everything, and the smell of piñon wood smoke drifts through the streets on cool evenings. The plaza is a good place to sit and watch the day go by.
t.lake bracciano easy scenic@42.6,12.4:
Amelia likes to say it is one of the oldest towns in Italy, and the stones back up the claim. Its huge, polygonal city walls, built of enormous interlocking blocks without mortar, date from long before Roman times, and the town's legend says it was founded in the second millennium BC, long before Rome. It sits on a hill in southern Umbria, in the Tiber valley, with Lugnano in Teverina and Giove a few kilometres away, on a green and quiet landscape of olive groves, oak woods and small farms.

The pin sits among them, a long way north of Lake Bracciano but in the same family of landscapes: soft hills, medieval towns on hilltops and winding roads between them. Amelia, with about five and a half thousand people, is the largest and has shops, fuel, restaurants and a pretty main square, and it is known for its figs, cooked in sweets and eaten fresh. Lugnano has a beautiful twelfth-century Romanesque church, the Collegiata, with a carved porch and a fine interior, and Giove is a small hilltop village with a Renaissance palace and a castle at its centre.

The riding is relaxed and rewarding. The roads wind gently through the hills, with long sweeping views over the Tiber valley, and the surface is generally good, although some rural stretches are rough and patched. Traffic is light, except on weekends, when Romans arrive in numbers for lunch. The best time is spring, when the fields are green and poppies bloom, or autumn, when the vineyards turn gold and the olive harvest begins. Summer is hot and bright, with good swimming spots in nearby lakes.

For the table, Umbria is a treat. Look for strangozzi, a hand-rolled pasta usually served with truffle or a rich sauce, torta al testo, a flat bread cooked on a hot stone and filled with meat or vegetables, and local olive oil, which is peppery and green. Many trattorias in the hill villages serve simple, honest food at fair prices.

The place makes an easy, pleasant halt, close enough to Rome for a day out and far enough for the noise to fade. Order lunch, linger over a coffee, and enjoy a view that has barely changed in centuries.
t.castelli romani dawn loop photo pull off:
Monte Soratte rises on its own above the Tiber valley, a long ridge of limestone that stands out against the flat plain like a ship on a calm sea. The Roman poet Horace mentioned it in one of his odes, describing it white with snow, and the mountain has been a landmark for travellers on the Via Flaminia since antiquity. The pin sits in the hills of the Sabina, on the east bank of the river, near Forano, Selci and Filacciano, with the big mountain to the south-west.

This is a quiet, rural part of Lazio, far from the crowds and noise of Rome. The villages are small and old, stone houses built on hilltops, with a church, a bar and a view. Olive groves cover the slopes, and the olive oil of the Sabina is among the best in Italy, protected by its own designation. Farfa Abbey, a short ride away to the east, is one of the great Benedictine monasteries of medieval Italy, once among the richest in the country, and still has a working community of monks and a well-kept church.

The riding is gentle and beautiful. Narrow roads wind between olive groves and oak woods, rising to ridges with long views over the Tiber and the Apennine foothills, and the surface is mostly smooth, though it is patched in places and strewn with gravel near farm gates. Traffic is light, apart from the occasional tractor, and the speed is relaxed. At dawn, which is the purpose of this stop, the valley fills with mist, the hills rise out of it like islands, and the light is soft and golden. It is one of the best views within reach of Rome, and few people see it.

Rignano Flaminio, fourteen kilometres away, is the nearest bigger town, with supermarkets, fuel and cafés, and the small villages have bars that open early for coffee and a cornetto, a sweet croissant that is the standard Italian breakfast. Bring a layer, as mornings can be cool even in summer, and dress for the mist.

If you have time, climb or ride up to the little hill villages and wander their lanes. Most have a small restaurant or osteria that serves local food at fair prices, and the welcome is warm.
t.abruzzo gran sasso weekend@42.0,11.9:
The Etruscans lived on this coast long before the Romans, and the evidence is everywhere. At Cerveteri, a few kilometres inland, the Banditaccia necropolis is a whole city of the dead, with grave mounds cut into the volcanic rock, streets, squares and carved interiors that imitate the houses of the living, and it is on the UNESCO list. At Santa Severa, the walled castle on the shore stands on the site of Pyrgi, an Etruscan port, and the little medieval fortress is open to visitors. The pin sits near Santa Marinella, on the Via Aurelia, the old road that runs along the Tyrrhenian coast from Rome toward Tuscany.

The coast here is a mixture of beaches, rocky headlands, pine groves and small resort towns, with a faint air of faded holidays and Sunday outings from Rome. Santa Marinella, with fourteen thousand people, has fuel, shops and plenty of seafood restaurants, and Ladispoli and Cerveteri, to the south, are larger. Inland, the Tolfa hills rise to wooded ridges, and the town of Allumiere owes its existence to the alum mines that supplied much of Europe in the fifteenth century.

For riding, the Aurelia is a busy, straight road, but the lanes into the Tolfa hills are the reward. They wind between oak woods, pastures and old stone farms, with views over the sea, and are quiet during the week. The surface is mixed, with patches and the occasional pothole, and in summer the coastal road is thick with beach traffic, so go early. In spring the hills are green and full of wildflowers, in autumn the light is golden, and in winter the coast is empty and calm.

The cuisine here is simple and excellent. Fresh fish, grilled or in a fish soup, spaghetti with clams, and fried calamari are the staples, and the nearby hills produce wine, olive oil and good cheese. Many seaside restaurants open at lunchtime, and a table near the water on a spring day is hard to beat.

The ride is the Abruzzo and Gran Sasso weekend, which lies to the east across the Apennines, so this stop is a pleasant place to begin: an hour north-west of Rome, with the sea at your back and the mountains ahead.
t.sognefjellet high road@60.6,10.5:
Mjøsa is Norway's largest lake, a long, deep arm of water stretching more than a hundred kilometres through farmland and forest north of Oslo, and the pin sits just west of it, on the Toten plateau, not far from Raufoss. The land here is gently rolling, with big fields of grain and potatoes, red barns and white farmhouses, and a view down to the lake on a clear day. On Mjøsa itself, the paddle steamer Skibladner, launched in 1856, still carries passengers in summer, and is said to be the oldest paddle steamer in the world still operating on a regular schedule.

The name on the label is Sognefjellet, the high mountain road that climbs through the Jotunheimen national park to nearly 1,500 metres, but it lies far to the north-west, and this stop is about 300 kilometres from it. Here the ride is a quiet, rural one, through the heart of Innlandet county. Raufoss, with a little over six thousand people, is an industrial town known for its munitions and metal works, and has fuel, supermarkets and cafés. Gjøvik, a little to the north-east, is the bigger town on the lake, with a good waterfront and a large Olympic cavern hall, an ice hockey arena built inside a mountain.

The riding is relaxed. Roads wind across the plateau, with long curves, gentle climbs and wide views, and the surface is good, as is usual in Norway. Traffic is light apart from a few lorries and tourists, and speed limits are low and strictly enforced, with automatic cameras and heavy fines, so keep within the limits. In summer, the evenings are long and bright, and in autumn the birches turn yellow and the farmland glows. Sudden rain showers are common, so carry waterproofs.

For a meal, the farm cafés on the Toten plateau serve waffles, coffee and local produce, and the region is famous for its potatoes and its dairy. A cup of coffee and a fresh waffle with jam and sour cream is a Norwegian ritual, and well worth the stop.

The pin is a start and finish point, so use it to check fuel, food and weather before heading toward the mountains. The Sognefjellet road beyond is spectacular, but the journey begins quietly here, in a landscape of fields and lakes.
t.telemark canal roads photo pull off@60.3:
Eidsvoll is the place where modern Norway began. On 17 May 1814, a group of delegates met in a manor house here and signed the constitution that declared the country independent after four centuries under Danish rule, and the date is still celebrated as National Day. The building, Eidsvollsbygningen, is now a museum, a handsome neoclassical house on a hill above the river, and the pin sits a few kilometres from it, near Råholt, Maura and Grua, in the farmland north of Oslo.

This is the southern end of the great Norwegian lake system. Mjøsa, the largest lake, empties through the river Vorma at Eidsvoll, and the river runs south to join the Glomma, the longest in the country. Oslo's main airport, Gardermoen, lies just to the east, and the sound of aircraft is common, but the land to the west, around Hurdal and the lake Hurdalssjøen, is quiet, forested and full of small farms. In the evenings the forests smell of pine and damp moss, and in autumn the birches turn gold.

The label talks of the Telemark Canal, which lies far to the south-west, and the pin belongs to a different part of the country. Riding here is gentle and rhythmic, with long, smooth roads through farmland and forest, wide bends and gentle hills. The E6 motorway runs through the district, but the side roads are better, and traffic is light on weekdays. Norway's speed limits are low and strictly enforced, with fixed and mobile cameras and heavy fines, so ride calmly. The weather is changeable, with sudden showers, and even in summer the evenings can be cool.

For fuel, food and coffee, Råholt and Eidsvoll have supermarkets, petrol stations and cafés, and Gardermoen has more. The roadside cafés sell open sandwiches, waffles and strong coffee, and the farm shops in the area offer fresh vegetables, cheese and berries in season. Prices in Norway are high, so bring a card, and expect to pay well for a simple meal.

Take a short detour to Eidsvollsbygningen if you have time. Walking through the rooms where the delegates debated, and looking out at the same view of the river, gives a sense of how small, quiet places can change the course of a country.
t.nullarbor roadhouse@-31.4,130.9:
The Nullarbor Roadhouse stands in one of the emptiest stretches of the Eyre Highway, the sealed road that connects South Australia with Western Australia across the flat limestone plain. The name comes from the Latin for no trees, and the description is mostly accurate: the land is low, pale and covered in saltbush and bluebush, with a horizon so far away that it feels like the sea. The roadhouse is a small island of services in all that space, with fuel, food, accommodation and a campground, and it is a place where truckers and travellers meet and compare notes.

Fuel is what matters most. Distances between roadhouses on the Nullarbor are long, commonly well over a hundred kilometres, and prices reflect the cost of delivery, so fill the tank whenever you can and carry a spare container if your range is short. The wind is the other major factor. A headwind can drink fuel and tire the rider, while a crosswind can push a bike sideways, and road trains, which are lorries pulling several trailers, create a powerful slipstream as they pass. Give them room and expect to be buffeted.

Wildlife is abundant. Kangaroos, wombats, emus and even camels wander the verges, particularly at dawn and dusk, and a collision can be fatal for rider and animal. Plan to ride in daylight and keep your speed sensible after mid-afternoon. Wedge-tailed eagles often sit on the road, feeding on roadkill, and take off slowly, so slow down when you see them.

The plain is an old sea floor, and under it lie caves and sinkholes, some of the longest cave systems in the world. Further south, the cliffs of the Great Australian Bight drop into the Southern Ocean, and from June to October southern right whales come to the Head of Bight to calve, a short drive from the highway. A golf course, the Nullarbor Links, runs along the highway with one hole at each roadhouse, a typically Australian joke on a vast scale. The night sky here, far from any city, is crowded with more stars than most people have ever seen.
t.pula@44.9,13.9:
Pula's amphitheatre is the first thing you see and the last thing you forget. Built in the first century AD, in the reign of Vespasian, it stands on the edge of the harbour with its outer wall almost entirely intact, three storeys of arches rising above the water, and it is one of the six largest Roman arenas still standing. Gladiators once fought here before a crowd of thousands, and today the arena hosts concerts and a film festival, with the bay glittering through the arches behind the stage.

The city, with about 59,000 people, sits at the southern tip of the Istrian peninsula, where Croatia pushes into the Adriatic, and it carries layers of history that show up in odd places. A Roman temple dedicated to Augustus stands on the main square, a triumphal arch commemorates the Sergii family, and the old Venetian walls climb the hill behind. The Austro-Hungarian navy based its main fleet here in the nineteenth century, and the great cranes of the shipyard still dominate the western shore. James Joyce taught English at the naval school in 1904 and 1905, and a bronze statue of him sits outside a café.

As a start and finish, Pula is easy. Fuel is plentiful, parking is simple outside the old core, and good roads fan out across Istria, a heart-shaped peninsula of red earth, olive groves, vineyards and stone hill towns. The road north to Poreč, where the sixth-century Euphrasian Basilica glitters with Byzantine mosaics, runs through quiet farmland and small villages, with long, easy bends and little traffic outside the summer season. The coast has pretty coves and pine woods, and the Brijuni islands lie just offshore.

Food is a pleasure here: truffles from the Istrian forests, local olive oil, fresh fish, and a dry white wine called Malvazija. The bora, a cold north-easterly wind, can gust hard in winter, so be careful on exposed roads. In summer the sun is strong, and the sea is warm and clean. At dusk the arena turns orange and the swifts circle above it, which is a fine way to end any day.
t.lake bracciano easy scenic@41.8,12.9:
East of Rome the land begins to lift, and the road from Valmontone to Cave is the first hint of it. The pin sits in a gap between the Alban Hills to the west and the Prenestini mountains to the east, in a corridor where the old Via Casilina and the A1 motorway run side by side. It is not wild country, but it is a useful, sensible place to take on fuel and coffee before the hills, and the towns of Cave and Valmontone have all the services a rider needs.

Valmontone is dominated by a big seventeenth-century palace built by the Doria Pamphilj family, and the town is also a place with a sad modern history. In the spring of 1944, as the Allies broke out of the Anzio beachhead, the fight for Valmontone and the road through it was a key moment in the push towards Rome, and the town was heavily bombed. Today it has been rebuilt, and a huge shopping outlet beside the motorway has become a local landmark, which means traffic at weekends can be heavy.

Cave, a little further east, is a hill town on the edge of the Prenestini, with a small old centre and a church overlooking the plain. From here the roads begin to climb, narrow and winding, through olive groves, chestnut woods and small villages, and the view back across the plain to Rome's hazy skyline is wonderful on a clear evening. The surface is variable, so watch for patched asphalt and gravel on the bends, and expect local drivers who know the road well and are often in a hurry.

Practical matters are simple. Fuel is in Cave, with more in Valmontone, and there are cafes and bakeries in both. Try a local pizza bianca and a coffee at the counter, standing up, as the Romans do. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the air is clear and the light is soft. In midsummer the heat on the plain is intense, and the best plan is to start early, climb into the hills and be back in the shade by the afternoon.
t.lake bracciano@41.8,12.9:
Cave is a hill town in the countryside south-east of Rome, at the foot of the Prenestini mountains, and the ride that ends here has come a long way round from Lake Bracciano to the north-west of the capital. The town has about 8,000 people, and it is a working place of old stone houses, cafés, bakeries and shops, with a church and a small square at its centre. Fuel and supplies are easy to find, and the local bars serve strong coffee early in the morning.

The country around is volcanic and fertile, with vineyards, olive groves and chestnut woods covering the slopes, and a number of old hill towns perched on spurs of rock. Palestrina, a few kilometres to the north-east, was the site of a vast Roman sanctuary of Fortuna, whose terraces climb the hillside, and its ruins are some of the most impressive in Italy. Genazzano, a little further, holds a castle and a pilgrimage church. Wine lovers know the region for Cesanese, a red grape that makes a rustic and fragrant wine.

For a rider, the pleasure is in the small roads. Lanes wind between stone walls and vines, climb to villages, and drop again through woods, and the corners are tight enough to be fun without ever being dangerous. Surfaces vary, with patches of rough asphalt, and locals drive fast, so keep to your side on blind bends. Rome is about thirty-five kilometres to the west, and the road back is busy at rush hour.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the air is clear and the colours are warm. In summer the heat is strong, and in winter the hills can be misty and cold. At the end of a long ride, a plate of pasta and a glass of local wine in a village trattoria is a very good way to say goodnight.
t.castelli romani dawn loop@41.8,12.3:
Rome is quietest at dawn, and this is the place to see it. Fiumicino and Ostia lie on the coast just west of the city, where the Tiber meets the Tyrrhenian Sea, and between them is a landscape of canals, pine woods and Roman ruins that most visitors miss. The pin sits near Isola Sacra, the low island between the river's two mouths, a strange place of reeds, farmland and houses, with Leonardo da Vinci airport humming beside it.

Ostia Antica, a few kilometres inland, was the port of ancient Rome, and its excavated streets, warehouses, baths and a theatre are among the best-preserved Roman remains in Italy. The harbour silted up, and the river changed course, leaving the city stranded, and it was buried in sand and mud, which preserved it. Close to the airport lie the remains of the harbour built by the emperor Claudius and expanded by Trajan, whose hexagonal basin is still visible as a pond. On Isola Sacra, an ancient cemetery has tombs with fine terracotta reliefs.

Castel Fusano, a great pine forest that stretches inland from the coast, was planted in the seventeenth century and is full of umbrella pines, which give the landscape its distinctive look. The roads that cross it, shaded and straight, are lovely at dawn when the light filters through the trees and the air smells of resin. Wild boar, and an occasional fox, still live in the woods.

Fuel is easy here, because Fiumicino and Ostia are big towns with many stations, and cafes open early for the airport workers. Take a coffee and a cornetto at a counter, as the locals do, then begin the ride. The traffic on the roads to Rome is heavy later in the day, so an early start is the secret. Heading towards the Castelli Romani, the volcanic hills south-east of the city, you will pass through quiet farmland and pine woods and find the hills turn to vineyards and villages. In summer, the beaches of Ostia fill with Romans, and the traffic on the coast road can be slow, so avoid it on hot weekends.
t.castelli romani dawn loop scenic road@42:
The hills north of Rome are the remains of a great volcano, and this stretch around Rignano Flaminio and Magliano Romano shows it well. The pin sits in a landscape of rounded ridges and wooded gullies, cut into soft volcanic tufa, with olive groves on the sunny slopes and oak and hazel in the shade. It is gentle, rural country, only forty kilometres from the capital, and the contrast with the city is striking.

The roads are narrow and winding, rising and falling between small villages, and they are among the best near Rome for a quiet ride. The surface is variable, with patches of gravel and broken edges, and the bends are often blind, so take them gently. Views open suddenly to reveal the long, isolated ridge of Monte Soratte, rising out of the Tiber plain to the north-east like a whale, a mountain that the poet Horace wrote about two thousand years ago.

Close by is the valley of the Treja, a small river that has carved a deep gorge through the tufa, and which is protected as a regional park. Magliano Romano lies within it, and the area is full of Etruscan tombs, waterfalls and woodland walks. Further along, the Via Flaminia, the old Roman road that led north from Rome to the Adriatic, passes through Rignano and still follows its ancient line in places.

Rignano Flaminio has nearly seven thousand people, so it has fuel, shops and cafes. The surrounding villages have trattorie that serve homemade pasta, roast lamb and local olive oil, which is green and peppery and worth buying. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the weather is mild and the colours are good, and a Sunday morning ride here is a good way to escape the city. In summer, the heat can be fierce, so start early and stop in the shade, and in winter the lanes can be wet and muddy.
t.castelli romani dawn loop@41.6,12.9:
The Pontine plain is one of the strangest landscapes in Italy, because almost all of it is artificial. For centuries, this was a malarial marsh, a broad band of swamp between the Alban Hills and the sea that defeated emperors and popes. In the 1930s Mussolini's government drained it, dug a network of canals and founded new towns, among them Latina, Sabaudia and Pomezia, laid out in a rigid, rationalist style. The pin is near Cisterna, at the northern edge of the plain.

Cisterna has a place in the history of the Second World War. In January 1944, as American troops advanced from the Anzio beachhead, a battalion of Rangers was cut off and almost wiped out in the fighting near the town, which was largely destroyed. Today it is a busy, modern town with nearly twenty-seven thousand people, which makes it a good place for lunch. Fuel is easy, the cafes are good, and the old Appian Way, the Roman road to Brindisi, runs close by, often as a straight, quiet lane lined with umbrella pines.

The riding is flat and straight, with long avenues of eucalyptus trees planted as windbreaks and a network of canals that flash in the sun. It is not technical, but it has a certain hypnotic quality, particularly in the early morning when the mist hangs over the fields. The farmland is rich, producing kiwi fruit, artichokes and the milk of water buffalo, which is made into the famous mozzarella di bufala. A plate of fresh mozzarella with ripe tomatoes, eaten at a roadside shop, is a better way to finish a ride than most.

The wind can be strong on the open plain, particularly in spring, and in winter fog is common, so take care. Mosquitoes are a nuisance in summer, a reminder of the plain's old reputation, so you may want to keep your visor down at dusk. The best seasons are spring and autumn, when the fields are green, the light is clear and the Alban Hills form a blue wall to the north. At the end of the day, the lights of the towns come on across the plain, and the traffic of the Appia heading for Rome gives the whole place a sense of evening.
t.ravenna@44.4,12.2:
Ravenna is a town that was once the capital of an empire, and then largely forgotten, which is why so much of it survives. In 402 AD the Western Roman emperor Honorius moved his court here, because the marshes around it were easier to defend than Rome. After Rome fell, the Ostrogoth king Theodoric ruled from Ravenna, and then the Byzantine emperor Justinian reconquered it, and left behind the churches whose mosaics are among the glories of early Christian art. Eight of its early Christian monuments are on the UNESCO World Heritage list.

The mosaics are the reason to come. In the church of San Vitale, the walls glitter with images of Justinian and his empress Theodora, their eyes looking out across fifteen centuries, while in the small mausoleum of Galla Placidia, a deep blue ceiling is scattered with golden stars. They are simple, silent places, small in scale and huge in effect, and you may need a ticket and a little patience in high season. Dante, exiled from Florence, died here in 1321 and is buried in a modest tomb close to the centre, which is still a place of pilgrimage for Italians.

For a rider, Ravenna is a flat, easy city, with cyclists on every street and a large car-free centre. Parking for motorcycles is generally easy on the edge of the old town. The Mille Miglia route, the great Italian road race, passes through Ravenna, and a handful of car and motorbike enthusiasts will always have a story about it. Fuel and food are no problem in a city of eighty thousand, and it is the home of piadina, a thin flatbread filled with cheese, ham or rocket, which is one of the best snacks in Italy.

Out of town, the coast and the pine forest of Classe offer a quiet ride, and the Po Delta, with its lagoons and flamingos, lies a short way to the north. The roads are flat and straight, with fog in winter and mosquitos in summer, but the light, in spring and autumn, is lovely. Plan to stay for a few hours, take your time with the mosaics and end the day with a plate of fresh pasta in one of the old town's trattorie. If you can, make an early start, because the churches are quieter in the morning.
t.tuscany val d orcia overnight photo pull:
The label on this one says Val d'Orcia, but the coordinates fall about a hundred kilometres south, in the Alto Lazio, the northernmost part of the Rome region, where the Maremma meets the volcanic hills. The villages nearby, Canino, Tessennano and Arlena di Castro, sit on a low tufa plateau of wheat fields, olive groves and deep green ravines, and the landscape has a lonely, ancient feel that is quite different from the postcard Tuscany.

This is Etruscan country. Just south of Canino lies the park of Vulci, once one of the richest Etruscan cities, whose remains include tombs, a necropolis and an enormous bridge, the Ponte dell'Abbadia, which spans a gorge on the Fiora river. The bridge, built by the Romans and rebuilt in the Middle Ages, is a stunning sight, and a small museum in the nearby castle displays Etruscan finds. The area is also known for its horses and cattle, the cowboys of the Maremma, called butteri, who still work the herds.

Canino is the capital of olive oil in this part of Italy, and its oil, which has a protected designation, is fruity, green and slightly peppery. Many farms sell it directly, and a tin or bottle is an ideal souvenir. Tuscania, nine kilometres away, has more than seven thousand people, fuel and cafes, and it also has two splendid Romanesque churches on a hill outside the walls, San Pietro and Santa Maria Maggiore, which are well worth a visit. The town was badly damaged by an earthquake in 1971, but has been carefully restored.

The roads here are quiet, undulating and straight, with sudden dips into the ravines, and surfaces that can be rough. There is little traffic, and in spring the fields are bright green and scattered with poppies. Summer is hot and dry, with the plateau turning to gold, and in autumn the olive harvest brings tractors and crates onto the lanes. The light at dusk, with the hills turning blue and the sun sinking over the Tyrrhenian Sea, is the reason many riders linger.
t.abruzzo gran sasso weekend@42.1,12.7:
Palombara Sabina stands on the edge of the Monti Lucretili, a compact range of limestone ridges that rises north-east of Rome, and the fuel stop here is the first real signal that the city is behind you. The pin sits on the plain below, among the villages of Cretone, Castel Chiodato and Sant'Angelo Romano, where the farmland begins to rise. The ride calls itself Abruzzo and Gran Sasso, and the Gran Sasso's pale summit, Corno Grande at 2,912 metres, lies a good hundred kilometres to the north-east, but on a very clear winter day you may see snow on distant peaks.

Palombara has a fortress built by the Savelli family above the old town, a tangle of steep lanes and stone arches, and a small centre with a few cafes. The surrounding hills belong to a regional park, and the highest point, Monte Gennaro, reaches 1,271 metres, with wide views over the Roman countryside. This is the land of the Sabines, the people whom the Romans, according to legend, robbed of their women in the earliest days of the city, and who were later absorbed into the Roman world. The poet Horace had a farm in these hills, near the village of Licenza, a gift from his patron Maecenas, and wrote about its quiet and simplicity.

Olive oil is the local pride, and the oil from the Sabina hills has a protected designation, with a fruity, green taste. In autumn the groves are busy with the harvest, and you will see nets spread under the trees and small tractors on the lanes. The land is a patchwork of oak woods, olives, pasture and stone villages, many of them perched on rocks.

Fuel is easy at the edge of the larger towns, and Palombara Sabina has more than six thousand people. The roads that climb into the Lucretili from here are narrow, steep and twisty, with surfaces that vary, and few barriers. The bends are tight, the views are good, and the traffic is mostly local. Start early on a spring or autumn morning, take a coffee at a counter and be on the lanes by the time the light turns gold. Summer is hot, and by midday the lowlands are hazy, while in winter the heights may bring frost and the odd snowfall.
t.abruzzo gran sasso weekend photo pull of:
A glance at the map shows that this pin falls in the sea, some fifteen kilometres off the coast of Lazio, south-west of Rome, so there is no road here to ride. The shore it looks toward is another matter. From Ostia to Torvaianica, a long, straight beach runs below a line of pines, backed by farmland and the vast, private estate of Castelporziano, a presidential nature reserve of woods and wildlife that stretches along the coast.

Torvaianica is the main resort, a seaside town of low-rise apartments and beach clubs that fill with Romans in July and August, and become almost deserted in winter. The sand is dark grey and the sea is shallow, and the sunsets, when the sun sinks into the Tyrrhenian in a blaze of orange, are worth a stop. In clear weather you can sometimes see the long profile of Monte Circeo, a limestone headland rising from the sea to the south, which the ancient Greeks identified as the island of the sorceress Circe in the Odyssey.

The landscape behind the shore is of reclaimed marsh. Pomezia, a few kilometres inland, was founded in 1939 as part of the drainage project, and has a rationalist centre built in a plain, geometrical style. Beyond, the Pratica di Mare airfield and the old Latin settlement of Lavinium recall a much earlier age. The country is flat, the roads are straight, and the winds from the sea can be brisk, so it is best to ride the coast road, which is often busy, on a weekday or in the early morning.

Fuel is easy at Torvaianica, a town of seventeen thousand people with several stations, and cafes and pizzerias along the front. Seafood is the best food: spaghetti with clams, fried calamari and grilled sea bass. The best times for the coast are May, June and September, when the sea is warm and the crowds are thin. Come in the evening, park the bike on the promenade and watch the sun go down, and you will see why Romans have been coming here to cool off for generations.
t.abruzzo gran sasso weekend high point@41:
Lariano lies on the eastern slopes of the Alban Hills, the old volcano that rises south-east of Rome, and the pin falls among woods and farms between it and the village of Giulianello, in the foothills. The Alban Hills are not high, with Monte Cavo at about 950 metres, but their volcanic soil is rich, and the slopes are covered with vineyards, chestnut woods and orchards. The old crater lakes of Albano and Nemi lie a short distance to the north-west.

The high point is a modest one, a ridge on the shoulder of Monte Artemisio, which reaches over 800 metres, and which has long been a boundary between ancient peoples. In Roman times the area was the territory of the Volsci and the Latins, and in 1744 a bitter battle was fought nearby, at Velletri, between the Austrians and the Spanish and Neapolitan armies. Today it is a quiet, wooded landscape, popular with Romans for Sunday picnics and walks among the chestnuts.

Velletri, close by, is the wine town of the hills, with a protected white wine made from Malvasia and Trebbiano, and its cellars are open for tastings. Cori, on the hillside to the south-east, is a gem of a town, with huge Cyclopean walls from the pre-Roman period and a Roman temple of Hercules. Both are worth the detour and give a sense of how many layers of history lie under the Roman countryside.

The roads here are the best in the region for a spirited ride. They are narrow, twisty and well surfaced, climbing through shady woods and descending in long bends towards the plain, with views to the sea on a clear day. Be careful of leaf litter, wet patches and the occasional gravel, and expect cyclists and walkers on weekends. Fuel is available at Lariano, which has nearly thirteen thousand people, and in Velletri. Spring brings blossom and fresh green, and autumn brings the chestnut harvest and woodsmoke. In summer, the hills are a cool escape from the heat of the plain, so many Romans head here.
t.abruzzo gran sasso weekend scenic road@4:
Palestrina was ancient Praeneste, and a place of pilgrimage long before Rome was a great city. Above the modern town, a huge sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia climbed the hillside in a series of terraces, ramps and arcades, built in the second century BC, and the town's medieval houses were built on top of its ruins. The pin sits in the hills nearby, among the villages of Castel San Pietro Romano, Gallicano and Poli, in the Prenestini mountains, a ridge of limestone that rises east of Rome.

Castel San Pietro Romano is one of the most photogenic villages in Lazio, a cluster of stone houses clinging to a rocky outcrop, with a ruined fortress above. It was used as a location for the 1950s film Bread, Love and Dreams, with Gina Lollobrigida, and it has changed little since. Poli has a medieval castle in the middle of the village, and Gallicano is a quieter farming town in the valley. Palestrina was also the birthplace of the composer Giovanni Pierluigi, who took the town's name and became one of the most important composers of the Renaissance.

The roads that wind through the hills are among the most enjoyable near Rome. They climb steadily through olive groves and chestnut woods, with tight bends and quick straights, and the surface is generally good. Views open over the Roman plain and the Alban Hills, with the haze of the city beyond. On the weekends, you will share them with cyclists and locals, so take care on the blind corners, and watch for sand and leaves after rain.

Palestrina has nearly fifteen thousand people and plenty of fuel, cafes and trattorie. The local specialities are simple: pasta with pecorino, roast lamb and fresh ricotta. Visit in spring, when the almond and cherry trees are in flower, or in autumn, when the woods turn bronze. The light in the late afternoon on the stone walls of the villages is warm and soft, and makes a good moment to stop and look out over the plain to Rome.
t.perugia@43.1,12.4:
Perugia sits on a ridge above the Tiber valley, with a long history and a student population that keeps it young. The Etruscans founded it, and the Etruscan Arch still stands in the old walls, with Roman lettering added later. From the top of the hill you can see across Umbria to Assisi, Spello and, on a clear morning, the line of the Apennines. The city is large, about a hundred and twenty thousand people, so you have every service you need.

Arriving by bike is fine but not relaxing. The old centre is partly closed to traffic, parking is awkward and the streets are steep and cobbled in places, with tight turns at low speed that can be tricky with luggage. Most riders leave the machine at a car park on the lower edge, and use the escalators that run up through the old Rocca Paolina fortress, which is an experience in itself, a tunnel through a medieval quarter buried under a papal fortress.

The city's story is full of conflict. It was a free commune, then fought neighbours for centuries, and in 1540 Pope Paul III built the Rocca Paolina to put it firmly under papal control, razing the houses of the Baglioni family who had ruled. The Fontana Maggiore in Piazza IV Novembre, finished in the thirteenth century, is the highlight, a marble fountain carved with scenes from the Bible, the months and local legends. Perugia is also known for chocolate, with an annual festival in October, and for Umbrian cooking: lentils, truffles, roast pork and strangozzi pasta.

For riding, the surrounding hills offer quiet roads with gentle curves, olive terraces and view after view. Fuel is easy to find on the ring roads around the city. Spring and early autumn are lovely, whereas midsummer is hot and winter mornings can be icy on shaded ground. Park low, walk up, and give the old streets an afternoon. The Tiber valley has a way of drawing you down again, and the ride out feels pleasant and unhurried.
t.pisa@43.7,10.4:
Pisa has one picture in the world's head, and it is of a tilted tower, but the town behind the picture rewards a rider who stays for lunch. It sits on the flat Arno plain a few kilometres from the sea, with about seventy-seven thousand people, many of them students at the university and the Scuola Normale. The mountain ridge of the Monte Pisano rises to the east, low and wooded, and gives the city an odd comfort, like a hand on the shoulder.

The tower itself began in 1173 and leaned almost at once, because the ground beneath is soft clay and sand. Construction stopped, started again after generations, and eventually reached its full height in the fourteenth century. The cathedral, baptistery and cemetery that share the grass of Piazza dei Miracoli are older and, honestly, just as lovely. Pisa was one of the great maritime republics, rivalling Genoa and Venice, and its wealth built all this before the harbour silted up and the sea retreated. Galileo was born here, and the story that he dropped weights from the tower is probably a legend.

For motorcycles, the city is slow, cyclists and one-way systems, and the centre has limited-traffic zones that catch visitors, so check before riding in. Park outside the walls and walk. The good riding lies elsewhere: the Monte Pisano roads toward Calci and the Certosa, a former Carthusian monastery, wind through olive terraces and chestnut woods. Along the coast, the San Rossore regional park shelters pine forest, marsh and wild boar, and a quiet road runs toward Marina di Pisa.

Fuel is available all around the ring road, and so is food. Try cecina, a thin baked chickpea pancake, or the Tuscan bread soups, and expect simple trattorie rather than grandeur. Summer is hot and crowded around the tower, so late afternoon is kinder, and winter has fog on the plain. After a day in the hills, Pisa is a good place to end: flat, easy, and with more going on than its famous leaning neighbour.
t.pikes peak and deckers photo pull off@39:
Fraser sits in a high, cold valley on the west side of the Continental Divide, a small mountain town of about twelve hundred people strung along US 40 beneath the ski slopes of Winter Park. Its main claim to fame is the weather: the town has long called itself the Icebox of the Nation, since its night-time temperatures can fall below freezing in any month of the year, and winter lows of minus thirty are not unheard of. At about 2,600 metres, the air is thin, and a warm layer is wise even in July.

The valley is a quiet, green trough of meadow and willow, with the Fraser River winding through it and the high peaks of the Indian Peaks and the Vasquez range rising on either side. Moose are frequent visitors to the wetlands, and elk wander the hillsides. The approach from the east is by Berthoud Pass, which climbs to 3,446 metres on US 40, a long, steep road of switchbacks with panoramic views of the Divide. The railway came by another route: the Moffat Tunnel, a six-mile bore completed in 1928, carries trains under the mountains, and the line is still busy with coal and freight.

Riding here is a pleasure in summer. US 40 over Berthoud is a fine pass road, if heavily travelled, and the ride down into the valley is a long, flowing descent with views over the range. Beyond Fraser, the road runs on to Granby and Grand Lake, the entrance to the western side of Rocky Mountain National Park, with a gentle ride beside the Colorado River. Thunderstorms build over the peaks in the afternoon, and snow can fall in any month at the pass, so check the weather.

Fuel and food are available in town, with a few cafés and a grocery store. The pass is generally open year-round but can close in storms. Mornings are cold and clear, with frost on the meadows, and the best light is early. Autumn, with aspens turning gold, is spectacular, though the nights are very cold. Take warm gloves and a spare layer, and allow time for photographs at the pass, where the wind often blows hard.
t.ceduna@-32.1,133.7:
Ceduna is the last proper town before the long emptiness. It sits on the western side of the Eyre Peninsula in South Australia, facing Murat Bay, and for most people it is the place where the Nullarbor Plain crossing begins: more than a thousand kilometres of the Eyre Highway to Norseman in Western Australia, with roadhouses spaced out like stepping stones. The town itself is small, with around two thousand people, but it has the sort of weathered, practical atmosphere of a place that serves travellers and fishermen.

Oysters are what Ceduna is known for. The bay and the nearby waters produce some of the best in the country, and they are sold fresh from sheds along the coast, usually at a very fair price. Eating a dozen on the jetty before heading into the desert is a sensible tradition.

The highway was named for Edward John Eyre, who in 1841 made an exhausting overland trek along this coast, helped by an Aboriginal man named Wylie. The road itself was only fully sealed in 1976, and before that, travellers had to cross hundreds of kilometres of dirt. Today it is a good, straight road, carrying road trains, caravans and the occasional cyclist. A rider should plan fuel carefully, because stations are far apart. After Ceduna, you will find roadhouses at Penong, Nundroo, Yalata, Nullarbor, Border Village and Eucla, with long gaps in between, and prices rise the further you go. Top up at every opportunity, and carry water.

Wind is the main enemy. It can blow from the side with great force, and on a bike the effect over hundreds of kilometres is tiring. Early mornings are calmer, but kangaroos and wombats are most active at dawn and dusk, so avoid riding at those times if you can. The stretch near the Head of Bight lets you walk to cliff edges and, from June to October, watch southern right whales that come into the Bight to calve.

The treeless plain itself, whose name comes from the Latin for no trees, gives an extraordinary sense of scale. The sky is huge, the road runs straight to the horizon, and you will feel very small.
t.penong@-31.9,133.0:
Windmills, of all things, are what Penong is known for. This tiny settlement on the Eyre Highway, a couple of hundred people on the western edge of South Australia's Eyre Peninsula, pumps its water from underground using wind, and old farm windmills stand in rows along the roadside and in a small museum at the edge of town. In a place where the horizon is a straight line and the sky fills most of the view, they make a strangely graceful sight.

Ceduna, about seventy kilometres to the east, is the last proper town, with supermarkets, motels and a pub, and the Nullarbor Plain proper starts a few hours further on. Penong is the last settlement of any size before the long empty run into Western Australia, and it has a store and a roadhouse-type stop, but supplies are limited and opening hours short. The sensible rule on the Eyre Highway is to fill up at every opportunity, carry water and not to assume a pump has fuel until you see it working.

About twenty kilometres south of Penong, down a gravel track, lies Cactus Beach, a wild surf spot at the edge of the Southern Ocean, famous among surfers for its powerful left and right breaks. The coast is a line of limestone cliffs and white dunes, with deep blue water, and the swell comes in from Antarctica with nothing to stop it. The area is also the edge of the Great Australian Bight, where southern right whales come to calve in winter, and the whale-watching at the Head of Bight, farther west, is world class.

The riding on this section is straight, flat and exposed. Wind is the main difficulty, since a crosswind from the south can push a loaded bike sideways, and a headwind can halve fuel economy. Road trains, long trucks with several trailers, use the highway, and their slipstream and the wind they push are strong, so give them room and expect a buffeting when they pass. Dawn and dusk bring kangaroos, wombats and emus onto the road, and hitting one at speed is dangerous, so slow down in the low light.

Summer days are hot and dry, and winter nights are cold, so carry layers, plenty of water and a basic repair kit. The silence and space are the reward.
t.pula@44.9,13.8:
Pula's Roman amphitheatre is the sixth largest in the world, and it stands right by the harbour, its limestone arches facing the sea. The pin lands at the southern tip of Istria, in the city, which has about sixty thousand people, a working shipyard and a long history as a naval base. The Austro-Hungarian navy made it a major port in the nineteenth century, and the cranes of the shipyards still dominate the bay.

From here, the road leads north into the hills. The Istrian interior is a patchwork of vineyards, olive groves and truffle woods, with hill towns like Motovun, Grožnjan and Buzet standing on top of ridges. The roads are narrow and twisty, with bends, short climbs and wide views, and the surface is mostly good. Summer brings heat and crowds on the coast, and the best time is spring or autumn, when the countryside is green or golden. Wind, the bura, can blow hard on the coast in winter and affect riders on exposed roads.

Pula has more to offer than the arena. The Arch of the Sergii, a Roman triumphal arch, and the Temple of Augustus are in the old centre, and James Joyce taught English here for a few months in 1904 and 1905. The city has a good fish market, and the coast has rocky bays for swimming. The Brijuni islands, a national park, are a short boat ride away.

Fuel and food are easy in Pula, with stations on the main roads and many restaurants, and it is wise to fill up before leaving for the hills, where stations are scarce. Istrian food is excellent, including fresh fish, fuži pasta with truffles, and wines like Malvazija and Teran.

Look at the arena before you go. At dawn, with the first light on the stone, it is quiet and almost empty.
t.castelli@41.8,12.3:
Fiumicino is a town most people know only from its airport, but the pin lands in the suburbs near the mouth of the Tiber, between the airport and the sea, at Isola Sacra. This low, flat island between two arms of the river is rich in history. It was the site of Portus, the harbour that the emperors Claudius and Trajan built to supply Rome, and the ruins of warehouses, docks and a hexagonal basin can still be seen. Ostia Antica, the old port town, is only a short ride away.

For a ride that began in the Castelli Romani, the hills south-east of Rome, this is a westward finish, down to the coast. The roads are flat, straight and often busy, with traffic lights and roundabouts, and the surface is mixed, with patches and potholes. The Via del Mare and the Via Ostiense connect Rome to the coast, and they are heavily used by Romans going to the beach, especially at weekends, so weekdays and early mornings are best. Pine woods and reed beds line parts of the coast, and the air smells of salt and resin.

The coast has a strange history. Ostia Antica was a major port for centuries and is now one of the best-preserved Roman towns, with a theatre, shops and mosaics that are far less crowded than Pompeii. Lido di Ostia, the modern seaside town, was developed in the 1920s and is where many Romans spend summer weekends. In winter, the beach is quiet, and the seafront restaurants serve fresh fish and fried calamari.

Fuel is plentiful in Fiumicino and Ostia, with large stations on the main roads. The area has many fish restaurants, especially around the old fishing port of Fiumicino, where the catch is landed each morning, and a plate of spaghetti with clams is the typical meal. Bars along the beach serve coffee and pastries.

Walk out to the sea wall if you have time. The mouth of the Tiber is muddy and plain, but there is something satisfying about seeing where the river that gave Rome its life reaches the sea.
t.parma@44.8,10.3:
Parma sits on the Via Emilia, the straight Roman road that crosses the plain from Rimini to Piacenza, and today it is known above all for what is eaten there. Parmigiano-Reggiano and Prosciutto di Parma both come from this corner of Emilia, and a visit is not complete without a slice of each, accompanied by a glass of local sparkling red such as Lambrusco, which is sold everywhere. The pasta here is stuffed with spinach and ricotta, and the fried bread called torta fritta arrives with plates of cured meat.

The old city is among the most elegant in northern Italy, with a Romanesque cathedral that has a famous dome painted by Correggio, and next to it the octagonal pink marble baptistery, a masterpiece designed by Benedetto Antelami in the late twelfth century. The great Teatro Regio is a temple of opera, and the town was the home of Giuseppe Verdi, who was born in a village nearby. The Pilotta, a huge palace complex, holds museums and a remarkable wooden theatre.

For a rider, the important thing is the limited traffic zone. Most of the historic centre is closed to non-resident vehicles, and cameras issue fines automatically, so park outside the ring of avenues and walk in. Several car parks and garages around the edge are fine for a motorcycle. Fuel is easy to find on the ring road and the roads out of town.

The Mille Miglia, the famous open road race that ran between Brescia and Rome from 1927 to 1957, passed through Parma, and each May the modern historic re-enactment brings long lines of classic cars through the same streets. If your trip coincides, the atmosphere in town is wonderful. The surrounding country is flat, but the foothills of the Apennines south of the town offer better riding.

Finishing in Parma means one thing above all: a proper dinner, and I would not skimp on it. Give yourself a couple of hours to walk through the old streets as the evening light warms the stone.
t.tuscany val d orcia overnight@41.5,12.6:
Anzio and Nettuno run together along the Lazio shore, about fifty kilometres south of Rome, and between them they have around ninety thousand inhabitants, which means petrol stations are never an issue. The fuel gate here is on the edge of Anzio, a working port and holiday town that has been busy since Roman times. Nero was born here, and the remains of his seaside villa, a sprawling palace on the cliffs, can still be seen at the western end of town.

Anzio is also a ferry port, with ships and hydrofoils to the islands of Ponza and Ventotene, which lie some forty miles out to sea, and these are well worth a visit if you have a spare weekend. The harbour is lively, with fish restaurants lining the quay and fishing boats unloading the day's catch. Next door in Nettuno, a squat fortress built in the sixteenth century, the Forte Sangallo, stands on the waterfront, and the old walled town behind it has narrow lanes and a pleasant piazza.

The name Anzio is also remembered for the Second World War landings of January 1944, and the beaches here were the scene of heavy fighting. There is a war cemetery and a museum, and it adds a sobering layer to a lively holiday town.

For a rider, the start of the Val d'Orcia overnight is a long way north. The ride begins on flat coastal roads and the straight, fast roads through the Pontine plain, and the best of the corners comes much later, among the hills of southern Tuscany. Start early to beat the summer heat and the holiday traffic coming the other way.

Take on a full tank here, grab a coffee and a pastry at one of the bars on the front, and make a start. The sea air at this hour is cool, and the smell of salt, pine resin and fried dough is typical of the Italian coast.
t.tuscany val d orcia overnight@42.3,13.6:
L'Aquila is the capital of the Abruzzo region, a mountain city at about 700 metres, ringed by the high peaks of the Apennines, and it carries a heavy history. In April 2009 a major earthquake struck the city, killing more than three hundred people and damaging much of the medieval centre. Reconstruction has been slow, but large parts of the old town have now reopened, with scaffolding giving way to restored churches and palaces, and the place has a quiet, resilient feel.

The villages nearby, Villa Sant'Angelo and San Demetrio ne' Vestini, lie in the Aterno valley, south-east of the city, and are small, stone-built and calm. L'Aquila itself has fuel, supermarkets and plenty of cafes and trattorias, so seventeen kilometres is a short hop from this food stop. The city's Fontana delle 99 Cannelle, a medieval fountain with ninety-nine spouts, is one of the old sights that survived, and the basilica of Santa Maria di Collemaggio is a beautiful piece of pink and white Romanesque stone where a pope was crowned in the thirteenth century.

The regional speciality is the arrosticino, a small skewer of lamb grilled over charcoal, which is cheap, delicious and served by the dozen. It goes well with local red wine and a bowl of pasta with a rich sauce. Saffron from the Navelli plain and pecorino cheese are also good, and the people tend to be generous with portions.

For the ride, the roads around L'Aquila are quiet and often excellent, rising into the mountains of the Gran Sasso, with wide views, fast bends and clean air. Winter closes the highest roads, and even in summer the temperature drops sharply at altitude. Wolves and even bears live in the mountains of Abruzzo, though you are very unlikely to see them from the road.

This is a fitting end to a long ride, a place to sit down with a plate of lamb and a glass of wine, and watch the sun go down over the mountains.
t.abruzzo@42.1,12.7:
Palombara Sabina rises on a rocky spur at the foot of the Monti Lucretili, and the pin lands in the plain below, near Cretone and Castel Chiodato, about thirty kilometres north-east of Rome. The Sabine hills start here, a landscape of olive groves, oak woods and small limestone ridges, with Monte Gennaro, at 1,271 metres, the highest peak of the range, rising above the villages. The Romans knew this area as Sabina, and it was the home of the Sabine people.

The ride that finishes here has crossed the Abruzzo and the Gran Sasso, so the Sabine foothills are the first sign of Rome's hinterland. The roads here are narrow and quiet, with bends along ridges and across small valleys, and the surface is generally good, though patchy near the villages. Evening light on the olive groves is the best, and the air is cool and fragrant. Traffic increases near the larger roads towards Rome, especially on weekday evenings.

Palombara has a medieval castle, the Savelli castle, which stands over the old town, and the streets below are narrow and full of small churches. Sabina oil is among the oldest in Italy, with a long history of production, and the local farms often sell it directly. The Monti Lucretili park, a protected area of woodland and pasture, has walking routes and a rich wildlife, including wolves and wild boar, though you are unlikely to see them.

Fuel and food are easy at Palombara Sabina, a town of just over six thousand people, with stations, shops and trattorias, and the surrounding villages have simple restaurants. Local dishes include pasta with wild boar sauce, grilled lamb and, in season, mushrooms and truffles. The nearest railway station is at Guidonia or Monterotondo, and the ride back to Rome is short.

If you have time, take the minor road towards Monte Gennaro. The views from the foothills over the Roman campagna, with the city on the horizon, are a satisfying end to a long journey.
t.hardanger fjord and waterfalls@60.0,11.3:
Sørumsand is a modest town on the plain east of Oslo, in the old Romerike district, and the point here is a practical one: a place to fill the tank and gather yourself before the real riding begins. The town has about three and a half thousand people, a supermarket, a few cafes and a station, and it sits beside the lower Glomma river system in flat farmland dotted with red barns and birch woods. It is not a destination, and it does not pretend to be one, but it does have one small treasure, the narrow-gauge railway.

That railway, the Urskog-Hølandsbanen, ran north-east from Sørumsand into the Urskog forests and is now a heritage line kept running by volunteers, with old steam locomotives and carriages on a track only 750 millimetres wide. On summer weekends you can ride it, and if you are early for a meeting with friends or have an hour to spare, it is a charming diversion. The line was built to haul timber from the forests of Urskog, which gives a clue to what the land around here was used for for centuries: forestry, farming and the floating of logs down the Glomma to the sawmills.

For a rider the surrounding roads are quiet, rolling and agricultural, with long straights between the fields and a few mild bends where the road dips to cross a stream. The east side of Oslo is not the dramatic part of Norway, and the Hardanger fjord in the ride's title is hundreds of kilometres west, but the gentle start does make an unhurried warm-up. Traffic builds around commuter hours near Lillestrøm, so plan to leave early or after nine.

Fuel is straightforward in town, and prices in Norway are high, so it is worth filling the tank here rather than in the mountains, where the stations are fewer and often dearer. Coffee is easy to find and the bakery goods are good. Take a moment to look at the weather, because the forecast for the passes to the west decides your day.
t.oslo norway scenic roads@60.3,12.5:
This stretch of country belongs to Finnskogen, the Finn forest, a broad belt of spruce and pine along the Swedish border that was settled in the seventeenth century by Finnish farmers who practised slash-and-burn agriculture. They arrived by invitation from the Swedish crown, who wanted the empty forests used, and the Norwegian side filled up with families who spoke Finnish for generations. Their culture left traces in place names, in log cabins and in a certain stubborn attitude toward the woods, and there is a modest Finnskogen trail for walkers who want to follow it.

The terrain is rolling and quiet, not mountainous, with low ridges, black tarns, bogs and a thousand small lakes, any of which can serve as a place to swim on a warm afternoon. The nearest towns are small, Kirkenær at some thirty kilometres to the west and Torsby across the Swedish line, and between them the roads are narrow, lightly used and bordered by tall trees. For a rider this means a ride of gentle curves and long, shaded straights, with the sun flickering through the trunks and the surface sometimes patchy after winter frost. Elk are the main hazard, particularly at dawn and dusk, and a collision with one is serious.

The forest is also one of the few areas in Norway where wolves have settled, in a zone shared across the border with Sweden. You will almost certainly not see one, but it adds a thrill to a picnic by a lake. Mosquitoes in June and July can be savage, so bring repellent if you plan to stop by the water.

Plan your fuel in advance. The better choice is Kongsvinger, a town of more than eleven thousand to the south, since services on the forest roads are sparse and many small stations close early or on Sundays. Pack a drink and something to eat as well. After a day in the forest, a swim in a clear lake with the smell of resin in the air is a good way to end the ride, and the cold water wakes you up in a way nothing else does.
t.rondane scenic route@60.3,12.3:
Between the Glomma river and the long wooded ridges of the Vinger district, a few kilometres from Kongsvinger, this is farming country where fields of barley and potatoes break up the forest and the farmhouses are painted red or white with dark roofs. The area is close to the Swedish border, and the history of the place is the history of that frontier: the fortress at Kongsvinger, begun in the 1680s under the Danish-Norwegian king, was built to guard the invasion route from Sweden, and it still stands on its hill above the town with views along the river.

The riding around here is relaxed. The roads follow the valley and the ridges, offering easy bends, a few climbs and descents, and the sort of Norwegian rural scenery that does not shout but is very restful. The surface is usually good and speed limits are strictly enforced, with cameras and police who know what they are doing, so keep to the limit. In late summer there are tractors and timber lorries to watch for, and in autumn the birch leaves turn gold and cover the road in places, which reduces grip.

As a food stop, the choice is the town of Kongsvinger, with some eleven thousand people and a good range of cafes, bakeries and grills. In the smaller villages you may find a petrol station with a grill counter and a coffee machine, which is often the best place for a hot dog and a long chat. Norwegian roadside food can be expensive, so many riders bring a thermos and a packed lunch and stop in one of the lay-bys that look out over fields.

The fortress deserves an hour if you have it, and the museum inside tells the story of the Swedish wars and the garrison that lived here. The hill is a good place to stretch and look out over the broad valley, especially in the late afternoon when the light turns golden. Fuel is easy in Kongsvinger.
t.atlantic road@60.1,11.1:
Kløfta is a small town on the Romerike plain north-east of Oslo, and the pin lands near Ask, a village in Gjerdrum, three kilometres to the south-west. The plain is the largest area of farmland in eastern Norway, a gently rolling landscape of grain fields, spruce woods and red wooden barns, with the E6 motorway and the main railway line running through it. Oslo's airport at Gardermoen is some thirteen kilometres to the north.

The ride's name speaks of the Atlantic Road, the famous bridge road on the west coast, but this is far away, and the finish here is a calm, rural one. The roads are straight and quiet, with long, gentle bends, and a surface that is generally good. Traffic builds near the E6 and the airport, but the lanes between the farms are peaceful. In summer, the fields are green and gold, and in winter, the snow is flat and deep. Light in the evening in early summer is long and soft.

The landscape has a geological story. The ground here is made of marine clay, laid down when the sea covered the plain after the last ice age, and when the land rose, the clay was left behind. Some of it is quick clay, which can turn to liquid when disturbed, and in December 2020 a large landslide at Ask destroyed homes and took lives. The event was a national tragedy, and it is remembered with respect locally. The area has made safety a priority since.
