Fuel and food are available in Kløfta, which has stations, supermarkets and small restaurants, and larger shopping areas are close by at Jessheim. Local bakeries offer fresh bread, and farm shops sell potatoes, strawberries and honey in season. The train to Oslo takes about thirty minutes.

Take a quiet moment at the edge of a field. The broad horizon and the soft light make a calm end to a ride.
t.aurlandsfjellet snow road@60.6,11.5:
Forget the snow road in the ride's name for a moment, because the ground here is Hedmarken, the broad lowland east of Lake Mjøsa that Norwegians think of as their bread basket. Fields of barley, oats and potatoes stretch between low forested ridges, with big white farmhouses and red barns, and the Mjøsa itself, Norway's largest lake, lies a short way to the west. It is a landscape that looks as though someone ironed it, and after the fjords and mountains it feels almost Danish.

A food stop in this part of the country usually means a village shop with a counter or a petrol station grill, and both are better than they sound. Norwegians take their coffee seriously, and waffles with jam and soured cream are served almost everywhere. The nearest real towns are Stange and, to the north-east, Våler in the Solør forests, so if you need a proper meal or a shop, plan around them rather than hoping for something on the lane you are riding.

The riding is calm and rhythmic. Roads follow the field edges and cross low ridges through spruce and pine, so you get a mix of open views and green tunnels, with long straights and occasional bends where a stream crosses. Surfaces are generally good, but the farmland produces mud on the road at harvest time and tractors that move at their own pace. Speed cameras and police checks are common on the main roads, and fines in Norway are severe, so keep to the limit.

This region also has a long history. Hedmark's farms were the economic base of the area for a thousand years, and old churches, some of them medieval stone buildings, stand among the fields. The Viking-age burial mounds dotted through the district are signposted. Late summer, when the grain is gold and the days are still long, is the best time to ride here, and the evening light on the fields is exceptionally good.
t.hardanger fjord@60.0,11.3:
Sørumsand is the home of a small railway that has nothing to do with fjords. The narrow-gauge line Urskog-Hølandsbanen, the only preserved narrow-gauge railway in Norway, runs steam and diesel trains from here on summer Sundays, and the museum in the old station shows the carriages and engines. The pin lands a few kilometres away, near Auli, in the Romerike district east of Oslo, with the town of Fetsund on the Glomma river ten kilometres to the south-west.

The ride's name speaks of the Hardanger Fjord, far to the west, but the day ends here, in a very different landscape: flat farmland, pine woods and the wide, slow Glomma, Norway's longest river. The roads are straight and quiet, with gentle bends along the river, and a surface that is generally good. Traffic is light, except near Lillestrøm and the main roads towards Oslo. In summer, the fields are full of grain and the air smells of cut hay, and in autumn, the birch woods turn gold.

The river has a long working history. For centuries, timber from the forests of the interior was floated down the Glomma to the sawmills, and at Fetsund, the Lenser, a series of log-sorting booms, stayed in use until 1985 and is now a museum, with a footbridge over the water. To the west, Øyeren, a large lake at the end of the river, has a vast inland delta, a protected wetland that is one of the most important places for migrating birds in northern Europe.

Fuel and food are easy enough, with stations and shops in Sørumsand and a wider choice in Lillestrøm, and small cafes open in summer. Norwegian bakeries sell fresh bread, and farm shops offer strawberries and potatoes. The train to Oslo runs from Lillestrøm in about fifteen minutes.

Walk onto the footbridge at Fetsund if you can. Looking down at the old booms, you can almost hear the logs.
t.barron island@-12.2,132.4:
I will be honest about this one: I cannot place a spot called Barron Island with any confidence, and the coordinates fall in a remote stretch of the Top End of the Northern Territory, in the tidal floodplains between Darwin and Kakadu. It is country that is more water than land for half the year, a mosaic of mangroves, mudflats, paperbark swamps and open grassy plains cut by creeks that rise and fall with the monsoon.

The landscape here is dominated by two seasons. From about November to April the wet season brings towering thunderstorms and flooded plains, with roads closed by water and the humidity close to unbearable. From May to October the dry season arrives, the floodwaters retreat, and the wetlands concentrate vast numbers of birds, including magpie geese, jabirus and egrets, in the shrinking billabongs. Crocodiles, both freshwater and the much bigger saltwater species, live in the rivers and are not to be underestimated. Never walk near the water's edge in the Top End, and take any warning sign seriously.

The riding in the region is largely along two main routes. The Arnhem Highway runs east from Darwin to the entrance of Kakadu National Park, and from there the Kakadu Highway runs south past the visitor centre at Jabiru, the wetlands of Yellow Water and the rock art sites at Ubirr and Nourlangie. Both roads are well-surfaced and straight, so the main challenges are heat, road trains and the constant risk of wildlife on the bitumen, especially buffalo, wallabies and feral pigs at dusk. Burning in the late dry season creates smoke haze, and the Aboriginal custodians of the land have managed the country with fire for tens of thousands of years, giving the landscape its mosaic character.

Kakadu is jointly managed by the traditional owners and the national parks service, and it is listed for both its natural and cultural values. Fuel and food in the region are available at Jabiru, Cooinda and a few roadhouses along the highway, but they are far apart, so top the tank before entering the park and carry plenty of water. Park entry requires a pass, which can be bought at the gate or online.

Check locally for current road conditions and closures, particularly in the wet.
t.trollstigen and@60.1,10.8:
The name suggests a mountain pass, but the coordinates drop you in Romerike, the flat farming plain north-east of Oslo, between Åneby, Rotnes and Kløfta. It is gentle country of clay fields, small woods and low ridges, where Norwegians who work in the capital have settled in neat suburbs and villages.

Rotnes is the main centre of Nittedal, a municipality with a mix of old farms and newer housing, and it is where you will find supermarkets and fuel. Åneby is a smaller community nearby, and Kløfta to the north, with around six thousand people, sits on the main railway line and close to the E6. Gardermoen, Oslo's main airport, is not far beyond, so the sky is full of arriving aircraft. To the west the land rises into the forested hills of Nordmarka, which is one of the capital's great recreation areas, with lakes, trails and cabins.

The landscape tells an old agricultural story. The marine clay left by the retreating ice age sea made this some of the best farmland in the country, and Romerike has long been known as the granary of Norway, with big fields of grain and potatoes. In late summer the plain turns gold, and you can see the red barns across fields from the road. Old churches stand in the villages, and the area has a long history of settlement.

The riding is straightforward, with good surfaces, long straights, and the odd roundabout. Speed limits are enforced by cameras and there is heavy commuter traffic at rush hour on the main routes, so try to avoid those times. If you want something more attractive, head onto the minor roads towards the forest edge, where bends and gentle climbs make a pleasant change. Watch for tractors, joggers and elk, which do wander across roads at dawn and dusk.

Fuel is easy at Rotnes and Kløfta, and the area is a good spot to stock up before continuing north or west. Norwegian prices are high, so a supermarket sandwich and a thermos coffee are the sensible choice.

Best from late spring to early autumn, when the days are long. This is not the dramatic Norway of the postcards, but it is a calm, agricultural pause in the journey.
t.lysefjord and suleskar scenic road@60.1,:
This is Krokskogen, the high, forested plateau north-west of Oslo, with Tyrifjorden glittering far below the edge of it. The name on the stop is a long way off, but the road here is a real scenic one in its own right. It runs across rolling moraine ground thick with spruce and pine, past dark tarns and little cabins, then drops suddenly toward Sundvollen and the fjord. The nearest towns are Hønefoss, about sixteen kilometres north-west, and Skui, a smaller place nearer the city.

Locals will tell you that the finest moment on this plateau is the view from the lookout at Kongens utsikt, the King's View, where the whole broad blue sweep of Tyrifjorden opens out with its islands and farmland. Below it lies the steep Krokkleiva, a short, tight, well-known climb that Norwegian cyclists treat as a rite of passage and motorcyclists enjoy for its hairpins and gradient. It is not a long road, but it is a satisfying one, with enough bends to make you pay attention and a view to remember at the bottom.

Krokskogen itself is one of Oslo's great recreation forests. Families come here to pick blueberries and chanterelles in late summer, and to ski the prepared tracks in winter, and the roads hum with weekend traffic on sunny Saturdays. For a quieter ride, go early on a weekday or in the golden evening light. After rain the forest smells of wet moss and resin, and fog collects in the hollows, which can be beautiful and treacherous.

Hønefoss or the stations around Sandvika, just east, are your safest bets. If you want food, the lookout at Kongens utsikt and the nearby hotels at Sundvollen have a reputation for a decent coffee and a long-view lunch, and there are forest car parks where a thermos and a sandwich serve just as well. The road is narrow in places, with cyclists and walkers who do not expect you, so keep your speed honest.
t.lysefjord and suleskar photo pull off@60:
North of the Oslo basin the land lifts into Hadeland, an open, farmed ridge country where Nordmarka's forests give way to fields, red barns and long views down to blue lakes. This stop is in the middle of it, with Grua and Jevnaker the closest villages and Hønefoss to the south-west as the real town for supplies. The name on the label belongs to a fjord in another part of the country, so take this as an honest piece of Norwegian countryside instead: a pull-off where you can get off the bike, look out over the farmland and let your ears recover.

Hadeland has an old identity as a place that makes things. The Hadeland glassworks, in the neighbouring parish, has been blowing glass since the middle of the eighteenth century and is still going, with a shop and demonstrations that make a good rainy-day excuse for a stop. The farmland itself is among the best in the east of the country, which is why you pass so many big, well-kept farmsteads with their outbuildings arranged around the yard. In early summer the fields are sharp green, in autumn they go gold, and in the long light of late evening the ridges throw soft shadows that are lovely to ride through.

The road is typical of inland south-east Norway: smooth surface, gentle gradients, medium-speed curves, and a surprising number of tractors in season. Where it rises over the ridges there are open views toward the Randsfjorden lake and the dark hills to the north, and you should keep an eye out for elk, especially around dusk and dawn. Hitting one at speed on a motorcycle is a serious matter, and signs along these roads are not decorative.

Fuel is available in Jevnaker, about twelve kilometres away, and in Hønefoss, farther. Neither is far, but outside the towns the petrol stations can be unstaffed card-only pumps, so carry a card that works on the Norwegian system. Coffee and a cinnamon bun at one of the village bakeries is the thing to look for.
t.r ros mining town cultural landscapes an:
Røros is a copper town built on cold and patience. It sits at the high end of the Gauldal valley, near the Swedish border, in a bleak, open plateau where winters are among the hardest in southern Norway, and the old wooden houses crowd together as if sharing warmth. UNESCO listed it in 1980, and it is one of the few places where you can see a mining town as it grew rather than as a museum.

The mine was founded in 1644 and operated for more than three hundred years, closing in 1977. The copper company ran everything, from the smelter to the farms that fed the workers, and the town's dark timber houses with their turf roofs, and the great stone church that dates from 1784, reflect that single-minded enterprise. Piles of slag still stand on the edge of town, and the smelter works, now a museum, has an impressive old hall. The surrounding landscape, called the Circumference, was reserved by royal decree for the company's use, with forests cut for charcoal and wood.

The local people include southern Sami reindeer herders, whose culture is older than the mine, and you can learn about them in the town. The winter market, the Rørosmartnan, takes place in February and attracts huge crowds despite the temperatures. In summer the town is quieter and the smell of woodsmoke and tar fills the lanes.

The riding in the area is open and gentle, with high plateau roads, birch scrub, bogs and long views, and traffic is light outside summer. Roads can be icy as early as September and as late as May, and there can be elk and reindeer on the road, particularly at dusk. The surface is generally good, and the bends are long and easy. Cross-country skiing trails begin right outside town in winter.

Røros has around three and a half thousand people, so fuel, groceries and cafes are all available, and the place is used to travellers. The nearest larger towns are a long way off, so fill up here before heading into the mountains or towards the Femundsmarka wilderness.

Walk the main street and look for the cafe that serves reindeer stew. Then look up; the stars here are very good when it is clear.
t.dolores@37.5,-108.5:
Dolores sits on the river of the same name, in a green, tree-lined valley on the western edge of the Colorado Rockies, and for most riders it marks the end of a long and thrilling run. The San Juan Skyway, a loop that links Ouray, Silverton, Telluride and Durango, passes over some of the highest and most dramatic roads in the country, and Dolores is where the mountains finally let go and the high desert begins. The name is Spanish for sorrows, and comes from a Spanish expedition that camped here in 1776, led by two Franciscan friars searching for a route to California, who named the river for Our Lady of Sorrows.

The town is small but has a bit of history. In the early twentieth century it was a station on the Rio Grande Southern railroad, a narrow-gauge line that wound its way through the mountains to the mining towns, and the line's strange, motorised railcars, known as Galloping Geese, were a lifeline for remote communities. One of these curious vehicles is preserved in a small park in town. A few kilometres north, the river was dammed in the 1980s to make McPhee Reservoir, and there is a museum at the Anasazi Heritage Center, which explains the Ancestral Puebloan people who once farmed this country.

The riding that leads here is superb. Over Lizard Head Pass, at more than ten thousand feet, the road runs through high meadows of wildflowers and under a distinctive spire of volcanic rock, then drops steadily through aspen and spruce toward the desert. The curves are long and open, the surface is good and the views are enormous. In September the aspens turn gold, and the whole valley glows. Snow can fall on the pass any month, so watch the forecast.

Dolores has fuel, a few cafes and a brewery or two, and the larger town of Cortez, about sixteen kilometres away, offers more services and is the gateway to Mesa Verde, where the cliff dwellings of the Ancestral Puebloans are worth a day. Take water, because the air is dry and the sun is strong. In the evening, with the river murmuring and the cottonwoods whispering, Dolores is a gentle place to end a ride.
t.twin lakes@39.1,-106.4:
Twin Lakes sits in a basin under the highest mountain in Colorado, and it is one of the places where the Rockies feel larger than life. The two lakes, glacial in origin, lie side by side at about 9,200 feet, fed by streams from the surrounding peaks, and the great pale bulk of Mount Elbert, at 14,433 feet the highest point in the whole Rocky Mountain range, rises behind them. The village is tiny, with a few dozen residents, and the road that runs past it is the approach to Independence Pass, one of the great mountain crossings in the American West. Leadville is the nearest town, twenty kilometres away, and Aspen is on the far side of the pass.

The historic part of the village is a cluster of old log buildings, including Interlaken, a nineteenth-century resort on the south shore of the lower lake, which has been partly restored and can be visited on foot. Visitors came here in the 1880s by stagecoach to fish, picnic and dance, and the old stables, icehouse and hotel still stand among the aspens. A mile or two up the valley the road narrows and begins to climb.

Independence Pass, at 12,095 feet, is a beautiful and demanding road, and it is closed in winter, usually from November until late May. The ascent from Twin Lakes is a steep, winding climb with tight hairpins and big views, and the top is alpine tundra, bare and windy, with wildflowers in July and snow in any month. The road on the far side descends in a long series of curves toward Aspen. It is narrow, with limited barriers and no room for error. Large vehicles are discouraged, and weather can turn quickly, so be off the summit before the afternoon storms.

Fuel is in Leadville and Buena Vista, and not reliably in the village, so fill up before you come. The lakes are cold and clear, with trout fishing in the summer and ice in the winter. Autumn here is magnificent, with aspens glowing gold on the slopes and the first snow on the high peaks. A hot drink from the little store, a plate of eggs, and a walk by the water are the best way to prepare for the pass.
t.minturn@39.6,-106.4:
Minturn was a railroad town and a rough one, built in the 1880s where the Denver and Rio Grande Railroad climbed the Eagle River valley toward Tennessee Pass, and it kept the character of a working place long after the trains stopped. The main street is a short row of old brick and timber buildings, a few bars and restaurants, and a farmers' market in summer. It lies in a narrow valley between steep slopes, with the Eagle River running through, and only a few miles from the resort of Vail, which was built in the 1960s on what had been sheep pastures. People in Minturn like to say that they are the real place, and they have a point.

The Top of the Rockies Scenic Byway runs south from here, up US 24 and over Tennessee Pass at 10,424 feet, then down to Leadville, the highest incorporated city in the United States. On the way you pass Red Cliff, with its high steel bridge, and the site of Camp Hale, where the Tenth Mountain Division trained for winter war in the Second World War, and where many of the soldiers who returned went on to found ski resorts across the West. The valley is quiet, with big meadows, aspen groves and views of the Sawatch Range, whose peaks include some of the highest in the state.

The riding is smooth and enjoyable, with long, broad curves, steady climbs and little traffic compared with the Interstate. The road is well surfaced and the grades moderate, though the altitude makes engines feel a little flat and riders a little breathless. Weather can change rapidly, with afternoon storms bringing cold rain, hail and lightning, and snow can arrive early in autumn and linger into late spring. Check pass conditions in the cold months.

Minturn is small, with about a thousand residents, but it has fuel and food, and Vail, eight miles away, has everything else. Shops there are pricey, so Minturn is the better place for a cheap breakfast. The best time to ride is June to September, with aspen colour in late September.
t.lake city colorado@38.0,-107.3:
Lake City is the sort of village that never quite got the memo about the twenty-first century. Tucked into a high valley of the San Juan Mountains at around 8,600 feet, it has about 370 residents, a short main street of wooden false fronts, a handful of cafes and a county courthouse that serves one of the emptiest counties in Colorado. It was a silver-mining town in the 1870s, and the mines lasted just long enough to leave behind a pretty centre and a ring of ghost towns. The nearest bigger place is Gunnison, and the closest for fuel is in the village itself, so check your tank before heading into the backcountry.

The Alpine Loop starts from here and joins Lake City with Silverton and Ouray over two high passes, Engineer Pass at about 12,800 feet and Cinnamon Pass at about 12,600. This is not a paved road, it is a rocky, steep, sometimes narrow mountain track, best suited to adventure bikes and 4x4 vehicles, and not a place for road bikes or heavy tourers. Snow blocks the passes from October to June, and even in summer, thunderstorms, mud and rockfall can slow progress. Check conditions before starting.

The land around is a lesson in geology and history. Lake San Cristobal, just south of town, was formed about seven hundred years ago when the Slumgullion Earthflow, a huge landslide, dammed Lake Fork of the Gunnison River, and the scar of that slide is still visible on the hillside, creeping slowly downhill. The area also has a grim footnote: in the winter of 1873–74, a prospector named Alferd Packer led a party into the mountains here and returned alone, admitting to cannibalism, and the story is retold with relish by local guides.

Beyond the passes lie old mining sites, among them the ghost town of Capitol City, and wide meadows with columbines, Indian paintbrush and lupines in July. Aspens in late September turn the slopes gold. Bring a jacket, carry water, and expect little phone signal. The best season is late June to mid September, and the high roads are often empty on weekday mornings.
t.cortez colorado@37.3,-108.6:
Cortez lies in the far south-west corner of Colorado, on a high, dry plateau between the La Plata Mountains and the red rock country of Utah, and it is the gateway to some of the most important archaeological landscape in North America. Mesa Verde National Park, about ten miles east, preserves cliff dwellings built into rock alcoves by Ancestral Puebloan people in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, with stone towers, kivas and rooms stacked in sandstone overhangs. The people who lived there left around 1300, and their descendants today include the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico and Arizona.

The town takes its name from the Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés, though he never came anywhere near. It is a practical, friendly place, with about nine thousand people, a main street with a few murals and an Anasazi Heritage Center nearby, where displays and a partly excavated pueblo explain the story. Ute Mountain, a long sleeping-giant outline to the south-west, belongs to the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, and the tribal park there protects further cliff dwellings, reached on guided tours.

The Trail of the Ancients, the scenic byway that links Cortez with Blanding in Utah, runs west across the high desert, past Hovenweep National Monument, where square stone towers stand on the rim of small canyons. The road is quiet and smooth, with gentle undulations, and the landscape opens into mesas, washes and distant buttes. Beyond Blanding, the byway continues past the Valley of the Gods and Bears Ears. Weather can be extreme, with fierce summer heat and sudden cold snaps, and afternoon storms can pour rain onto dry washes, which flash flood. Keep an eye on the sky.

The Four Corners, the only spot in the United States where four states meet, lies about forty miles to the south-west, and many riders add the photo stop. Cortez has fuel, supermarkets and good Mexican and southwestern food, and its position at nearly 6,200 feet means that nights are cool even in summer. Services on the byway are sparse, so fill the tank and carry water. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.mesa verde@37.2,-108.5:
The cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde sit in the folds of a high green tableland south of Cortez, and the first thing that surprises you is how far you still have to ride after the entrance gate. The park road climbs onto the mesa top and then keeps going for a good while, twisting along the canyon rims at a speed limit that will feel slow and turns out to be right, because the edges are close and the deer are careless. Treat it as a gentle, scenic hour rather than a spirited one.

The people who built here were Ancestral Puebloans, farmers who lived on these mesas for centuries and who moved their homes into the sandstone alcoves in the 1200s. By around 1300 they had left for good, heading south toward the Rio Grande and Arizona. Cliff Palace, the largest of the dwellings, was found by local ranchers in 1888, and the area became a national park in 1906. Several of the big sites are visited on ranger-led tours that need a ticket, so it is worth checking ahead rather than arriving at the gate on a whim. The mesa-top villages and pit houses, which you can walk to on short paths, tell the older half of the story and are often quieter.

For a rider the practical points are simple. Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms off the La Plata Mountains, and the mesa top can be cooler than the valley by a good margin, so a liner earns its place on the bike. Late May and September to early October give the best mix of light and quiet.

What stays with you is the silence. Piñon and juniper smell sharp after rain, the canyons fall away in layers of tan and rust, and you realise that this was a crowded, ordinary neighbourhood once. Fire has also shaped the mesa in recent decades, leaving stands of pale dead trunks among new growth, which gives the ride an odd, open, windswept look. Give it half a day if you can, and take a jacket you do not need.
t.hovenweep@37.4,-109.1:
Hovenweep is the kind of place you reach by deciding to, because nothing else lies along the way. The monument sits on the Utah and Colorado line out on a quiet, dry plateau, and the nearest settlement of any size on the Colorado side is Towaoc, thirty-odd kilometres off. The road in rolls over sage flats and slickrock edges with almost no traffic, and in the late afternoon you can ride for a long time without seeing another vehicle. That emptiness is half the charm and also the warning: fill up before you leave Cortez or Blanding, carry water, and assume your phone will have given up.

The towers are what you come for. Ancestral Puebloans built clusters of square, round and D-shaped stone towers on the rims of small canyons here in the 1200s, and nobody is entirely sure what they were for. Granaries, lookouts, ceremonial rooms, a way of guarding a spring, all have been argued. The walls still stand to a startling height, fitted with a care that makes the ruins feel recent rather than ancient. Square Tower Group, near the visitor area, is the easiest to walk around and the one with the clearest sense of a village perched above a drainage. It was protected as a national monument in 1923.

The land around is high desert in the proper sense. Expect big sky, a fine dusting of red dirt, ravens, and in warm months lizards that sprint across the tarmac. Spring and autumn are comfortable; midsummer can be fierce by midday, and winter nights go well below freezing. Because the lights are so far away, the monument has a reputation for dark skies, and if your plans allow an overnight in Blanding or Cortez, the stars from here are the kind you remember.

Ride it slowly. The surface is generally fine but the junctions are few and the shoulders soft, and cattle can wander out onto open range. You are on the Trail of the Ancients here, and unlike its busier neighbour Mesa Verde, the story is told mostly by silence and masonry. Bring a camera, bring a spare bottle of water, and give the towers a full hour.
t.golden@39.8,-105.2:
Golden is where Denver's western edge hits the mountains. The town sits at the mouth of Clear Creek Canyon, squeezed between the twin flat-topped bulks of North and South Table Mountain, and its main street still looks like a western town that grew up respectable. Golden was the territorial capital of Colorado in the 1860s before Denver took over, and it has kept a few reminders, including the banner that arches over Washington Avenue welcoming visitors, and the Colorado School of Mines, the college that trains mining and petroleum engineers. Coors Brewing has made beer here since 1873, and the brewery still dominates one end of town, with a tour that finishes at a tasting room.

For a rider, the value is practical and geographic. Golden has several fuel stations and plenty of places to eat, which makes it a natural starting and finishing point for the roads into the Front Range. The road up Lookout Mountain winds in a series of hairpins to the grave of Buffalo Bill Cody, who died in 1917 and was buried on the summit with a view over the plains, and the museum beside it is a small treat. The Lariat Loop, a scenic route that circles up through Lookout Mountain and down through Genesee and Morrison, packs a lot of road into a short space.

Further on, Clear Creek Canyon leads west along Highway 6 with rock walls on both sides, the creek foaming beside the road, and a handful of tunnels. Beyond it, Highway 119 and Golden Gate Canyon Road climb toward the Peak to Peak Highway, which links mountain towns such as Nederland, Estes Park and Black Hawk at heights of eight or nine thousand feet, with the Continental Divide glittering to the west. From there, Trail Ridge Road in Rocky Mountain National Park reaches over twelve thousand feet, and only opens when the snow has cleared, usually from around Memorial Day until mid or late October.

Weather on the Front Range moves quickly. Mornings are often clear and calm, and afternoon thunderstorms can build over the mountains, bringing hail and sudden cold. Start early, carry rain gear and layers, and be aware that the temperature difference between Golden and the high passes can reach twenty degrees Celsius. Golden itself is easy: parking is manageable, the creek-side path is pleasant, and a coffee at the edge of town is a good way to start or end a ride.
t.l aquila@42.3,13.4:
L'Aquila lies in a high bowl of the central Apennines, at about 700 metres, ringed by the snow-covered limestone of the Gran Sasso to the northeast and the Sirente-Velino range to the southeast. It is the capital of Abruzzo, and looks more like a mountain fortress than the coastal region's reputation suggests. The city was founded in the thirteenth century when the people of dozens of surrounding villages came together under imperial authority, and the legend says that each village built its own piazza and church within the walls, hence the Fontana delle 99 Cannelle, a long wall of ninety-nine spouts, one for each of them.

On the night of 6 April 2009, a powerful earthquake destroyed much of the old centre and killed more than three hundred people. The scaffolding and cranes that filled the historic quarter for years have gradually given way to restored palaces and churches, but you will still see the signs of the scale of the damage, and the rebuilding continues. It is respectful to treat the place as somewhere people live and are putting back together. The Basilica of Santa Maria di Collemaggio, with its pink-and-white patterned facade, is one of the most beautiful Romanesque churches in Italy, and is where Pope Celestine V was crowned in 1294. The ceremony of the Perdonanza, a pardon granted to pilgrims, takes place here every August.

For a motorcyclist, L'Aquila's role is practical: it has fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and it is the last place with real services before the mountains. From here, the roads climb to Campo Imperatore and the high plateau beneath the Gran Sasso, or head east through Santo Stefano di Sessanio, a stone village on a hilltop that has been carefully restored. The roads are twisty and quick, with good surfaces in places and potholes in others, and winter closures are common at altitude, so check before heading up in the cooler months.

Food in Abruzzo is hearty and straightforward. Arrosticini, small skewers of mutton grilled over charcoal, are the signature, along with saffron grown on the plateau and pecorino cheese from shepherds who still move flocks between pasture and plain. Watch the weather, because at this height, a clear morning can turn to cold fog in an hour.
t.orvieto@42.7,12.1:
Orvieto stands on a block of volcanic tufa that rises abruptly from the plain, a flat-topped rock with cliffs on every side and a town built to the edge of them. It is in southwestern Umbria, near the border with Lazio and Tuscany, with the Paglia river winding below. The Etruscans made it an important city, and the caves cut into the soft rock beneath the streets are still used for storing wine. In the Middle Ages, it was a papal refuge and a town of some power, and the legacy of that is the Duomo, begun in the late thirteenth century.

The cathedral is the reason many people come, and the facade is a dazzling thing, covered in mosaics and carved reliefs, the sort of surface that changes with the light. It was built to honour a miracle at nearby Bolsena, where a host was said to have bled during Mass, and the town still celebrates Corpus Domini with a procession. Inside, the Chapel of San Brizio has frescoes by Luca Signorelli, whose depiction of the end of the world is among the most vivid of the Renaissance. Another stop is the Pozzo di San Patrizio, a deep well with a double spiral staircase, built in the sixteenth century to give the town water if it were besieged.

Orvieto is also wine country, known for Orvieto Classico, a light and dry white wine made from grapes grown on the volcanic soils around the town. A glass with lunch is the sensible way to taste it, though perhaps not on the way to a day's riding.

For a rider, this is a good place for a coffee and a stretch. The hill town has narrow cobbled streets and a restricted traffic zone, so most visitors park at the base and take the funicular up from the station, or leave the bike in one of the car parks below. The riding in the area is excellent, with the roads from Orvieto toward Lake Bolsena, Pitigliano and the Tuscan border running through green, rolling country with views of tufa towns and olive groves. Surfaces vary, but the traffic is light outside the high season.

Fuel is easy, with stations at Orvieto Scalo, down by the railway, and along the main roads. Come in spring or autumn for the best conditions, and take care on wet cobbles, which are slick.
t.mora@61.0,14.5:
Mora sits at the northern end of Lake Siljan, in the heart of Dalarna, the province that Swedes think of as the soul of the country. The lake, formed by a meteorite impact some three hundred and sixty million years ago, is nearly round, a huge ring of water set among forested hills, and the villages around its shore have kept their folk traditions: red-painted wooden houses, midsummer poles hung with flowers, and fiddlers in regional costume.

Mora is known for several things. The Vasaloppet, a cross-country ski race of ninety kilometers, finishes here every March, with thousands of skiers streaming down the main street. The race commemorates the winter of 1520, when Gustav Vasa, fleeing Danish troops, skied to Mora and rallied the Dalarna men to his cause, and he later became king. The painter Anders Zorn, one of Sweden's most famous artists, was born near Mora, and his house and museum are well worth a visit. The Mora knife, with its red wooden handle, is made here, too, and the Dala horse, the carved red wooden horse that became a national symbol, is made in Nusnäs, just outside town.

The riding around Siljan is a joy. A road circles the lake, through Rättvik, Leksand and Orsa, with gentle curves, views across the water and farmland on the hills, and the surface is excellent. Traffic is light apart from midsummer weekends, when the whole region comes alive with celebrations. Side roads climb to old summer farms, fäbodar, on the hills, where in past centuries women took cattle to graze for the summer.

Mora has fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels, and it is a good base. Orsa, north of town, has a bear park. The best months are June to August, with the midsummer festival in late June the high point, and September has golden light. Winter is long and snowy, and the season for riding is short. Elk and reindeer cross roads, and speed limits are strictly enforced, so ride with care in the forest stretches.
t.montalcino@43.1,11.5:
Montalcino is a wine town that happens to have a fortress, or maybe the other way round. It sits on a hill at about five hundred and fifty metres south of Siena, with views across the valleys of the Orcia and Ombrone rivers, and its name is known to wine lovers around the world because of Brunello, a red wine made from a local variety of Sangiovese and aged for years before release. The vineyards and olive groves cover the slopes around the town, lined with cypress, and in autumn the leaves turn the hills copper and gold.

The history is just as rich. The fortress was built in the fourteenth century by the Sienese, and it later became the last stronghold of the Republic of Siena. After Siena fell to Florentine and Spanish forces in 1555, many of its citizens retreated here and held out for four more years, a last independent flag in Tuscany. The walls are still intact and you can climb to the ramparts for the view, and the town has a lively collection of wine shops, called enoteche, where you can sample the local product. Not far away is the Abbey of Sant'Antimo, a Romanesque church in a quiet valley, which is worth visiting for its stone and its Gregorian chant.

The riding is gentle but charming. The roads around Montalcino are narrow, twisting and often lined with cypress, with the occasional white gravel strada bianca branching off. Tarmac is mostly good, but some stretches are patched, and farm traffic and cyclists are common. The climb into the town is steep, with a few tight bends, and parking in the old centre is limited. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons, when the light is soft and the vines are green or golden. Summer is hot and the roads can be busy at weekends.

Services are fine, since the town has cafes, restaurants, bakeries and shops and has been catering to wine visitors for a long time. A glass of Rosso di Montalcino, the younger sibling of Brunello, with a plate of pici pasta or a slice of local pecorino is a very civilised pause. For fuel, though, you will need to plan. The village of Torrenieri, about six kilometres away, is the nearest stop, and larger towns such as Buonconvento and Abbadia San Salvatore have more choice.

If you ride with a pillion or sit for lunch, pace yourself. Italian police take drinking and riding seriously, and the roads here are very good at punishing the unwary.
t.pienza@43.1,11.7:
Pienza is the ideal city that one man built for himself, and it is as extraordinary as that sounds. It began as a village called Corsignano, the birthplace of Enea Silvio Piccolomini, who rose to become Pope Pius II. When he returned in 1459 as pope, he decided to turn his home town into a model Renaissance city, and he hired the architect Bernardo Rossellino to do it. In only a few years, the place was rebuilt around a perfect trapezoid piazza, with a cathedral, a papal palace and a town hall, all in the new classical style. The pope died in 1464 and the plan was never completed, which is why Pienza is still so small and so perfect, like a stage set frozen in time. It was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.

The setting is the Val d'Orcia, a landscape of rolling hills, cypress-lined drives and isolated farmhouses that has become one of the most photographed in Italy. The clay soils create gentle, bare ridges, and in spring the fields are bright green, in summer golden, and in winter often wrapped in mist. The town stands on a ridge above it all, with a terrace behind the cathedral that gives views across the valley to Monte Amiata. It is the sort of scene that makes you want to stop on every corner.

Riding here is a pleasure. The roads are narrow, curving and well maintained, passing between fields and vineyards at an easy pace, and the corners are mostly gentle. Traffic can be heavy in summer, with coaches and rental cars, so the best times are early morning and late afternoon, when the light is golden. The town centre is restricted to traffic, and you will need to leave the bike outside the walls and walk in.

Pienza is also famous for its cheese. Pecorino di Pienza, made from sheep's milk and aged in various ways, is sold in dozens of shops along the main street, and the sampling is generous. The town has plenty of restaurants and bakeries, and a lunch of pasta, pecorino and a glass of Vino Nobile from nearby Montepulciano is as good as it gets.

For fuel, the small town of San Quirico d'Orcia, about six kilometres to the west, is the nearest option, and Chianciano Terme, about twelve kilometres, has more choice. Fill up before climbing into the hills, as pumps in the countryside are few.

Take time to wander the narrow lane called Via dell'Amore, a path around the walls with the view over the valley. It is worth the ten minutes even if the name makes you smile.
t.montepulciano@43.1,11.8:
Montepulciano sits on a long limestone ridge at about 600 metres, overlooking the Val di Chiana to the east and the Val d'Orcia to the west, and it has the appearance of a town that has been polished by centuries of owners with taste. It is a Renaissance town, built largely by Florentine families and architects, with palaces such as the Palazzo Contucci and the Palazzo Comunale, and a main street, the Corso, that climbs in a long, steady slope toward the Piazza Grande at the top. The Duomo, the well and the town hall are here, and the view from the tower over the Tuscan hills is long.

The wine is the reason many people come. Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is a red made mostly from Sangiovese, known locally as Prugnolo Gentile, and it has been prized since the Middle Ages. The cellars are dug into the rock beneath the town, and many offer tastings. Do be sensible about drinking and riding, which are not compatible, and consider a spit bucket or a taxi. Pecorino cheese from nearby Pienza and pici, the thick hand-rolled pasta of this part of Tuscany, are the best things to eat.

The riding approach is lovely. The road climbs from the valley with views of cypress-lined drives, farmhouses and fields of wheat that go green in spring and golden in June. The surface is generally good, and the curves are gentle, but the roads are popular with cyclists, particularly in spring, and tourist traffic builds in summer. Go early and again late, when the light is low and soft, and the hills show their folds. Autumn, with the harvest and mist in the valleys, is a magical time.

Practical points: the old town is limited-traffic, so park outside the walls and walk up. Montepulciano has fuel stations on the approach roads and in the nearby villages, and plenty of cafes and restaurants inside. The town gets busy at midday, so a late afternoon arrival is easier. Stay for sunset, when the stone turns honey-coloured and the whole valley fades to blue.
t.greve in chianti@43.6,11.3:
Greve is the sort of town that makes you want to put the kickstand down and wander. Its heart is an odd, wedge-shaped piazza lined with arcades, with a statue of the explorer Giovanni da Verrazzano in the middle. He was born in a castle nearby, and he is remembered as the first European to sail into New York Bay. Under the porticoes are butchers, wine shops and cafes, and on market days the square fills with stalls selling cheese, sausage and local produce. It is the natural capital of Chianti, in the best sense, a working market town, not a museum.

The Chiantigiana, the old state road that runs between Florence and Siena, passes right through, and it is a classic of Tuscan riding. The bends are easy, the surface is generally good, and the landscape rolls past in a pattern of vineyards, olive groves, cypress and stone farmhouses. The black rooster, the symbol of the Chianti Classico wine league, appears on signs and bottles everywhere. It is not a road for speed, because there are too many cyclists, camper vans and rental cars, but it is a road for pleasure, especially on a weekday in spring or autumn. Summer is hot and crowded, and the light at midday is flat.

Wine is the point, and the wine of the region is made mainly from Sangiovese. In the shops of Greve you can taste Chianti Classico, from young and fruity to aged and complex, and buy bottles to take home, if you have luggage space. A plate of ribollita, the hearty Tuscan bread and vegetable soup, or a slice of bistecca alla fiorentina is a fine reward. If you are riding, a small taste is enough, and a coffee will do the rest.

Greve has everything a rider needs. There are petrol stations on the edge of town, supermarkets, banks, pharmacies and plenty of places to eat, and it is a good base for a few days in the area. Tavarnelle Val di Pesa, about twelve kilometres away, is a larger town with more services. The hills around are dotted with castles and villas, many of which offer tours and tastings.

The best times to ride the area are May to June and September to October. In October the grape harvest brings tractors and the smell of crushed fruit to the roadside, and the slopes turn gold and red.
t.panzano@43.5,11.3:
Panzano sits on a ridge above a natural amphitheatre of vineyards that the locals call the Conca d'Oro, the golden shell, and the name is not an exaggeration. The terraces face south and catch the sun from morning to evening, and the wine grown on them is among the most respected in Chianti. The village itself is small, with a single main street, a ruined castle, a church and a handful of shops, but it has the confident air of a place that knows its worth. The views from the edge of the village across the valley are some of the best in Tuscany.

Panzano is also famous for meat. It is home to a butcher who became a celebrity, known for reciting passages from Dante to his customers while he cuts, and for turning the shop into a kind of theatre, with long tables, wine and platters of cured and cooked meat. Whatever you think of the performance, the quality is high, and Tuscan beef is a serious business. If you arrive at the right time, you can eat very well in the village, and there are other restaurants and wine bars serving local dishes.

The riding here is a delight. The Chiantigiana runs along the ridge, with long, easy bends and views on both sides, and the side roads that drop into the valleys are narrow and quiet. Some of them turn to white gravel, and a road bike may prefer to keep to the tarmac. The surface is generally decent but can be patchy after winter, and the traffic includes plenty of tourists, so the best times are early morning and weekdays. In spring, the hills are green and the broom is in flower, and in autumn the vineyards turn to gold and rust.

For fuel, Greve in Chianti, about four and a half kilometres to the north, has stations and shops, and Tavarnelle Val di Pesa, about twelve kilometres away, offers more choice. Panzano has a few shops and a bakery, but it is best to fill before arriving. Parking is easy at the edge of the village, and a short walk takes you to the main street.

The village hosts a few events during the year, and the church of San Leolino, a Romanesque building a short way out of town, is worth a quiet visit if you want a change from the wine.
t.castellina in chianti@43.5,11.3:
Castellina in Chianti is a fortress town that once guarded a frontier. In the Middle Ages, the hills between Florence and Siena were the front line of a long rivalry, and Castellina was on the Florentine side, with a stout castle built to watch the enemy. The fortress, the Rocca, still stands in the centre of the village, and part of it is now a small museum. Nearby is a covered street, the Via delle Volte, which runs under arches along the old walls and feels like a medieval alley, with cool air and stone vaults overhead. The town was one of the three original members of the Chianti League, a military and political alliance of the fourteenth century that gave the region its name.

The history goes back much further than the Middle Ages. Just outside the town is an Etruscan burial mound, a reminder that people were living on these ridges long before Florence or Siena existed. The museum in the Rocca has finds from the area, and the landscape of vines and olives has been farmed for thousands of years. The wine is the heart of the local economy, with Chianti Classico produced by the estates all around.

For a rider, the ride to Castellina is a classic. The Chiantigiana, the state road between Florence and Siena, runs through the town, with easy bends and long views across the vineyards. The surface is generally good and the gradients are gentle, but the road can be busy with traffic, especially at weekends and in high summer, so weekdays are better. On the side roads, you will find narrow lanes and gravel tracks, with farmhouses and cypress avenues. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with soft light and green or golden hills.

Castellina has several wine shops, cafes and restaurants, and the food is typical of the region, with Tuscan bread, pasta with boar sauce, and grilled meats. It is a good place for a leisurely lunch, with plenty of choice. For fuel, there is a station on the main road in the area, but it is wise to fill in larger towns such as Poggibonsi, about eleven kilometres away, where you will find more services and supermarkets.

On the way south towards Siena, the road passes some of the most beautiful stretches of the Chianti, with the vines in neat rows and the old stone houses sitting in the folds of the hills. Take it slowly and enjoy it.
t.praiano@40.6,14.5:
Praiano gets the sunset that Positano hogs the postcards for. The village faces west, stacked up a cliff halfway between Positano and Amalfi, and in the evening the light drops behind the little islands of Li Galli and sets the water on fire while the people of the terraced bars hold their glasses and go quiet. It is a fishing village that has stayed more or less itself, with a tiny harbour at Marina di Praia tucked into a cleft in the rock, a church with a bright majolica dome, and houses climbing the hillside in tiers of pink, ochre and white. The whole Amalfi Coast is a UNESCO site, and Praiano is the part of it that feels least staged.

The road is the SS163, the Amalfitana, and it is as hard as its reputation. It is a single ribbon of tarmac cut into the cliffs, with the sea hundreds of feet below, a retaining wall on one side and rock overhangs on the other, and it never stops bending. Visibility around the corners is poor, and the buses that serve the coast are wide enough that you will sometimes have to stop and wait while the driver folds in the mirrors and makes the turn in three goes. It is slow, intense riding that rewards patience far more than skill. Go early, before the day-trippers, or in the shoulder months when the lemon terraces are quiet. In high summer there can be queues in both directions, and the authorities have used rules such as alternate number-plate days to control traffic, so check before you go.

The coast has been inhabited for a very long time. Amalfi was once a powerful maritime republic and its sailors traded with the Levant, and the old watchtowers that stand on the headlands, including one in Praiano, were built to warn of raiders from the sea. The terraces on the slopes, held up by dry stone walls, grow lemons and vines, and the lemons of this coast end up in the local liqueur, limoncello, and in cakes and pastries.

For practical matters, Praiano has restaurants and bars with terraces, mostly small family places, and the fish is excellent. Fuel is the thing to plan. The village is small and pumps are scarce on this stretch, so fill in Amalfi or in the hill town of Agerola, a few kilometres above, before you set out along the cliffs. Parking is difficult and often paid, so a small bike has a real advantage here.
t.ravello junction@40.6,14.6:
Ravello sits so far above the Amalfi Coast that it feels like a different place entirely. Where the seaside towns are crowded onto ledges at the water's edge, Ravello perches on a ridge some three hundred and fifty metres up, in cooler air, with the sea a bright floor far below. In the Middle Ages it was a rich and proud town, part of the maritime republic of Amalfi, and the merchant families built palaces and gardens that are still the main attraction. Composers, writers and artists have come here for a century and a half, and Richard Wagner is said to have found the model for the magic garden of his opera Parsifal in the grounds of Villa Rufolo.

The junction is the place where the road up from Amalfi meets the roads towards Scala and Minori and Maiori, and it is a hinge in many riding plans. The climb from the coast is a delight, a narrow road that winds through lemon terraces and woods with views opening and closing at every bend. It is steep, tight and sometimes rough at the edges, with little room for error, and it is shared with buses, vans and the odd Vespa. Hairpins come quickly and the gradients are punchy. The descent down the other side, toward the Maiori valley, is quieter and often shaded by chestnut woods, and a pleasant change after the cliffs of the main coast road.

The town itself is a place for walking. Cars and bikes are kept to the edge, and you wander the lanes to the cathedral, with its bronze doors, to the Villa Cimbrone, whose terrace of infinity gives a vast view along the coast, and to the gardens of Villa Rufolo, which are open to the public. In summer, the town hosts a music festival, with concerts staged on a terrace above the sea. The cafes and gelaterie around the main square are an excellent place to wait out the midday heat.

Fuel and services are mostly on the coast. Maiori, about three kilometres away, is the nearest larger town with fuel and supermarkets, and Amalfi has stations too. Do not rely on pumps in Ravello itself, and fill before you climb. Parking at the edge of the old centre is limited and paid, so arrive early.

Come in spring or autumn if you can, when the air is clear, the crowds are small and the light is kind to the lemon groves.
t.vietri sul mare@40.7,14.7:
Vietri sul Mare is where the Amalfi Coast begins, or ends, depending on which way you are riding, and the town marks the point with a cascade of colour. It stands on a steep slope at the eastern end of the Costiera, just beyond Salerno, and it is famous for ceramics. Painted tiles decorate the church domes, the benches and the house fronts, and the shops sell plates and jugs in blue, yellow and green. The craft goes back centuries, and in the early twentieth century German artists settled here and gave the local style a new life. Cava de' Tirreni, a proper town of nearly fifty thousand, is just up the hill, and Salerno is a few kilometres east, so supplies and fuel are easy.

The coast road here is the SS163, the Amalfitana, and it is among the most celebrated and most congested in Italy. From Vietri it runs west, clinging to cliffs above the Tyrrhenian Sea, with tight bends, short tunnels, and views of lemon terraces falling to the water. The road is narrow, and buses and coaches take the bends in the middle, so riders have to be alert. In July and August the queues are long, and a motorbike can be a real advantage, though patience is still required. Spring and autumn are far more pleasant, and weekdays are better than weekends.

The geology is striking. The coast is limestone, folded and fractured, rising steeply from the sea to peaks of over a thousand metres, and the terraces, built by hand over centuries, support lemons, vines and olives. The Amalfi lemon, known as sfusato, is large and fragrant and is used in limoncello. The whole coast is a UNESCO World Heritage Site for this working landscape.

For rest, Vietri is less crowded than Positano or Amalfi, and its seafront is a good place to sit with a coffee and a sfogliatella. Seafood is the obvious choice for lunch: anchovies from Cetara, just along the coast, are famous, as is the colatura, a fish sauce descended from Roman garum. Take care with the parking regulations, which are enforced firmly. At the end of a day, the sea light on the tiles is a fine finale.
t.asciano@43.2,11.6:
South of Siena the Tuscan hills lose their vines and cypress and turn into something stranger: the Crete Senesi, a landscape of bare, rounded clay hills the colour of a wet pigeon, cut by gullies that geologists call calanchi. Asciano is the town that sits at the heart of it. It is a compact brick-and-stone place inside medieval walls, with a handful of churches, a small collection of Etruscan and sacred art in its museums, and a main street that the locals walk up and down in the evening. Nobody comes to Asciano for a famous monument, and that is the nice thing about it.

The country around is the draw. In spring the clay slopes turn a soft, bright green with young wheat, in early summer they ripen to gold, and after the harvest the fields are ploughed to a grey-brown that can look like the surface of the moon. Single farmhouses, each ringed by a few cypresses, stand on the ridges like ships. Riding through this country is slow and pleasant, with long gentle gradients, wide views and not much in the way of traffic once you leave the main roads. The tarmac is generally fine, though some of the side roads turn to white gravel, the strade bianche that cyclists race on, and a loose surface needs some respect on a road bike.

The clay is no accident of nature in a simple sense. The hills are the bed of an ancient sea, and the sediments laid down there erode into the characteristic gullies when the rains come, which is why the farmers here have always fought a battle with the soil. In summer it bakes hard and cracks, and in wet weather the unpaved tracks become slippery, so that is another reason to be wary of leaving the asphalt.

Asciano has the services of a working Tuscan town. There are fuel stations on the approach roads, a supermarket, bakeries and a good choice of simple restaurants, where the local specialities are pici, thick hand-rolled pasta, boar sauce, pecorino cheese and the honey of the district. A train line links the town to Siena. Sinalunga, about fifteen kilometres to the east, is a larger town and handy if you need something more.

The best time to come is spring or early autumn. Midsummer is hot and a bit flat, but the light at the end of the day is lovely on the clay.
t.abbazia monte oliveto maggiore@43.2,11.5:
At the end of a long avenue of cypress trees, in a hollow of the clay hills south of Siena, stands a great red-brick monastery. Monte Oliveto Maggiore was founded in the early fourteenth century by a Sienese nobleman who gave up his career and his comforts to live as a hermit, and who was soon joined by others. They built here, on what was then a wild and wooded slope, and the community grew into the mother house of the Olivetan Benedictines. The abbey is still home to a small number of monks, and it feels like it: quiet, ordered and slightly outside time.

The brick buildings rise from a forest of cypress and oak, with a gatehouse tower and a church with a leaning bell tower, and inside are some of the finest frescoes in Tuscany. The great cloister is decorated with a cycle of scenes from the life of St Benedict, painted at the end of the fifteenth century and in the early sixteenth, begun by Luca Signorelli and completed by the painter known as Il Sodoma. The scenes are full of life, with elegant courtiers, animals, tricks played on the saint and a number of gleefully worldly details that suggest the artists did not take themselves too seriously. It is worth an hour of anyone's time.

The monks make honey, liqueurs and herbal products, which are sold in a shop by the entrance, and there is a restaurant nearby for a simple meal. Visitors are asked to dress modestly and to keep quiet in the church and cloister, and opening hours are fixed and sometimes interrupted by monastic services, so check before you go. The place has a spiritual calm that is a pleasant contrast to the busy Tuscan towns.

The ride to the abbey runs through the heart of the Crete Senesi, with long, gentle bends over bare clay ridges and a few sections of white gravel on the side roads. The main approach is paved and in good order, with views opening on each crest, and the cypress avenue at the end is one of the great sights of the district. Go on a weekday if you can, since coaches visit in summer. Cyclists are common, so give them room.

The village of San Giovanni d'Asso, about five kilometres away, is known for its truffle festival in autumn, and Asciano, a little further, has stations, supermarkets and cafes. Fill the tank in Asciano before heading out.

If you can, come in the morning, when the mist often fills the hollows between the hills and the abbey rises out of it.
t.terrace bay@-20.0,13.0:
Terrace Bay is a handful of buildings on the Skeleton Coast of Namibia, and it is as remote as a place can be while still having a name. The coast here is one of the harshest in the world: cold Atlantic water, thick fog rolling in from the Benguela current, and the dunes of the Namib running straight to the sea. The name Skeleton Coast comes from the whalebones and shipwrecks that litter the shore, and from the sailors who survived the wrecks only to die in the desert. The area is part of the Skeleton Coast National Park, and a permit is needed to enter, so plan this properly with a booking, because it is a tightly controlled area.

There is no town nearby. Terrace Bay was built as a base for diamond prospectors in the 1950s, and it is now a small tourist camp, with a few simple rooms, a bar and a gravel airstrip. Fuel is a serious matter: the nearest reliable supplies are at Henties Bay or Khorixas, far away, so riders carry extra and plan their range with care. A satellite phone or at least a tracking beacon is sensible. The gravel roads are made of salt and clay, often hard and flat, but soft sand and washouts can appear.

The ride along the coast is stark and beautiful. The salt road runs beside a grey sea, with fog banks lying offshore and then burning off in the afternoon. You may see seal colonies, particularly at Cape Cross, where tens of thousands of Cape fur seals crowd the beach, and the smell is overwhelming. Desert-adapted elephants, lions and rhinos live in the dry riverbeds further north, though sightings on the coast are rare. The light, in the late afternoon, makes the dunes glow gold and the sea turn pewter.

Wind is the constant companion, and temperatures swing from cold mornings to hot afternoons inland. Carry plenty of water, spare tyres, tools and a good map. Avoid driving in the dark, and do not leave the road, as the desert crust is fragile. It is a place of silence, with only the sound of the surf, and it is better enjoyed with respect and preparation.
t.enden@61.8,10.1:
Enden lies on the edge of the Rondane mountains in Innlandet, and the name is apt, because the road here runs close to the end of the inhabited country and the beginning of the open fell. Rondane was Norway's first national park, created in 1962, and it is a landscape of rounded peaks, ten of which top 2,000 metres, with Rondeslottet the highest at about 2,178. The slopes are covered in reindeer lichen, which gives the hills a pale, silvery look, and the valleys hold lakes and bogs. The nearest towns, such as Otta and Vinstra, are over thirty kilometres away, so this is remote territory.

The Rondane road is a National Tourist Route, with viewing platforms and rest areas designed by architects to blend into the landscape. At Sohlbergplassen, the viewpoint above the forest, a simple wooden pavilion frames the mountains. The road itself is quiet and smooth, with gentle gradients and wide, open curves, and it climbs through pine forest to the high plateau. The surface is generally very good, and traffic is light, apart from the occasional camper van.

Wild reindeer, one of the last herds in Europe, roam the Rondane area, and musk oxen live on the nearby Dovrefjell. Your best chance of seeing wildlife is early in the morning or at dusk, and you should slow down for animals on the road. The weather is typical for the mountains: sunny and fresh one hour, cold and wet the next. In summer, temperatures can reach twenty degrees, but nights are cool. The road can close in winter, and in spring and autumn, snow is possible.

Be prepared for limited services. Fuel is not available on the road, and a full tank is important before you set off from Otta or Vinstra. Mountain lodges offer food and drink, including waffles, soup and strong coffee. The area is popular with hikers, and the trails are well marked. The smell of pine resin and the vast, soft hills make this a place for slow riding and long pauses.
t.sohlbergplassen@61.9,10.1:
Harald Sohlberg painted his famous winter landscape of a snow-covered peak under a vivid night sky in the Rondane mountains, and the viewing point called Sohlbergplassen is named after him. It sits beside the road at the edge of the national park, and from it you look across to Rondeslottet, the highest peak of the range at about 2,178 metres, and the long line of rounded summits that make up this part of the Norwegian interior. The painter's view is familiar to many Norwegians, who know the picture from school, and the viewpoint has a sculptural platform that frames the mountains without spoiling them.

Rondane was Norway's first national park, set up in 1962, and it is a high, open, bare place. Ten peaks rise above two thousand metres, with a landscape of reindeer moss, dwarf birch, boulders and small lakes. Wild reindeer live here, in one of the last herds of their kind in Europe, and you may see them in the distance in late summer. Weather can change in minutes, and a bright morning can become a wet afternoon with low cloud on the tops.

For a rider, this is easy, uncomplicated mountain riding. The road, a scenic route across the high country, runs in long, graceful bends over open ground, with enough climb to give you a sense of altitude and little in the way of traffic. The surface is good, the speed limit is moderate, and the views extend a long way. The main hazards are wind and rain, the occasional sheep and the low sun in autumn, which can dazzle. Summers are short, and the road is open all year, though winter driving here is a serious business.

Fuel is not available at the viewpoint. Folldal and Otta, the closest places, are the nearest options, and both are small, so do not expect a big choice. Fill up before you set out, and take food with you. A flask of coffee on the platform, with the mountains laid out in front of you and the wind rustling the grass, is the right way to spend a half hour.
t.animas forks@37.9,-107.6:
Animas Forks is a ghost town that looks as though the residents stepped out an hour ago and forgot to come back. At about 3,400 metres it sits in a high basin where several creeks meet to form the upper Animas River, ringed by steep slopes, and a scatter of weathered wooden buildings still stands among the grass and wildflowers. The Duncan House, with its bay window and painted trim, is the most photographed, and the old jail and the remains of the Gold Prince mill can be seen nearby.

The town was founded in the early 1870s during the silver and gold rush in the San Juans, and for a few years it flourished, with a few hundred residents in summer, a hotel, a post office, a newspaper and the usual saloons. Winters were another matter. In the winter of 1884, a single storm is said to have buried the town under many feet of snow, and people tunnelled between buildings for weeks. Eventually the ore played out, and by the 1920s the last residents had gone, leaving the buildings to the weather. Today the site is managed by the Bureau of Land Management and the local historical society, and the best advice is to look but not climb on the walls.

The road to Animas Forks is a gravel track, in decent shape in summer, and it is easier than the passes on either side. The approach from Silverton follows the river upstream, past more old mines, with the surface a mix of packed dirt and stones. A cautious rider on a decent bike will manage it, though the narrow bends and the oncoming jeeps need care. Rain makes the dirt greasy, and thunderstorms in the afternoon can flood the creek crossings. The road is usually open from about June until the first heavy snow in autumn.

Nothing here sells anything. Silverton, about fifteen kilometres to the south, is a narrow-gauge railway town with fuel, cafes and a tough, handsome main street, and Ouray is the other source, a longer ride. Carry water, wear warm clothing and give yourself time. The altitude is serious, and you may be breathless walking between the buildings. The light on the slopes at the end of the day, when the shadows lengthen, is lovely, but plan to be off the track before dark.
t.cinnamon pass@37.9,-107.5:
Cinnamon Pass is the friendlier of the two high passes on the Alpine Loop, though friendly is relative at 3,852 metres on a dirt road. It links Lake City with Animas Forks over the shoulder of the San Juans, and its name is supposedly from the cinnamon-coloured rock of the slopes, which glow rust and orange in the right light. The summit is a broad, open saddle with a marker, a wide view of ragged peaks, and usually a few jeeps, a few motorcyclists and a few marmots arguing over the best rock.

The road is a long, rocky climb from the east, past old mining sites and meadows full of wildflowers in July. The surface is rough but generally less technical than Engineer, with loose stones, some washboard, and a few exposed bends. The descent toward Animas Forks drops through high valleys, with the old town laid out below, and the effect is a little like arriving in another century. Handies Peak, a fourteen-thousander, stands nearby, and keen walkers use the pass as a starting point.

The region has a long history. The Ute people used these mountains for centuries, until pressure from miners led to treaties and removal in the 1870s and 1880s. Then came prospectors, then towns, then the collapse. Alferd Packer, the notorious Colorado cannibal, was said to have wandered into this country in the winter of 1873 and 1874, an unfortunate tale that is part of the local lore of Lake City. The old mining camps and roads left an extraordinary legacy of trails for modern travellers.

The road is open only in summer, usually from late June through September or early October, and you should check conditions with the Lake City or Silverton visitor offices. Afternoon storms are common, and the high basins catch cold, wet wind. Fuel is available in Lake City, to the east, and Silverton and Ouray, but not on the pass, so fill up before leaving. Bring tools and a tyre repair kit, because help is slow to arrive. The air is thin, the drop-offs are serious and the scenery is a good reason to stop often. Take your time, and enjoy it.
t.bernalillo@35.3,-106.6:
Bernalillo is an old Spanish and Pueblo town on the Rio Grande just north of Albuquerque, and it has a quiet identity of its own, a mix of adobe walls, cottonwoods, cafes, a few vineyards and a long history. The Sandia Mountains stand to the east, with a ridge that turns watermelon pink at sunset, which is what the name Sandia means in Spanish. The town has about nine thousand people and holds a festival of San Lorenzo each August, with traditional dances.

Francisco Vásquez de Coronado came this way in 1540, in search of the fabled cities of gold, and wintered in a Pueblo village near here. The ruins of that village, Kuaua, are preserved at Coronado Historic Site, where the restored kiva walls contain colourful painted murals that are hundreds of years old. The Spanish settled the valley in the following centuries, and the old plaza and the church still reflect that heritage. The region is also a mixture of cultures, with several Pueblo communities nearby, each with its own traditions.

The Jemez Mountain Trail heads northwest from here, through desert and canyon country of astonishing colour. The red and orange cliffs near Jemez Pueblo, the white gypsum bluffs, and the green river valley make a series of vivid contrasts, and the road, narrow and curving, follows the Jemez River up into pine forest. Hot springs bubble up at Jemez Springs, and farther on, the road climbs to the rim of the Valles Caldera, a huge volcanic crater formed about one and a quarter million years ago, now a green grassland where elk graze.

Bernalillo has fuel, supermarkets and several well-known New Mexican restaurants, so it is easy to start. The local food is built around chile, red or green, and the question of which one you want is asked at every table, and the answer, Christmas, means both. Try a breakfast burrito or a plate of enchiladas. Summers can be hot, with afternoon thunderstorms, and winter can bring snow on the high road, so check conditions. Autumn, when the cottonwoods turn gold along the river and the air smells of roasting chile, is a good time.
t.jemez pueblo@35.6,-106.7:
Jemez Pueblo is a living community, not a monument, and the first thing to understand about it is that the people who live here call it Walatowa, meaning this is the place in their language, Towa. The village sits at the foot of the Jemez Mountains, in a valley of red sandstone cliffs along State Route 4, and the pueblo's lands run up the canyon of the Jemez River toward the high country. The Jemez people have lived in this region for many centuries, and are the only remaining speakers of Towa, a language they share with the people of the former Pecos Pueblo.

The cliffs along the road here are spectacular, a wall of red and cream rock streaked with black, rising a few hundred feet above the river and catching the evening light. Cottonwoods line the river, and the land around the pueblo is green with fields and orchards. The Walatowa Visitor Center, on the highway, has a small museum and sells local crafts and food. Jemez is known for its pottery, and for its feast days, especially the one held on 12 November, when the village welcomes visitors with dances and stalls selling red and green chile stew and fry bread. Photography and sketching are not permitted in most parts of the pueblo, so ask first.

The road is the Jemez Mountain Trail Scenic Byway, and the ride up the canyon is a joy. From Bernalillo, Route 4 follows the river past the pueblo, with long, easy curves through red rock country, then climbs through pine forest toward the volcanic caldera of the Valles Grande. The surface is good, the traffic moderate, and the views change at every bend. Weekends can be busy, particularly in autumn, but weekday mornings are calm. Winter brings ice at higher levels, and summer thunderstorms bring flash floods.

Further up, past the pueblo, lie Jemez Springs, with its hot springs and the ruins of the seventeenth-century Franciscan mission of San Jose de los Jemez, and Soda Dam, a curious calcium-rich formation across the river. The nearest large towns are on the other side of the mountains, around Bernalillo and Rio Rancho, where petrol and supermarkets are plentiful. Small shops in the valley sell snacks, but fuel is more limited. Treat the pueblo with respect, stay on public roads, and be aware that some areas are closed to visitors.
t.unaweep canyon@38.9,-108.6:
Unaweep Canyon is a geological oddity. Most canyons have a river running through them, in one direction, from a high end to a low one. This one has two creeks, East Creek and West Creek, flowing in opposite directions from a low divide in the middle, so that the valley appears to drain both ways at once. The canyon was carved by an ancient river, probably the Colorado or Gunnison, that flowed through it millions of years ago before something diverted it, and geologists are still arguing about what. The name is generally given as a Ute word, sometimes translated as canyon with two mouths.

It is a majestic place. The walls are towering cliffs of dark Precambrian granite and gneiss, with red sandstone above, and the valley floor is a wide green strip of meadow, cottonwood and ranch fields. State Highway 141 follows it for about fifty miles between the Grand Valley and Gateway, the road running in a gentle, curving line between the walls, with long straights and sweeping bends. It is a quiet road, with little traffic, big sky and a sense of being very far from the interstate. The Unaweep-Tabeguache byway takes its second name from the Tabeguache band of the Ute, who lived in this country.

The ride is excellent in spring and autumn, when the temperatures are mild and the light is soft. In summer, the heat can be fierce on the west side, and thunderstorms build over the plateau in the afternoon. In winter, the upper canyon sees snow and ice. Watch for cattle on unfenced stretches, for deer at dusk, and for rock fall after storms. The canyon is a favourite with climbers and mountain bikers, and you may see vehicles with bikes on the roof.

Farther south, the road emerges into the red cliffs of the Dolores River country, with old uranium workings and the remains of a remarkable hanging flume, a wooden water channel built along the cliff face in the 1880s to carry water to gold diggings. Fuel needs thought. Grand Junction, about twenty kilometres from the east end, has everything, and Orchard Mesa has stations too, but the canyon itself and the village of Gateway have limited services, and Naturita, to the south, is the next sizeable place. Fill up in Grand Junction, carry water, and take your time.
t.gateway@38.7,-109.0:
Gateway, Colorado, sits where the Dolores River squeezes out of a red-rock canyon and the land opens into a wide, flat valley, and the name describes the geography exactly. Cliffs of rust-coloured sandstone rise on every side, stained with desert varnish and carved into fins, towers and shelves, and the town fits into the gap like a pebble in a doorway. There are a few dozen residents, a post office, and a very comfortable-looking resort, and not much else for miles.

The resort has an odd story.
