It was created by John Hendricks, who founded a well-known documentary TV network, who bought up ranch land here and built an upmarket lodge with an auto museum, where a collection of rare and beautiful cars sits in the middle of the desert. That is a strange thing to find at the end of a long road through uranium country, and you may feel faintly underdressed in motorcycle boots, though the restaurant and cafe are open to passers-by. The surrounding country has an older history, as the home of the Ute people, and later of uranium prospectors, cattlemen and a few hardy homesteaders.

The riding in is the real draw. Highway 141 runs through the Unaweep Canyon and then down into the Dolores valley in a long series of flowing bends, with red cliffs overhead and the river meandering in the bottom. It is one of the quietest scenic roads in Colorado, with long views and very little traffic. The best time is the cool end of the day, when the setting sun turns the rock the colour of embers. Summer afternoons are hot and thundery, and in winter the road is open but icy in places. From Gateway you can ride on south along the river through narrow gorges toward Naturita, passing the old hanging flume, or turn back toward Grand Junction.

Services are limited, and this is where planning matters. The resort has a restaurant and a small store, but I would not count on petrol, and the nearest large town is Grand Junction, about ninety kilometres to the north-east. Naturita, to the south, has more basic services. Fill up in Grand Junction, carry water and a spare layer, and keep an eye on the sky, because desert thunderstorms can send flash floods down the washes within minutes. The stars, on a moonless night, are astonishing.
t.placerville@38.0,-108.1:
Placerville is a handful of buildings beside the San Miguel River in the southwest Colorado mountains, and it is barely more than a name on the map, but it has a good one. The word placer refers to a deposit of gold in a streambed that can be washed out by hand, and the hunt for it brought prospectors here in the 1870s. Later, the Rio Grande Southern Railroad ran through the village, carrying ore and passengers down the canyon, and some of the old railroad buildings and grades can still be seen.

The setting is lovely. The river runs clear through a narrow valley of red cliffs, cottonwoods and aspen, with high peaks of the San Juan Mountains to the south and the mesas of the Uncompahgre Plateau to the north. At roughly seven thousand feet, the air is dry and clear, summer days are warm, and nights are cool. Nearby, a mountain called Lone Cone stands apart from the rest of the range, a solitary peak above the plateau, and is a landmark from many miles around.

The Unaweep-Tabeguache Scenic Byway runs north-west from the area through country that few travellers see, passing through Unaweep Canyon, an odd, wide valley with a peculiar secret. In the middle of the canyon, there is a divide, and the two creeks on either side run in opposite directions, one to the east and the other to the west, and geologists still debate how the canyon formed. The road is quiet, with long curves, red cliffs and ranch land, and it is a very relaxed ride. The Tabeguache name comes from a band of the Ute people.

Telluride and Mountain Village, about twenty-three kilometres south-east, have services, and the small town of Norwood, to the west, has basic supplies. Weather can change quickly, with summer thunderstorms and early snow at higher elevations. Autumn is wonderful, with golden aspen on the hillsides and clear blue skies, and wildlife, including deer, elk and wild turkeys, can be seen. Keep an eye out for cattle on the road in places.
t.questa@36.7,-105.6:
Questa announces itself as a working town, not a tourist one. Sitting at the foot of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains in northern New Mexico, it has a small plaza, an adobe church, a few cafes, a gas station, and the feeling of a place that has long been busy with other things. That is one of its charms. On the Enchanted Circle, which loops around Wheeler Peak through Taos, Questa, Red River, Eagle Nest, and Angel Fire, this is the community that has not been polished for visitors, and so it is a good place to eat a plain, honest meal and top up the tank.

The name is Spanish for slope, and the land really does tilt: the town stands above the Red River valley with the high peaks rising behind. The first Hispano settlers came here in the nineteenth century to farm and graze, and the old church of San Antonio de Padua still anchors the village. The molybdenum mine up the valley was for decades the main employer, and its presence has shaped both the economy and the landscape. These days the surrounding country has been recognised as part of the Rio Grande del Norte National Monument, a high, wide, wild stretch of river gorge and volcanic plateau.

Riding out of Questa toward Red River is where the loop earns its name. The road follows the canyon up through aspens and pines, climbing steadily past Bobcat Pass to a little under ten thousand feet, with long, flowing curves rather than tight hairpins. The surface is generally good. Traffic is light on weekdays and heavier on summer weekends. The weather matters more than the corners: afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, and snow can close or slow the high sections in winter and spring.

Practical matters are easy here. Questa has fuel and a handful of places for lunch, and Taos, about thirty kilometres south, is the larger town for anything more. Come in autumn if you can, when the aspens turn and the air has a snap to it. The quiet in the evening is real, with a smell of woodsmoke and piñon, and the stars arrive in numbers that remind you how far you are from a city.
t.lookout mountain@39.7,-105.2:
A few minutes from Golden's brewery smoke and red-brick downtown, the road tilts upward and begins a series of switchbacks that make Lookout Mountain Road feel like a proper mountain pass. The views build quickly: first the town and the creek below, then the whole Front Range plain spread out to the east, Denver's towers a faint cluster in the haze. On a clear evening the light on the city is worth the ride on its own.

This is the high point of the Lariat Loop, a scenic route built to showcase the mountains west of Denver. The road itself was completed in the early twentieth century, and it carries a lot of history. Near the summit is the grave of William F. Cody, better known as Buffalo Bill, who died in 1917 and asked, so the story goes, to be buried on a mountaintop overlooking the plains. A small museum beside the grave tells his story, with all its showmanship and some of its complications. Whatever you think of the legend, the site has a fine, windy outlook.

The riding is tight and rhythmic. The switchbacks are well-engineered and steady in gradient, but they are narrow, and the road is popular with cyclists who climb it as a training run, so take care on blind turns. Weekend mornings can be crowded. Early weekday rides or late evening runs are quieter and let you enjoy the corners, though in the dark you will want to watch for deer. Wind can be strong on the exposed bends near the top, and summer storms build quickly over the foothills.

Golden, three kilometres below, is a real town with fuel, groceries, and plenty of food. It is also the home of a famous brewery that gives tours, though a rider will prefer a coffee. The geology around here is worth a glance: tilted sandstone ridges, flatirons, and the dramatic mesa of North Table Mountain across the valley, all products of the uplift that created the Rockies. Pull off at the viewpoint, take a few photographs, and then go back down for lunch, remembering that the downhill needs your brakes more than the climb needed your throttle.
t.evergreen@39.6,-105.3:
Evergreen is the mountain town that Denver residents escape to, and you can feel it as soon as you arrive. Pine trees close in around the road, the elevation has crept above seven thousand feet, and the lake in the middle of town reflects aspen and sky. After the open prairie and the busy suburbs, this feels like a different state, and it takes only forty minutes by bike to get from one to the other.

The approach is the best part. Highway 74 follows Bear Creek through its canyon, with rocky walls, shaded curves, and a surface that is generally smooth and well-kept. The corners are flowing rather than fierce, and in the morning you may have it nearly to yourself. By midday the traffic fills in, with cyclists, cars, and the occasional slow truck. The loop around via Lookout Mountain and Morrison is easy to ride in either direction, though many riders prefer to arrive in Evergreen from the east so that the canyon comes at them fresh.

The town has roots in ranching, logging, and tourism, and it still feels half like a village and half like a suburb. A historic homestead, now a museum, tells the story of an early family who built a big mountain house here, and the lake offers a path for strolling. Elk are common around the edges of town, and in autumn the bulls can be loud and bold. Treat them with respect. Mount Blue Sky, once called Mount Evans, rises to the southwest, and its summit road is among the highest paved roads in North America, though it is seasonal and a separate commitment.

Practically, Evergreen is the place on this loop where you will find everything: fuel, grocery stores, bakeries, and a choice of restaurants and coffee shops along the main street. It is a good place to rest properly rather than snatch a sandwich. Kittredge, a smaller community nearby, is on the way back toward Morrison. Spring can bring surprise snow, and winter ice lingers on the north-facing corners of the canyon, so check the forecast. Late summer and early autumn are the easiest and most colourful seasons to ride.
t.morrison@39.7,-105.2:
Morrison is a small town squeezed into the mouth of a canyon, with high red sandstone walls on one side and the flat plain on the other. It is easy to ride through quickly, and that would be a mistake. The town sits at the edge of one of the most distinctive geological spots in Colorado, where the great tilted slabs of the Front Range come right up to the prairie like a row of rust-red sails.

Two things make the neighbourhood famous. Red Rocks Park, just up the road, holds an open-air amphitheatre set between giant sandstone monoliths, opened in the early 1940s and known worldwide as a concert venue. And the Morrison Formation, a layer of rock that gave its name to a vast swath of dinosaur country across the American West, was first described near here; the first big fossil finds of the late nineteenth century helped start the American dinosaur rush. Dinosaur Ridge, close by, still shows tracks in its tilted rock beds.

For riders, Morrison is the quiet corner of the Lariat Loop. Coming in from Evergreen, you follow Bear Creek down out of the mountains and drop into town with the canyon walls around you, then head north toward Golden on a road that runs along the foothills. The corners are gentle, the views of the plain are wide, and the traffic is thick on summer evenings when the amphitheatre has a show. If a concert is scheduled, expect backed-up roads and expensive parking, and plan your timing accordingly. Any other time, it is a pleasant, easy ride.

The town itself has a short main street of shops, cafes, and a few old stone buildings, and a stream running through. There are places to eat and drink but not a full-service stop for fuel, so use Evergreen or Golden, or the bigger suburb of Ken Caryl, to the southeast, for petrol and groceries. The light is best late in the afternoon, when the red rocks glow, and in spring the grass is green and the creek runs fast. In winter the road is usually clear, though shaded corners can hold ice for a while.
t.madrid new mexico@35.4,-106.2:
Madrid, pronounced the American way with the stress on the first syllable, is one of the more unlikely success stories in New Mexico. It began as a coal-mining town, with company housing strung along a narrow canyon in the Ortiz Mountains, and for a while it was known for its extravagant Christmas lights, which the coal company strung up each year and which could be seen from miles away. When the mines closed, the town was nearly abandoned. Artists began moving in during the 1970s, buying cheap cottages and turning the old storefronts into galleries and workshops, and the place found a second life.

Today the main street is a lively, slightly shabby, thoroughly enjoyable row of galleries, craft shops, cafes, and a saloon that has become a regular meeting place for motorcyclists. The town was used as a film set, notably for a comedy about a group of riders that did no harm to its reputation among them. On a sunny weekend the street fills with bikes, and the porch of the old tavern is a good place to watch them arrive.

The road is the Turquoise Trail, New Mexico 14, running between Albuquerque and Santa Fe along the east side of the Sandia Mountains. Between those cities it is a gentle ride rather than a technical one: rolling high-desert country with piñon and juniper, big views, and a surface that is generally good. Traffic is steady on weekends, and the speed limit drops sharply through the villages. Be careful of the gravel at the junctions and of wind gusts across the open stretches, which can be strong in spring.

Madrid is small, and fuel is not something to plan around. The reliable plan is to fill in Santa Fe or Albuquerque, or in one of the bigger communities on the way, and treat the village as a place for lunch, coffee, and a look around. Pastries and a decent cup are easy to find; a proper meal takes a little longer on busy days. Summer is hot at midday, so mornings and evenings are best, and winter brings occasional snow that closes nothing for long but can leave patches of ice on the shaded bends.
t.cerrillos@35.4,-106.1:
Cerrillos is the sleepy older sibling of Madrid, a dusty, unhurried little place a short ride away that feels like a film set because it has been used as one. Its wide main street of adobe and wooden storefronts, its church, and its dry hills all suggest the nineteenth-century frontier, and the village makes little effort to dress it up. Chickens, dogs, and cats are more in evidence than crowds, and that is part of the pleasure.

The reason there is a town at all is the rock. The low hills around here have been mined for turquoise for centuries, long before the Spanish arrived, and the Pueblo peoples traded the blue-green stone widely across the Southwest. Later came silver, lead, and coal, and the village boomed and faded as each ran out. Cerrillos Hills State Park, just beside the village, protects some of the old workings and has trails across the hills, with views toward the Sandias and the Ortiz range. A short walk is a good way to get a sense of the landscape's long history.

For a rider, the access is a short spur off the Turquoise Trail. The road in is narrow and quiet, and the village streets are slow, with gravel at the edges and the occasional pothole. It is a place to dawdle, not to hurry. The surrounding country is classic high desert: scattered piñon and juniper, red earth, and the kind of enormous sky that makes distances hard to judge. Late afternoon light on the hills is excellent, and the air smells of dust and sage after rain.

Cerrillos has a few small shops and cafes, but no real services for a motorcycle. Fuel is a matter for Santa Fe or one of the larger communities to the north or south; Eldorado is the nearest town of any size, about twenty kilometres away. Bring water, especially in summer, when the sun is fierce, and check the sky in the afternoon, when storms can build quickly over the mountains. Spring and autumn are the kindest seasons, and a winter morning can be crisp, bright, and almost empty of traffic.
t.bear creek falls@38.0,-107.7:
Between Ouray and Red Mountain Pass, the Million Dollar Highway does something that makes first-time riders slow right down: it clings to a cliff, with no guardrails in places, while a waterfall drops into the gorge beside it. Bear Creek Falls is that moment. The creek tumbles hundreds of feet from the heights above, passes beneath the road on a bridge, and then plunges into the canyon of the Uncompahgre River far below. A small pull-off lets you stop, though you should do it deliberately, because the traffic behind you will not.

The scenery is as dramatic as anything in Colorado. The San Juan Mountains here are young, steep, and cut by glaciers, and the walls of the canyon are layered rock in rust, grey, and cream. Ouray itself, a short ride north, sits in a deep bowl of peaks and is sometimes called the Switzerland of America, a title that feels more earned than most. Hot springs bubble up through the town, and an hour in one after a long day on the bike is a fine idea.

The ride here is the headline. US 550 south from Ouray is a narrow, winding mountain road, with tight bends, steep drops, and few places to recover from a mistake. The surface is generally good, but frost heaves, patches, and rockfall can appear. Weather changes quickly, and snow can arrive in any month at the top of Red Mountain Pass, which stands at a little over eleven thousand feet. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, so an early start is wise, and winter riding is not advisable.

Fuel and food are in Ouray, three or four kilometres away, which is a good small town for both. Telluride lies on the far side of the mountains by a different route, and Silverton is the next town beyond the pass. Park only where it is safe and legal at the falls, and keep a wide margin for the bend that follows. The light on the gorge is best in the late morning, and the best months are late June through September, with the aspens turning in the last weeks of that window.
t.truchas@36.0,-105.8:
Truchas clings to a ridge at around eight thousand feet in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, and from its edge the land drops away westward toward the Rio Grande valley in a vast spread of mesa and desert. Behind it the Truchas Peaks rise to over thirteen thousand feet. The name is Spanish for trout, from the streams that run off the mountains, and the village has a sense of being at the end of something, which in a way it is.

This is one of the oldest Hispanic settlements in the region, founded in the middle of the eighteenth century as a land grant community on the frontier. Families farmed small plots, grazed sheep, and wove wool, and the village has kept many of its traditions. Weavers and woodcarvers still work here, and a few galleries open to visitors. Robert Redford chose Truchas as a setting for the 1988 film The Milagro Beanfield War, and locals still talk about it, with the mix of pride and weariness that film attention tends to bring.

The High Road to Taos, New Mexico 76, is a rewarding ride, winding between small villages, orchards, and old adobe churches, with the mountains rising on one side and the big western views on the other. The curves are gentle and frequent, the surface is generally decent, and traffic is lighter than on the main highway through the Rio Grande gorge. Climbing up toward Truchas, the road tightens and the views widen. Beware of loose gravel at the edges, and of livestock and dogs on the road, since this is a working village.

There is little here in the way of services, and none you should rely on for fuel. Española, the closest larger town, is about twenty-five kilometres back toward the valley, and Chimayo is nearer but small. Bring water, and be prepared for weather: snow can fall in the high villages in any month except midsummer, and storms build in the afternoons. Autumn is excellent, when the aspens on the mountain slopes turn gold and the air has a crisp bite. The smell of woodsmoke in the evenings is one of the best things about it.
t.las trampas@36.1,-105.8:
Las Trampas is a village that is easy to ride through and very much worth stopping in. Its centrepiece is the church of San Jose de Gracia, a big adobe building with twin bell towers, built in the second half of the eighteenth century and still in use. It is regarded as one of the best-preserved Spanish colonial churches in the United States, and the simplicity of the building, with its thick walls, wooden beams, and carved details, has a power that more elaborate churches often lack.

The village was founded in the 1750s by families who took up land on the frontier between the Spanish settlements and the Plains. They were exposed to raids and the hardships of high-country life, and their descendants have stayed here for centuries. The fields are small, the irrigation ditches, or acequias, still carry water in the old way, and the houses are low adobe with tin roofs. It is a place that has changed slowly and has its own rhythm.

The High Road to Taos passes right through. New Mexico 76 here is a narrow, slowly climbing road with long curves, orchards and pastures on the lower slopes, and the mountains near at hand. It is a gentle ride, with enough bends to keep a rider interested, and the scenery is the real point. Watch for children, dogs, and the odd tractor in the village itself, and treat the speed limit with respect. In winter the road can be icy, especially in shaded corners, and spring brings a lot of grit and loose stone at the edges.

Do not expect services here. The village is small, and fuel or a full meal will be found elsewhere: Española is about thirty kilometres away on the valley road, and Chimayo is nearer but also small. If the church is open, step inside quietly, and remember that it is an active place of worship, not just a monument; visitor hours can be limited, and it is reasonable to ask in the village before assuming. Take water, and plan your day so that you are not hurrying the corners in the long, low light of late afternoon. Autumn light on the adobe is exceptional.
t.ranchos de taos@36.4,-105.6:
The church at Ranchos de Taos is one of the most photographed buildings in the American Southwest, and it deserves it. San Francisco de Asis is an adobe mission with massive buttresses, rounded and sculptural, that seem to flow out of the ground. Georgia O'Keeffe painted it several times, Ansel Adams photographed it, and generations of artists have tried to get its shape right. Every year or so, the community re-plasters it with fresh mud in a tradition that goes back generations, so what you see is partly the work of recent hands.

The village sits at the southern edge of the Taos Valley, with the Sangre de Cristo Mountains rising to the east and the vast sagebrush plain running west to the Rio Grande gorge. It is old farmland, once worked by Taos Pueblo and then by Spanish settlers in the eighteenth century, and a few ranches still graze the fields. The mountains on a clear morning are a strong blue, and the light is the reason so many painters settled here.

On the bike, Ranchos de Taos is the end of the High Road, the point where New Mexico 76 reaches the main highway, and the ride from Truchas and Las Trampas leaves you well prepared for a break. The road in is relaxed, and traffic through the village slows to a crawl on summer days, when tour buses and visitors crowd the church square. Go early for a quieter experience, and treat the pedestrians and cyclists with care. The high-desert wind can be strong across the open land, particularly in spring, and thunderstorms in summer arrive in the afternoons.

This is a good place to refuel in every sense. Taos, only six kilometres away, is a proper town with stations, restaurants, and supplies, and Ranchos de Taos has a number of small cafes and galleries of its own. If you can, walk around the back of the church, where the buttresses are most dramatic, and respect the notices about photography and services inside. Autumn is the best season, with clear air and golden cottonwoods along the creeks, and winter brings snow to the mountains and a quiet beauty to the valley.
t.the via appia across alban hills@41.7,12:
The Romans built the Appian Way straight as a ruler across the Campagna, but when it reached the Alban Hills, the old volcanic massif south-east of Rome, even they had to bend a little. At Ariccia, the road crossed a deep valley on a huge viaduct of stone blocks, parts of which still survive, and climbed past Albano and Genzano toward Velletri and the south. Ariccia and Albano Laziale, where the coordinates sit, are on the stretch of the Via Appia included in the UNESCO listing of Via Appia, Regina Viarum, inscribed in 2024.

The Alban Hills are the Castelli Romani, a ring of hill towns where Roman nobles and later popes built summer villas to escape the heat of the city. Castel Gandolfo, overlooking the crater lake of Albano, was the summer residence of the popes for centuries. In Ariccia, Bernini designed the main square and church, and the modern bridge across the valley offers dramatic views. The town is famous for porchetta, whole roast pork with herbs, sold in fraschette, simple taverns where you eat it with bread and local white wine.

Nearby, Lake Nemi, a smaller crater lake, was where the emperor Caligula kept two enormous ceremonial ships, recovered in the 1930s and later destroyed by fire during the Second World War. Nemi is also known for its tiny wild strawberries. Genzano holds the Infiorata, when the main street is carpeted with flower petals in elaborate designs.

For riders, the Castelli Romani offer winding roads through chestnut woods, vineyards and olive groves, with views over the lakes and the Roman plain. The roads can be busy, especially at weekends, when Romans flock to the hills, and town centres are narrow, with traffic restrictions. The SS7, the modern Via Appia, runs through Albano and Ariccia, and is a busy main road. Fuel and food are easy to find. Come on a weekday morning, ride around the crater rims, and stop for porchetta at lunch.
t.halfway house@36.4,-107.9:
The Chacoans built roads that do not seem to go anywhere. From Chaco Canyon, the centre of an extraordinary culture that flourished in the San Juan Basin of north-western New Mexico around a thousand years ago, a road known as the Great North Road runs almost due north for about fifty kilometres, straight as a ruler across mesas and washes, toward Kutz Canyon. Along it stand small great houses, and the site known as Halfway House is one of them, a stone structure about halfway along the road, possibly a waystation or a ceremonial marker. Chaco Culture, including outliers like this one, was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1987.

The Great North Road and its sites are on public and tribal land, and many are not open to the public or are difficult to reach, on rough dirt tracks across the desert. Respect closures and signs, do not disturb anything, and remember that these sites are sacred to the Pueblo and Navajo peoples. Chaco Culture National Historical Park, to the south, is the place to see the great houses, such as Pueblo Bonito, and the road to it is partly unpaved and can be impassable after rain.

The landscape is high desert, at around 1,900 metres, with sagebrush, juniper, sandstone mesas and wide skies. Summer is hot, with afternoon thunderstorms, and winter can be cold and snowy. The light is intense, especially at sunrise and sunset, when the mesas glow red and gold.

For riders, the area is about long distances and solitude. Highway 550 runs north-south through the basin, a fast road with little traffic, and fuel stations are far apart, so fill up whenever you can. Bloomfield, Aztec and Farmington, to the north, have fuel, shops and services. Carry water, and be aware that dirt roads can turn to deep mud after rain.
t.twin angels@36.6,-107.9:
South of Bloomfield, on the edge of the badlands of Kutz Canyon, a small Chacoan great house sits on a ridge with views over the San Juan Basin. Twin Angels Pueblo is one of the outliers of Chaco Culture, a stone building with rooms and a kiva, built around a thousand years ago by people connected with the great centre at Chaco Canyon, about eighty kilometres to the south. It lies near the end of the Great North Road, the long, straight Chacoan road running north from the canyon, and it is part of the UNESCO-listed Chaco Culture. It is managed by the Bureau of Land Management, and reached by a rough dirt road and a short hike.

Kutz Canyon is a maze of eroded badlands, grey and red clay hills, cut by washes, and it is a strange, beautiful landscape, especially in the low light of morning and evening. The Bisti/De-Na-Zin Wilderness, to the south-west, has even more spectacular badlands, with hoodoos and petrified wood.

Bloomfield, fifteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and services, and Salmon Ruins, a large Chacoan great house on the San Juan river, is in the town, with a museum. Aztec Ruins National Monument, a few kilometres north, has a reconstructed great kiva. Mesa Verde National Park, across the border in Colorado, with its cliff dwellings, is a couple of hours' ride away.

For riders, the area offers long, open roads through desert and mesas, with little traffic. Highway 550 and the roads around Farmington are good, and the dirt roads to the sites are rough and can be impassable after rain. Summer is hot, with thunderstorms, and winter can be cold. Carry water, leave every potsherd exactly where you find it, respect the sites, and enjoy the vast landscape and the night skies, which are among the darkest in the country.
t.piazza del duomo@43.7,10.4:
Nothing prepares you for that first glimpse through the gateway. A wide green lawn, and set on it like ornaments on a cloth, the white marble cathedral, the round baptistery, the cemetery cloister of the Camposanto, and of course the bell tower, leaning at an angle that looks wrong no matter how many photographs you have seen. The Piazza del Duomo in Pisa, also called the Field of Miracles, was one of the first places in Italy to be listed by UNESCO, back in 1987.

The buildings date from the eleventh to the fourteenth centuries, when Pisa was a rich maritime republic trading across the Mediterranean, and they were built partly with the spoils of its wars. The tower began to tilt soon after construction started in the late twelfth century, because the ground beneath it is soft, and work stopped and started over almost two centuries. Engineers stabilised it in a major project around the turn of the millennium, and you can climb the worn spiral stairs to the top if you book ahead. Galileo was born in Pisa, and legend says he dropped weights from the tower to study falling bodies, though historians doubt the story.

Riding into Pisa requires a little care. The historic centre has limited traffic zones, the ZTL, monitored by cameras, and entering without permission brings fines that may follow you home months later. Park at the edge, in designated motorcycle areas, and walk the last few hundred metres. The roads around are mostly flat and busy, but the hills to the east, the Monte Pisano, offer winding routes towards Lucca, and the coast road towards Livorno and beyond leads to some of Tuscany's best riding further south.

Pisa will not leave you short of a pump or a meal. The area around the piazza is crowded with souvenir stalls and street vendors, so step a few blocks away for better food at better prices. Try cecina, a thin chickpea flatbread baked in wood ovens, and walk along the Arno in the evening, when the palaces glow in the low light and the crowds by the tower thin out.
t.torre annunziata villa a@40.8,14.5:
In the busy, scruffy town of Torre Annunziata, on the coast south of Naples, a high wall hides one of the most extraordinary Roman villas ever found. Villa A at Oplontis, often called the Villa of Poppaea because it is thought to have belonged to the family of Nero's second wife, was buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in 79 and rediscovered in the eighteenth century, with large-scale excavations in the twentieth. It is part of the UNESCO site that includes Pompeii and Herculaneum, but sees a fraction of their visitors, which is one of its great pleasures.

The villa is huge, with dozens of rooms, gardens, a swimming pool and porticoes, and its walls are covered in some of the finest Roman frescoes anywhere: painted architectural perspectives, gardens full of birds, masks, still lifes and peacocks, in vivid reds, yellows and blues. Walking through the rooms, almost alone, you can imagine the luxurious life of the Roman elite on the Bay of Naples. Above it all looms Vesuvius, still very much active and closely monitored, a reminder of the forces that preserved this place.

Torre Annunziata has a long history of pasta making, with mills and drying racks once lining its streets, and the whole area is packed with towns, roads and people. Riding here is chaotic and demanding, with dense traffic, scooters weaving in all directions, potholes and creative interpretations of the rules. Keep calm, stay alert and keep your bike secure when parked. The rewards come with a ride up Vesuvius, on a road that climbs through vineyards and lava fields to a car park near the crater, or along the Sorrento peninsula and the Amalfi coast, among the most spectacular coastal roads in Europe, though traffic in summer can be intense.

Fuel stations are plentiful, and the town has bars and pizzerias. Neapolitan pizza, born just up the coast, is the obvious order, along with fresh pasta dishes with tomatoes from the volcanic soil, seafood and sfogliatella, a crisp pastry filled with ricotta. Visit in spring or autumn to avoid the summer heat and crowds.
t.evaporitic karst and caves of northern a:
Gypsum dissolves in water far faster than limestone, and in the upper valley of the Secchia, in the Reggio Emilia Apennines, that simple fact has produced a strange landscape of white cliffs, sinkholes, caves and underground rivers. The Evaporitic Karst and Caves of the Northern Apennines were added to the World Heritage list in 2023, and this area near Castelnovo ne' Monti and Villa Minozzo holds some of the most striking outcrops, ancient Triassic gypsum that glitters in the sun and forms steep walls above the river. Near the Secchia, the springs of Poiano gush out of the rock with a strong flow of slightly salty water, fed by the karst system.

The great landmark of the area is the Pietra di Bismantova, a sheer-sided sandstone block rising above Castelnovo ne' Monti like a stranded ship. It is visible from miles around, and Dante mentioned it in the Divine Comedy, comparing the steep climb of Purgatory to the effort of reaching its summit. Today it is a popular spot for climbers and walkers, and there is a small hermitage at its foot.

The riding in these mountains is excellent. The main road through Castelnovo ne' Monti, the SS63, climbs from the Po plain towards the Passo del Cerreto and on into Tuscany, with long, flowing bends, good surfaces and fine views over the Apennines. The smaller roads that branch off towards Villa Minozzo and the Secchia valley are narrower and twistier, with steep gradients, tight hairpins and occasional rough patches. Traffic is light during the week, but busier on summer weekends with riders and day trippers from the cities.

Castelnovo ne' Monti, a town of about ten thousand people, is the main centre of the area, with fuel, shops and restaurants. This is Parmigiano Reggiano country, and the cheese from the mountain dairies is especially prized. Look also for tortelli filled with herbs, potatoes or pumpkin, and for the local cured meats. Mountain weather can change quickly, and winter brings snow to the higher roads, so check conditions before setting out. In autumn, the beech and chestnut woods turn spectacular shades of gold and red.
t.teatro dell aquila@43.2,13.7:
Fermo sits on a hill above the Adriatic, and its theatre is the jewel inside the town. The Teatro dell'Aquila was built in the late eighteenth century, designed by the architect Cosimo Morelli, and it is one of the largest and finest historic theatres in the Marche, a region that has an extraordinary number of them, almost every town having its own little opera house. Inside, tiers of gilded boxes rise in a horseshoe around the stalls, and the painted ceiling glows above. If you can catch a performance, or join a guided visit, do so.

The town itself rewards a slow walk. The Piazza del Popolo, long and arcaded, is one of the most elegant squares in the region, and the cathedral sits on top of the hill, at the Girfalco, with a view stretching from the Adriatic to the Sibillini mountains. Under the town lie the Roman cisterns, a vast system of interconnected chambers built to collect and purify water, which can be visited and are cool and atmospheric on a hot day.

For riding, the Marche is underrated. The hills between the coast and the Apennines are crossed by a dense network of quiet roads, linking hilltop towns and villages, with endless bends, short climbs and wide views over fields of sunflowers, wheat and vines. The roads are generally good, though the smaller ones can be rough and narrow. Inland, the Sibillini mountains offer more dramatic riding, with high passes, plateaus and the great Piano Grande near Castelluccio, famous for its flowering lentil fields in early summer, although the area is still recovering from the earthquakes of 2016.

Fermo, a town of about eighteen thousand people, has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants. The coast, at Porto San Giorgio and Lido di Fermo, is only a short ride away, with beaches and seafood. The local cuisine includes vincisgrassi, a rich baked pasta dish similar to lasagne, and the famous olive all'ascolana, stuffed and fried olives from nearby Ascoli Piceno. Summer can be hot on the coast, but the hills are cooler, and the evenings are perfect for a ride with the sun setting over the mountains.
t.the via appia in fundi@41.4,13.4:
The Via Appia, the queen of Roman roads, runs straight through the middle of Fondi, and the town's grid of streets still follows the plan of the Roman settlement it once was. Built from 312 BC to link Rome with Capua and later extended to Brindisi, the Appia crossed the coastal plain here, between the mountains and the sea, and Fondi grew up around it as a stopping place. In the historic centre, the main street follows the line of the ancient road, and stretches of the Roman walls survive, built of huge polygonal blocks. The Via Appia was recognised by UNESCO in 2024 as a World Heritage Site, with Fondi as one of its components.

The town has more to offer than the Roman road. The Castello Caetani, a medieval castle with a tall round keep, stands at the edge of the old town, and the noble Caetani family left their mark on many buildings. Fondi today is also known for its huge wholesale fruit and vegetable market, one of the largest in Europe, which supplies much of Italy with produce from the surrounding plain.

The modern road that follows the line of the Appia, the SS7, is busy and not particularly exciting to ride, with heavy traffic and plenty of trucks. But the roads that climb into the Ausoni and Aurunci mountains around Fondi are a different story, with narrow, winding routes through olive groves and oak woods, small villages and wide views over the plain and the sea. Lenola, about six kilometres away, is a hill village with a sanctuary and a good view.

The coast is close by, with the lagoon-like Lake of Fondi and the beaches of the Riviera di Ulisse, named after Ulysses, who according to legend stopped here on his travels. Sperlonga, a white hilltop village above the sea, has the ruins of a villa built by the emperor Tiberius, with a grotto where spectacular sculptures were found. Terracina and Gaeta are other fine towns along the coast. Fondi has fuel, shops and restaurants, and the local food includes buffalo mozzarella, fresh vegetables and seafood. Summers are hot, so the mountain roads are best in the morning or evening.
t.diamantina@44.9,11.5:
The Este dukes of Ferrara loved their countryside retreats, the delizie, and they scattered them across the flat land around the city like jewels on a cloth. The Diamantina, near Vigarano Pieve west of Ferrara, was one of them, an estate of farmland, woods and buildings named after the diamond, a symbol of the Este family. The delizie are part of the UNESCO listing of Ferrara, City of the Renaissance, and its Po Delta, which recognises the city's planned urban layout and the way the Este shaped the surrounding landscape, draining marshes and creating farms and hunting grounds.

Ferrara itself, a short ride away, is one of the great Renaissance cities of Italy, with a massive moated castle in the centre, a cathedral, and a perfectly preserved ring of walls that you can ride around, or better, walk or cycle on top of. In the late fifteenth century, Duke Ercole I commissioned the architect Biagio Rossetti to design a new quarter, the Addizione Erculea, with wide straight streets and elegant palaces, one of the first examples of modern urban planning in Europe.

The riding in the Po plain is flat and straight, through fields of wheat, maize, fruit trees and rice, with long roads running along the embankments of rivers and canals. It is not exciting, but it has a certain hypnotic charm, especially in the early morning, when the mist rises from the fields and the poplars stand like ghosts. In winter, dense fog can settle for days, making riding dangerous, and the summer can be hot and humid, with mosquitoes near the water. Watch out for tractors and cyclists, who are everywhere in this flat land.

Bondeno, about seven kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel and shops, while Ferrara has everything you could need. The local food is rich and distinctive: cappellacci filled with pumpkin, salama da sugo, a spiced pork sausage cooked for hours, and the coppia ferrarese, a twisted bread with protected status. Further east, the Po Delta is a world of lagoons, marshes and flamingos, with quiet roads along the dykes and the sea on the horizon, a fine destination for a gentle ride.
t.teatro serpente aureo@42.9,13.7:
Offida sits on a ridge in the southern Marche, a small walled town of brick and stone looking across rolling hills towards the Adriatic in one direction and the Monti Sibillini in the other. In the arcaded town hall on the main square hides one of the region's many jewel-box theatres, the Serpente Aureo, the Golden Serpent, with its horseshoe of boxes, gilded decoration and painted ceiling. The Marche has dozens of these little opera houses, built when every proud town wanted its own stage, and this one is among the prettiest, small enough that you feel you are in someone's very ornate living room.

Offida is also famous for lace. Women here have worked bobbin lace, merletto a tombolo, for centuries, and you may still see them on doorsteps, bobbins clicking, turning out delicate patterns. At the end of town, the Gothic church of Santa Maria della Rocca stands on a rocky spur, its brick bulk and crypt frescoes giving a sense of the place's medieval importance. The local wines carry the town's name: Offida Pecorino and Offida Passerina whites and robust Rosso Piceno reds, and the carnival in February is a lively, ancient tradition.

The riding in this part of the Piceno is a constant roller coaster of small ridges and valleys, the roads climbing to hilltop towns and dipping into river valleys planted with vines and olives. Bends are frequent but rarely extreme, surfaces are mostly decent with some rough stretches, and traffic is light outside the busy valley roads near the coast. The views shift constantly between the sea and the mountains, and in late spring, when the fields are green and the poppies are out, the landscape is gorgeous. Winter brings fog in the valleys.

There is fuel in Offida and in the larger towns in the Tronto valley below; Ascoli Piceno, with its travertine squares, is a short ride away. Stop for olive all'ascolana, stuffed and fried olives that are the local snack, and a glass of Pecorino in one of the bars on the square. The theatre is not always open, but it can sometimes be visited, and it is worth asking at the town hall if the doors are shut.
t.gessi di onferno@43.9,12.5:
The hills behind Rimini hide a surprising piece of geology. Around the hamlet of Onferno, in the comune of Gemmano, the ground is made of gypsum, laid down when the Mediterranean dried out millions of years ago and then pushed up into these ridges. Water dissolves gypsum easily, so the landscape is pocked with sinkholes, blind valleys and caves, and the Grotta di Onferno winds for hundreds of metres beneath the village. The name is often linked to inferno, supposedly because vapour rising from the cave mouth in cold weather looked like the breath of hell.

The cave is the heart of a regional nature reserve and shelters a large colony of bats, several species of them, which pour out at dusk in summer. Guided visits run through galleries of glittering gypsum crystals and odd formations, cool even in August. Above ground the reserve is a patchwork of oak woods, scrub, meadows full of orchids in spring and abandoned terraces. In September 1944 these quiet ridges were the scene of savage fighting on the Gothic Line, when British troops battled for days to take Gemmano, and the area is sometimes called the Cassino of the Adriatic.

For riders, the Valconca behind the Adriatic Riviera is a fine playground, ignored by most of the beach crowd below. Narrow roads climb from the Conca valley through Mercatino Conca, Montescudo and Gemmano, with tight bends, steep pitches and sudden views of castles on hilltops: Montefiore Conca's fortress is close, and San Marino's three towers loom on Monte Titano just to the north. The tarmac is patchy in places and gravel collects on bends after rain. Spring and early autumn are perfect; summer weekends bring more traffic as people escape the coast.

Morciano di Romagna, nine kilometres away, is the nearest proper town with fuel, shops and a market. The hill villages have a bar or two, and the piadina, the flatbread of Romagna filled with ham, squacquerone cheese and rocket, is the obvious lunch. If you visit the cave, bring a light jacket, and note that visits are guided and timed, so check before you plan around one. Rimini's beaches and nightlife are only half an hour away if the evening needs livening up.
t.sasso fratino@43.8,11.8:
Sasso Fratino is a forest you are not allowed to enter, and that is precisely the point. High on the Romagna side of the Apennine ridge, in the national park of the Casentino forests, it was declared Italy's first integral nature reserve in 1959, and since then nature has been left almost entirely to itself. Ancient beech woods cling to steep slopes, with silver fir, maple and ash mixed in, and dead trees are left to rot where they fall, feeding fungi, beetles and birds. In 2017 it became part of the transnational World Heritage listing of ancient beech forests of Europe.

The surrounding park is open, and it is one of the wildest corners of central Italy. Wolves have returned, deer are everywhere, and in autumn the rutting stags bellow through the woods at dusk, a sound that stops you in your tracks. The monastery and hermitage at Camaldoli, founded by Saint Romuald around a thousand years ago, sit in the fir forest on the Tuscan side, and the sanctuary of La Verna, where Saint Francis is said to have received the stigmata, stands on its cliff not far away. Mount Falterona, where the Arno rises, is just to the north.

The roads through here are superb. From Stia and Pratovecchio in the upper Casentino, the road climbs to the Passo della Calla on the ridge and drops down the Romagna side to Santa Sofia, with an endless succession of bends through dense forest. Other routes to Camaldoli, Badia Prataglia and La Verna are just as twisty. Surfaces can be rough, wet leaves make the corners treacherous in autumn, and fog and snow are common in winter, when the pass can be closed. The light filtering through the beeches in October is something special.

Pratovecchio and Stia are the nearest villages, small but with services, and Bibbiena, down in the valley, is the place for a full tank and a choice of trattorias. Casentino specialities include tortelli stuffed with potato, mushrooms in season, and the thick wool cloth once woven at Stia. Respect the closed reserve and enjoy the forest from the many trails around it.
t.monte cimino@42.4,12.2:
Monte Cimino is the highest point of the Cimini hills, an old volcanic range rising to just over a thousand metres between Viterbo and the Tiber valley in northern Lazio. Its top is clothed in one of the most beautiful beech forests in Italy, unusually low for beech in this latitude, and UNESCO counts these trees among Europe's ancient beech forests. On a hot summer day, climbing into its shade from the baking plain feels like entering a cathedral.

Near the summit lies the Sasso Menicante, a huge block of volcanic rock balanced so finely that, according to tradition, it could be rocked by a person's push. Pliny the Elder mentioned it. Below the mountain, on its western side, the Lago di Vico fills an ancient caldera, a round lake surrounded by forest and hazelnut groves, protected as a nature reserve. Hazelnuts are the main crop of the whole area; you will see orchards of them everywhere, and chestnuts too, which are celebrated in autumn festivals.

The Romans regarded the Ciminian forest as dark and impenetrable, and Livy describes the army hesitating at its edge during the war against the Etruscans. Today the hill towns around it are among the most charming in Lazio. Soriano nel Cimino is crowned by a massive Orsini castle, Caprarola has the extraordinary pentagonal Villa Farnese, and Canepina and Vallerano are quiet villages of grey stone.

For riders this is a superb playground. The roads climbing from Viterbo, Soriano and Ronciglione to the summit and around Lago di Vico are twisty, well graded and lightly trafficked on weekdays, with a mix of tight hairpins in the forest and faster bends through the orchards. Watch out for leaves and moss on shaded corners, hazelnut harvest machinery in late summer, and local riders who know every bend. Soriano nel Cimino, with five and a half thousand people, has fuel, bars and restaurants; Viterbo is a larger city with everything. Try the local pork, chestnut dishes in autumn, and the wines of the nearby Lake Bolsena area. Rome is less than an hour and a half away, so the Cimini make a great escape from the capital.
t.via appia regina viarum@41.3,13.3:
Terracina is the point where the Via Appia, the queen of roads, meets the sea after its long straight run from Rome across the Pontine plain. The Romans built the road in 312 BC under the censor Appius Claudius, and for its time it was a marvel: paved, drained and as straight as engineering allowed, linking Rome to Capua and later to Brindisi. The stretch through the Pontine marshes was notorious for mosquitoes and malaria, and travellers often took a canal boat alongside the road instead, as the poet Horace describes in one of his satires.

Here the road hit an obstacle: the Monte Sant'Angelo, whose spur, the Pisco Montano, dropped straight into the sea. In the early second century the emperor Trajan had his engineers cut through the rock to carry the road along the shore, removing a vertical wall of limestone some thirty-six metres high. The cut is still there, with Roman numerals carved into it at intervals marking the depth, and you can stand beside it and marvel. High above town, on the mountain, the ruins of the Temple of Jupiter Anxur look out over the coast with a view that stretches to Circeo and the islands.

The Pontine plain itself was drained and settled under Mussolini in the 1930s, and the new towns built then, Latina, Sabaudia and Pontinia, have a distinctive rationalist architecture. The Appia's modern successor, the SS7, still runs dead straight for tens of kilometres across the plain, lined with eucalyptus and pine trees; it is fast, monotonous and full of lorries, but there is something haunting about following a route that is over two thousand years old.

Terracina, a lively seaside town of thirty thousand people, has everything: fuel stations, beaches, a fish market and restaurants serving clams and fresh seafood. The coast road west towards Sabaudia and Monte Circeo, with dunes on one side and lagoons on the other, is a pleasant ride, while the hills inland towards Sonnino and the Monti Ausoni have tight, quiet roads with lovely views. Summer weekends bring heavy beach traffic from Rome, so plan accordingly.
t.kin ya a@35.7,-108.1:
A broken stone tower rising out of the sagebrush is what you see first at Kin Ya'a, and it is one of the strangest sights in the Southwest. This was a Chacoan great house, built in the eleventh and twelfth centuries by the same Ancestral Puebloan culture that raised the monumental buildings of Chaco Canyon, some forty kilometres to the north. What makes Kin Ya'a special is its tower kiva, a round ceremonial room built up four storeys high, much of which still stands. Its name is Navajo and is usually translated as tall house. It is one of the outlying sites included in the World Heritage listing of Chaco Culture, linked to the canyon by what archaeologists believe was a formal road.

The country is wide, high and empty: the eastern edge of the Navajo Nation in northwestern New Mexico, about two thousand metres above sea level, with mesas, sandstone cliffs, sagebrush flats and enormous skies. Crownpoint, the nearest community, is a small town that is the administrative centre for the Eastern Navajo Agency, and it is famous for its regular Navajo rug auctions, where weavers sell directly to buyers.

Getting here is an adventure. The last stretch to the ruin is on unpaved roads and tracks that range from well graded gravel to rutted sand, and when wet the clay turns into a slick, sticky mess that is close to impossible on a road bike. Check conditions locally, ask permission where needed, and be aware that much of the land around is Navajo Nation or allotted land, where respect and permission matter. Never climb on the walls or collect anything; these sites are fragile and protected by law.

Services are thin. Crownpoint has a few shops and basic facilities, and the nearest dependable fuel and food are along Interstate 40 at Thoreau or in Gallup, a sizable town further west. NM 371 runs north from Thoreau through Crownpoint to Farmington, a long, lonely road with wonderful views and almost no traffic. Carry plenty of water, check the weather, especially in the summer monsoon season, when afternoon thunderstorms can be violent, and plan your fuel before you set out. At sunset, the tower glows red against the sky.
t.pierre s site@36.2,-107.9:
North of Chaco Canyon, the Ancestral Puebloans built something that still puzzles archaeologists: a road. Not a trail, but a wide, carefully engineered path, about nine metres wide in places, running almost dead straight north across the desert for some fifty kilometres. It is known as the Great North Road, and Pierre's site sits right on it. This is a cluster of small structures built on and around a prominent sandstone outcrop, including what may have been signalling stations or shrines on top of the hill, and from its height you can see far across the San Juan Basin. Like Kin Ya'a to the south, it is protected as one of the Chaco outliers on the World Heritage list.

Why the road went north, to an empty canyon edge at Kutz Canyon, is the mystery. Some archaeologists think it had a symbolic or religious purpose, connecting Chaco to a sacred direction or to the place of origin in Puebloan tradition, rather than being a practical trade route. Seen from the air or in low light, its faint line across the land is still visible. Twin Angels, another small Chacoan site, lies nearby.

The country here is badlands and mesas, grey and buff clay hills eroded into strange shapes, sagebrush flats and wide horizons. It looks barren, but in spring there are wildflowers, and at any time of year you may see pronghorn, coyotes and hawks. The weather is extreme: hot in summer, cold in winter, with sudden storms and strong winds.

Access is by dirt roads off US 550, the highway between Cuba and Bloomfield, and they become impassable when wet. This is Bureau of Land Management land, but there are no facilities at the site and very few signs; a GPS track, local advice and plenty of water are essential. Do not climb on structures or remove anything. For fuel, food and accommodation, Bloomfield, Aztec and Farmington to the north are the closest towns, and Aztec has its own impressive Chacoan great house at Aztec Ruins National Monument, inscribed together with Chaco itself. US 550 itself is a good, fast road across the high desert, with wide curves and little traffic outside the towns.
t.vatican city@41.9,12.5:
The smallest state in the world is about forty-four hectares of walled hill on the right bank of the Tiber, and somehow it contains the largest church in Christendom, one of the greatest art collections ever assembled and a population that would barely fill a village. The Vatican exists as an independent country since the Lateran Treaty of 1929 between the Holy See and Mussolini's Italy, but the popes have been building here for far longer. St Peter's Basilica stands over the traditional site of the apostle's grave, and its dome, designed by Michelangelo, dominates the skyline of western Rome. Bernini's colonnade, sweeping round the square like two great arms, was meant to embrace every visitor who arrived.

Inside the Vatican Museums you walk past ancient sculpture, Raphael's rooms and at the end the Sistine Chapel, with its ceiling and the Last Judgement. Go early and expect queues anyway. For the basilica, a simple rule: shoulders and knees covered, or you will not get in, which is easy enough in riding kit and less so in shorts.

Riding into Rome is a sport for people with quick reflexes. Scooters swarm around you, lanes are a suggestion and the horn is a form of conversation. The good news is that Rome is very motorcycle-friendly in one important way: two-wheelers can park in many places where cars cannot, and spaces near the Vatican are reasonably easy to find. The bad news is the ZTL, the limited traffic zones of the historic centre, watched by cameras that send fines to foreign owners months later; study the rules before you enter, because they differ for motorcycles and change with time of day. The Lungotevere along the river is a lovely way to cross the city in the evening, when the traffic thins.

To escape, head north-west on the Via Aurelia or the Via Trionfale over Monte Mario, the highest hill in Rome, and then out towards Lake Bracciano and the beech forests of Monte Raschio near Oriolo Romano, part of the ancient beech forest heritage site. In the other direction the old Via Appia leads south past tombs and catacombs to the Alban Hills. Fuel is plentiful throughout Rome. For food, step a few streets away from the Vatican walls to Prati, where the prices drop and the quality rises.
t.assisi@43.1,12.6:
From the valley floor Assisi looks like a long pale ribbon draped across the lower slope of Monte Subasio, and the colour comes from the mountain itself. The town is built of Subasio stone, a limestone that ranges from cream to rose, and in the evening light the whole place glows pink. It is, of course, the town of Francis, the merchant's son who gave away everything in the early thirteenth century and founded the Franciscan order, and of Clare, who followed him. The great basilica built over his tomb, begun in 1228, has two churches one above the other, and the frescoes inside, including the cycle of the saint's life traditionally attributed to Giotto, changed the course of European painting.

In 1997 an earthquake brought down part of the vault of the upper church, killing four people inside, and the restoration that followed, piecing together tens of thousands of fragments, is a story of extraordinary patience. Down on the plain, Santa Maria degli Angeli is an enormous later basilica built around the Porziuncola, the tiny chapel where Francis began his community and where he died.

For riding, the Umbrian valley around Assisi is gentle and pretty, but the real treat is Monte Subasio. A road climbs from the town past the Eremo delle Carceri, the hermitage where Francis went to pray, and on up through woods onto the open grassy top of the mountain, then down towards Spello or Collepino. It is narrow, with tight bends and some rough patches, and the views over the valley towards Perugia and the Apennines are superb. Elsewhere, the roads to Gualdo Tadino and Nocera Umbra climb into quieter, greener hills, and south past Spello and Foligno you reach the Fonti del Clitunno and its little Lombard-era temple.

The historic centre of Assisi is a limited traffic zone, so leave the bike at one of the car parks below the walls and walk; the lanes are steep and the paving can be slippery when wet. Santa Maria degli Angeli has fuel and supermarkets, and the town has plenty of trattorias. Try strangozzi, thick hand-rolled pasta often served with black truffle or a simple tomato sauce, and a glass of Sagrantino from Montefalco, on the hill across the valley.
t.the via appia on the route from benevent:
East of Benevento, the Via Appia leaves the Calore valley and heads into the green, rolling hills of Irpinia on its long way to Brindisi, and near Venticano and Pietradefusi you are travelling over one of its quieter stretches. The road the Romans laid here is mostly lost under fields and later tracks, but the line still guides the landscape, and a short way south-east lie the remains of Aeclanum, near Mirabella Eclano, a Roman town that grew rich on the traffic. Benevento itself was the great junction: from here the original Appia ran over the hills to Venusia and Tarentum, while the Emperor Trajan built a faster route, the Via Traiana, through the plains of Apulia. His triumphal arch, raised in AD 114, still stands in Benevento, its reliefs remarkably sharp.

This is wine country first and foremost. The hills around Venticano and Taurasi produce Taurasi, a powerful red from the Aglianico grape, and the white wines of Greco di Tufo and Fiano di Avellino come from just to the west. Vineyards share the slopes with hazelnut groves and wheat, and small towns perch on the ridges above. Benevento has its own legends: for centuries it was said that witches gathered under a walnut tree by the river, and the town's famous yellow liqueur, Strega, takes its name from them.

The A16 motorway between Naples and Canosa passes close by, but it is the minor roads that make the area worth riding. The old SS7 and the provincial roads between villages roll over the hills in wide, open bends, then tighten into hairpins as they climb into hilltop towns. Traffic is light, surfaces are mixed, and in places landslips have left wavy patches or narrowed lanes, typical of this part of southern Italy. Irpinia is earthquake country, and the 1980 earthquake left deep scars; some villages were rebuilt in new locations, which can make old maps misleading.

Venticano and the other villages here are small, so for fuel and supplies look to San Giorgio del Sannio, a few kilometres north, or Benevento itself, which also offers a fine old centre with a Lombard church, Santa Sofia. Lunch should involve local cheese, cured meats and pasta with a slow-cooked meat ragù, and if you can get a seat in a family trattoria on a Sunday, do so.
t.casamero@35.4,-108.1:
Casamero is a small sandstone pueblo on the edge of a valley below the red cliffs of north-western New Mexico, near Prewitt and Thoreau, and it was built about a thousand years ago by people connected to the great Chaco culture. It is one of the Chacoan outliers, communities that shared the architecture, pottery and probably the beliefs of the great houses of Chaco Canyon, more than eighty kilometres to the north, and that were connected to them by a network of straight roads. The walls of Casamero, made of carefully laid stone, still stand to a good height, with the outlines of rooms and a great kiva, a large round ceremonial chamber, nearby. It is part of the Chaco Culture World Heritage site.

The landscape around is classic high desert. Red and buff sandstone mesas rise above valleys of sagebrush and juniper, and to the south-east, Mount Taylor, a volcano sacred to the Navajo and the Pueblo peoples, dominates the horizon. The sky is enormous, the light is clear, and the summer monsoon brings dramatic thunderstorms in the afternoons, with lightning and sudden downpours that can flood dirt roads. Winter nights are cold, and snow is not unusual.

The main road through the area is Interstate 40, which follows the route of the old Route 66 across New Mexico. Sections of the old road still run alongside the interstate, through small towns like Thoreau, Prewitt and Milan, and they are a much more enjoyable way to travel, with less traffic and a sense of history. North of Thoreau, the road to Crownpoint, on the Navajo Nation, crosses open plains and mesa country; Crownpoint is known for its Navajo rug auctions. The road to Chaco Canyon itself includes long stretches of rough dirt, best avoided after rain on a heavy bike. Wind can be fierce on the open plains.

The nearest fuel and supplies are in Thoreau, and the town of Grants, about thirty-five kilometres east, has more choice, including motels and restaurants. Try New Mexican food, with green or red chile on almost everything, and a Navajo taco, fry bread topped with beans, meat and vegetables. Carry plenty of water, as services are few and far between.
t.villa d este@42.0,12.8:
Cardinal Ippolito II d'Este, son of Lucrezia Borgia, had expected to become pope. When that did not happen, he was made governor of Tivoli and consoled himself by turning an old Benedictine convent on the hillside into a villa with a garden that would astonish Europe. Built in the sixteenth century, the Villa d'Este is a hillside of terraces, stairs and fountains, all fed by gravity from the river Aniene: the Hundred Fountains, a long wall of spouting masks and eagles, the Fountain of the Organ, which plays music driven by water, and the Oval Fountain, with its cascade falling into a pool. The villa and its gardens are a World Heritage Site.

Tivoli sits on the slopes of the Monti Tiburtini, east of Rome, above the plain of the Aniene, and it has been a resort since Roman times. Below the town, the Villa Adriana, the vast country palace of the emperor Hadrian, is another World Heritage Site, with ruins of pools, theatres, baths and libraries spread over a huge area. The Villa Gregoriana, with its gorge and waterfalls, is another sight in town.

Riding from Rome to Tivoli on the Via Tiburtina is slow and busy, with traffic and lights, but the climb into the hills beyond Tivoli is more rewarding. The roads into the Monti Simbruini and toward Subiaco, where Saint Benedict founded his first monasteries, twist through valleys and mountains, with good surfaces and views. The Valle dell'Aniene is especially lovely.

Tivoli has petrol stations on its approach roads and no shortage of trattorias. In the town's restaurants, try pasta all'amatriciana or cacio e pepe, and the local wines from the hills. The Villa d'Este is busy, especially on weekends, and the gardens are at their best in spring and early summer, when the fountains sparkle in the sunshine. Parking near the villa can be tight, so arrive early.
t.the system of italian style condominio t:
The Marche has more historic theatres per head than almost anywhere in Italy. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, almost every hill town built its own opera house, often paid for by local families who then owned their boxes, like apartments in a condominium, and passed them down through generations. The result is a network of jewel box theatres in small towns, with tiers of boxes, painted ceilings and gilded stucco, many of them restored and still in use. San Severino Marche, a few kilometres away, has the Teatro Feronia, one of these, and the network of such theatres across the region has been put forward for World Heritage recognition.

San Severino itself is a lovely town, with an elongated piazza ringed by porticoes, the Piazza del Popolo, and an old upper town on the hill with a cathedral and tower. The Pinacoteca has works by the local painters Lorenzo and Jacopo Salimbeni. Matelica, to the north, is known for its white wine, Verdicchio di Matelica, and Castelraimondo for its medieval tower.

The landscape here is the heart of the Marche: rolling hills of wheat, sunflowers and vineyards, with the Apennines rising to the west and the Sibillini mountains to the south. The hill towns are close together, each on its own ridge, and the roads between them are a delight.

For riders, the Marche is one of the best kept secrets in Italy. The roads twist over hills and through valleys, with good surfaces, light traffic and endless views. The Sibillini, an hour's ride south, offer mountain roads of real quality, including the climb to the Piano Grande at Castelluccio, where the lentil fields bloom in early summer. The area was hit by earthquakes in 2016, and some roads and villages are still being repaired, so check routes.

San Severino Marche covers the practical side, with pumps and places to eat, as do Matelica and Castelraimondo. Local food includes vincisgrassi, a rich baked pasta, ciauscolo, a soft spreadable salami, and porchetta. A night at one of the old theatres, if there is a performance, is a memorable way to end the day.
t.montecatini terme@43.9,10.8:
The water at Montecatini has been drunk for health since the Middle Ages, but it was in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries that the town became one of the great spa resorts of Europe, with grand thermal establishments built in neoclassical, Liberty and Art Deco styles, set in parks of plane trees and pines. The Tettuccio, with its marble colonnades and frescoes, is the most famous, a temple of water where visitors drink from taps along a counter. In 2021 Montecatini became part of the Great Spa Towns of Europe World Heritage Site, alongside Baden-Baden, Bath, Vichy and others.

The town is a place of hotels, gardens and wide avenues, built for a leisured clientele that included Verdi, Puccini and a long list of celebrities. A funicular, opened in the late nineteenth century, climbs from the town to Montecatini Alto, the medieval hill town above, with its piazza, cafés and views over the Valdinievole and the plain toward Florence.

The Valdinievole is a lovely area, with hill towns, olive groves and villas. Pescia, nearby, is a centre of flower growing, and Collodi, a little further, is the home of the Pinocchio park, named after the author of the story, who took his pen name from the village. The hills toward Pistoia and the Apennines offer some excellent roads.

Riding in Montecatini itself is town riding, with traffic and one way streets, but the hills around are rewarding. The road up to Montecatini Alto is twisty and fun, and the roads through the Valdinievole and up into the Pistoia mountains are good, with views and light traffic. Summer heat can be strong in the valley.

Montecatini has fuel on the main roads and more hotels and restaurants than it can fill outside high season. Try the cialde di Montecatini, thin wafers filled with almonds, a local speciality, and the Tuscan dishes of the area, such as pappa al pomodoro and ribollita. The spas offer treatments and the parks are pleasant for a stroll.
t.the clitunno tempietto@42.8,12.8:
A few steps from the Via Flaminia, in the green flatland below Spoleto, there is a little building that scholars have argued about for centuries. The Tempietto del Clitunno looks like a miniature Roman temple, with a gabled front, columns and a carved cornice, but it is actually an early medieval church, made largely of reused Roman pieces and probably dating from somewhere between late antiquity and the time of the Lombards. It is among the group of Lombard sites in Italy that UNESCO listed in 2011, and part of its charm is that nobody is quite sure who built it or when.

The setting is the other half of the story. Just up the road are the Fonti del Clitunno, a set of springs that feed a small, clear pool shaded by weeping willows and poplars, with ducks and swans moving across water that looks almost impossibly still. The Romans thought the place sacred, and Pliny the Younger wrote a letter describing it in warm detail, noting the shrines and the clear water. Virgil mentioned the white bulls that grazed here, and the nineteenth-century poet Carducci wrote about it too, so literary pilgrims were arriving long before motorcycles.

The riding in this part of Umbria is very good. The old Flaminia, now the SS3, runs straight and quick along the valley floor, and the real pleasure comes when you turn off toward Trevi, perched on its hill among olive groves, or head south into the Monteluco hills above Spoleto with their tight, shaded bends. Montefalco, home of Sagrantino red wine, is a short run away, and the surfaces on the main roads are generally good, though the minor lanes can be patchy with gravel and leaves. Late spring and early autumn are the best times; mid-August can be hot, and the roads fill with weekenders.

Campello sul Clitunno is a small village with a few cafes, and for fuel and larger shops Spoleto, about eleven kilometres south, is the sensible choice. Try the local olive oil on bread if you get the chance, because the Trevi area is known for it. The little temple opens at set hours and is small enough that a visit takes only a few minutes.
t.teatro ventidio basso@42.9,13.6:
Ascoli Piceno is made of travertine, and in the right light the whole town looks like it has been carved from cream. The pale stone paves the great Piazza del Popolo and lines the arcades and towers, and the theatre is one of the quiet treats of a place that rarely makes the big lists. It is named after Ventidio Basso, a local boy who rose from humble beginnings to become a general under Mark Antony, defeated the Parthians in the first century BC and, so the story goes, was the first Roman to hold a triumph over them. The people of Ascoli remember it with civic pride.

The theatre itself is a nineteenth-century neoclassical building, handsome and intimate, in the middle of the old town. The town sits where the Tronto river meets a smaller stream, in the Marche region, with the Sibillini mountains to the west and the Monti della Laga to the south, and it feels like a place that has always been slightly out of the way and is quietly content with that. In August the Quintana, a medieval tournament with costumes, drums and competing districts, fills the streets, and it is worth timing a ride for if you like crowds and noise.

For the riding, Ascoli is a very good base. The roads climb west into the Sibillini through the Valle del Castellano and over to Castelluccio, among tight bends, forest and wide upland views, while the valley road towards the Adriatic is fast and easy. Surfaces vary after winter, and sections of road in the mountains have been affected by earthquakes in recent years, so check for closures before committing to a long loop. Summer is hot in the town but delightful in the hills; spring and autumn are best.

Food is part of the point. Olive all'ascolana, large green olives stuffed with meat, breaded and fried, are the local pride and are sold in paper cones, and a small plate of them with a glass of Rosso Piceno is a very good reason to park the bike. Ascoli is a proper city, with several fuel stations around its edges, plenty of cafes in the old centre, and some lovely evening light on the piazza.
t.evaporiti di san leo@43.9,12.3:
San Leo stands on a limestone block that rises sheer out of the Marecchia valley, and from a distance it looks like a fortress that nobody could possibly have captured. The ground under it tells a longer and stranger story. The evaporite rocks in this area, gypsum and associated salts, were laid down around six million years ago, when the Mediterranean nearly dried out in what geologists call the Messinian salinity crisis. Seawater evaporated, minerals crystallised, and the beds you see in the cuttings are the leftovers of that event.

Above them the fortress dominates the skyline, remodelled by Francesco di Giorgio Martini for the Montefeltro dukes in the fifteenth century, and it was later used as a prison. The most famous inmate was the adventurer Count Cagliostro, who died here in 1795 after being condemned by the Inquisition. Dante mentions San Leo in the Purgatorio, as an example of a place hard to climb, and Saint Francis is said to have been given Monte Alverna by a count at a gathering in the area. The village itself is small, quiet and made of the same pale stone as the rock, with a Romanesque parish church and cathedral that are older than the fortress.

On the bike, the main road along the Marecchia from Rimini is smooth and fast, and then you reach the climb to San Leo, a short, twisting road cut into the cliff with hairpins and a view that gets better with every turn. Further inland the Montefeltro hills give lovely, quiet riding on roads that wander through villages and past castles, though the surface can be broken after winter and the corners tighten without warning. Spring and autumn are best; in August the heat gathers in the valley and the car parks fill.

San Marino is only a short distance away, which means a lot of cheap fuel on that side of the border and a lot of souvenir shops. In San Leo itself there is little more than cafes and small restaurants, so buy fuel in the valley, in Novafeltria, Pennabilli or Borgo Maggiore, before you climb. A strong coffee and a sit on the small piazza under the fortress is a good way to pass the middle of the day.
t.villa de il trebbio@44.0,11.3:
The Medici came from the Mugello, and Il Trebbio is one of the places where you can see it. The family's rise to Florentine power in the fifteenth century began in these hills north of the city, among farms and woods where they held land long before they held banks and palaces. Il Trebbio is a fortified villa near San Piero a Sieve, redesigned for Cosimo the Elder by the architect Michelozzo, and its crenellated walls, tower and gardens mark it as a country retreat that is also, quietly, a statement of status. It is one of the Medici villas listed by UNESCO in 2013.

Nearby, the larger villa-castle of Cafaggiolo has a similar history and is slightly easier to see from the road. The surrounding Mugello is a broad, green basin ringed by the Apennines, where the Sieve river flows, with tidy fields, cypress lines and oak woods. The villas were hunting lodges and working farm estates as much as places of leisure, with vines, olives and grain feeding the household in town.

For anyone who rides, the Mugello means two things. First, the Autodromo del Mugello, where MotoGP stages one of its most-loved races each year, and the local villages are full of fans in the summer. Second, the roads: the old Via Bolognese over the Passo della Futa and the Raticosa to Bologna, with long, fast bends, stone bridges, forests of beech and chestnut and a number of tight, shaded corners.
