The Futa pass reaches about nine hundred metres and carries heavy motorcycle traffic on weekends, so go early if you can, and be careful with the surface in the wet. Police and speed cameras are present on the busy stretches.

San Piero a Sieve is a small town with fuel and cafes, and Barberino di Mugello, a few kilometres up the valley, has more shops and a wide choice of places to eat. Tuscan bread is made without salt, which can come as a surprise, and it is meant to go with strongly flavoured cured meats and cheese. If you are lucky enough to be here in autumn, the chestnut woods and the first mushrooms make the whole valley smell of woodsmoke and leaves.
t.herculaneum@40.8,14.3:
On the morning of 24 August in AD 79, as the story is usually told, Vesuvius blew its top, and Herculaneum, a small seaside town on the Bay of Naples, was buried under around twenty metres of volcanic material. Pompeii gets the headlines because it was buried in ash and pumice, but Herculaneum was overwhelmed by superheated surges of gas and ash, and that violence did something kinder to the evidence: it carbonised wood. Roof beams, doors, beds, shop shutters and even food were preserved in a way that Pompeii cannot match, and the town feels smaller, closer and more intact.

The site was found in the early eighteenth century when a well-digger struck marble, and the first excavations were tunnels cut by the Bourbon rulers in search of statues. Today the town is open to the sky, with mosaics, painted walls and two-storey houses on view, and the old boat sheds near the former shoreline hold the skeletons of the people who sheltered there, found in the 1980s. The Villa of the Papyri, a short distance away and still largely buried, yielded a library of charred scrolls that scholars are still trying to read.

This is not a place for a leisurely ride, and the bike is a tool for avoiding the worst of it. The streets around Ercolano and Portici are crowded, noisy and chaotic, with scooters, delivery vans and double-parked cars, and the Neapolitan approach to junctions is to treat them as a negotiation. Take your time, keep your distance and watch for loose manhole covers and slick basalt paving, which is slippery in the wet. Parking for bikes is easier than for cars, but leave nothing on the machine. Early morning is calmer.

Fuel is no trouble in a town of fifty thousand people, and the area is full of pizzerias, bakeries and bars serving good coffee. Once you have seen the ruins, the road up the flank of Vesuvius to the crater car park gives some tight bends and a fine view across the bay, though it can be busy at weekends and in summer. The wine of the slopes, Lacryma Christi, is worth tasting off the bike, when the day is done.
t.villa de castello@43.8,11.2:
The Villa di Castello stands on the north-western edge of Florence, in the flat land below Monte Morello, and the huge city has grown right up to its gates. Sesto Fiorentino, a town of forty-five thousand people, is three kilometres away, and the centre of Florence a few more. The villa is one of the Medici villas that UNESCO inscribed in 2013, and it is an unusual one, because the garden is the main attraction and the house inside is plain.

The Medici bought the property in 1477, and in 1537 Cosimo I took it as his own country retreat and had the Florentine designer Niccolò Tribolo lay out a garden in a rigorous geometric plan, with fountains, a hedge-lined labyrinth and an artificial grotto decorated with carved animals and shells. This was the model for the Italian Renaissance garden, imitated in France and England, and it is still a pleasure to walk in. In the late fifteenth century, Botticelli's Primavera and the Birth of Venus were hung in the earlier villa on this site, which is why people mention it. The house today holds the Accademia della Crusca, the body that guards the Italian language, and it is not generally open the way a museum is, so check access before coming. La Petraia, a nearby Medici villa on a hill, has a tower and a garden too.

For a rider, the interest lies in what lies beyond. Florence's ring roads are fast and confusing, and the historic centre is a restricted traffic zone, with fines for entering the wrong street, so do not wander in by bike. The hills to the north offer the real pleasures. Fiesole, with its Etruscan and Roman remains, is a short climb, and farther on the Apennine roads towards the Mugello wind through chestnut woods. The Mugello circuit, where the Italian MotoGP is held each summer, is about thirty kilometres away, and the whole valley is full of bikes at weekends.

Fuel and food are easy at Sesto Fiorentino, and there are bars everywhere. A Florentine lunch means ribollita, a bread and bean soup, or lampredotto, tripe in a bun from a street stall. Come in spring or autumn for fewer crowds and clear light. July and August are hot, humid and noisy with traffic.
t.the via appia at the itri pass@41.3,13.5:
Ancient Rome's first great highway, the Via Appia, was begun in 312 BC by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus, and it ran from Rome south to Capua and later on to Brindisi on the Adriatic. At Itri, in the hills behind the Gulf of Gaeta, it squeezes through a narrow pass between the Monti Aurunci and the sea, and the road still crosses the same gap today. A stretch of the old paved line survives near the pass, with its big, rounded basalt blocks, though you will need to get off the main road and look carefully to find it.

The pass has always been a place of ambush and trade, and of stories. The most famous local figure is Michele Pezza, known as Fra Diavolo, who was born at Itri in 1771 and led a guerrilla band against the French in the Napoleonic wars. He was captured and hanged in Naples in 1806, and the town has never quite decided whether to call him a bandit or a hero. The medieval castle above Itri is a good place to see the lie of the land. The surrounding hills grow the Itrana olive, a small black fruit that is eaten and pressed locally, and the olive groves climb the slopes in terraces, grey-green and silvery in the wind.

On a motorcycle, the way in from Fondi or from the coast is quick and enjoyable. The old Appia, the SS7, climbs from Fondi in a series of broad curves with moderate gradients, and the road through the pass is busy with trucks, particularly on weekday mornings. A better option is to leave the main road and ride the quieter provincial roads towards Sperlonga and Gaeta, where the coastline is rocky, the sea changes colour from deep blue to green, and the cliff-top villages have steep, narrow lanes that need care on wet tiles. Sperlonga has the remains of a villa of the emperor Tiberius, where a banquet grotto, partly collapsed, once held huge marble sculptures.

Fuel, food and coffee are plentiful. Itri has about eight thousand people and Fondi over twenty-six thousand, so there are stations and bars in both. Come in spring or in September and October to avoid the summer traffic to the beaches, and be wary of heat and Saturday congestion between June and August, when the coast road backs up for kilometres.
t.pueblo pintado@36.0,-107.7:
Pueblo Pintado stands in the high desert of northwestern New Mexico, on Navajo land, and it is the easternmost of the great houses connected to Chaco Canyon. Around a thousand years ago the people we call Ancestral Puebloans raised masonry walls here, several storeys tall, laying thin sandstone into patterns that still look careful today. The ruin has been roughened by weather, but the arrangement of rooms, the circular kivas and the long arc of the building are clear, and you can walk around it on a short trail.

The land is what you notice first. It is big, tawny country of mesas, arroyos, sagebrush and piñon-juniper, with a sky that does a lot of the talking. Wind is nearly constant, and storms in July and August arrive with walls of rain, so check the clouds before you set off. The Chaco world was linked by roads, including the Great North Road, and Kin Ya'a and Casamero, other outlier sites on this route, were parts of the same network, set along lines that only make sense when you have seen the distances.

Riding here is open and a little lonely. The paved highways, long and straight with the occasional smooth bend, carry little traffic and plenty of space, and the Navajo Nation roads that spur off toward the ruins can switch to rough dirt that turns to glue after rain. Distances are huge and services thin. Fuel is limited to small towns and trading posts, so fill up before you go, with the nearest bigger centres in Farmington to the north and Cuba or Bernalillo in the east and south.

Respect matters here. This is the Navajo Nation, so follow local rules about where you may walk and photograph, and treat the ruins, which are fragile, as you would a cemetery. Come in spring or fall, when daytime temperatures are mild and the light on the sandstone turns amber at either end of the day. Winter brings snow and mud, and midsummer afternoons are hot and thundery.
t.torre annunziata villa b@40.8,14.5:
Under the shadow of Vesuvius, in the middle of a modern working town, there is a Roman villa that was buried in the same eruption of AD 79 that destroyed Pompeii. Torre Annunziata stands on the ancient site of Oplontis, a seaside suburb of Pompeii, and its two excavated villas are part of the UNESCO listing of Pompeii, Herculaneum and Torre Annunziata, inscribed in 1997. Villa A, the grander one, is famous for its frescoes and is linked with Poppaea Sabina, the wife of Nero. Villa B, the one on this ride, is different, a commercial building where wine and other goods were stored and traded, with a large courtyard and many amphorae found when it was dug up.

The eruption buried the coast under metres of ash and pumice, and the excavation in the twentieth century of buildings preserved by it, with painted walls, furniture and even bread, gave scholars a priceless record of Roman life. At Oplontis, the villas stand a few metres below the modern street level, and a visit to Villa B takes you down into the Roman world through the middle of a town. Vesuvius, a grey cone with a broad crater, dominates the skyline, and the smell of the sea mixes with the smell of exhaust.

Torre Annunziata was for centuries a centre of pasta making, and the dry pasta of nearby Gragnano still trades on that tradition. The Bay of Naples is one of the most beautiful in the world, and the old coast road leads to Sorrento and the Amalfi Coast.

Riding around Naples demands nerve. Traffic is dense and fast, drivers are inventive, and scooters weave through gaps. The surface has potholes and basalt paving stones, which are slippery in the wet. The road to the crater of Vesuvius, a series of tight bends climbing the cone, is worth the effort, with a view across the bay. Torre Annunziata has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Boscotrecase and Trecase are neighbouring towns. A pizza and a coffee are the right lunch. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.tarquinia@42.3,11.8:
Tarquinia sits on a hill a few kilometres inland from the Tyrrhenian coast, in the northern tip of Lazio where the land starts to feel more like Tuscany. The town was called Corneto until 1922, when it took back the name of the Etruscan city of Tarchna that once stood on the neighbouring plateau. The old centre is tight, brownish stone, medieval towers, and a few good small piazzas; the main reason people come, though, lies on the Monterozzi ridge just outside, where the Etruscans built their necropolis.

Those tombs are the real wonder. Many are cut into the soft rock and painted inside, with banqueting scenes, dancers, musicians, hunters and fishermen in colours that still look fresh. Names like the Tomb of the Leopards and the Tomb of the Augurs are worth looking up before you arrive. They give a rare sense that the Etruscans were people who enjoyed themselves, and the necropolis is a UNESCO site shared with Cerveteri. In the town, the national museum is housed in a fifteenth-century palace and holds the famous winged horses from a temple of the city.

The riding is a pleasant mixture. Coming up from the Via Aurelia, which runs along the coast, you cross low rolling country of olive groves, cornfields, grazing and the odd cypress line. The roads around Monte Romano and the Tuscia are rarely crowded, the surface is generally decent, and the corners are gentle, not technical. This is a landscape for easy cruising, not hard attacking. Heat in July and August is heavy, and the middle of the day on the ridge feels like an oven; spring and autumn are far kinder.

Tarquinia is a proper town of twelve thousand people, so fuel, a pharmacy, bars and restaurants are all here. The seafood in this part of Lazio is straightforward and good, and a plate of pasta with local fish is the right reward after the necropolis. If you want a swim, the beaches at Tarquinia Lido are a short ride away, flat and dark-sanded, and not especially pretty but welcome after a hot day.

Rome is not far south, which is why this is a natural start for the Vatican ride. Heading north towards Assisi, you leave the coast behind and climb into Umbria with the day getting cooler as you go.
t.baraccano@44.5,11.4:
Baraccano is not a village, it is a corner of Bologna: a gate in the old thirteenth-century walls where the Via Santo Stefano runs out of the centre. The name comes from the barbican that once defended it. Next to the gate stands the small sanctuary of the Madonna del Baraccano, a Renaissance church whose fresco of the Virgin drew pilgrims after a reported miracle, and beside it a lovely little courtyard, a place most visitors walk straight past on the way to the Two Towers.

Bologna rewards that kind of slow looking. The city is famous for its porticoes, roughly forty kilometres of them in the historic centre, which UNESCO recognised in 2021, and the long covered walk up to the sanctuary of San Luca on the hill is the famous example. The old university, the oldest in the Western world according to its own proud claim, still gives the place a young, loud energy in the evenings. And the food is, simply, serious: tagliatelle with ragù, tortellini in broth, mortadella, and the sort of lasagne that has no business being cheap.

For riders, the main thing to know is that the historic centre is a limited-traffic zone watched by cameras, and fines arrive by post weeks later. The practical answer is to leave the bike outside the ring, in one of the supervised parking areas, and walk. Baraccano itself is just inside the line of the old walls, so approach with care and read the signs. Fuel is plentiful anywhere on the ring road and in the suburbs; Bologna has more than three hundred thousand people, and it is never short of pumps.

The rides from here head off in two quite different directions. To the west, the pale gypsum outcrops around Zola Predosa, known as the Gessi, give the first hint of the unusual geology of the Emilian hills: soft white rock, sinkholes, small caves. South, the Apennines begin almost at the city's back door, and the road over the Futa or Raticosa passes toward Tuscany is a classic day for anyone with a free weekend.

Early morning is best if you want the city to yourself. The light on the red-brick arcades is warm, the cafés are opening, and the traffic has not yet found its stride.
t.historic centre of florence@43.8,11.3:
Florence is the kind of city where the problem is not finding something to look at but deciding when to stop. The historic centre sits on a bend of the Arno, a compact grid of Roman origin with the Duomo at its middle, Brunelleschi's dome rising over the roofs, the Palazzo Vecchio at the civic heart and the Ponte Vecchio, the only bridge the retreating Germans spared in 1944. The Medici bankers who ran the place for much of the fifteenth to eighteenth centuries paid for most of what you are about to see, and they were rather good at it.

On a motorbike, Florence is mainly a place to arrive at, leave the bike, and walk. The centre is a limited-traffic zone with camera enforcement, and visitors who ignore it receive fines by post long after they have gone home. Check the current rules and park outside the ring, ideally in a supervised lot. The Fortezza da Basso, the Oltrarno side and the hills above the city are all easier. Fuel is no concern in a city of three hundred and fifty thousand people.

The better riding begins as soon as you climb out. The road up to Fiesole is a short, twisting hill climb through villas and cypresses, with Florence spread behind you in the haze, and beyond it the lanes of the Mugello and Chianti open up. Towards San Gimignano the road goes through the vineyards of Chianti, a landscape of low hills, olive terraces, small stone villages and the occasional hairpin. Cerreto Guidi, the other ride from here, takes you west into gentler country with a Medici villa waiting at the end.

Food is simple and meaty: the huge bistecca alla fiorentina, ribollita soup made with old bread, and lampredotto, the tripe sandwich that locals eat at street stalls. A glass of Chianti is the obvious accompaniment, though riders may prefer the espresso. In 1966 the Arno flooded the city badly and the marks are still visible on some walls, a quiet reminder of how fragile all this beauty has been.

Summer is hot and crowded, so aim for spring or early autumn, and leave early in the morning when the stone is cool and the tour groups are still having breakfast.
t.ville d assise@43.1,12.6:
Assisi sits on the western flank of Monte Subasio, and the first thing you notice is the colour. The stone, quarried from the mountain itself, is a pale pink-white that glows at sunset, and the whole town seems to hang off the slope above the Umbrian plain. It was the home of Saint Francis, born here around 1181, who gave up his father's cloth business to live in poverty, and the town built one of the great pilgrimage churches of Christendom around his tomb. The Basilica of San Francesco has two layers of frescoes by Giotto and his circle, and was badly shaken by the earthquake of 1997, when part of the vault fell. It reopened after careful restoration, and UNESCO listed Assisi in 2000.

Down below, around the great domed church of Santa Maria degli Angeli, is the busier modern settlement, with the Porziuncola, the little chapel that Francis rebuilt with his own hands. Rivotorto, a few kilometres away, is where his first brothers lived in a hut. That is the useful geography: the old town up the hill, parking and petrol on the plain.

Motorcycles are a good way to arrive, because the narrow old centre is restricted and bikes are easier to place than cars, though you will have to walk. The road up from Santa Maria degli Angeli is straightforward. A better ride is to head up over Subasio itself on the minor road that climbs to the Eremo delle Carceri, where Francis and his friars used to retreat to pray in the woods. The surface is mixed, the bends are tight and blind in places, and it can be misty in spring and snowy in winter. Late spring and early autumn are the sweet spots, when the plain is green or gold and the crowds are thinner.

Practicalities are easy. Santa Maria degli Angeli has the larger shops and pumps, and Assisi's own lanes are full of places for coffee, a plate of strangozzi pasta with truffle, or a slice of torta al testo, the flatbread stuffed with greens.

Go quietly, and if you can, be there when the day trippers have left and the bells begin. It is a town that deserves an evening.
Ravenna is the odd one out in Italian history, a small flat city on the edge of the Adriatic that for a while was the capital of an empire. In 402 the Western Roman emperor Honorius moved his court here from Milan, because the marshes and lagoons around the town made it easy to defend, and for the next century and a half it passed through the hands of Roman emperors, the Ostrogoth king Theodoric, and then the Byzantines, who ruled Italy from here through an exarch. Each left buildings, and eight of them, decorated in dazzling mosaics, make up the Early Christian Monuments of Ravenna that UNESCO listed in 1996.

You can walk the whole set in a day, since the old centre is small and mostly pedestrian. The point of the mosaics is not their age so much as their colour. Gold, deep blue and green glass tesserae catch light from small windows, and the ceiling of the so-called Mausoleum of Galla Placidia looks like a night sky. Dante died here in 1321 after years of exile and is buried beside the church of San Francesco, so literary pilgrims arrive too.

The land is the surprise for riders. Ravenna once sat on the sea. Silt and a falling coastline have left it several kilometres inland, with pine forests near Classe and the Po delta's wetlands to the north, full of herons and, in winter, flocks of ducks. The ride into the Apennines from here is a classic. You cross the plain through Faenza or Brisighella, then the road starts to climb into the Tuscan-Romagnol Apennines. The Foreste Casentinesi with its Sasso Fratino strict nature reserve, one of Italy's oldest forests, lies on the other side.

Practically, leave the bike outside the restricted traffic zone and walk. Fuel is no problem in a city of eighty thousand, and the food is hearty Romagna cooking: piadina, cappelletti in broth, and sardines from the Adriatic. Be careful on the plain in winter, when fog and frost can combine on the flat roads, and in summer the mosquitoes are famous.
t.mambo@44.5,11.3:
Not every checkpoint on a ride needs to be old. MamBo, the Museo d'Arte Moderna di Bologna, opened in 2007 in a former municipal bakery on the northern edge of the old centre, and the building says a lot about how Bologna thinks. The city turned the factory where it once baked bread for its people into a home for twentieth-century and contemporary art, with a strong collection of Giorgio Morandi, the painter who spent his whole life in this town painting bottles and jugs on a table, and whose little house lies not far away.

Bologna itself is a joy for anyone who likes a city that works. The porticoes, nearly forty kilometres of covered arcades, were added to UNESCO's list in 2021, and they make walking pleasant in any weather. The two leaning towers, Asinelli and Garisenda, are the symbol, and the old university, founded in the eleventh century and often called the oldest in the world, still fills the streets with students. Bologna is nicknamed la Grassa, the fat, for its food, and it earns it: tortellini in broth, tagliatelle al ragù, mortadella, and a glass of Pignoletto.

For a rider, Bologna is a place for care. The historic centre is a restricted traffic zone with cameras, and fines arrive by post months after you have gone home, so park outside and walk or take a bus. The ring roads and the Via Emilia are busy, and trams, cyclists and delivery scooters keep you alert. Fuel is everywhere, and nearby Casalecchio di Reno on the Reno river has more of the same.

The reward is leaving it behind. A short ride south-west puts you on the winding roads of the Apennines, with the Porrettana and the old roads through Sasso Marconi climbing past chestnut woods and little villages. The Tuscan border lies a morning away, and Cafaggiolo in the Mugello, the Medici villa on the ride list, makes a handsome destination for a day.

Come in spring or autumn, when the air is clear and the terracotta roofs hold the light.
t.church of st vitale@44.4,12.2:
San Vitale does not look like much from the outside. It is a squat octagon of plain brick, built in the sixth century, and the first reaction of many visitors is mild surprise. Then you step through the door and the interior opens up in layers of marble, arches and light, and the apse is covered in mosaic so bright it seems to glow. It was begun under the Ostrogothic king Theodoric's rule, around 526, and finished and consecrated under Byzantine rule in 547, in the years after Justinian's generals had reconquered Italy.

The two panels everyone comes for face each other across the apse. On one the emperor Justinian stands with his court and the bishop Maximian, carrying a golden bowl; on the other his wife Theodora, in a jewelled crown, sweeps in with her ladies. Neither ruler ever came to Ravenna. They are present by proxy, which was the point: this was Byzantium's statement of power in a recaptured Italy, pressed into glass and gold.

Take your time here, and look at the details: the peacocks, the vines, the lambs. It is a good example of why the monuments of Ravenna are inscribed together, because the building sits next to the Mausoleum of Galla Placidia in a quiet courtyard, so you can visit both in the same short walk.

For riders the connection to the ride list is the Vena del Gesso Romagnola, the long white ridge of gypsum that runs across the Apennine foothills south of Faenza and Imola. The gypsum is the same family of rock that dissolves into caves and sinkholes, and Monte Penzola is a good place to see the stripped, bright slopes. After the dark, glowing interior of San Vitale it makes an interesting contrast: the same pale material that Romans used for plaster, still lying in the open.

Parking in Ravenna's historic centre is restricted, so use the car parks on the edge and walk the few minutes. The town has plenty of fuel on its outskirts, and the cafes around the Piazza del Popolo make a pleasant place to sit and wait for the queue to ease, which in high season it must.
t.arian baptistry@44.4,12.2:
The Arian Baptistry is small, plain and easy to miss, tucked on a side street east of the old centre, and that is half of its appeal. It is an octagon of brick, built by Theodoric in the early sixth century for the Arian Christians, the faith the Goths followed. Arians believed that Christ was subordinate to God the Father, a view the orthodox church condemned as heresy, and so Theodoric's Ravenna had two communities, two cathedrals and two baptisteries, living side by side with surprising tolerance for an age of war.

Inside the dome, the mosaic shows Christ's baptism in the river Jordan. Christ stands naked in the water while John the Baptist pours water on his head, and a river god sits beside them holding a reed, a pagan figure borrowed from Roman art that lingers in a Christian scene. Around the rim the twelve apostles walk in a circle, in procession towards an empty throne. It is compact and strangely moving, and you can take it all in within ten minutes.

When the Byzantine army took Ravenna, the Arian buildings were seized and rededicated, and the baptistry became a Catholic chapel. The mosaics survived, and parts of the original decoration were restored. The ground in Ravenna has risen with centuries of silt while the buildings stayed put, so you often step down into these old rooms rather than up.

For riding, the nearest good reward is Baraccano, a Bologna landmark on the route list, reached across the Via Emilia, an hour away. Between the two, the Po plain is as flat as a table, and the roads, canals and drainage ditches run in straight lines. Fog in November can hide a cyclist at ten metres, so slow down.

Fuel is available all around the city, and the old town is a short walk. Stop for a piadina or a coffee on the Via di Roma and give the baptistry a quiet moment before the next building.
t.neonian baptistry@44.4,12.2:
You have to be nearby to find the Neonian Baptistry at all, a plain brick octagon beside the cathedral that looks more like a service building than a monument. It is the oldest of Ravenna's surviving mosaic monuments, built around the end of the fourth century as the baptistery of the orthodox cathedral, and redecorated in the middle of the fifth century by Bishop Neon, whose name it carries. It was raised on the site of a Roman bath house and reused older marble, typical of a city busy turning pagan stone into Christian rooms.

Look up, and the dome opens in circles. At the centre Christ is baptised by John in the river Jordan, with a bearded personification of the river holding a cloth. Around him the apostles march in a ring, their robes in gold and white against a blue sky, and below them are empty thrones and altars, framed by stucco prophets. The colours are more restrained than San Vitale's, which makes the beauty feel earlier and slightly stricter.

The floor is the quiet clue to the city's history. Ravenna was a lagoon town, and the land under it has settled while silt built up around it, so the original floor lies well below today's. Walk down a few steps and you are standing in the fifth century.

For the ride list the connection is the Vena del Gesso Romagnola and Monte Penzola, the dazzling ridge of gypsum on the first folds of the Apennines. After a morning among tesserae, the contrast is nice: a place where the geology is the art. The route there leaves Ravenna on flat farm roads and enters the hills near Faenza, where vineyards for Sangiovese and Albana, a local white, line the slopes.

Fuel is easy in Ravenna and along the Via Emilia towards the hills. The old centre is mostly closed to traffic, so park at the edge and go on foot. Coffee at a table in the square next to the cathedral costs about what you would expect from a tourist city, and is still worth having.
t.mauseoleum of theodoric@44.4,12.2:
Theodoric's tomb stands alone on the northern edge of Ravenna, among trees and grass, a squat two-storey block of white stone crowned by a single enormous dome. The king of the Ostrogoths ruled Italy from Ravenna for thirty-odd years until his death in 526, and he planned his own mausoleum before the end. It is built of Istrian limestone, dressed so tightly that no mortar was needed, and the roof is a single slab hollowed into a shallow dome, carried across the Adriatic from the Istrian coast. How they lifted it is still discussed.

It is a strange monument, partly Roman and partly Germanic. The ten-sided lower storey has arched niches, and a decorative frieze runs around the top in a motif of pincers that scholars link with Gothic metalwork. Theodoric had been educated as a hostage at the court in Constantinople, and admired Roman civilisation, yet he remained an Arian Christian and a Gothic king, and the building holds both identities. His body was later removed, and the porphyry basin in the upper chamber is thought to have been his sarcophagus.

The location has its own interest. Ravenna's harbour once lay near here, and the name of the village of Porto Fuori nearby preserves a memory of it. The coastline has retreated several kilometres since, and the rows of tall pines that border the flat land to the east are the remains of what was once a dense forest between the city and the sea.

This is an easy stop for a rider because the tomb has its own small park with room for a bike nearby and is outside the tightest restricted streets. The road in from the ring road is wide and fast, then slows as it nears the city. Fuel is available throughout Ravenna, and the northern outskirts, towards the Adriatic coast, have plenty of options.

The ridge of gypsum at Monte Penzola on the Vena del Gesso lies two hours away, a good ride south and west over the hills, and the natural material there makes a good companion to this stone.
t.historical centre of naples@40.8,14.2:
Naples does not wait until you are ready. The historic centre is one of the oldest continuously inhabited urban areas in Europe, founded by Greek settlers as Neapolis, the new city, in the sixth century BC, and the grid they laid out is still visible in the long straight street the locals call Spaccanapoli. Roman, Byzantine, Norman, Angevin, Aragonese, Spanish and Bourbon rulers each added a layer, and UNESCO listed the centre in 1995 as one of the great palimpsests of European history.

Beneath the streets is a second city. The Greeks and Romans quarried the soft tuff stone to build above, and left cavities that became cisterns, passages and air-raid shelters, and you can still walk down into them with a guide. Above ground the churches are crammed with baroque marble and paintings, including Caravaggio's Seven Works of Mercy at the Pio Monte della Misericordia, a wonderful dark picture that stands comfortably among the street noise.

For a motorcyclist, Naples is a test. The scooter is king here, the traffic flows in a way that looks chaotic and somehow works, and the centre is a restricted zone with its own rules. Park at the edge, lock the bike properly, and walk. Theft is a real concern in this city, so use a disc lock and leave nothing on the bike. In the Montecalvario and Spanish Quarters, alleys are narrow, steep and busy with washing lines and shrines to Maradona. Fuel is available throughout the city, and the surrounding districts have no shortage of pumps.

What you come for, besides the monuments, is the food. Pizza was born in this city, and the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo has been recognised by UNESCO. A margherita with a blistered, soft edge, a coffee at the counter standing up, a sfogliatella at the pasticceria: these are the real attractions, and they are cheap.

The ride list starts here for the old Via Appia, the Roman road that ran south-east to Brindisi, and the first miles out of the city lead through suburbs before the countryside begins. Leave early to beat the traffic.
t.basilica of st apollinaire nuovo@44.4,12:
Theodoric did not build Sant'Apollinare Nuovo as a monastery church. He built it around the year 500 as the palace chapel for his Arian court, a hall with a wooden roof and two long walls of marble columns, and it still carries the finest strip of mosaic in the city. High on the left wall, a procession of virgins in white robes moves from the port of Classe toward the Virgin and Child, led by the three Magi. On the right, a line of martyrs advances from the palace towards Christ enthroned. The walking figures look calm, and their gold background makes the whole nave shimmer.

Look closely, and you can find the edit. When Justinian's armies took Ravenna and the church became orthodox, the mosaics that showed Theodoric's palace and his courtiers were altered, and the figures were removed, leaving curtains and the stray hands of courtiers still resting on the columns. It is a rare physical record of a regime changing its mind, and a favourite detail of guides.

The church changed its name in the ninth century, when the relics of Saint Apollinaris, the city's first bishop, were brought here from Classe for safety, and the word nuovo, new, distinguishes it from the older church that stands out among the pines near the old port.

For riders, Ravenna's historic centre is a restricted zone, so leave the machine at the edge and walk in. The church sits close to the Via di Roma, a short stroll from the station, and the cafes nearby are good for a morning stop. Fuel is easy on the city's outskirts and along the roads to the coast.

The ride that leads on from here goes to the Gessi Bolognesi, the gypsum hills and caves south of Bologna, which are a regional park with sinkholes and old quarries. The road crosses the flat Romagna plain, then climbs to a country of farms and small villages. Evening light on the plain makes the cypress lines glow, and the flatness gives you long views of the distant ridge. Fog in winter, though, can hang in the valleys until mid-morning.
t.district of casale and santo strato@40.8:
Posillipo takes its name from a Greek phrase meaning a pause from pain, and the Romans, who knew a good view when they saw one, covered the ridge with villas. It is the green promontory that divides the Bay of Naples from the Gulf of Pozzuoli, a hill of soft yellow tuff thrown up by the volcanoes of the Phlegraean Fields, and its western slope falls into the sea in cliffs and small coves. The Casale and Santo Strato district sits on the sea side of the hill, where terraced gardens, old walls and tiny ports survived the building boom that swallowed so much of Naples.

On the headland below, the Gaiola underwater park protects a small archipelago, and the fragments of Roman villas, including the ruins of the Pausilypon theatre cut into the rock, show what this coast looked like when rich Romans came for a holiday from Rome. The local stories are full of ghosts and curses, and the little Gaiola island has a name for bad luck among its owners.

Riding the coast of Posillipo is a slow, scenic thing. The Via Posillipo and the Via Francesco Petrarca follow the hillside with views over the bay to Vesuvius, Capri and Ischia, and the road winds between high garden walls. It is busy, and Neapolitan drivers expect a bike to keep up, so keep your wits and your lane. Evening is the time for it, when the light slants across the bay and the sea turns copper.

Practicality is simple, since this is a built-up part of Naples, and the nearby districts of Bagnoli and Fuorigrotta have pumps and bars. Parking along the coast is the hard part, so look for a space in the side streets and walk down to the water. Be careful with the bike and take anything valuable with you.

The ride list continues south to Punta Licosa in the Cilento, a wilder and quieter coast, and the contrast between the two is part of the pleasure.
t.properties of the holy see in that city:
The Vatican is the world's smallest state, and you ride in and out of it without noticing. The line between Italy and the Holy See is marked on the pavement of St Peter's Square, and the entire country covers less than half a square kilometre, with fewer than a thousand residents. What UNESCO listed, together with the properties of the Holy See in Rome beyond the walls, is a great collection of art and architecture: the basilica built over the supposed tomb of the apostle Peter, the dome that Michelangelo designed, Bernini's colonnade, and the Sistine Chapel and its ceiling, painted in the early sixteenth century.

From a rider's point of view, the Vatican is a place to approach thoughtfully. Motorcycles cannot enter the square, and the area around it is thick with coaches, scooters and pedestrians. The wide Via della Conciliazione, begun under Mussolini in the 1930s after the Lateran Treaty, leads straight to the basilica, and the Tiber embankments to the north and south offer places to park a bike if you look carefully. Rome has a restricted traffic zone, and parking inside the walls fills early in the morning. Fuel is no concern in the capital, which has stations on every major road, so fill the tank in the suburbs and ride in light.

Historically, the little state is the successor to the Papal States, which once ruled central Italy and fell to the Italian kingdom in 1870, leaving the pope a self-declared prisoner in the Vatican until the treaty of 1929. The Swiss Guards in their striped uniforms have been recruited from Switzerland since the early sixteenth century, and they remain one of the smallest and oldest military units in the world.

The ride list from here sets off down the Via Appia, the Queen of Roads, over the Alban Hills, past the lakes of Castel Gandolfo, where the pope has a summer residence. Early morning is the right moment to leave Rome, when the traffic is light, the air is clear and the pine trees along the old road hold the light.
t.mausoleum of galla placida@44.4,12.2:
It is a surprise how small Galla Placidia's mausoleum is. A cross-shaped brick chamber no bigger than a modest chapel, it stands hidden behind the church of San Vitale in a quiet corner, with plain walls that give no hint of what is inside. Step in and the dark opens into a deep blue night. The vault is covered in tiny gold stars on a field of lapis-coloured glass, and a gold cross shines in the dome above, with figures of the apostles and doves drinking from a fountain in the lunettes. The only light comes through thin alabaster windows, which turn the daylight amber.

It was built around the middle of the fifth century and named after Galla Placidia, the half-sister of Emperor Honorius and a formidable figure, who ruled in the name of her young son after a life that included capture by the Goths, marriage to one of their kings and a return to the imperial court. Tradition names the building as her tomb, though she most likely died in Rome and was buried there, and the three sarcophagi in the chamber probably held other members of the imperial family. The legend is better than the evidence, but the building does not need it.

The best mosaic is the Good Shepherd above the entrance, a Christ in gold and purple who sits among sheep in a green landscape and holds a cross like a staff, an image that is almost pastoral. It is a rare survival of the very early style, when Roman artists made Christian subjects with a classical sense of space.

The ride list takes you from here to the Vena del Gesso and Monte Penzola, and the contrast is fun. After the closed jewel of the mausoleum, you can ride into the open karst country, the bright cliffs and the hollows of gypsum, about an hour's ride out from the flat Romagna coast. The route climbs through chestnut and oak woods before the cliffs appear.

Practical points: queues can build in busy periods and are shortest early, and Ravenna's centre is closed to most traffic, so park outside and walk. The city of eighty thousand has fuel on all approaches.
t.santa fe@35.7,-105.9:
Route 66 used to go to Santa Fe, and then in 1937 it did not. The original alignment of the Mother Road ran over Glorieta Pass into the old Spanish capital of New Mexico, before dropping south to Albuquerque, and then engineers cut a straight line across the desert from Santa Rosa to Albuquerque, shaving about a hundred miles off the journey and leaving Santa Fe on a bypassed loop. The ride from Amarillo to Santa Fe follows that early route, and this is the end of it, in a city at about seven thousand feet in the foothills of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains.

Santa Fe is the oldest state capital in the United States, founded by the Spanish in about 1610, and the Palace of the Governors on the plaza has been in continuous use for most of that time. The city has an adobe look, with earth-coloured buildings, flat roofs and wooden beams, because the town's planners decided long ago to keep a consistent style, and it is full of galleries and museums, including one devoted to Georgia O'Keeffe, who painted the desert landscape nearby. The Santa Fe Trail from Missouri ended on the plaza, and traders arrived here with wagonloads of goods. Under the portal of the Palace, Native American artisans sell silver, turquoise and pottery, a tradition of long standing.

The riding is the most pleasant at the end of the journey. The high desert is a landscape of mesas, pinon and juniper, wide sky and sharp light, and the roads that run into Santa Fe from the east climb through pine woods. If you have time, take the High Road to Taos, which winds through old Hispanic villages with adobe chapels, or the Turquoise Trail south toward Albuquerque, through old mining towns. Weather at this altitude can change quickly, with summer thunderstorms in the afternoon and cold nights even in July, and snow can fall from October to April.

Santa Fe has a population of more than eighty thousand, so fuel, hotels and restaurants are not hard to find, though accommodation is expensive. The local food is New Mexican, with red or green chile on almost everything, so when asked red or green, the answer is Christmas, which means both. Parking for bikes is easy in public lots near the plaza. Take a jacket for the evening, and allow time to sit on the plaza with a cold drink and watch the light fade on the mountains.
t.chaco culture national historical park c:
Chaco is a place where you have to earn the silence. The way in is a long dirt road, many miles of corrugations and dust, that leaves the paved highway in the high desert of north-west New Mexico and runs across open range before dropping into a wide canyon, and by the time you arrive, you have been shaken and quiet for a good while. Then you see the walls. Between about the middle of the ninth century and the twelfth, the Ancestral Puebloan people built a dozen huge stone buildings here, called great houses, of which Pueblo Bonito is the largest, with hundreds of rooms in a D-shaped plan, stacked several storeys high, and a vast number of ceiling timbers carried in from forests far away.

Nobody is sure exactly what Chaco was, whether a ceremonial centre, a trading hub, a capital or all of those, but the builders clearly understood the sky. Many of the buildings are aligned to the solstices and the cycles of the moon, and on Fajada Butte, a slab of rock sits against the cliff in such a way that a spiral petroglyph was once crossed by daggers of sunlight at the solstices. Roads, perfectly straight and built across the landscape, link Chaco to outlying sites such as Kin Ya'a, and Halfway House, which belong to the same wider network. The park was listed as a World Heritage site in 1987.

The road is the challenge. The main access from the north, from the village of Nageezi on the highway, is about twenty miles of unpaved county road, rutted and washboarded, and after rain it can become impassable, so check conditions with the park before you set out. On a motorbike, a steady pace and some off-road skill are needed, and the dust can be thick, so carry a visor or goggles. Flash floods can fill the washes in summer, in the monsoon season of July and August, and the temperature swings widely, from hot afternoons to cold nights. The park is at about 6,200 feet.

A small campground is the only place to stay, and it fills quickly. The night sky here is among the darkest in the country, and the stars are spectacular. Walk quietly, stay on the paths, and leave everything as you found it.
t.kakadu national park@-12.8,132.8:
Kakadu is big in a way that is hard to take in until you have driven in it. The national park covers nearly twenty thousand square kilometres of the Northern Territory, about the size of Wales, and holds a whole series of landscapes: sandstone escarpments, floodplains, billabongs, monsoon forest, tidal rivers and open woodland. It is one of Australia's few World Heritage Areas listed for both natural and cultural values, and it is owned by its Aboriginal traditional owners, who lease it to the government and manage it jointly.

People have lived here for at least sixty-five thousand years, according to archaeological finds, and the rock art galleries at sites like Ubirr and Burrungkuy are some of the most remarkable in the world. Paintings of fish, animals, spirit beings and even early European ships cover the rock shelters, in some cases layer on layer. It is a living culture, and visitors are asked to respect restrictions on certain sites and to follow signs.

The wildlife is spectacular. Saltwater crocodiles are common in the rivers and billabongs, and swimming is dangerous except in designated, safe pools, so obey the signs. Yellow Water Billabong, near Cooinda, is full of birds, with jabirus, egrets, whistling ducks and sea eagles, and a dawn boat trip is the best way to see them. In the late dry season, grass fires are lit deliberately by rangers, and you may ride through smoke.

The Kakadu Highway and Arnhem Highway are well-sealed but long and straight, with heat, sun and road trains, and distances are large. The dry season, from May to October, is the time to go. From November to April, the wet season brings floods and road closures, humidity and storms. Fuel is available at Jabiru, about eighteen kilometres from here, and at Cooinda, and you should fill up whenever you can, since the next station could be a hundred kilometres away. Carry plenty of water, and buy a park pass at the entrance.
t.rome@41.9,12.5:
Rome is the end of the line for the Mille Miglia, or at least the halfway mark, because the old race ran out from Brescia to Rome and back again, a thousand Italian miles in all, which is where the name comes from. It ran from 1927 until 1957, mostly through towns and villages with the roads left open and crowds standing at the kerb, and the drivers flew down the Via Cassia and through the Apennine passes at speeds that make the whole thing seem barely believable now. It ended after a crash in 1957 that killed spectators, and was later revived as a rolling classic-car parade, which still comes through Rome every spring.

Riding in Rome itself needs a particular frame of mind. The streets are old, narrow and often cobbled with the little black basalt blocks called sampietrini, which are slippery when wet and punishing on a heavy bike. Scooters pour past on both sides, buses own the bus lanes, and drivers use their horns as punctuation. Much of the historic centre is a restricted traffic zone, the ZTL, where entry without a permit earns a fine by camera, and motorcycles are not exempt in every area, so check before you go and park outside it. The ring road, the GRA, is fast, busy and sometimes badly surfaced.

The reward is that few cities pay you back so well for the trouble. Early morning, when the streets are washed and empty, the Colosseum and the Forum seem to have been waiting for you. A few hundred metres from the Vatican, the dome of St Peter's rises over a skyline of pines, domes and terracotta roofs. The Appian Way, built in 312 BC, still runs south from the city with its old basalt paving, tombs and cypress trees, and it is one of the finest places in Italy for a slow ride on a Sunday, when parts of it are closed to cars.

There is no problem finding petrol, food or coffee, since a city of over two million does not run short, and a coffee taken standing at a bar for a euro or so is one of the pleasures of Italian life. Try carbonara, cacio e pepe or supplì, and keep away from restaurants that put photographs of the dishes on the door.

Spring and autumn are best, as summer heat is severe and August half-empties the city, with many places closed.
t.florence@43.8,11.3:
Florence was one of the great stops on the Mille Miglia, and it is easy to see why the race came through. Drivers arriving from Bologna had crossed the Raticosa and Futa passes in the Apennines, a long, twisting run of hairpins that tested both engines and nerves, then dropped down into the Arno valley to the city where Brunelleschi's red dome rises above a sea of terracotta roofs. The dome, completed in the fifteenth century over the cathedral, was a feat of engineering that was done without a conventional wooden frame, and it still defines the skyline.

Riding into Florence from the north is a different thing from the old race. The city centre is small, dense and heavily restricted, with a ZTL traffic zone covering most of the historic core, and the camera system issues fines to anyone who enters without permission. The best plan is to leave the bike in a car park or on the outskirts, such as near Piazzale Michelangelo or in the suburbs, and walk. Cobbles and tram lines call for care, and summer heat can be fierce. The city is crowded from April to October, and the queues for the major museums, including the Uffizi and the Accademia, can be long, so book ahead.

For fuel, food and coffee, Florence has everything, and the outskirts have large petrol stations and supermarkets. Fiesole, on a hill north of the city, is a charming small town with Etruscan and Roman remains, an old cathedral and fine views back over the rooftops, and the road up to it is a pleasant short ride, with bends through cypress and olive groves. For a longer day, the roads south of the city into Chianti are among the best in Italy for relaxed riding, with gentle hills, vineyards and stone villages.

The food is robust and local. Look for bistecca alla fiorentina, a thick T-bone steak cooked rare over coals, ribollita, a bread and vegetable soup, and lampredotto, a tripe sandwich sold from street carts. Gelato was famously refined here, and the cafés still make it well.

Aim for early morning or late afternoon, when the golden light on the Arno is worth the effort.
t.the porticoes of bologna@44.5,11.3:
Bologna is a city built for walking in the rain. More than forty kilometres of covered arcades line its streets, some medieval, some Renaissance, some modern, and the Porticoes of Bologna received UNESCO status in 2021 as a distinctive urban form. They began as a practical fix: the university, founded in the eleventh century and often called the oldest in the world, drew so many students that the city needed more living space, and builders were allowed to extend rooms outward over the street on timber beams. Later they were rebuilt in brick and stone and required by law, so that people could move along any main street without getting wet.

The longest of all leads out of the city to the Sanctuary of the Madonna di San Luca on a hill south-west of the centre. It runs for nearly four kilometres and has around 660 arches, and climbing it on foot is a local ritual, particularly at the time of the annual procession of the icon. The Basilica at the top gives a view across the red roofs to the Po plain, and on a clear day you can see the Alps.

A motorbike in the old centre needs care. Much of it is a restricted traffic zone, and the porticoes themselves are for pedestrians, so ride outside the walls and walk. Cobbles, tram-free but bus-heavy streets and cyclists make the old town a bit of a maze, while the ring road, the tangenziale, is fast and often congested. Summer is hot and humid, and the arcades give welcome shade.

You need not worry about fuel, food or coffee, because Bologna, with more than three hundred and sixty thousand people, is full of all three, and the city is known as La Grassa, the fat one, for good reason. Tagliatelle with ragù, tortellini in broth, mortadella and lasagne with green pasta are all native to the city, and the wine bars serve Pignoletto with a plate of local cold cuts. Casalecchio di Reno, on the southern edge, is a larger suburb with petrol and shops, and the gateway to the Apennine roads.

Those roads are the reason so many riders come to the area: the hills south of Bologna offer curves in abundance, from the Futa and Raticosa passes toward Florence to the quieter valleys of the Reno and Setta.
t.strada maggiore@44.5,11.4:
Strada Maggiore is one of the oldest streets in Bologna, running east from the Two Towers along the line of the Roman road toward the Via Emilia, and it is a street where the arcades seem to be a different style every hundred metres. Some are medieval and made of timber, with beams that look too old to hold anything up, others are Renaissance and graceful, with slender columns. Along the way the street passes tall palaces, small shops, old churches and, on the right, the lovely porch of Santa Maria dei Servi, a Gothic church whose portico is among the most beautiful in the city.

Gioachino Rossini, the composer of The Barber of Seville, lived in a palace on this street in his later years and made it his home in Bologna, and the museum of music in a nearby palace now houses a collection of instruments, portraits and scores that tells the story of European music. A short distance away is the Casa Isolani, a medieval house from the thirteenth century with a wooden portico that is one of the oldest surviving in the city.

For anyone arriving by motorbike, this is a walking street, not a riding street. The centre has traffic restrictions, and the roads are narrow, so it is better to leave the bike outside the old walls in the supervised parking areas or on the street on the outskirts, such as the Ponticella district to the east. From there, the walk toward the heart of town is gentle and pleasant, and the arcades keep off sun and rain.

Ponticella is a small place with a few shops and cafés, but for fuel, supermarkets and larger services, Bologna itself is the place to look. Food is, as everywhere in the city, a pleasure: look for a trattoria where tortelloni with butter and sage or tagliatelle al ragù are made by hand, and a plate of mixed fried food, the fritto misto, if the season allows.

The best time of day is late afternoon, when the light slants under the porticoes and students gather on the steps.
t.cavour@44.5,11.3:
Via Cavour and Piazza Cavour are the elegant face of Bologna, the part of the city where the nineteenth century left a more formal imprint. After Italian unification, the city's rulers cut broad, straight streets through the medieval maze, built palaces in a grander style and created squares where the aristocracy and the newly rich could stroll. Today the area around Via Cavour, close to Piazza Maggiore, is lined with shops selling jewellery, fashion and fine food, beneath the same continuous arcades that cover most of the city.

The contrast with the old centre is part of the pleasure. A few steps from the narrow lanes of the Quadrilatero, where market stalls sell cheese, fresh pasta and cured meats, you reach quiet streets of tall, shuttered buildings and well-dressed pedestrians, with cafés where an espresso comes in a small white cup and a pastry on a saucer. In the evening, the aperitivo hour brings crowds to the bars, with small plates of snacks served alongside a glass of wine or a spritz.

On a bike, the centre is largely off limits or tightly controlled, as in most Italian historic cores, and the cobbles and tram-like sprawl of buses make the streets unpleasant to ride. The best approach is to find a parking spot for motorcycles, which are plentiful in marked bays near the old walls, then walk. Take care with the one-way system and the cycle lanes, which cut through the streets in unexpected places.

The city is generous with services. With over three hundred and sixty thousand inhabitants, it has fuel stations on the ring road, supermarkets and large hotels, and Ponticella, a small place nearby, can supply the basics. The best coffee is drunk standing at the bar, and the best ice cream is made in small workshops with seasonal flavours, rather than in the big, brightly lit shops.

Bologna's reputation for left-leaning politics, student life and gastronomy is deserved, and the mix creates a city that feels lived in, not preserved. Early autumn is a wonderful time, when the heat softens, truffles and mushrooms appear on menus and the arcades fill with students returning for the new year.
t.pavaglione@44.5,11.3:
Not many places have a portico named after a silk market, but Bologna is not many places. The Pavaglione is the long, wide arcade that runs along the side of the Palazzo dell'Archiginnasio, near the great Piazza Maggiore, and its name comes from the pavilion, a tent or covered market where silk cocoons were once traded. Bologna was a major centre of silk production in the late Middle Ages and Renaissance, and the water-powered mills of the city, fed by canals from the Reno, supplied thread to much of Europe. A stroll under the arches today, among the shops and cafés, is a stroll through that history.

The Archiginnasio itself was the main seat of the University of Bologna from the sixteenth century, built to bring the various schools together in a single building. Its walls and corridors are covered in thousands of coats of arms painted by students and professors over the centuries, a dense, colourful archive of academic life. Inside, the Anatomical Theatre, a small wooden chamber with a carved ceiling and statues of famous physicians, was used for public dissections, and is among the most unusual rooms in Italy. Visits are possible, but opening hours vary, so it pays to check.

Practicalities are simple. This is the very heart of the city, with traffic restrictions in force, so leave the bike outside the centre and walk in. With the old stones underfoot and the sound of bicycle bells, it is a pleasant walk, and the arcades give shelter if the weather turns.

Bologna has everything a traveller needs, from fuel stations on the outskirts to supermarkets and restaurants in every district, and the neighbouring place of Ponticella has some small shops. A good spot for lunch is any of the small trattorias in the lanes near the market, where the menu changes daily and the pasta is made by hand.

The real treat at the Pavaglione is the people-watching. Students, shoppers and pensioners drift past in the afternoon, and on warm evenings the area comes alive, with buskers, couples and groups of friends. If you are a coffee drinker, try a caffè in one of the old-fashioned bars, standing at the zinc counter among the regulars.
t.santa caterina e saragozza@44.5,11.3:
Via Saragozza runs south-west from the city's old gate, the Porta Saragozza, toward the hills, and it is the start of the longest portico in the world, the covered way that climbs to the Sanctuary of San Luca. The arcades begin at the gate, run along the street, and then, from the monumental Arco del Meloncello, begin to climb in earnest, a long, steady ascent of steps, ramps and arches that carries pilgrims and joggers up the hillside. It is a favourite local walk, and on summer evenings it fills with people.

Santa Caterina, the neighbouring street, is a narrower, quieter lane lined with old houses, small shops and cafés, a good way to see the less polished side of Bologna. The area is mostly residential and feels like a neighbourhood, with washing hanging from windows, bicycles chained to railings and small groups of neighbours chatting on the pavement. It is an easy place to spend an hour, and one of the best spots for finding the sort of everyday restaurant where the locals eat.

For a motorcyclist, this side of the city is the gateway to the best roads. From Casalecchio di Reno, a larger suburb on the edge, you can follow the Reno valley or climb into the Apennines, with winding roads through chestnut woods, small villages and open farmland, and in spring the slopes are covered with blossom. The roads here are popular with riders from all over northern Italy, and on a fine weekend you will share the bends with plenty of other bikes, as well as cyclists, who train on the hills in large numbers.

The centre is a restricted traffic zone, so it is best to park outside the walls and walk to the arches. Fuel, shops and cafés are never far away, since Bologna and Casalecchio have everything you could want. The hills can be hot and hazy in summer, with temperatures in the mid thirties, and cool and clear in autumn.

The sanctuary on the hill has a long tradition. According to legend, a Greek hermit brought an icon of the Virgin to the hill in the twelfth century, and it has been honoured ever since, with a procession carrying it down into the city each year. Whether or not you share the faith, the walk up is worth the effort for the view from the top.
t.santo stefano e mercanzia@44.5,11.3:
Where Strada Maggiore begins, in the shadow of the Two Towers, a very particular little cluster of buildings stands: the Palazzo della Mercanzia, a Gothic building of the late fourteenth century that housed the merchants' guild and its court, a body that settled commercial disputes and regulated trade. Its façade is decorated with the coats of arms of the guilds, and it forms part of the dense core of medieval Bologna, an area of narrow lanes and tall brick houses. Nearby stand the two leaning towers, Asinelli and Garisenda, the former rising nearly a hundred metres and the latter famously tilted, a symbol of the city.

Close to the Mercanzia, the Piazza Santo Stefano is a quiet, beautiful square surrounded by porticoes and old palaces, with a group of interconnected churches known as the Sette Chiese, the seven churches, which from the outside look like a single rambling, irregular building. According to tradition, the complex was founded as a copy of the holy sites of Jerusalem, and the inner courtyard, with a basin said to have been used by Pontius Pilate, is a calm place for a pause. The atmosphere is wonderfully old, with the smell of candle wax and damp stone.

For the rider this is, again, a place to leave the bike. The roads of the historic core are mostly restricted, and the streets are narrow and thick with pedestrians and cyclists, so the sensible plan is to park outside and walk in. A short walk leads to the large central square, Piazza Maggiore, with the huge unfinished basilica of San Petronio.

There is nothing to worry about on the practical side: Bologna has all the fuel, shops, restaurants and hotels one could ask for, and the suburb of Ponticella adds a few more. Good restaurants cluster around the Piazza Santo Stefano, and the aperitivo hour fills the area with chatter.

The towers can be climbed, with a long wooden staircase inside the taller one, and the view at the top across the red roofs, the hills and, on a very clear day, the Alps is the best in the city. Tickets must be booked, and the climb is not recommended for anyone nervous of heights or narrow stairs.
t.villa de careggi@43.8,11.2:
Cosimo de' Medici chose a quiet slope just north of Florence for his country house, and in the late 1450s he had the architect Michelozzo rebuild an older castle-like farmhouse at Careggi into a villa. It was not a grand showpiece. It was a working retreat where a banker who ran a city without holding office could think, farm, and entertain scholars. Cosimo died here in 1464, and so did his grandson Lorenzo the Magnificent in 1492, which makes the walls rather weighty with Florentine history.

The house is best known for what happened inside it. Cosimo gave Marsilio Ficino a home nearby and encouraged him to translate Plato and the Neoplatonists into Latin, and the circle of friends that gathered here to read, argue and dine became what later generations called the Platonic Academy. Whether it was ever a formal institution is debated, but the idea of rich merchants spending an evening on Greek philosophy tells you much about the early Renaissance. The villa belongs to the group of Medici villas that UNESCO lists together, and the building is today part of the grounds of a large hospital, which gives the visit a slightly odd texture: ambulances at the gate, cypresses and a formal garden beyond. Access is limited, and the villa has been opened to visitors only on certain days, so check before riding out.

For a motorcyclist this is city-edge Florence, three kilometres from the centre, and the roads are the usual busy suburban ones, with hospital traffic, buses and parked cars squeezing the lanes. It rewards going early. Fiesole, a small hill town of under three thousand people, is only a few kilometres north, and the climb up to it through villas, walled gardens and olive terraces is one of the best short rides in Tuscany, with bends tight enough to keep you awake and views that open out over the dome of the cathedral. Weekend traffic can slow it, and in midsummer the heat sits heavily in the walled lanes.

Fuel, food and coffee are no problem in Florence itself, with plenty of stations on the ring road and bars on every corner. Take a short break at a bar for a coffee at the counter, and ask about the schiacciata, a flat, oily, salty bread that makes a good second breakfast. Remember the ZTL restrictions in the centre if you drift south into the old city.
t.abruzzo@41.9,13.8:
The high Apennines of Abruzzo are the least tamed part of central Italy. At these coordinates you are near Scanno and Pescasseroli, in a landscape of beech forest, bare limestone ridges and alpine meadows, with peaks that rise above two thousand metres and keep their snow into late spring. Most of it lies within the Abruzzo, Lazio and Molise National Park, created in 1922, one of the oldest in Italy, where the Marsican brown bear, a distinct population found nowhere else, still survives in small numbers. Apennine wolves, chamois, red deer and golden eagles live here too, and in autumn the roaring of stags carries through the beech woods.

The riding is unusually good and unusually quiet. The road from Sulmona up to Scanno passes through the Sagittario gorge, a tight, narrow defile where the tarmac clings to the rock and tunnels cut the corners, and then opens onto the high plateau and the little lake of Scanno, which is said to have a heart-shaped outline when seen from above. The village itself is a tangle of steep stone lanes and arches, with a tradition of women's costume in dark colours and elaborate headdresses, and goldsmiths who still work the filigree jewellery that locals once gave as wedding gifts. To the west, the road toward Pescasseroli crosses a pass and then runs along the valley of the Sangro river, with beech forests on both sides. Bends are frequent, the surface is mostly good, and traffic is thin outside the school holidays.

Fuel is the point to watch. Scanno and Pescasseroli, both small towns of two thousand people or so, have fuel and a few shops, but the stations are limited and not always open late, so the larger town of Sulmona, about twenty kilometres away, is the safe place to fill up. Pescasseroli sits at roughly twelve hundred metres, so even in summer evenings are cool, and in winter the passes can ice up or close.

Sulmona is known for its confetti, sugared almonds shaped into elaborate flowers, and the local food is shepherd's food: lamb, pecorino, sausages, lentils, and a spicy chilli oil. Pescasseroli was the birthplace of the philosopher Benedetto Croce. Go in late spring or in October, when the beech woods go copper, and keep your speed down at dusk, when wildlife crosses the road.
t.jardin de pratolino@43.9,11.3:
Pratolino is a hill north of Florence where, in the 1570s, Francesco I de' Medici decided to build a pleasure ground that would amaze Europe. He commissioned Bernardo Buontalenti, an architect, engineer and theatre designer, and the result was a park of grottoes, fountains, water-powered automata and hidden jets, which wrecked visitors' clothes and delighted them in equal measure. The great survivor is the Appennine, a gigantic statue by Giambologna, about ten metres high, crouched beside a pond, a stone giant with caves inside his body and a face emerging from rock and moss. It is one of the strangest and most impressive garden sculptures in Italy.

Much of the original villa is gone, and the garden was reshaped in the nineteenth century as an English-style landscape park by the Demidoff family, so the place is a layered mixture rather than a pure survival. UNESCO includes it in the list of Medici villas and gardens. The park is seasonal, and visits are generally limited to certain days and months, so check before you go. Walking in, you pass a huge old fish pond, long avenues of beech and chestnut, and quiet corners where moss grows over damp stone.

The road up from Florence is the old Via Bolognese, the route that leads north to Bologna, and it climbs quickly past villas and hillside gardens. Beyond Pratolino, the road becomes rural, with chestnut woods, small farms and the slopes of Monte Senario, where a monastery sits among firs. The riding on the lanes nearby is excellent, with tight bends, narrow tarmac and light traffic outside weekends. The old road to Bologna over the Futa pass was part of the route of the Mille Miglia and attracts a steady stream of riders, so expect company on sunny Sundays.

Caldine and Pian di Mugnone are small villages with a bar or two, but for fuel, supermarkets and larger choices, Sesto Fiorentino, a town of about forty-five thousand people some nine kilometres off, or Florence itself, is the place to head. In summer the hills are a few degrees cooler than the city, and a picnic under the trees is a pleasure.

Go in spring, when the camellias and magnolias bloom, or in October for colour. The giant is at his best on a quiet weekday morning.
t.peak to peak highway@39.8,-105.6:
Central City was once called the richest square mile on earth. Gold was found in the gulches here in 1859, and within a few years thousands of miners had crowded into a narrow valley in the Front Range, building a town of brick and stone, an opera house and hotels on a steep slope. Today Central City and its neighbour Black Hawk are known for their casinos, which fill the old buildings with slot machines, but the Victorian streets remain, and the Teller House and the Central City Opera, which still holds a summer season, are a reminder of the boom years. The pin sits just above the town, in the gulch country of Clear Creek County, at an elevation of some two and a half thousand metres.

Idaho Springs, in the next valley, is an old mining town with a main street of false-fronted buildings, hot springs and a mine tour, and Georgetown, with its Victorian houses, is the base for the Georgetown Loop Railroad, a narrow-gauge line that crosses a high trestle in a series of loops. From Idaho Springs, the road to Mount Evans, which climbs to over 14,000 feet, is the highest paved road in North America, and in the warm months a stream of riders makes the climb, though the upper section is closed for much of the year.

The Peak to Peak Highway is a different kind of road. It runs for about 55 miles along the front of the Rocky Mountains, from Black Hawk to Estes Park, crossing a series of high saddles at over 8,000 feet, with views of the peaks of the Continental Divide, forests of aspen and pine, and mountain towns. The curves are long and flowing, the surface is generally good, and the traffic is moderate, though it grows heavy on summer weekends. In autumn the aspens turn gold, and the whole road glows. Weather changes quickly at this altitude, with afternoon thunderstorms in summer and snow as early as September.

Fuel, food and coffee are available at Black Hawk, Central City and Idaho Springs, and the mountain towns have cafés and diners, many with decks that look out over the valley. Evergreen, twenty-seven kilometres away, is the nearest big town. Fill the tank before climbing and carry a warm layer.

The altitude can be a problem for riders from sea level, with headaches and shortness of breath, so drink plenty of water and take it easy. A hot coffee and a slice of pie in a mountain diner is the perfect reward.
t.red mountain pass@37.9,-107.7:
Red Mountain Pass crosses the San Juan Mountains at 11,018 feet, and the road over it, US 550 between Ouray and Silverton, is part of the stretch known as the Million Dollar Highway, one of the most famous and most frightening roads in the United States. The pin sits at the summit, with huge, red and orange mountains rising on all sides, coloured by the iron in the rock, which gives the pass its name. The old mining district of Red Mountain lay to the south, and the rusty remains of mills and shafts can still be seen on the slopes, where the Yankee Girl and other mines once produced silver.

The road was built in the 1880s to serve the mines, and the origin of its nickname is disputed: some say it cost a million dollars a mile, others that the fill contains gold ore, and others that the views are worth a million dollars. Whichever, the road is spectacular, a ledge cut into the cliffs, with no guardrails in places and drops of hundreds of feet, and a series of tight hairpins. The towns at either end are beautiful: Ouray, in a narrow box canyon ringed by cliffs, is known as the Switzerland of America, with hot springs and Victorian buildings, and Silverton is a restored mining town at the end of the narrow-gauge railroad from Durango.

For a rider, the pass is a challenge and a joy. The surface is paved and generally good, but narrow, with sharp bends and blind corners, and the edges are unprotected, so concentration is essential. Traffic includes large trucks, RVs and tourists, and the weather can change in minutes, with sudden thunderstorms in summer afternoons and snow at any time of year. Ice and avalanches close the road in winter, and avalanche control may stop traffic for hours. Altitude affects both bike and rider, with a loss of power and shortness of breath.

The nearest stations are at Ouray, on the north side, and Silverton, on the south, so fill the tank and carry a warm layer. Both towns have cafés, restaurants and bakeries, and a cup of hot chocolate in Silverton is a fine reward.

Go early, before the clouds build, and take the descent slowly, using the engine to brake. The views of the red mountains, the snow patches and the deep valleys below are some of the finest in Colorado.
These coordinates fall on the high ground west of Denver, among the pine and aspen of the foothills near Evergreen, a mountain town of about nine thousand people on a small lake. A short way south is the valley of Bear Creek, where the road climbs through the narrow canyon toward Idaho Springs. This is the doorway to some of the best motorcycle riding in the Front Range, and a good place to pull over and look back at the plains.

The ride is named for Trail Ridge Road in Rocky Mountain National Park, which lies a good way to the north, but in this area the great attraction is Mount Evans, the highest paved road in North America, which climbs to over 4,300 metres. Both roads share the same character: they are open only in summer, closed by snow for the rest of the year, and the opening dates change from season to season, so check before you set out. Trail Ridge itself reaches just over 3,700 metres, the highest continuous paved road in the United States, and crosses the Continental Divide in open alpine tundra where the wind cuts straight through your jacket.

The foothills here are a pleasant warm-up. Bear Creek Canyon on Highway 74 is narrow and curvy, following the stream between steep, rocky walls, and Evergreen Lake is a good place to stop for coffee. The road surface is mostly good, but gravel gathers in corners and deer are a danger at dusk. Elk herds often graze on the meadows near Evergreen, and in autumn the bulls roar in the mating season, a sound that carries across the valley.

Fuel and food are easy in Evergreen, which has several stations and a lively main street. After that, services thin out quickly. The weather in the Rockies is changeable, and afternoon thunderstorms in summer can bring hail and lightning to the high roads, so aim to be down from the ridges by early afternoon. A warm layer and a rain jacket are essential, even on a day that begins in sunshine. At this altitude the air is thin, sunburn is quick and you will feel the cold much faster than you expect.
t.oslo norway scenic roads@60.5,10.7:
Lake Mjøsa is Norway's largest lake, about a hundred kilometres long and over four hundred metres deep in its deepest place, and this pin lies in the farming country that rolls down toward its southern end. It is the Toten plateau, a broad upland of fields, birch woods and low ridges where Norwegians grow much of their grain and potatoes, with the lake glinting below to the east. The small settlements of Reinsvoll and Lena are the nearest, and Gjøvik, the main town of the district, is a short ride north.

Mjøsa has its own character. A paddle steamer, the Skibladner, has run on the lake since 1856 and is the oldest of its kind still in regular service, calling at the lakeside towns with a plume of smoke and the clack of its engine. The shores are lined with farms and orchards, and in the old days timber was floated down from the mountains to the sawmills along the lake. In summer, the water is surprisingly warm for a Norwegian lake, and swimming from small beaches is a popular pastime.

The riding on the plateau is relaxed. County roads rise and fall in easy bends over the ridges, with views of the lake and the surrounding hills, and traffic is light.
