The surface is usually good, though winter frost leaves patches that need watching. Wind across the open fields can be strong, and rain showers pass quickly. For a start, the road down to the lakeshore is a pleasant run, and the early morning light on the water is excellent.

For practical needs, fuel is easy at Gjøvik and Raufoss, and small shops in the villages sell basic supplies. If you want a swim, look for the public beaches on the lake, which have changing huts in some cases. The water is cold in May and pleasantly mild by August. Carry a towel and a flask of coffee, and watch for farm vehicles on the narrow lanes. A late evening swim, with the sun low over the water, is one of the pleasures of a Norwegian summer.
t.hardanger fjord and waterfalls@60.3,10.0:
Hønefoss is the gate to the mountains, and this pin lies a short ride west of it, in the green country of Ringerike where the lowland farms begin to climb into forest. The town itself grew around a waterfall, the Hønefossen, which drops through the middle of the centre and powered sawmills and paper works for centuries. Today the falls are floodlit at night, and a small park beside them is a pleasant place for a coffee. Hønefoss has a population of nearly fourteen thousand, so fuel and food are no problem.

The road that matters here is the Rv7, which leaves Hønefoss and heads north-west along the Krøderen lake and up the Hallingdal valley, then climbs over the Hardangervidda plateau to the fjord country around Eidfjord. It is the main route from Oslo to the Hardanger region, and a classic ride. Beyond the plateau, the road drops into the fjord, past the great Vøringsfossen waterfall, which tumbles nearly a hundred and fifty metres into a gorge. The ride from Oslo to Eidfjord is a long day, but the scenery is marvellous.

Ringerike has an older story too. The district was an important centre in Viking times, and it gave its name to the Ringerike style of Viking art, all twining beasts and tendrils. The old King's Road, the main route between Christiania and Bergen, passed through here, and sections of it can still be walked or ridden. Farms along the way still have old log buildings, and the soil is rich and dark. Lake Tyrifjorden, to the east, is a long, deep lake with islands and sheltered bays.

For a food stop, the town has many cafés and bakeries, and the roadside kiosks along the main road sell the usual waffles, sausage and coffee. Fuel is easy in Hønefoss and Jevnaker, but fill the tank before heading into the mountains, since stations are far apart on the high plateau. Winter closures and snow affect the higher parts of Rv7, so check conditions between November and April. Carry warm layers in any case, as the weather changes fast.
t.atlantic road coastal bridges@60.1,11.1:
Ask is the name of a place, and also, by a happy chance, an English word for what a rider should do before heading into this district: ask whether the roads are clear. The pin lies in Gjerdrum, on the Romerike plain north-east of Oslo, a flat, productive land of grain fields and low ridges near the airport at Gardermoen. Kløfta, the nearest sizeable place, is a few kilometres away and has everything a motorbike needs, including several stations and a good supermarket.

The ground here has a hidden character. The soil is marine clay, laid down when the sea covered the land after the last Ice Age, and some of it is quick clay, which can turn to liquid when disturbed. In December 2020, a quick-clay slide at Ask swept away a number of homes and took ten lives, a tragedy that is still remembered in the community and led to a national review of such risks. The area is calm and beautiful, but it carries this memory with it.

For riders, this is a starting point. The roads here are straight and well surfaced, with wide shoulders and heavy traffic around the airport and the E6 motorway, and a ride north or west quickly leads into quieter country. Early starts help, since the roads between Oslo and Gardermoen fill with commuters from seven. Cameras are frequent, and speed limits are low, so keep an eye on the signs. In winter, snow and ice make the going slow.

Fuel is easy at Kløfta, Ask and Jessheim, many stations being unmanned with card payment, so carry a card that works. Cafés and bakeries are common in the centres. The coast of the Atlantic Road is far to the north-west, a long day's travel, so check that you have everything before you set off. A good breakfast in a local café is not a bad idea. The farmland around is gold in late summer.
t.oslo norway scenic roads@60.5,11.9:
The Solør district lies in the east of Norway, where the land flattens and the forest closes in, and this pin sits in the heart of it, between Kirkenær and the Glomma river. The country is a mosaic of spruce and pine, small farms, bogs and long, slow lakes, running east toward the Swedish border, and it has a quiet, lonely character that suits a rider who has had enough of crowds. Kirkenær, the nearest town, has barely twelve hundred people.

The woods here have a distinctive history. In the seventeenth century, Finnish settlers, drawn by the chance of cheap land and a way of farming that involved burning the forest to grow rye, moved into the area and became known as the forest Finns. They brought their language, their log smoke saunas and their folklore, and their culture survived in the Finnskogen for centuries. At Grue, a church fire in 1822 killed more than a hundred people, one of the worst such disasters in the country, and the present church stands as a memorial.

Riding here is calm, with long, straight roads through the forest, gentle rolls and few bends. The surface is generally good, and traffic is light, though timber lorries use the main routes. The risk is moose, which are common and can cross the road at dawn and dusk, so keep your speed down in the woods and watch the verges. The forest is at its best in September, when the birch leaves turn and the light is low.

The lakes are good for swimming, with soft, brown water and quiet beaches that are often empty. Fuel is available at Kirkenær and Våler, but pumps may be unmanned, and cards are the norm, so carry one that works in Norway. Shops close early, and distances are long, so plan your meals. Bring mosquito repellent in summer, because the forest is full of insects, and a warm layer for the evening. The silence at night is deep.
t.telemark canal roads scenic road@60.2,10:
Nordmarka is Oslo's backyard, a huge tract of forest, hills and lakes that begins at the edge of the city and runs north for dozens of kilometres, and this pin sits at its north-eastern fringe, near Nittedal. The landscape is rolling, with spruce and pine on the ridges, black lakes in the hollows and a few farms in the valleys, and it is criss-crossed by trails that Oslo families walk, ski and cycle every weekend. Rotnes, the nearest sizeable place, is a small town on the Nitelva river.

The forest has been a working landscape for centuries. Timber from here fed the sawmills of Oslo and the shipyards of the coast, and ironworks used charcoal burned in the woods. The old logging roads and floating channels remain, and many of the lakes have dams built to regulate the flow. Today, the forest is mainly a recreation area, and cabins, many of them simple wooden huts without electricity, are a Norwegian tradition. In winter, the skiing here is excellent.

For a rider, the roads around Nittedal and Grua are quiet county routes with a mix of forest and farmland. The bends are easy, the surface is generally good, and the traffic is light. In the early morning, mist hangs in the hollows, and the smell of pine and damp earth is strong. The road is not a challenge, but it makes a pleasant backdrop for a morning, and the lakes are beautiful in the evening. In winter, snow tyres are a must.

Cafés and small shops offer snacks and coffee. If you are stopping for photographs, find a lake with a view of the forest, and be careful on the roadside. Bring a warm layer, since the forest holds the cold, and watch for moose at dusk. The silence under the trees is remarkable, given how close the capital is.
t.telluride@37.9,-107.8:
The road ends here, in the most literal sense. Telluride sits at the head of a box canyon in the San Juan Mountains, at about 2,670 metres, with cliffs on three sides and a waterfall tumbling down the back wall. Mount Bierstadt, one of Colorado's fourteeners, stands at the head of the valley, and the road on which this pin sits, Guanella Pass, climbs almost to its feet. t.million dollar highway weekend high poin:

The coordinates here are on Interstate 70 in the Rockies, right beside the old silver town of Georgetown, at roughly 2,600 metres in the valley of Clear Creek. t.tivoli and sabine hills@42.1,12.6:

Do as the locals do and drink it standing at the counter, with a cornetto, before you set off. A coffee at a Roman roadside bar is a better introduction to Italy than most museum tickets.

What gives the area its character is the landscape behind. To the north-east, the isolated limestone ridge of Monte Soratte rises out of the plain like a ship, nearly seven hundred metres high, a landmark the Latin poets knew as Soracte. Horace mentions it in one of his odes, snow-covered in winter, and on a clear day it is easy to see why it caught the eye. The Tiber, brown and unhurried, runs below, and beyond it the Sabine hills rise in successive blue ridges.

Practical points matter on this side of Rome. The ring road, the Grande Raccordo Anulare, carries heavy traffic at almost any hour, and the roads feeding it can back up on Sunday evenings, so aim to be moving before the morning rush or after it. Riano has about seven thousand people, with stations, supermarkets and bars, so fuel is no problem. Expect fast, impatient local driving and take the first quiet side road toward the hills, where the Roman traffic thins out within a few kilometres.
t.tivoli and sabine hills scenic road@42.0:
This stretch lies on the edge of the Monti Cornicolani, a little group of limestone hills north-east of Rome where the plain starts to wrinkle toward the Sabine mountains. Montecelio and Sant'Angelo Romano are both old hill villages, one perched on a spur above the Roman plain and the other crowning a rocky hill, and the road between them winds through olive groves, scrub oak and small farms, with the dome of St Peter's occasionally visible far to the west. Guidonia, the large town below, is a newcomer, founded in 1937 as a model aviation city, and its flat, rational layout contrasts sharply with the tangled lanes of the old villages.

The scenic part is the old villages. Montecelio has a medieval centre of steep lanes and stone houses, with a long view back over the Roman Campagna, while Sant'Angelo Romano sits close beneath a rocky outcrop with a small castle, and the old stone is warm in the evening light. The surrounding hills have been quarried for centuries, and below Guidonia the pale travertine stone that comes from the plain around Tivoli has been cut for two thousand years, giving Rome many of its great buildings, including the colonnade of St Peter's.

The riding is varied and good for the area, with short, winding climbs and drops, tight bends in the villages and some open, fast stretches between them. The surface is uneven in places, with patches left by heavy lorries from the quarries, and Italian drivers have a relaxed attitude to the centre line, so approach blind bends with caution. Early mornings are best, since the lanes are quiet, the air is clear and you can see the Apennines beyond the plain, and weekends are busier, with Romans out for lunch.

Fuel is straightforward, since Guidonia Montecelio, with more than sixty thousand people, has plenty of stations and supermarkets, and Montecelio and Sant'Angelo have a few bars and small shops. If you want lunch, look for a trattoria in one of the hill villages, where the menu is likely to feature pasta with cacio e pepe, grilled lamb and local olive oil, and the wine comes in a carafe. Book ahead on Sundays, when families fill the tables.
t.tivoli and sabine hills high point@41.8,:
The Alban Hills are an old volcano, and the road across their eastern flank near San Cesareo is the place where Rome's rolling plain begins to climb. The Colli Albani erupted for hundreds of thousands of years, and the last significant activity was thousands of years ago, leaving a ring of hills around two crater lakes, Albano and Nemi. The summit, Monte Cavo, is just under a thousand metres, and this stretch, on the plateau's edge, sits well below it. High point is a modest label here, but the ground does rise noticeably, and the air is a degree or two cooler.

The land is a patchwork of vineyards, chestnut woods, villas and small towns, the Castelli Romani, where the Roman nobility and the popes built country houses, and the local wine is the pale, dry Frascati, drunk in the old osterie. San Cesareo lies on the edge of this, a busy town of ten thousand, and the roads around it carry heavy local traffic, with a mix of lorries, commuters and weekend visitors. Colle di Fuori is a smaller village nearby, with a view across the plain.

The riding in the hills proper is some of the best near Rome. The roads wind through woods in tight bends and short climbs, with sudden views of the lakes, and the surface is mostly good, though it can be broken by tree roots and winter damage. Around San Cesareo, the roads are straighter and busier, but a few turns bring you into quieter lanes among the vineyards. Autumn is a good season, with the grape harvest, the chestnut festivals and the fresh smell of pressed grapes.

Fuel is available in San Cesareo, with several stations and supermarkets, and the nearby towns of Monte Compatri and Colonna have more. For a bite to eat, look for the roadside stands selling porchetta, the roast pork sandwich that is a local speciality, especially in the town of Ariccia on the other side of the hills. Weekends bring heavy traffic from Rome, so try to ride on a weekday, or start early on Sunday.
t.tivoli and sabine hills photo pull off@4:
The Tyrrhenian coast south of Rome is flat, sandy and green with pines, and Ardea sits just inland from it, a small town on a low tufa hill above a plain of fields and umbrella pines. It has an old history, much older than it looks. Ardea was the capital of the Rutuli, the people whose king, Turnus, fought Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid, and ancient walls and an earthwork still survive on the hill. The town today is quiet, with a museum devoted to the twentieth-century sculptor Giacomo Manzù, who lived and worked nearby.

The photo pull-off is on the flat road between Casalazzara and Ardea, where the landscape opens up. This is the Agro Romano, the old farmland of the Roman Campagna, with its long, level horizons, rows of eucalyptus and umbrella pine, and the occasional ruined farmhouse. In the evening, the light is warm and golden, and the sea is visible as a thin glimmer to the west. It is not dramatic scenery, but it has a calm, open quality that is typically Italian and very different from the hills to the east.

The riding is flat and easy. Roads here run straight across the fields, with the occasional roundabout and a lot of traffic heading to the beaches at weekends, particularly in summer, when the coast fills with Romans escaping the heat. The surface is generally good, though a few roads have been worn by lorries and farm vehicles. The wind off the sea can be strong, and the sandy soil gets blown across the road, so be careful of loose grit on the bends.

Ardea has about seventeen thousand people, so fuel, food and supplies are no problem, with stations and supermarkets on the main road. The beaches nearby, such as Lido dei Pini and Tor San Lorenzo, have a long strip of dark, volcanic sand and a row of seafood restaurants, which are good for lunch, particularly in spring and autumn when the crowds are thin. In summer, the traffic and the heat make midday riding unpleasant, so start early or ride in the evening.
t.buonconvento@43.1,11.5:
Buonconvento sits on the Via Cassia in the valley of the Arbia river, south of Siena, a small walled town built of red brick that most travellers pass on the way to somewhere grander. That is a mistake. The walls still stand in a tidy rectangle, with a gate at each end, and inside the streets are quiet and clean, lined with old brick houses, with a long, narrow main street that gives the place an unusual, almost theatrical order. The town has a historical connection to the Holy Roman Emperor Henry VII, who died here in 1313 while on campaign in Italy.

The landscape around Buonconvento is the Crete Senesi and the Val d'Orcia, a land of bare clay hills, cypresses, wheat fields and isolated farmhouses, and the colour changes with the seasons, from the green of spring to the gold of summer and the grey of winter. The ridge-top town of Montalcino, about ten kilometres to the west, makes Brunello, one of Italy's greatest red wines, and the great abbey of Monte Oliveto Maggiore, set among cypress trees, lies a short ride to the north-east. Both are well worth the diversion.

A small museum in the town is devoted to the sharecropping system, the mezzadria, that shaped Tuscan farm life for centuries, until it was abolished in the 1960s, and it gives a good picture of how people lived and worked on these hills. The town has a number of bars and small restaurants, and a bakery or two, and it is a pleasant place for a coffee or a light lunch before the next stretch of hills. There is a Friday market on some weeks, though the days vary, so ask.

The riding around Buonconvento is some of the best in Tuscany, with long, rolling roads through the hills, open bends and fine views, though the surface can be patchy and gravel appears on the corners. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with warm light and fewer tourists. Buonconvento has fuel in town, but stations can be thin on Sundays, so fill up in Siena or Sinalunga, about twenty-three kilometres away, which is a bigger town. In July and August the heat is serious, and shade is scarce, so carry water.
t.terminillo mountain road@41.7,12.4:
Rome's south-western edge is a patchwork of planned suburbs, pine woods and wide, fast roads that run to the sea, and this fuel stop sits among them, near Casal Palocco and Vitinia, a few kilometres from the great ring road. Casal Palocco itself is a leafy 1960s residential estate, laid out among umbrella pines, with big gardens and quiet streets, a long way from the Rome of the postcards. It is the sort of place where the supermarkets have wide parking lots and the bars open at six in the morning.

The reason for the stop is the day ahead. Terminillo, the mountain the Romans call their own, lies north-east of the capital in the central Apennines, beyond Rieti, rising to just over two thousand metres, and it is the closest real ski area to Rome. The day starts here because the ride crosses the city and then climbs through hills and mountain roads, and the first serious fuel station on the other side of the Apennine foothills is a long way off. Fill up, check the tyres and take a coffee at the bar, and you will be ready.

The ring road is the thing to think about. Rome's Grande Raccordo Anulare is one of the busiest roads in Italy, and the wise rider avoids it at peak times, so an early start, ideally before seven, makes a big difference. Traffic moves fast and in a lively fashion, with little use of indicators, and lane discipline is a matter of opinion. Take it steadily, keep your distance and watch the mirrors, and you will be out the other side before long.

Casal Palocco has about thirty thousand people and plenty of stations, shops and cafés, so the services are good. Vitinia, a smaller neighbour, has a few places too. The landscape here is flat and green, with pines and a hint of the sea breeze, and the nearby Castelporziano estate, the president's country property, preserves a big tract of coastal forest. If you have a little time before leaving, it is worth a glance at the pines in the early light.
t.terminillo mountain road high point@41.7:
No one comes to Castel Fusano for height, and the label is a joke the map is playing. The ground near Lido di Ostia is nearly at sea level, a flat coastal strip of sand, marsh and pines behind the beaches where Romans go for a day at the sea. What it does have is the Pineta di Castel Fusano, a large forest of umbrella pines that has grown here for centuries, planted to shelter the coast and to supply pine nuts, and its big, flat-topped trees make a strange, beautiful canopy over the dunes and the old roads.

The forest has a long history. In Roman times, this was the coastline around the port of Ostia, and the old Via Severiana, a coastal road built by the emperor Septimius Severus, runs beneath the trees, with traces of Roman villas and farms around it. The seventeenth-century castle that gives the forest its name still stands inside, in the middle of the pines. Fires have damaged parts of the forest in recent decades, and you will see stretches where the trunks are blackened and the replanting is young.

The riding is flat and sleepy, with long, straight roads through the pines, a few roundabouts and plenty of cyclists and joggers. The light under the trees is soft, dappled and green, and the smell of resin is strong on a warm day. Surfaces can be dusty, with pine needles and sand on the bends, which are slippery when dry as well as when wet, and the speed limits are low. Early morning and late afternoon are the best times, as the midday heat can be oppressive, and the weekends fill with beach traffic.

Lido di Ostia is a big seaside town of about eighty thousand people, and fuel, food and parking are straightforward, with stations on the main roads and a long promenade of bars and fish restaurants. The ruins of ancient Ostia, a few kilometres inland, are one of the best-preserved Roman towns and deserve a visit if you have time. After the ride, a plate of spaghetti with clams on the seafront is the classic reward.
Lake Bracciano is a perfectly round crater lake, a few kilometres across, north-west of Rome, and the roads around it give some of the pleasantest riding near the capital. The lake fills a collapsed volcano, and its water is clear and clean, since it supplies Rome with drinking water and motorboats are banned. Anguillara Sabazia sits on a small peninsula on the southern shore, a handsome old town of narrow lanes and stone houses, with views over the water to the hills on the far side.

The old town is worth a walk. Its streets climb a short hill to a church and a small square, and the lakeside promenade below has bars and restaurants serving freshwater fish from the lake, including eel and whitefish. Across the lake, the town of Bracciano is dominated by a great Orsini castle, one of the best-preserved medieval castles in Italy, with moats, towers and rooms that can be visited. The lake has been a destination for Romans for centuries, and on summer weekends the beaches are packed.

The road around the lake is a gentle, scenic loop, with long, flowing curves between olive groves and woods, and the lake glinting between the trees. The surface is generally good, though the road is narrow in places, and traffic can be heavy on summer weekends. There are plenty of places to stop for a view or a swim, and the best light is in the morning, when the water is still and the mist rises. In autumn, the hills around the lake turn gold and red.

Anguillara Sabazia has about fourteen thousand people, so fuel, shops and cafés are readily available, and Osteria Nuova, a smaller settlement nearby, has a few services. The surrounding villages have trattorias that serve local specialities, including pasta with wild boar and grilled meat, and the white wine of the area is light and dry. Parking in the old town can be tight on summer weekends, but there are car parks near the lake, and motorcycles can usually find a space close to the centre.
t.terminillo mountain road photo pull off@:
The Treja valley is a secret in plain sight, a deep green cleft in the volcanic tufa north of Rome, where a small river has cut a gorge through soft stone and left the old towns standing on pinnacles above it. Mazzano Romano clings to a rocky spur above the river, its houses growing straight out of the cliff, and Magliano Romano and Campagnano di Roma sit on the plateau around. The whole district is a regional park, with woods of oak and chestnut, waterfalls and small caves, and it is only about half an hour from the capital.

The valley was once a heartland of the Faliscans, a people who spoke a language related to Latin and lived between the Etruscans and Rome, and the cliffs are riddled with ancient tombs and cut paths. The ruins of their city, Falerii Novi, lie a short distance north, with the Roman walls still standing in a field. Near Mazzano is the Monte Gelato waterfall, a small cascade over a ledge of tufa, a favourite picnic spot where Romans come to cool off in summer, and where scenes in some well-known films were shot.

The photo pull-off gives a view across the valley toward the old town, with the cliffs, trees and rooftops in a single picture, and the best light comes in the late afternoon, when the stone turns gold. The roads around here are narrow and winding, with tight bends, short climbs and blind corners, and the surface is variable, with patches of rough tarmac and the odd pothole. There is little traffic, apart from locals and the occasional cyclist, so the pace can be relaxed, and the silence is a pleasure after the city.

Fuel is the matter to plan. Mazzano Romano has about two and a half thousand people and basic services, but fuel is limited, so fill up in Campagnano di Roma, about five kilometres away, a town of seven thousand with stations, shops and bars. Several trattorias in the valley serve simple Roman food, including pasta with pecorino, grilled lamb and fresh vegetables, and a long lunch there on a Sunday is a classic way to spend the day.
t.terminillo mountain road@41.8,12.9:
Cave is a hill town in the Prenestini mountains, east of Rome, a plain, workaday place of about eight thousand people that sits below the better-known town of Palestrina. It has the feel of a place that lives for its own sake, with a busy main street, a market and a few bars where old men play cards in the afternoon. The name means caves, and refers to the quarries and tufa cavities in the hillside. For a rider, it is a useful and honest stop, with fuel, food and a roof, and the road beyond promises better scenery.

Palestrina, a few kilometres away, has an extraordinary past. As ancient Praeneste, it was the site of a great sanctuary of Fortuna, the goddess of fate, built on a series of terraces up the hillside in the second century BC, and one of the largest sanctuaries in the Roman world. The medieval town was built on top of the ruins, and a museum in the old palace now holds a famous Roman mosaic of the Nile. The composer Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, a giant of Renaissance church music, took his name from the town, where he was born.

The food here is simple and good. The bars and trattorias of Cave serve pizza by the slice, supplì, which are fried rice balls with a core of melted mozzarella, porchetta sandwiches and plates of pasta with pecorino cheese. Prices are modest, and a good lunch is easy to find. The red wine of the Lazio hills is an easy companion, and the local olive oil is excellent, so a small bottle is a good souvenir.

The riding from Cave is a delight, with winding roads climbing through olive groves and oak woods into the Prenestini mountains, and some tight hairpins and good views. The surface is variable, so take care, and weekends bring Roman day-trippers, with plenty of cyclists and other motorbikes. The nearby town of San Bartolomeo is small, but Cave has several stations, so fill up before heading for the mountains. In summer, the heat is intense by mid-afternoon, so an early start is a good idea.
t.positano@40.6,14.5:
Positano is a town built on a staircase. Houses in pink, ochre and white pile up the steep hillside above a small, pebbly beach, so close together that they seem to hold each other up, and from the coast road above, the whole place looks like a painting hung on a cliff. It is the most photographed town on the Amalfi coast, and the view of it from the road, with the sea spread out below and the green-domed church at the bottom, is the reason for the stop.

The place has a story of its own. In the mid-twentieth century, it was a poor fishing village that attracted artists and writers, and the American author John Steinbeck, who visited in 1953, wrote an essay that helped make it famous, saying that Positano bites deep, and is a dream place that isn't quite real when you are there. The church of Santa Maria Assunta has a dome of coloured majolica tiles, and below the beach, three small islands called Li Galli are said in legend to be the home of the Sirens who tempted Odysseus.

The road is the Amalfi Drive, the SS163, a narrow ribbon cut into the cliff above the sea, with hairpins, tunnels and blind corners at every turn, and it is one of the great coastal rides of Europe, though not an easy one. In summer the traffic is heavy, with buses, cars and scooters, and the road is so narrow in places that buses and large vehicles have to wait for each other. A motorcycle makes much better progress than a car, but you need to keep your wits about you, watch for oncoming buses and expect the road to close for roadworks or rockfalls. Rules on traffic and parking change from season to season, so check them in advance.

There is almost no room in Positano for parking, and fuel is not easy to find along the coast, so fill up in Sorrento or on the plateau at Agerola, about five kilometres away, before you start. The town itself is a maze of steep stairs, boutiques, cafés and restaurants, with lemons and ceramics at every corner, and prices that match the view. Early morning or late evening are the best times to visit, when the day-trippers are gone.
t.amalfi@40.6,14.6:
Amalfi was once the capital of a maritime republic that traded across the Mediterranean, and it is hard to believe, looking at the small, crowded town squeezed into a ravine at the water's edge. For a few centuries around the year 1000, it rivalled Pisa and Venice, with a fleet that sailed to Constantinople, Egypt and Syria, and a population many times larger than it has now. Its maritime laws, the Tabula Amalphitana, were respected in ports across the sea. A great earthquake and storm in the fourteenth century swept much of the old town into the sea, and Amalfi never regained its power.

Its cathedral, dedicated to Saint Andrew, still dominates the main square, with a striped facade of black and white and gold mosaic, approached by a broad flight of steps, and a bronze door cast in Constantinople in the eleventh century. Next to it, the Cloister of Paradise is a quiet courtyard with slender columns and palms. The town was also famous for paper-making, and a museum in an old paper mill in the Valley of the Mills explains how it was done, with water-powered hammers and handmade sheets, and shops still sell the paper.

Lemons are the local pride, big, fragrant and sweet, grown on terraces carved into the cliffs and shaded by wooden pergolas. They go into limoncello, in pastry, in granita and in the food at every restaurant, and a glass of fresh lemon juice on a hot day is a small miracle. The small town of Atrani, a few hundred metres away, is a tiny, whitewashed village and quieter than Amalfi, and a short walk away.

The coast road to and from Amalfi is spectacular and demanding, with hairpins and tunnels and a great deal of traffic, particularly buses, so patience is needed. The harbour area has parking, but spaces fill quickly, and motorcycles are usually easier to place than cars. Amalfi has about five thousand people, with a few stations nearby, and Maiori, about four kilometres along the coast, is another source of fuel and supplies. Visit in spring or autumn if you can, when the crowds are smaller and the light is soft.
Norway begins to open up not far north of the airport. This fuel gate sits at the edge of the Romerike district, a few kilometres from Rotnes and Aneby, north-east of Oslo, where suburbs give way to farms and forest, and it is the traditional starting point for a long ride up through the country. The land here is green and gently rolling, with red barns, birch woods and small lakes, and in the early morning, mist lies in the hollows. Oslo's airport at Gardermoen, opened in 1998, is not far to the north.

The route to Trollstigen from here is long, more than four hundred kilometres, and it follows the E6 northward through the great valley of Gudbrandsdalen, where the river Lagen runs between wooded hills and old farms, and then turns west at Dombas, over the mountains to the Romsdalen valley and Andalsnes. Dombas is a crossroads of Norway, a small town at the meeting of roads and railways, and a good place for a rest. The Romsdalen is dramatic, with steep cliffs and the Rauma river, and it leads to the Troll Wall.

Fuel prices in Norway are high, and the first stop is a chance to fill up and to check what you carry. Klofta, the nearest town of any size, has almost six thousand people and every facility, and Rotnes and Aneby have smaller stations. Many pumps are unmanned and take cards only, so make sure that your card works with a PIN. Road tolls are automatic, charged through a tag or by number plate, and a rental bike should come with an account, so check before setting off.

Speed limits in Norway are low, and fines are heavy. Radar and cameras are common, and the limit on most roads is eighty or less. Drive with patience, and enjoy the view. Wildlife is a risk, especially elk and reindeer at dawn and dusk, so scan the verges. Weather can change in an hour, with sun giving way to rain, so carry waterproofs. A long day in the saddle, with a break every couple of hours, is the way to do it, and the first sight of the high mountains, as the road climbs out of the valley, is a thrill.
t.trollstigen and geiranger expedition sce:
The land north-east of Oslo is a surprise to those who expect fjords. Around Frogner, Leirsund and Klofta, the countryside is a broad, gently undulating plain of farms and woods, with rivers meandering through clay and sand, and the view from the road is of fields of barley and oats, red-painted barns and stands of spruce and birch. This is Romerike, one of Norway's biggest areas of arable land, and it has been farmed since the Iron Age. Burial mounds from that period lie in some of the fields.

The ground itself was shaped by the ice. At the end of the last glaciation, vast moraines were laid across the district, known as the Raet, and the sand and gravel plains that remain, including those around Gardermoen, are among the largest in Norway. The rivers here, the Nitelva and the Leira, wind through soft ground, and their banks are home to herons, ducks and, in spring, cranes. Lake Oyeren, to the east, has the largest freshwater delta in Europe, which attracts thousands of migrating birds.

For the motorcyclist, the roads here are not famous, but they are pleasant, with quiet lanes between fields, good surfaces and little traffic outside rush hour. There are curves, though gentle ones, and the road follows the contours of the land, with views across the fields and small lakes. In summer, the smell of cut grass and warm earth is strong, and the evenings are long, with light until almost midnight in June. In autumn, the birches turn yellow, and the mist forms in the hollows.

Klofta, five kilometres away, has nearly six thousand people, with fuel stations, supermarkets and a railway station. Frogner and Leirsund are smaller, with shops and a few services. Norway's roads are well maintained, but speed limits are low, and the police enforce them. Keep an eye out for farm vehicles and for elk, which are common in the forest edges. Rain can arrive quickly, so keep waterproofs handy. The light in late afternoon, with long shadows over the fields, is the time for a photograph, and a short stop at a farm shop for coffee or fresh berries is a pleasant break.
t.jemez springs@35.8,-106.7:
Jemez Springs is a small village strung along the Jemez River in a canyon of red and cream cliffs in northern New Mexico, and it feels a long way from anywhere. State Route 4 follows the river here, winding through a gorge of banded sandstone, with cottonwoods along the water and juniper on the slopes. It is a land of hot springs, tucked into the base of the Jemez Mountains, and the village has baths and a few small inns where tired riders can sit in mineral water.

The history is deeper than the size of the place suggests. The ancestors of the people of Jemez Pueblo lived here for centuries, and at Giusewa, where the village now stands, Spanish Franciscans built a mission church early in the 1600s, the walls of which still stand within the state historic site. Nearby, Soda Dam, a lump of travertine built by mineral springs, forces the river through a hole in a natural bridge. Jemez Pueblo, downriver, keeps the Towa language and holds feast days, and the red mesas along the road are part of its homeland.

The road is a joy, with wide, easy bends through the canyon, easy gradients and few straights. Red Rocks, a stretch of towering cliffs north of the village, is the highlight, glowing in the afternoon sun. Weather in the mountains can change quickly, and summer afternoons bring thunderstorms with sudden rain and lightning. Winter can leave ice on the shaded corners, and in late autumn the cottonwoods turn gold. The surface is generally good, but rockfall can drop stones onto the pavement.

Services in Jemez Springs are limited, and the village is small, with a couple of cafés and a general store. For reliable fuel, plan around Los Alamos, thirty-seven kilometres away over the mountain, or San Ysidro on the other side. Take water, wear a layer and allow time for a soak.
t.valles caldera@35.9,-106.5:
Pull over where State Route 4 opens onto the Valle Grande and the first reaction is usually silence. The meadow in front of you is the floor of a volcano, a vast grassy bowl some thirteen miles across, ringed by forested domes and ridges, with elk grazing in the distance and the sky arching over it all. About 1.25 million years ago a colossal eruption emptied a magma chamber here, and the ground collapsed into the void, leaving a caldera. The ash from that blast settled into the pale tuff that forms the cliffs of Bandelier and the Pajarito Plateau nearby.

Later eruptions raised lava domes inside the bowl, and Redondo Peak, the largest, stands in the middle like a green shoulder. Hot springs, fumaroles and rich, deep grassland lie within. For years the land was a private ranch, and it passed to the public in 2000 as a national preserve. Elk are the stars, with big herds and a bugling rut in the early autumn, and prairie dogs, coyotes and hawks are easy to spot. Streams run clear in the folds, and trout swim in some of them. The altitude is well above eight thousand feet, so the air is thin, clear and cool even in summer.

The road along the southern rim is a pleasure. It curves gently across the meadow edge, rises through ponderosa and aspen and gives wide views over open grass. Traffic is moderate, the surface is generally smooth, and the corners are easy. Weather turns quickly at this height, with afternoon thunderstorms in July and August, snow in winter and cold nights even in early summer. Mornings are best, when mist hangs on the grass and the elk are close to the road.

The visitor area has water and restrooms, and entry has a fee that is easy to pay. Bring warm clothes and binoculars, and give yourself time to stand and look.
t.red river@36.7,-105.4:
Red River is a mountain town that remembers being a mining camp, and it keeps a bit of the frontier in its main street. Prospectors arrived in the 1890s after gold and copper turned up in the canyon, and for a while the place was rough, with saloons and claims everywhere. The mines faded and the town reinvented itself as a ski and summer resort, and now it fills in winter with skiers and in summer with families, hikers and, on Memorial Day weekend, a large motorcycle rally that takes over the town.

It sits in a narrow valley at the foot of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, and Wheeler Peak, at 13,161 feet the highest point in New Mexico, stands a few miles to the south. The Red River itself runs clear and cold through the middle of town, and trout fishing is a long-running pastime. In autumn the aspens on the hillsides turn gold, a vivid ribbon against the dark green of the spruce. The air is high, dry and thin, with the town sitting at around 8,700 feet.

The riding is a highlight of the Enchanted Circle, the roughly eighty-four mile loop around Wheeler Peak. From Red River, State Route 38 climbs over Bobcat Pass, a bit under ten thousand feet, in a long series of bends through spruce and fir. The road is well surfaced, though with sections of frost damage, and the corners are open and flowing. Weather can change very quickly, and snow can fall in any month except perhaps July. Mornings are the best time for the climb, and thunderstorms often gather in the afternoon.

Red River has fuel and a decent selection of restaurants, from steak and green chile to pizza and breakfast burritos. New Mexican food is built around red or green chile, and if you are asked which you want, the answer 'Christmas' gets you both. Taos, thirty-seven kilometres away, is the nearest larger town. Bring a warm layer and give yourself time, since the scenery calls for it.
t.eagle nest@36.6,-105.3:
Eagle Nest sits on the high Moreno Valley floor, where the wind has room to run, and the first thing you notice is the lake. Eagle Nest Lake was formed by a dam on the Cimarron River finished in 1918, a large, shining sheet of water against a backdrop of mountains. Anglers come for trout and kokanee salmon, and in winter ice-fishing shacks dot the surface. The village itself is little more than a strip of motels, cafés, and gift shops along the highway, with a population of a few hundred, and it lives on the traffic of the Enchanted Circle.

The valley is a broad bowl of grass at over eight thousand feet, ringed by the peaks of the Sangre de Cristo range. It was a ranching region for generations, and the old Maxwell Land Grant, once one of the largest private estates in America, covered much of the land around. A little to the west lies the ghost town of Elizabethtown, where a gold rush in the 1860s briefly built New Mexico's first incorporated town. Elk graze the meadows in spring and autumn, and the sky is huge and often filled with raptors.

From a rider's standpoint, this is the easy, scenic part of the loop. The road is wide and straight, with long views, and the main hazard is the wind, which can blow hard across the valley in spring. To the east, US 64 drops into Cimarron Canyon, a spectacular gorge of granite cliffs and tall pines along a trout stream, with a narrow, winding road that rewards a slower pace. The surface can be rough in places, and deer are a danger at dusk.

There is fuel in Eagle Nest, and cafés that serve breakfast and burgers. Taos, thirty-two kilometres away, has more choice. The valley can be cool even in summer, with frost possible in September, so carry a layer and gloves. Late spring and autumn bring the most dramatic skies, with storms rolling across the valley and the light breaking through in shafts.
t.angel fire@36.4,-105.3:
Angel Fire is best known for a single building, a small white chapel on a hillside that has nothing to do with skiing. Dr. Victor Westphall, a New Mexico man whose son David died in the Vietnam War in 1968, built the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Chapel in his son's memory, and it grew into a state park that honours all those who served. The curved white walls rise against the mountains and the plain inside is deeply affecting. It is a place where people drop their voices without being asked.

Beyond the memorial the village is a mountain resort, with ski runs on the slopes in winter and mountain bikers in summer. It stands in the Moreno Valley, a high, wide basin of grass at about 8,400 feet, rimmed by the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, and it forms the southern anchor of the Enchanted Circle loop around Wheeler Peak. The air is clear and dry, the nights are cold even in summer, and the stars are bright.

For the bike, the roads around here are broad and gentle, with long curves across the valley floor and views to the mountains. To the south, US 64 climbs over Palo Flechado Pass, just over nine thousand feet, and drops through pine forest to Taos in a series of tidy bends. The surface is good, and the traffic is steady but not heavy. Weather is the main variable, with summer storms and a sudden drop in temperature when clouds build. In October the aspens glow, and the road is busy with leaf-watchers.

Angel Fire has fuel, groceries and a handful of restaurants, and the village is built for visitors, so services are easy to find. Taos is twenty-six kilometres away, and has a bigger selection and a famous old plaza. The Enchanted Circle can be ridden in a day with stops, and this is a good place for a break around the middle, with a coffee and a few quiet minutes at the chapel.
t.atnbrua@61.9,10.1:
Atnbrua is a bridge over the river Atna, where the Fv27 scenic road crosses water on its way through the high valleys east of Rondane. Rivers in this part of Norway are clear and cold, running fast over smooth stones, and the Atna, which drains the mountains, is a good example, with fish in it that anglers travel a long way to catch. From the bridge you can look down into pools the colour of tea, and the sound of water is a constant background. There is a parking place close by, and a short walk along the bank is easy enough for anyone.

The country around here is forest and bog, with spruce and birch, and in autumn the colours are warm and various. The mountains show themselves in the distance, round and bald. This is Østerdalen's upland edge, old farming country where small farms and summer pastures, called seters, dot the hillsides, and where the people lived for centuries by cattle, forestry and mining. Folldal, to the west, was a mining town, with copper and sulphur dug from the ground until the last century, and the old works are now a museum.

The road is a pleasure for a rider who wants to relax. It follows the valley in a series of easy bends, with the river on one side and the forest on the other, in good condition and without much traffic. Overtaking is not a big question, because the roads are quiet and the limits low. In autumn, elk are active at dusk and dawn, and they are large enough to ruin a day if you meet one, so slow down in forest stretches, especially in low light. In winter the road is dark and cold, with ice and snow, so travel only if you have the equipment.

Folldal and Alvdal are the nearest villages, both small, and both have a pump or two, though hours are short outside the weekday daytime. Carry water and a snack, because shops are few. The mosquitoes along the river in early summer can be fierce, so a little repellent is a better companion than a poncho. The light in September on the river is gentle and gold.
t.grand mesa@39.1,-108.0:
Grand Mesa is said to be the largest flat-topped mountain in the world, and when you climb onto it you understand why. From the orchards and desert canyons of western Colorado, the road rises through scrub oak and aspen onto a lava-capped plateau about forty miles long, at around eleven thousand feet. The top is forest, meadow and lake, cool in summer and buried in snow in winter, and it feels like a different region from the hot valley floor below.

The lava is the reason. Millions of years ago, basalt flows covered the area, and as the softer rock around them wore away, the hard cap was left standing as a table above the landscape. Glaciers later carved the surface, scooping out hollows that now hold hundreds of small lakes, so many that the mesa is a paradise for anglers. The old stories say that the Ute people used the mesa for hunting in summer, and the name Grand Mesa comes from Spanish and French trappers who saw its vast, flat profile from afar. Spruce, fir and aspen cover much of the top, and in autumn the aspens turn the slopes gold.

The byway, Colorado 65, climbs from the Cedaredge side and runs across the top before descending toward Mesa Lakes and Interstate 70. It is a smooth, easy road with long bends, sweeping views from the rim over the Gunnison and Colorado river country, and little traffic outside holidays. Watch for deer and elk at dusk, for cattle in open areas, and for sudden weather: afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, with lightning on the exposed plateau, and snow can arrive in September. The road is usually open from late spring to late autumn, depending on snow, and winter closures apply to some sections.

Services are limited on the mesa itself, with a lodge or two and a visitor centre in season. Cedaredge and Delta, to the south, have fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, and Palisade, famous for peaches and wine, makes a pleasant stop on the way down, so fill the tank before you climb. Take a jacket, as temperatures at the top can be twenty degrees cooler than in the valley.

Pull over at an overlook near the rim, and look out across the desert far below. The contrast between cool forest and hot canyon country is the best part of the ride.
t.mesa lakes@39.0,-108.1:
Mesa Lakes is a cluster of small lakes and forest cabins on the north slope of Grand Mesa, just below the rim, and it is where Coloradans go to fish, walk and avoid the summer heat. The lakes sit in hollows scooped out by ice, surrounded by spruce, fir and aspen, with meadows opening between them and the air cooler by many degrees than the valley of the Colorado River far below. There is a resort feel to the place, with a lodge, a few cabins and a campground, but it is quiet and woodsy, not busy.

The mesa has more than three hundred lakes, and these are among the easiest to reach. Anglers cast for trout from small boats and from the shore, and in morning light the water sits like glass, with mist rising slowly. Walking trails circle some of the lakes and lead into the forest, where you may see mule deer, elk and, if you are lucky, a moose, which has been reintroduced in Colorado. In summer the meadows fill with wildflowers, lupine, paintbrush and columbine, and the smell is of pine resin and warm earth. In autumn, the aspens glow yellow.

The ride from the north is a steady climb on Colorado 65 from the interstate, in a series of bends that gain height quickly and open up views across the valley. The road is paved and smooth, but narrower and slower than the main highway, with deer and sometimes cattle on the road, and rain or hail can arrive suddenly in summer afternoons. It is usually clear of snow from late spring to autumn, but check conditions, as early storms can close it. A rain jacket and a warm layer are sensible.

Facilities are simple. A lodge and small store operate in the main season, and may offer meals, but opening times vary, so do not rely on them. For fuel and supplies, Palisade and Clifton on the valley side, and Cedaredge on the southern flank, are the nearest towns of any size, and it is worth filling the tank and buying water before the climb.

Sit by a lake in the early morning if you can, and watch the light come across the water. The silence, broken only by the occasional splash of a fish, makes the climb feel worthwhile.
t.buena vista@38.8,-106.1:
Buena Vista sits in the Arkansas River valley at the foot of the Collegiate Peaks, and the first thing to know is that nobody there says it the Spanish way. Locals call it Byoo-na Vista, and they will tell you so with a smile. The town is small, with a few thousand people, a main street of brick buildings and a courthouse square, and it stands on a broad, high valley floor with the wall of the Sawatch Range rising to the west, a line of fourteen-thousand-foot summits capped with snow for most of the year.

Those peaks bear the names of colleges. Mounts Harvard, Yale, Princeton and Columbia were named by a Harvard-led survey party in the 1860s, and the range has been called the Collegiate Peaks ever since. Some of them rise more than fourteen thousand feet, and on a clear morning they look close enough to touch across the sagebrush and the river. The Arkansas River, born in the mountains to the north, runs through the valley here, and this stretch is one of the most popular white-water rafting stretches in the country, with rapids that range from gentle to wild.

The ride along the byway through Buena Vista is a pleasure. The roads are wide and smooth, with easy bends, long views of the mountains and generally light traffic, and the climb to the west, toward the mountains, gives better views still. Weather can change quickly, with afternoon thunderstorms in summer, and snow possible in the high country from September. The best times are late spring to early autumn, with the aspen colour in late September particularly beautiful. Watch for cyclists, rafting buses and wildlife, including mule deer, which wander into town.

The valley is dotted with natural hot springs fed by water heated deep underground, and several resorts and pools welcome visitors. A soak after a day in the saddle is a fine thing, and the mountain views from the water are worth the entrance fee. Buena Vista itself has petrol stations, groceries, outdoor shops, bakeries and a brewery or two, so it is a useful place to fill the tank and have a proper meal; Salida, about thirty-six kilometres south, is larger.

Take a stroll down the main street, grab a coffee and look west. The mountains are the reason you came, and they do not disappoint.
t.black hawk@39.8,-105.5:
Black Hawk is the last place you would expect to find slot machines wedged into a gold-rush canyon, and yet there they are, stacked up the sides of Clear Creek in glass and brick. The town sits in Gilpin County, a short drop from Central City, in a steep cleft where gold was first struck in 1859. John Gregory found the lode that set off the Colorado rush here, and for a few years this narrow gulch was said to be among the richest bits of ground in the country. Mills clustered at Black Hawk to crush the ore, which is why milling, not gambling, was its first business.

Gambling came back in the early 1990s, when Colorado voters allowed limited-stakes casinos in Black Hawk, Central City and Cripple Creek as a way of rescuing old mining towns. The result is a high-rise gaming strip with large parking structures, which is a surreal sight in a canyon where nineteenth-century brick storefronts still hang on. If you are a rider, it is less about the tables and more about the geography: Black Hawk is the point where the Peak to Peak Highway meets the canyon road down to the plains, so it is a useful hinge of the route.

The riding around here is good in bursts. Highway 119 descends Clear Creek and Black Hawk Canyon toward Golden in a series of tight curves with rock walls tight beside the road, and the climb toward Nederland is a lovely sequence of swingy bends in thin mountain air. Traffic is heavy on weekends because of the casinos, with buses and drivers on a mission, so I would aim for a weekday or early morning. The old road to Central City, a mile or two up the gulch, is slower and more interesting, passing the remains of mine tailings and weathered headframes.

For practicalities, Black Hawk has food, plenty of coffee and the sort of buffet that has not changed since the nineties. Fuel is available in the canyon area, though I would check ahead, and Idaho Springs and Evergreen both have more reliable stations. There is no shortage of parking, and it is generally safe, but do not leave anything visible on the bike. Winter ice makes the canyon descent treacherous, and the road can be closed during storms.
t.natural bridges@37.6,-110.0:
The strange thing about Natural Bridges is how quiet it is. Three great sandstone spans, Sipapu, Kachina and Owachomo, arch across dry canyon floors a short distance off Highway 95, in a corner of Utah that most people drive past on the way to somewhere with a more famous name. President Theodore Roosevelt made this Utah's first national monument in 1908, and the monument has stayed small, sparsely visited and unspoilt ever since. The bridges were carved by running water, not by wind, which is easy to forget when the creek beds are bone dry.

For a rider the one-way loop road is a pleasant detour, with short walks to overlooks, though the real ride is the highway on either side. Highway 95 crosses Cedar Mesa here, rising among pinyon and juniper to a high, cool plateau, with long, graceful curves and wide views to the Abajo Mountains and, farther off, the twin ears of the Bears Ears buttes. Heading east toward Blanding the road descends through slickrock canyons with a few tight bends. Heading west it drops toward Lake Powell. The surface is good, the traffic light, and the main hazards are livestock on unfenced stretches, crosswinds, and the occasional rock fallen from a cut.

The place is also rich in human history. Ancestral Puebloan people lived in these canyons for centuries, and the names Sipapu and Kachina come from Hopi tradition, with sipapu referring to the place of emergence from an earlier world. Rock art and cliff dwellings are scattered across Cedar Mesa, and you should treat all of it with care: do not touch the rock art and stay out of ruins. The monument is also an International Dark Sky Park, recognised in 2007 as the first of its kind, and on a clear night the Milky Way is startling.

Blanding is the nearest proper town to the east, with petrol and motels, and Bluff is another good base; Hanksville is the other direction and far. Spring and autumn are lovely, summer mornings are fine, and afternoon thunderstorms can fill the dry washes with sudden floods.
t.devils playground@38.9,-105.1:
Devils Playground is the name of a stack of weathered pink granite boulders beside the road, on the shoulder of Pikes Peak at around 3,900 metres. The wind, frost and violent temperature swings of the high country have broken the rock into jumbled tors and slabs, and the effect is a landscape that looks half-built by a bored giant.

Up here the trees are gone and the vegetation is the tough, ground-hugging sort that clings on above timberline. You may see marmots on the rocks and, with luck, bighorn sheep on the slopes. The air is noticeably thin, which makes your head swim if you walk quickly and costs a motorcycle engine a visible slice of its power. The summit is still about four hundred metres of climb above you, and the final miles are the exposed ones, with hairpins and open drop-offs and a view over the Great Plains to the east that goes on far beyond reason.

Riding the highway is a long job: nineteen miles, plenty of low gears, and a descent that tests brakes and nerve in equal measure. Use engine braking, not your front disc alone, and take the rangers' warnings seriously, because overheated brakes are the commonest problem on the way down. Check the forecast before leaving Cascade. Snow can fall at any time of year at the top, and the road closes when conditions are bad. Fog can hide the edge, and cold wind will find any gap in your gear.

At the summit the visitor centre sells hot drinks and the famous high-altitude doughnuts, which are a small reward for the climb. Fuel is not available on the mountain. Cascade-Chipita Park has a few small shops, and Woodland Park, about ten kilometres off, has proper petrol stations, so top up there. Allow plenty of time, because the speed limit is low and the pull-outs are tempting, and reserve some energy for the descent, which takes concentration.
t.independence pass@39.1,-106.6:
Independence Pass has a reputation for scaring people, and it earns about half of it. The road is narrow, with tight hairpins and in places no guard rail, and it tops out at 3,687 metres on the Continental Divide. But it is also a marvellous, bracing ride, and quite short, which makes it feel like a gift. The east side climbs from the Twin Lakes valley in a series of long, graceful bends, then the road bunches up into tight switchbacks above the trees. At the top you step onto tundra, with snow in the shaded gullies even in July and a view of ranks of peaks all the way around.

The west side down to Aspen is the more dramatic. The road is cut into the slope, with steep drop-offs on one side and the Roaring Fork River tumbling far below, and a couple of hairpins demand real attention and a good hold on the brake. Large vehicles are restricted, which keeps the traffic tamer than you might expect, though caravans and rental cars crawl through on busy summer weekends. Pick a morning and the whole thing feels clean and clear.

The pass takes its name from the town of Independence, a mining camp on the west side that boomed in the 1880s and later faded. Its ruins are a short drive below the summit, and the story goes that the camp was named for a find made on the Fourth of July. The high, wet meadows around the top are fragile alpine tundra, so stay on the paths and boardwalks. Across the valley to the south, you may spot Mount Elbert, the highest peak in Colorado at 4,401 metres, a long and unglamorous hump rather than a spire.

The highway is closed in winter, usually from around November until late May, so check before you plan. The air is thin and cold, with fast-changing weather and frequent afternoon storms, so aim to cross early. Aspen, about 24 kilometres west, has stations and every possible type of coffee, and Leadville, further east, has fuel and a more down-to-earth feel. Twin Lakes has a few small stores, but I would not rely on them.
t.tennessee pass@39.4,-106.3:
Tennessee Pass is the pass nobody photographs, which is part of its charm. At 3,186 metres, it carries Highway 24 across the Continental Divide between Leadville and the valley of the Eagle River, and it does so with a long, open, rather gentle gradient and a wide, forested saddle. A small sign marks the divide, and that is about it. The riding is smooth, steady and a good place to settle into a rhythm after more demanding passes.

The history is the interesting bit. A few miles north is Camp Hale, where the US Army's 10th Mountain Division trained for mountain warfare in the early 1940s, learning to ski, climb and fight in the cold before shipping out to the Italian Alps. After the war many of its veterans helped to create the American ski industry, and the nearby ski hill at Cooper, which they used to train on, still runs in winter. The old railway line over the pass, once a major route for freight, has been silent since the 1990s, though the line is still visible in places.

South of the pass lies Leadville, the highest incorporated city in the United States, at over 3,000 metres. It began as a silver boom town in the late 1870s, with mining fortunes that produced characters such as Horace Tabor and his second wife Baby Doe, and today it is a tough, slightly scruffy mountain town with a colourful main street. The mountains around it include Mount Elbert and Mount Massive, the two highest peaks in Colorado, which on a clear day give the horizon an unusually serious look.

The road is open year round, though winter brings snow and ice, and storms can slow things down. In summer expect warm sun, big cloud and afternoon showers. The pass has no services of its own, so top up in Leadville, about twelve kilometres south, which has several stations, a few good cafes and a diner or two with proper breakfasts. Minturn and Vail, down the north side, have more options. The wind picks up in the open saddle, so a windproof layer helps, and remember that your engine will feel the thin air, even on this gentle climb.
t.engineer pass@38.0,-107.6:
Engineer Pass is a gravel road, which matters, because up here the word gravel means rock, ruts, shale, creek crossings and exposure. At nearly 3,900 metres it is the highest point on the Alpine Loop, the long dirt circuit that links Ouray, Silverton and Lake City through the heart of the San Juan Mountains, and it is a proper high-country dual-sport ride. This is no place for a heavy tourer or an inexperienced rider on a road bike. A light adventure bike with good tyres, a competent rider and a sensible start time make it a different story.

Everything about the scenery is vast. The pass sits above treeline in a world of scree slopes, tundra and ragged peaks, with the colours of the rock shifting from rust to grey to yellow as the minerals change. The San Juans are volcanic in origin, shaped by huge eruptions and then carved by ice, and the Colorado mining boom that followed in the 1870s left its mark everywhere: old tailings, collapsed cabins, rusting machinery. Roads like this one were built for ore wagons and mules, and it shows in the width and the hairpins. The climb from the Ouray side is steep and exposed in places, and the drop-offs are long. Oncoming vehicles require patience, with passing places few.

Weather is the real hazard. Afternoon thunderstorms are routine in summer, and lightning on a ridge is not a game. Snow can fall in any month, and the road is normally open only from around late June until October, depending on drifts. Start early, carry a layer, and turn back if the sky looks wrong. The air at this height is thin, so engines run weak, and you will feel it too. Altitude sickness is a real possibility for riders who go straight up from low ground.

There are no services at the pass. Ouray, about nine kilometres away as the crow flies but much further by road, has fuel, restaurants and motels, and Silverton and Lake City have the same on other sides of the loop. Fill up every time you can, and carry food and water, tools and a means of calling for help, though mobile coverage is poor. Respect the old buildings and mine sites, which are unstable and sometimes still dangerous, and pack out your rubbish.
t.silverton high town@37.8,-107.7:
Silverton sits at about 2,830 metres in the San Juan Mountains, and it looks like a town on the edge of the world. Mountains close in on every side, snow lingers on the peaks well into summer, and the main street is wide and dusty, lined with false-front buildings from the silver boom. It was founded in the 1870s as a mining camp, and the miners dug deep into the surrounding hills for silver and gold. The town is now a National Historic Landmark, and it still has the feel of the frontier, with a population of only a few hundred people.

A narrow-gauge steam railway runs into Silverton from Durango, and the coal-fired locomotives still pull passenger trains on the line that opened in 1882, to carry ore and supplies. When the train arrives, the whole town fills with visitors, and the whistle echoes off the mountains. Blair Street, once the town's notorious red-light district, has restored buildings that house cafés, shops and saloons, and a walk down it gives a sense of the roughness of the old days.

For riders, Silverton is the beginning or the end of one of the most celebrated roads in the American West. The Million Dollar Highway, US 550, runs north to Ouray over Red Mountain Pass at about 3,350 metres, a narrow road with sheer drops, no guardrails in places and tight switchbacks cut into the cliffs. It is a thrilling ride, but it demands full concentration, and it can be closed by snow or avalanche from late autumn to spring. Even in summer, storms can bring hail and slick roads. Take it slowly, stay in your lane, and use pull-outs to let faster traffic pass.

The altitude is a serious matter too. Air at this height is thin, so engines run slightly less strongly, and riders can feel headaches or breathlessness if they have come up quickly from sea level. Drink water, eat well and pace yourself. Fuel is available in Silverton, but supplies can be limited and prices are high, so fill up when you can. Telluride, to the west, is the other nearest town, though it is reached by a longer road.

Food in town ranges from diner breakfasts to green chile stews and burgers, and many places close early or shut for the off season. Check hours before you plan a meal, and leave before dark.
t.ridgway view@38.2,-107.8:
Ridgway is a small town on the northern edge of the San Juan Mountains, and it sits in one of the most photogenic corners of Colorado. To the south, the peaks of the Sneffels Range rise in a jagged line, often snow-capped, and to the north the land opens to the plateau and the valley of the Uncompahgre River. The view from the road above town, with the mountains framed by cottonwoods and ranch fences, looks so much like a postcard that it has been used as a backdrop in films. The 1969 western True Grit was filmed in the surrounding country, and the red cliffs and aspen groves still look much as they did.

The town grew as a railway junction in the 1880s, where narrow-gauge trains carried ore from the mines of Ouray and Telluride. It is quiet now, with a main street of cafés, galleries and a few shops, and a reservoir nearby with a state park popular for boating. Ranches still graze cattle in the valley, and the air smells of sagebrush and woodsmoke.

For a rider, Ridgway is the gateway to the northern end of the Million Dollar Highway. From here, US 550 runs south to Ouray, a small town in a deep box canyon, often called the Switzerland of America, with hot springs and Victorian buildings at its feet. The approach is gentle at first, with open curves in a wide valley, then tightens as the canyon walls close in, and the road begins to climb. The views along this stretch, with waterfalls dropping from the cliffs and the peaks looming above, are among the best in the state.

The Dallas Divide road to the west climbs through aspen forest toward Telluride, and in late September the leaves turn a blazing yellow, drawing crowds of photographers. Weather in the mountains can change quickly, and afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, so plan to be down from high roads by mid-afternoon. Snow can arrive as early as September.

Fuel is available in Ridgway and in larger Montrose, about thirty-eight kilometres to the north, and prices are lower in Montrose. Ouray has fuel too, but it is smaller and more expensive. Stop at a viewpoint for a few minutes and look south. The mountains here have a way of making a rider feel small.
t.campo imperatore@42.4,13.6:
Campo Imperatore is a high plateau of grass, stone and sky under the Gran Sasso, so wide and bare that Italians call it Little Tibet. It lies at about 1,800 metres in the Abruzzo, a long basin among the highest peaks of the Apennines, and above it rises the Corno Grande, at 2,912 metres the highest mountain in the range. The landscape feels unlike most of Italy. There are no villages on the plain itself, only distant ridges, sheep and horses grazing among the tussocks, and a road that crosses the middle like a thin grey thread.

The plateau has a long working history. For centuries shepherds drove their flocks up here from the lowlands in summer, a seasonal migration known as transhumance, and the tradition survives in a quieter form. Sheep cheese, pecorino, and the grilled skewers called arrosticini, made with mutton, are the local food, and the small lentils grown around Santo Stefano di Sessanio are prized. On the plateau's edge stands a hotel and cable car station that played a part in modern history. In 1943, after Italy's armistice, Mussolini was held prisoner there, until German paratroopers landed gliders nearby and flew him out in a daring raid.

Riding here is a pleasure of distance and light. The road climbs from the valley in a series of bends, then runs along the plateau with long views in every direction and few vehicles. The surface is generally good, though winter frost leaves patches, and snow can close the road from late autumn well into spring, so check before you go. Wind is a constant companion, and cloud can drop quickly onto the high ground, cutting visibility to a few metres. Even in midsummer, bring a warm layer, because the air at this height is cool and the temperature falls fast after sunset.

Nature is part of the draw. Below the Corno Grande lies the Calderone, once described as the southernmost glacier in Europe, though it has shrunk dramatically and is now a small remnant. Golden eagles and chamois live on the crags, and in June the meadows bloom with wildflowers. At night, the stars are fierce.

L'Aquila, about seventeen kilometres away, and Isola del Gran Sasso on the other side are the nearest places to fill up, and small mountain refuges and kiosks serve coffee and simple food in season. Check opening hours, since many close early or shut outside the summer and ski months.

Stop at a pull-off and switch off the engine. The silence is large, and it is a fine reward for the climb.
t.gran sasso view road@42.5,13.6:
The northern side of the Gran Sasso looks like a different mountain from the southern one. Here, on the Teramo side, the slopes are steeper, greener and wetter, the villages cling to ridges, and the great rock face of the Corno Grande rises abruptly above forest and meadow. On a clear morning, the view from the road stretches in two directions, up to the pale wall of limestone and down to the foothills rolling toward the Adriatic, which shows as a thin silver line far to the east.

Isola del Gran Sasso is the nearby town, and it is better known than its size suggests. Above it stands the sanctuary of San Gabriele dell'Addolorata, a modern pilgrimage site that draws large numbers of visitors every year, especially on feast days, when the roads fill with coaches and cars. A short distance away, villages such as Pietracamela, high on the mountainside, preserve stone houses and steep lanes, and the ski area of Prati di Tivo lies above them. Below, in the valley of the Vomano, the town of Montorio al Vomano offers a more ordinary mix of shops and cafés.

The riding on this side is more tightly wound. The roads wind up through beech and oak forest, with narrow bends and a surface that varies from smooth to patched, and hairpins that need care when the road is wet. Traffic is light, apart from weekends and pilgrimage days, and the climb is rewarded with open views as the trees fall away. The Gran Sasso road tunnel, one of the longest in Europe, runs under the mountain, but the old road over the top is the better way to see it.

The wildlife here is notable. The Apennine chamois, once nearly extinct, has been reintroduced in the park, and wolves and brown bears live in the wider region, though you are unlikely to see them from the saddle. Eagles patrol the cliffs, and in spring the slopes are full of birdsong.

Fuel is available at Montorio al Vomano, about fifteen kilometres away, and in Isola del Gran Sasso, which is smaller. Higher up the road there is nothing, so fill up beforehand. Small restaurants in the villages serve local dishes, such as pasta with lamb sauce, grilled meats and soft cheeses, but they often close in the afternoon and on weekdays out of season.

Weather changes fast, and cloud can swallow the road in minutes. Take a rain layer and warm clothing, and enjoy the high air.
t.val d orcia cypress road@43.1,11.6:
There is a stretch of white gravel road in the Val d'Orcia that climbs a gentle hill between cypress trees in a perfect zigzag, and it has become the most photographed piece of Tuscany. The trees stand in careful rows, the fields roll away in green and gold, and a farmhouse sits on the crest with the sky behind. It looks arranged, and in a sense it is, because this landscape has been shaped by farmers and landowners for centuries, and in 2004 UNESCO listed the valley as a cultural landscape for its harmony of nature and human work.

The valley lies south of Siena, between Montalcino and Pienza, with the extinct volcano of Monte Amiata closing the horizon to the southeast. The soil here is clay, pale and crumbly, and in late summer it turns the colour of biscuit, while in spring the wheat is vivid green. Pienza, a few kilometres away, was rebuilt in the fifteenth century by Pope Pius II as an ideal Renaissance town, and its small square is an elegant lesson in proportion. Bagno Vignoni, with its steaming pool in the middle of the village, is another curiosity. The old pilgrim road, the Via Francigena, runs through the valley, and the villages of San Quirico d'Orcia and Torrenieri are stops along it.

For riders, the main roads here are easy and gracious, with long curves, a good surface and views that open at every ridge. The famous white roads, strade bianche, are gravel, and they are fine for a careful rider on the right bike, though they can be dusty in summer and muddy after rain. Traffic is moderate, with tour buses, cyclists and photographers, and on a sunny weekend you may find cars stopped in the road for pictures. Go early or in the late afternoon, when the light is soft and the shadows long, and the hills glow.

San Quirico d'Orcia, about three kilometres away, has shops, cafés and a lovely Romanesque church, and Torrenieri is a smaller village. For fuel, Torrenieri and Buonconvento are the nearest places, and Chianciano Terme and the towns along the main road have more. Many small farms sell olive oil, pecorino and honey at the gate.

Do not park in the middle of the road to take your picture. Locals tolerate a lot, but a safe pull-off is better, and the view is the same from the verge.
t.montalcino food@43.1,11.5:
Montalcino sits on a hilltop above a sea of vineyards and olive groves, and it has been making a wine that carries its name around the world. Brunello di Montalcino is made from a local clone of the Sangiovese grape, aged for years in oak and in bottle, and in 1980 it was among the first wines in Italy to be awarded the highest quality classification, DOCG. A glass of it with a plate of cured meats or a thick stew of wild boar, called cinghiale, is the classic way to eat here, and the menu in most trattorie follows that rhythm.

The town is small and handsome, with narrow stone streets climbing to a fourteenth-century fortress, built by Siena, that dominates the skyline. The history of the fortress holds a strange footnote. When Siena fell to Florence and its Spanish allies in 1555, a group of Sienese loyalists withdrew to Montalcino and kept the idea of the republic alive for four more years, until 1559. A short walk takes you up to the walls, and the view across the vines and the distant Monte Amiata is worth it. In the countryside to the south, the Romanesque abbey of Sant'Antimo stands in a quiet valley of olive trees, and if you arrive when the monks are singing, the sound in the stone church is memorable.

For a rider, Montalcino is a lunch and a pause, a place to park, walk and eat slowly. The ride in from the Val d'Orcia or from Buonconvento is a series of gentle curves through vineyards, with good surfaces and open views, and the road up to the town is short and steep. Parking near the centre is limited, so use the lots at the edge and walk in. Streets are narrow and cobbled, and boots with a bit of grip help.
