Food is the reward. Besides cinghiale, look for pici, thick hand-rolled pasta served with garlic and tomato or with a rich meat sauce, and for pecorino cheese from the nearby Pienza area, often paired with honey. Many restaurants close in the afternoon, so aim for lunch before two, and book ahead on weekends and in the harvest season. If you plan to taste wine, remember that you are riding, and a sip is enough.

Fuel is at Torrenieri and Buonconvento, and the larger town of Abbadia San Salvatore is farther away, so fill up before you climb. In the evening, the walls glow and the town quietens, which is the best hour to be there.
t.basilique de santa maria degli angeli et:
Below the hill of Assisi, on the plain, stands a church that was built to cover a tiny one. The Basilica of Santa Maria degli Angeli, a huge baroque building from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, has at its centre the Porziuncola, a small chapel of stone, only a few metres long, where Francis of Assisi received his first followers and founded the Franciscan order in the early thirteenth century. He died in a hut beside it in 1226, and the chapel was so precious that the basilica was raised over it, like a case around a jewel.

Behind the church, a rose garden is said to grow thornless roses, which, according to legend, sprang from the thorns on which Francis rolled to resist temptation. You can see the roses in May and June, and the garden also holds a small museum. The town around the basilica, Santa Maria degli Angeli, has about seven and a half thousand people, with cafes and shops, and it is a practical base for visiting Assisi, whose medieval centre is listed by UNESCO.

Umbria is called the green heart of Italy, and the ride around it shows why. The roads from here lead through olive groves and vineyards, past hill towns of pink and white stone, with the long ridge of Monte Subasio behind. The afternoon run to the Tempietto del Clitunno, a small early medieval chapel beside a spring, passes through Spello and Foligno, with soft hills and cypress lines. Traffic is moderate, the surface is generally good, and the bends are gentle, though mornings can be foggy in autumn.

Fuel and food are easy, with petrol stations near the main road and plenty of bars, and the nearby town of Bastia Umbra, with about eighteen thousand people, has supermarkets. Try a plate of strangozzi pasta with truffle, or porchetta in a roll, and a glass of Sagrantino. Visit the basilica quietly, since it is a place of pilgrimage, and cover your shoulders and knees. The light on the hills in late afternoon is lovely.
t.gallup@35.5,-108.7:
Gallup is a long, thin town squeezed between red sandstone cliffs and the railroad tracks, on the old line of Route 66 in northwestern New Mexico. It sits at about 2,000 metres, with a dry, high-desert climate and a landscape of mesas and pale grassland, and it is known as the Indian Capital of the World, since it serves as a trading centre for the Navajo, Zuni and Hopi nations. Galleries and trading posts in town sell turquoise jewellery, woven rugs and pottery, and the quality of the work is high, though prices reflect that.

Route 66 runs straight through the middle of Gallup, along the main street, past neon signs and old motels, one of which, the El Rancho, was built in the 1930s and hosted movie stars during the days when Westerns were filmed in the red rock country. The hotel's lobby is full of signed photographs and a wide staircase. The town is also famous for the Navajo code talkers, who used their language as an unbreakable code in the Pacific in the Second World War, and a memorial in town honours them.

For riders, the old highway is the attraction, between Santa Fe in the east and Winslow, Arizona, in the west. The stretch around Gallup is high desert, with long straights, big skies and the occasional sweeping bend where the road slips between mesas. Interstate 40 now carries most of the traffic, and the old road survives in segments, some well paved and some rough. Wind is a regular feature, and storms, with hail and flash floods, appear quickly in July and August. Winter nights are cold, and snow and ice are possible, but daytime skies are usually clear.

Gallup is a town of more than twenty thousand, so fuel, food and repairs are readily available, and you will find plenty of motels. Services between towns can be far apart, with Church Rock and Twin Lakes small and limited, so fill the tank whenever you are in a large place. Navajo tacos, fry bread topped with beans, meat and cheese, are a local favourite and a filling lunch.

Take time to look at the Native American arts, buy only from reputable sellers, and consider an evening at one of the old motels, with its neon glow.
t.grand junction@39.1,-108.6:
Grand Junction sits where the Gunnison River flows into the Colorado, in the high desert of western Colorado, and it takes its name from that meeting of waters. Red sandstone mesas close it in on one side, the Book Cliffs on the other, and in between is a fertile valley full of orchards and vineyards. Peaches from nearby Palisade are famous in Colorado, and the town of Palisade has become a small wine region, with tasting rooms among the fruit farms. Orchard Mesa, a short way south, is part of the same agricultural belt.

The surrounding landscape is full of dinosaurs. This part of the Colorado Plateau was a floodplain in the late Jurassic, about 150 million years ago, and the rocks of the Morrison Formation have given up some of the most complete skeletons ever found. The Dinosaur Diamond, a loop of scenic roads through western Colorado and eastern Utah, links museums and quarries, and a number of fossil trackways and bone quarries are open to visitors. Dinosaur Journey, a museum in the area, is a good introduction.

Another natural wonder is the Colorado National Monument, just west of town, a canyon landscape of tall red monoliths and sheer cliffs. Rim Rock Drive, a road built in the 1930s by workers of the Civilian Conservation Corps, runs along the edge with tunnels cut through the rock, and it is one of the best short rides in the state. The bends are open, the surface is good and the views stretch for miles, though bicycles and tourists slow traffic in summer. In the heat of July, the red rocks radiate warmth, and it is best to ride early.

Grand Junction is a city of sixty thousand, the largest between Denver and Salt Lake City, so fuel, food and repairs are easy. The road toward Vernal, in Utah, passes through very empty country, with long gaps between stations, so fill the tank here and again at any town you pass. Cash and water are good to carry. Mobile signal can be absent.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild days and clear light, while summer is hot and winter can be cold. Eat a good meal before you go, and consider a stop at a Palisade fruit stand for peaches in August.
t.trondheim@63.4,10.4:
Trondheim was once Nidaros, the capital of Norway in the Viking Age, and the story of the country's conversion to Christianity runs through it. King Olav Haraldsson, later Saint Olav, was buried here after he fell at Stiklestad in 1030, and the cathedral that grew over his grave became the destination of pilgrims from across northern Europe. Nidaros Cathedral is still the biggest medieval building in Norway, its west front crowded with carved saints, and the pilgrim paths still arrive from the south and east.

The city lies on a loop of the river Nidelva where it meets a long fjord, and the old bridge across it, the Gamle Bybro, leads into Bakklandet, a district of brightly painted wooden houses and small cafes. Along the river the old warehouses stand on stilts above the water, a view that every visitor photographs. The people are friendly and a bit dry, and with the technical university in town the place has a young, busy feel even in a long Nordic winter.

As a riding base it is excellent, with a catch. The roads out of town are good, but the main route south is the E6 and the traffic on it is steady, with tolls collected electronically around the city. The reward comes when you leave it: the valley of the Gaula leads up toward Røros on a quiet road through farmland and then through forest, rising slowly onto the high plateau. Heading west and north along the coast road brings fjord views and ferries. Rain can arrive at any time of year, and at the start of the day a warm layer is cheap insurance.

Fuel is easy here, with stations all around the city and along the major roads. If you are starting early, a good coffee is easy to find, and Trondheim takes its coffee seriously. In the summer the light never fully fades, so a late departure is an option, and in the autumn the birch turns yellow along the river and the whole valley goes gold for a few weeks.
t.r ros mining town and the circumference@:
Røros is a town built on copper, and it looks like it. Miners began digging here in 1644, and for more than three centuries the works shaped everything: the dark timber houses with turf roofs, the great heaps of slag that sit at the edge of town, and the smelter that still stands in the middle. The mines finally closed in 1977, and the whole town centre and a wide ring of countryside around it, called the Circumference, are now a World Heritage Site. The Circumference matters because the mining company had rights over wood, water and farmland in that ring, and the landscape was organised to feed the works.

It stands high, a little over six hundred metres above the sea, on a plateau of low hills, bogs and birch. Winters here are among the coldest in southern Norway, and the old wooden houses were built close together to share warmth. In summer the sky is wide and the air is clean, with the smell of woodsmoke and resin in the evening. The big stone church, finished in the eighteenth century, stands over the roofs like a lantern and was once the pride of the miners. Reindeer meat is on local menus, and the area is part of the southern Sami homeland, which you will see in the shops and craft stalls.

The riding is some of the calmest in the country. The road up from Trondheim along the Gaula valley climbs gradually, and the final stretch onto the plateau is open, forested and pleasant at a relaxed pace. Surfaces are generally good, but the farm roads around town can be rough in spring when the frost heaves them. You will meet more reindeer than lorries on the quieter lanes, and they cross the road without warning.

Røros is large enough for fuel and groceries, and the main street has cafes where a waffle with sour cream and jam is the proper thing to order. The best light is late in the afternoon, when the wooden facades turn amber. The place is busy at midsummer and in the winter market season, and calm in between.
t.golden@39.6,-105.2:
Here the plains of Denver finish and the Rockies begin, and they do not ease into each other. The point lies in the foothills west of Golden, near Indian Hills, in a steep, pine-dotted landscape where red sandstone fins stick up from the slopes and the city's glow is only a few miles behind the ridge. Evergreen, the nearest sizeable town, sits in a mountain valley beyond.

The red rocks here are part of the same geology that produced Red Rocks Park, the famous amphitheatre in Morrison, where huge slabs of sandstone tilted upward by the rise of the mountains form a natural concert hall. The Dakota Hogback, a long ridge of tilted rock, runs along the front of the range, and the road through Bear Creek Canyon cuts through it in a narrow gap. Mount Falcon Park, nearby, has the ruins of a burned-out house on a hilltop, with views over the whole Front Range.

For riders, the lure is how fast the roads change. Within twenty minutes of the suburbs you can be on bends carved into the side of a canyon, with Bear Creek running below and the walls close on either side. Colorado Highway 74 is a popular route, busy on weekends with riders, cyclists and day-trippers, so patience helps. Further west, the road toward Squaw Pass leads up toward Mount Blue Sky, once called Mount Evans, which carries the highest paved road in North America, topping out at over 4,000 metres. That road is only open in the warmer months, usually late May to early September, and weather at the top can turn nasty with little warning.

Golden, just east, is a handsome little town with the Coors brewery and the School of Mines, and Lookout Mountain above it holds the grave of Buffalo Bill, a local legend whose Wild West show toured the world. The view from up there on a clear evening is one of the best of the metro area.

Fuel is easy in Golden and Evergreen, less so once you climb. Mornings are best for quiet roads, and afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, with lightning on the ridges, so plan to be lower by mid-afternoon. In autumn, the aspens turn gold and the whole Front Range glows.
t.tivoli and@42.1,12.6:
Here you are north of Rome, close to Riano, in the broad Tiber valley, on the volcanic plain between the river and the Sabine foothills. It is the other end of the day for a ride that left Rome by the Via Flaminia or Via Salaria, and the character of the land is gentle: fields of wheat and sunflowers, old farm towers, olive groves on the first low hills and always, to the north, the shape of Monte Soratte.

Soratte is a limestone ridge that rises abruptly from the plain to about 690 metres, an isolated whale-backed mountain that seems to have been dropped in the wrong place. The Roman poet Horace wrote of it covered in snow in one of his odes, and in the Second World War, German forces dug a vast tunnel complex into its rock, which later served as a nuclear shelter for the Italian state. In the middle ages a monastery stood on the summit, and monks gave the place a long tradition of pilgrimage. It is visible from nearly all the roads around here and makes a good landmark.

The riding is pleasant and not demanding. The old Via Flaminia, built in 220 BC and the main road from Rome to the Adriatic, runs just to the east, and the Via Salaria, the old salt road used by the Sabines, passes through Monterotondo and over the plain. Both roads are straight and busy, but behind them lie quieter lanes through villages with a church, a bar and a fountain, and on a clear spring morning, with the poppies out, they are lovely. Mist rises from the Tiber in autumn. Heavy lorries serve the quarries and industrial areas, and you should keep your distance.

Riano, a town of nearly seven thousand, is four kilometres away and has fuel stations, bakeries and bars. Nearby are plenty of places for a pizza by the slice or a plate of pasta, often in family-run trattorias that fill at lunchtime on Sundays with whole families. Roman drivers are fast and expect you to keep up, so stay alert in traffic. It is a gentle landing before the city, with the evening light coming across the fields.
t.terminillo@41.7,12.4:
The coordinates land on the south-western side of Rome, near Casal Palocco and Vitinia, on the long Via Cristoforo Colombo corridor that links the city to the sea at Ostia. The suburbs here were built in the twentieth century, with gardens and villas in the shade of tall umbrella pines, and the atmosphere is leafy and a little dated, like a resort for families who had cars before most people did. This is the end of a ride from Terminillo, and it is an easy ride in, mostly straight and quick.

What lies around is the interesting part. A few kilometres south-west is the Castel Porziano estate, a huge stretch of Mediterranean forest and dune that belongs to the Italian presidency and is mostly closed to the public, where cork oak, holm oak and pine shelter wild boar and deer, and the coastline is one of the last stretches of unspoilt sand near Rome. Beyond the pines of Castelfusano is the sea, and to the north is the old Roman port town of Ostia Antica, with its theatre, shops and apartment blocks, one of the best-preserved Roman towns anywhere.

The road is a dull pleasure. The Colombo is a wide dual carriageway with fast cars, many traffic lights and heavy summer traffic of families heading to the beaches on Sundays. Take care at the junctions, where scooters cut across and roots from the pines have buckled the surface at the edges. The side roads are quiet and shaded, and the sea air is noticeably cooler, which in summer is a relief. In winter the beach towns are almost empty, and a ride out to the sea for a coffee and a sunset is a pleasant detour.

You are in a district of more than thirty thousand people, so fuel, shops and restaurants are everywhere. On the way to the coast, many roadside places grill fish or serve fried seafood, and a paper cone of fried anchovies is a good snack. Be careful of the speed cameras on the Colombo, which are common, and keep to the limits. Take your time over the last kilometres, and let the pines and the smell of the sea clear your head.
t.tuscany val@41.5,12.6:
Anzio and Nettuno are twin towns on the Lazio coast, about fifty kilometres south of Rome, sharing a beach, a harbour and a great deal of history. The Roman emperor Nero was born in Antium, as Anzio was known, and the ruins of the imperial villa survive on the cliff above the sea, with a grotto and a sweep of brickwork. In the twentieth century the place was in the news in a different way. In January 1944, Allied forces landed here in Operation Shingle, hoping to outflank the German lines at Cassino and race to Rome, and instead found themselves pinned to the beachhead for months in hard fighting.

The aftermath is still visible. At Nettuno, a few kilometres east, the Sicily-Rome American Cemetery holds the graves of more than seven thousand American soldiers in rows of white marble crosses and stars, in a calm, formal landscape of lawns and pines, with a chapel and a wall inscribed with the names of the missing. It is a sobering place, quiet and beautifully kept, and worth a stop. Anzio's war museum records the landing from several viewpoints, including those of the local civilians.

Today the towns are a seaside resort for Romans, with long sandy beaches, a busy harbour where ferries leave for the islands of Ponza and Ventotene, and restaurants lining the front that serve spaghetti with clams and fried fish. It is lively in summer and almost deserted in winter, when the sea turns grey and storms pound the breakwater. A walk on the pier at sunset is the best way to end a day.

For riders, the roads to the coast, the Via Nettunense and the Via Pontina, are flat and busy, with lots of lorries and holiday traffic, and are best avoided on summer weekends. A better route runs inland through the hills toward Lanuvio and the Castelli Romani, with bends, shade and views. The surface is fairly good, but patches of loose gravel appear after storms. Both towns have fuel stations and shops, with more than forty-five thousand people in Anzio alone, and parking is easy outside high season. In summer, arrive early to find a place near the beach.
t.bologna@44.5,11.3:
Bologna rewards the person who arrives by bike and then walks. It sits where the flat Po plain meets the first fold of the Apennines, a red-brick city of just under four hundred thousand, and you can feel the shift in the road long before you see the towers. From the south, the old Via Emilia and the Futa and Raticosa passes bring you down from the mountains in long, easy sweeps that end very suddenly in traffic lights and delivery vans.

The centre is gloriously walkable and badly suited to riding, so leave the bike on the edge. Piazza Maggiore is the heart, with the vast, unfinished face of San Petronio, a church planned to outsize St Peter's and held back by the Pope of the day. The cathedral proper, San Pietro, is a short walk away on Via Indipendenza, and it is a quieter, more reserved affair than its neighbour. Look up at the two leaning towers, Asinelli and Garisenda; the taller reaches about ninety-seven metres, and the shorter one has been under watch for years because of its tilt.

What makes Bologna unusual is the arcades. Some forty kilometres of porticoes shelter the streets, which is why you can stroll in a downpour and stay dry, and why the city earned its UNESCO listing for them. The university here dates from 1088 and is usually called the oldest in the Western world, which explains the student bars, the book stalls and the general cheerful disorder. Food is the other half of the story: tortellini in broth, tagliatelle with ragu, mortadella, and a lot of generous people insisting you eat more.

Practically, Bologna has a limited traffic zone in the centre, so check before you ride in, and parking for motorcycles is available at designated bays around the ring. Fuel is easy on the tangenziale. The best riding is south: take the road up the Reno valley or toward the Futa pass, which tops out around nine hundred metres, and be back for dinner when the portico lights come on.
t.naples@40.9,14.3:
Naples is loud, fast and generous, and it does not much care what you thought of it before you arrived. Almost a million people live in the city proper, and a good many of them seem to be on scooters, so the first rule of riding here is to pick a line and hold it. Cars stop where they like, pedestrians cross on faith, and horns are a form of conversation. It sounds worse than it is: the traffic has a rhythm, and once you find it, it flows.

The city is also one of the oldest continuously lived-in places in Europe, founded by Greeks as Neapolis and layered ever since with Roman, Norman, Angevin, Spanish and Bourbon history. Spaccanapoli cuts a dead straight line through the old town, with churches, shrines to Maradona and pizzerias along the way. This is where pizza was perfected, and a Margherita from a wood oven costs a couple of coins and weighs on the soul nicely. Add a small, strong espresso at a standing bar and you have the day's fuel for the body.

Over everything sits Vesuvius, the volcano that ended Pompeii and Herculaneum in 79 AD, and its shape is always in the corner of your eye. The ride from here goes out to the Pompeii excavations, which lie about twenty-five kilometres around the bay. You can take the coastal road through a chain of towns, or the motorway for speed, and both are busy. If you want a proper curve or two, the road up the volcano climbs a good way toward the crater rim, and the view over the gulf with Capri in the haze is worth the detour.

Practical points: do not leave anything on the bike, use a heavy chain, and park in a guarded space where you can. There is fuel all around the city and along the autostrada. Go early to Pompeii, because by noon in summer the ruins are a hot, shadeless grid of crowds, and the afternoon is better spent with a cold drink on the waterfront.
t.los alamos@35.9,-106.3:
Los Alamos is a town that exists because of a secret. In 1943 the US government chose this remote mesa, once the site of a boys' ranch school, for the Manhattan Project, and J. Robert Oppenheimer's team built the first atomic bombs in the pine forest at the end of a single winding road. The laboratory is still the biggest employer, which gives the town an odd, educated, slightly fenced-in feel. Street names, museums and a surprising number of PhDs in the grocery queue all hint at it.

The setting is dramatic for a different reason. The town spreads across fingers of the Pajarito Plateau, flat-topped mesas of hardened volcanic ash that spill off the Jemez Mountains and end in sheer canyon edges above the Rio Grande. At roughly seven thousand feet the air is thin, dry and bright, and afternoon thunderstorms in July and August can build fast enough to make you reconsider the plan. The road up from the river through the canyon is a good one, climbing in long bends from the valley floor with the whole Rio Grande rift laid out behind you.

For riders, this is a place to arrive and look around rather than to race through. The roads out the back are the real prize: Highway 4 heads west over the rim of the Valles Caldera, a huge collapsed volcano whose grassy floor holds elk herds and mist at dawn, then drops through red rock country toward Jemez Springs and its hot baths. Heading the other way, the same highway passes Bandelier National Monument, where Ancestral Pueblo people cut homes into soft tuff cliffs and left petroglyphs that are still easy to find.

It is also a practical stop. The town has plenty of fuel, a proper main street and ordinary places to eat, and White Rock, a little way down the hill, has more of the same with a canyon overlook. Be aware that the weather up here can run ten degrees cooler than Santa Fe, and in winter the roads carry snow and sometimes ice in the shade. Have a jacket in the bag even when the valley is warm.
t.golden colorado@39.8,-105.2:
Golden has a bit of everything a rider wants at the end of a day. It is wedged into a gap where Clear Creek slips out of the Front Range and onto the plains, with flat-topped Table Mountain on one side and Lookout Mountain on the other, so the town feels like it was dropped into a doorway. For a few years in the 1860s it was even the capital of Colorado Territory, until Denver took the title and the weight along with it.

It is better known today for Coors, whose brewery has dominated the east side of the valley since the nineteenth century and still gives the town a faint grain smell when the wind is right, and for the Colorado School of Mines, one of the world's famous engineering colleges. The main street is walkable and pleasant, with a creekside path where kids swim in summer and a good scatter of cafes and restaurants. With about twenty thousand residents, fuel and food are never an issue.

What makes Golden a great base is how quickly the road changes. Within ten minutes of the center, Lookout Mountain Road leaves the suburbs and rises through a string of tight switchbacks to the summit, where Buffalo Bill Cody's grave and a small museum sit with a view over the plains all the way to the Denver skyline. It is a classic Colorado hill climb, narrow and steep with tight bends and a fair number of cyclists to share it with, so patience is rewarded. The wider Lariat Loop Scenic Byway links the mountain with the foothill towns of Evergreen and Morrison, and the old railway grades and canyon roads give you more options than a single day can use.

Heading west, Highway 6 follows Clear Creek Canyon up toward Idaho Springs, a narrow, rock-walled gorge with tunnels and a busy flow of trucks and rafters. In the opposite direction, Golden Gate Canyon rewards early starts with quiet bends through aspen and pine. Mornings are best for all of it. Afternoons bring weekend traffic, summer thunderstorms and, in shoulder seasons, ice in the shade that survives long after the sun has cleared the road in town.
t.taos pueblo@36.4,-105.5:
Taos Pueblo has been lived in for roughly a thousand years, which makes it one of the oldest continuously inhabited communities in the United States. The core of it is a pair of multi-story adobe buildings, North House and South House, which rise in stepped terraces against the backdrop of Taos Mountain. A small stream, the Red Willow Creek, runs between them, bringing water from the Sangre de Cristo range, and that stream is the reason the people settled here in the first place.

The pueblo is home to the Taos people, who speak a Tiwa language and have kept many of their traditions through Spanish rule, Mexican rule and the arrival of the United States. In 1680 the pueblos of the Rio Grande joined together in a revolt against the Spanish that drove the colonists out for more than a decade, and Taos was one of its centers. The village was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1992, and its adobe walls are still re-plastered by hand every year. The church of San Geronimo, with its low whitewashed facade, stands close to the plaza.

The ride from Santa Fe is a highlight of northern New Mexico. The High Road, via Chimayo, Truchas and Las Trampas, winds through old Hispanic villages with adobe churches, apple orchards and steep views toward the mountains. It is narrow and curvy, with sharp turns and the occasional dirt shoulder, and it is quiet outside harvest time. The faster option is Highway 68 along the Rio Grande Gorge, with sheer basalt walls and the river far below. Near Taos, the Gorge Bridge crosses a canyon about six hundred feet deep, and the view from the walkway is staggering.

A few rules apply at the pueblo itself. Visitors pay an entrance fee, may pay extra to take photographs, and are asked to stay out of private homes and the cemetery. The pueblo sometimes closes to visitors for ceremonies or tribal events, so check ahead. At that altitude of about seven thousand feet, the sun is strong and the evening can be cool.

Taos itself, a few miles south, has fuel, cafes and galleries. Try the fresh bread baked in the outdoor horno ovens at the pueblo, a small thing that tastes of real place.
t.palmwag@-19.9,13.9:
Palmwag is a small oasis in the dry, stony north-west of Namibia, named for the palm trees that cluster around a spring on the Uniab River, and it is one of the few places in Kunene where you can find shade, cold water and a bed. The surroundings are a huge concession of desert and rocky hills, a wilderness of red earth and pale grass where animals roam freely, and the lodge sits at the edge of it like a small green island.

The ride in on the gravel is a classic. The roads out of Khorixas, Kamanjab and the south pass through a country of flat-topped hills, dry riverbeds and scattered mopane trees, with distances that feel endless and few other vehicles. The surface is wide gravel, mostly graded, though it can be badly corrugated, stony or sandy in places, and flash floods in the rainy season can cut the road or leave deep ruts. Care is needed with speed, because loose stones are easy to underestimate. Early morning and late afternoon are best, since midday heat is fierce. Fuel is normally available at the lodge, which is one of the few supply points in this part of the country, but it is wise to carry extra and check before relying on it.

The surrounding area is famous for desert-adapted wildlife. Desert elephants, which have longer legs and wider feet than their savanna cousins, roam the dry riverbeds, moving long distances in search of water, and black rhinos live in the rocky country, among the largest free-roaming populations in Africa. Lions, giraffes, oryx and springbok are also present, and the area is a haven for birdwatchers. Do not stop near elephants on the road, and give them space, since they can be unpredictable.

The history of the region is tied to its people. Himba pastoralists live farther north, herding cattle and goats and covering themselves with a paste of ochre and butterfat, and Damara and Herero communities live in the south. A veterinary cordon fence runs across the country to the south, and you will pass a control gate where officials may ask about your route. Good manners and a smile will go a long way.

The landscape's colours are spectacular, from orange rocks to the dry yellow grass and the green line of the palms. The air smells of dust, hot rock and sweet acacia flowers after rain.

Carry water, food, spare tyres or repair kit, and a satellite beacon if you have one. Distances are huge and help is slow, so ride conservatively and never at night.
t.kamanjab@-19.6,14.8:
Kamanjab is a farm-service town on the edge of Damaraland, a place of dust, cattle trucks and big skies that serves as the practical heart of north-western Namibia. It sits at a junction where the tarred road from Outjo and Etosha meets the gravel routes heading west into the empty country of Kunene, and for travellers it is the last place to buy proper supplies for a long way. The surroundings are a mix of commercial cattle farms and scrub-covered hills, dry for most of the year and briefly green after rain.

Practicalities come first. The town has fuel, a supermarket, a few small guesthouses and a couple of simple places to eat, and it is also the sensible spot to check tyres, fill water bottles and buy snacks before going west. The roads out of town are tar in places and gravel in others, with the C40 heading toward the Grootberg Pass, where the gravel drops steeply off a plateau in a series of tight bends with wide views of the valley below. The surface is usually good but can be corrugated, and the road is often shared with cattle, donkeys and goats. The best time to ride is the dry season, from May to October, when the days are warm and the nights cold.

The town's history is typical of this country. It began as a farming settlement, and it has long been the home of Herero communities, as well as German-descended and Afrikaner farmers whose families came a century ago. Further north, Himba people live in scattered settlements, and you may see their distinctive appearance in the market or by the road. The region's earlier story involves San hunter-gatherers and later waves of herders, and rock engravings can be found on some farms, though visiting them requires local guidance and permission.

Western Etosha is a natural next step. The park's western areas, with fewer visitors and drier landscapes, are known for desert-adapted wildlife and big waterholes, and the approach from here is quiet and scenic. Entry fees apply, and park rules on speed and conduct are strict, with gates closing at sunset. The land around Kamanjab also holds small private reserves offering game drives and, in some cases, cheetah and carnivore centres.

The scenery has a stark beauty: flat-topped hills, termite mounds like gravestones, and acacia trees with umbrella crowns. The air smells of warm dust and dry grass, and sunsets come in a blaze of orange.

Fill the tank here, carry plenty of water and plan to arrive before dark, since animals are hard to see at night.
t.folldal@62.1,10.0:
Folldal is a small mining village in the Østerdalen district, and it carries a curious history for a place so quiet today. Copper was mined here from the seventeenth century until the 1970s, and the old workings at Folldal Verk are now a museum, with buildings and shafts that give a picture of the life of the miners. About 600 people live in the village centre, and the surrounding municipality is large, with mountains, forests and pastures. The nearest towns are Alvdal, a long way south, and the larger settlements are far enough that fuel is something to plan for.

The village sits at the northern edge of the Rondane range and close to Dovrefjell, and the landscape is typical of eastern Norway's high country: broad valleys, rolling hills and birch forest that gives way to bare mountain above the tree line. The Folda river flows through the village, and in summer the meadows are bright with wildflowers. In autumn, the birches turn gold and the mountain slopes glow red with dwarf shrubs, and it is one of the most beautiful seasons.

The Rondane road ends here, and the last stretch is a gentle descent through forest and farmland. The road is smooth and quiet, with moderate curves, and you pass through a landscape of small farms, summer pastures and old wooden buildings. Elk, reindeer and sheep may appear on the road, so keep watch, particularly at dawn and dusk. The weather can be changeable, and rain showers come and go quickly. In winter, snow and ice make riding impossible, and the best months are June to September.

In Folldal, you can find a small shop, a petrol pump and a cafe, though hours may be limited, so check before you rely on it. Local food includes cured meats, cheese and the brown goat cheese, brunost, that Norwegians love, which tastes of caramel. A visit to the mining museum is a good way to spend an hour, and the surrounding mountains are ideal for walking. After the open fell, the village is a calm, friendly place to rest.
t.cedaredge@38.9,-107.9:
Cedaredge is a small orchard town on the south-eastern flank of the Grand Mesa, a place of about two thousand people where apples, peaches, cherries and pears are grown in the warm lower slopes and the main street holds a few cafes and a museum of pioneer buildings. It sits at about six thousand feet, with the huge bulk of the mesa filling the sky to the north, and from here the byway starts to climb. The town is a quiet, friendly stop, and Delta, with larger stores, is down the valley.

The Grand Mesa is often described as the largest flat-topped mountain in the world. Its surface is a capping layer of hard volcanic basalt that protected the softer rock below from erosion, and the plateau stands more than five thousand feet above the valleys around it. On top, at over ten thousand feet, there are hundreds of small lakes, left by glaciers, set among spruce forest and meadows. Elk, deer and black bears roam there, and the fishing is popular.

The Grand Mesa Scenic Byway climbs in a series of switchbacks and long bends, from orchard country through scrub oak and aspen into dense spruce and fir. As it climbs, the temperature falls and the views get wider, with the Gunnison River valley and the West Elk range visible to the south, and, from a few lookouts on the north side, the Grand Valley with the Colorado River. The road is well maintained, with a good surface, easy gradients and pull-offs. Traffic is light, and the best times are late spring, when the lakes thaw, and early autumn, when the aspen turn gold.

Take fuel in Cedaredge, since there is little on the plateau. The services on top, a lodge or two and seasonal stores, are open mainly in summer. Afternoon thunderstorms are common, and hail can arrive without much notice, so start early and be down before the sky darkens. It can be cold, with snow possible in any month, so carry a warm layer, and watch for deer at dusk. Later in the season, the road can close for winter.
t.palisade@39.1,-108.3:
Palisade is a small town in the Grand Valley of western Colorado, and it smells of peaches in summer. The orchards that surround it, nourished by water from the Colorado River and baked by long hot days and cool nights, produce fruit so good that people drive from Denver to buy it from roadside stands. The harvest runs from July through September, with peaches at their best in August, and the town holds a festival to celebrate. It sits at about forty-seven hundred feet, which makes it one of the warmest places in the state.

The same combination of sun and cool nights has made the valley a wine region as well, and many small wineries and tasting rooms are scattered among the orchards, along with cideries, lavender farms and a few craft breweries. The backdrop is dramatic: pale cliffs of the Book Cliffs to the north, the flat-topped Grand Mesa to the east, and the red and orange rock of the Colorado National Monument to the west. Mount Garfield, a bare slope above the town, glows in the evening light.

For a rider finishing the Grand Mesa byway, the descent into Palisade is a sudden change in the world. After the cool forest and lakes of the plateau, you drop through winding canyons and into dry, bright orchard country, and the temperature rises by twenty degrees or more. The roads here are flat and straight, running between fruit trees and vineyards, and are best enjoyed slowly, with a stop at a stand for a cold drink and a peach.

Fuel and food are no problem, since the nearby towns of Clifton and Grand Junction, the main city of the valley, have all the services you could need, and Palisade has its own small selection. The Colorado River here is popular for rafting and floating, and cycling is a local passion, so share the road with bikes. Summer is hot, with temperatures often above thirty-five degrees Celsius, so ride in the morning or evening. Autumn is gentler, with harvest festivals and golden light, and the roads are quieter.
t.salida@38.5,-106.0:
Salida stands where the Arkansas River leaves its mountain valley and starts to spread out, a former railroad town of about five thousand in central Colorado, at about seven thousand feet. The old brick downtown is on the National Register of Historic Places, and has the kind of independent bookshops, galleries, bakeries and brewpubs that make it a pleasant place to spend an evening. The river runs right through town, and in summer it is full of kayakers, rafters and paddleboarders enjoying a whitewater park.

To the west, the Collegiate Peaks rise like a wall. This part of the Sawatch Range holds a cluster of the highest summits in the state, over fourteen thousand feet, and several of them are named after Ivy League universities, which is how they got their name: Harvard, Yale, Princeton and Columbia. Geologists from Harvard surveyed the area in the 1860s and gave their college a mountain, and the others followed. The peaks are often snow-capped into July, and their sharp outlines are visible from many points on the ride.

The byway runs through the valley of the upper Arkansas, a wide, open landscape of sagebrush, cottonwoods and ranches, with the river flickering in the distance. The road is mostly straight, with gentle curves and the occasional climb, and the surface is good. This is a relaxed road rather than a technical one, and the views are what matter, especially in late September, when the aspens on the lower slopes turn yellow. Weather can change fast at this altitude, with afternoon thunderstorms in summer and a chance of snow outside it.

Fuel is plentiful in Salida, and so are restaurants, and it is worth taking time to wander the old streets. The Mount Princeton hot springs, up the valley, offer a soak after a day on the road. Buena Vista, the next town north, has its own services if you need them. Salida means exit in Spanish, and the name suggests the way the railroad once escaped the mountains. A cup of coffee on the riverside patio is a good way to begin the day, and the long summer evenings suit a slow dinner.
t.central city@39.8,-105.5:
Central City climbs a steep gulch in the Colorado Rockies, a little brick town of a few hundred people at about eight and a half thousand feet, and it is a monument to the gold rush. In 1859, a prospector named John Gregory struck gold in the gulch, and within a few years, tens of thousands of people had arrived. The hills around were so full of ore that the town called itself the richest square mile on Earth, and the street names, the headframes, the tailings piles and the tilted miners' cottages still tell the story.

The grand buildings from the boom survive, among them the Teller House hotel and the Central City Opera House, which opened in 1878 and is still used for a summer season of opera. The miners, many of them Cornish, wanted culture as well as gold, and they built a fine hall in a mining camp. In the past few decades, gambling was legalised in the town, and casinos now fill several of the old streets, which gives the main drag a slightly odd mix of Victorian charm and neon.

For the ride, the roads that climb here from the east are steep and winding, narrow in places, with hairpins and sharp turns that follow old wagon tracks. The scenery is a combination of forest, rock outcrops, abandoned mine buildings and long views over the Front Range. Surfaces can be rough after winter, and in summer, tour buses and casino traffic can make progress slow. The Peak to Peak Scenic Byway runs a long way north from nearby Black Hawk through mountain villages toward Estes Park.

You can buy fuel at Idaho Springs, in the valley below, about seven kilometres away, which is on the interstate and has plenty of stations and restaurants, so it is wise to fill up there. The town has a handful of cafes and bars, and a small museum devoted to its history. Weather at this altitude can be changeable, with fog, thunderstorms and a chance of snow outside summer. Autumn, when the aspen turn gold in the surrounding gulches, is a lovely time to visit, and the evening light on the old buildings is warm.
t.aspen@39.2,-106.8:
Aspen was a silver town before it was a ski town, and the old buildings still show it. In the 1880s, miners poured into the Roaring Fork Valley after rich veins of silver were found in the hills, and the little camp became one of the biggest producers in the country in only a few years. The Hotel Jerome opened in 1889, and the streets filled with banks, opera houses and saloons. When the silver price crashed in 1893, the town went quiet for half a century, until skiers arrived after the Second World War and turned it into a resort.

Today Aspen has fewer than seven thousand year-round residents and a reputation as one of the most expensive towns in America. Boutiques and galleries sit alongside old brick buildings, and private jets fill the little airport. But the setting is genuinely lovely, with four ski mountains, dense stands of aspen trees, and the high peaks rising on all sides, among them the Maroon Bells, two perfectly shaped summits that are often called the most photographed mountains in Colorado. Hunter S. Thompson lived at nearby Woody Creek, and his shadow hangs over the local bars.

Out of town, the ride heads up the valley toward Independence Pass, which crosses the Continental Divide at over twelve thousand feet on a narrow, winding highway, with sharp curves, steep drop-offs and few guardrails. It is a spectacular road, and in summer the wildflowers on the high tundra are magnificent. The pass is closed in winter, usually from November until Memorial Day or later, and large vehicles are not permitted on the narrowest section. Afternoon thunderstorms are common, so make an early start, and take care on the descent.

Aspen has everything, from fuel stations to supermarkets, restaurants and bike shops, so take care of the basics before you go. Prices are high, so if you are on a budget, shop in Basalt or Glenwood Springs down the valley. In autumn, in late September, the aspen groves turn a vivid gold, and the road is crowded with photographers. Be considerate of other road users, and remember that the air up high is thin and cold, so layers and gloves are a good idea even in July.
t.grootberg pass@-19.8,14.1:
Grootberg means big mountain in Afrikaans, and the name fits a flat-topped plateau that rises out of the stony plains of Kunene in north-western Namibia. It is part of the Etendeka formation, a thick stack of ancient lava flows that now forms a long escarpment, and the pass is a steep gravel descent off the edge, with sharp bends and loose stones. At the top, a lodge perches on the rim with a view that runs across the valley of the Klip river to a horizon of red, brown and purple hills.

This is desert-elephant country. A small population of elephants that have adapted to the dry conditions roams the dry riverbeds and valleys of the Kunene region, walking long distances between water and feeding grounds, and they are sometimes seen near the road. They are wild, and they can be dangerous, so keep a safe distance, never ride between a mother and her calf, and be ready to back off. Local communities manage conservation efforts, and tourism provides valuable income.

The riding is serious. The gravel road is rough in places, with deep corrugations, sharp rocks and washouts after rain, and the pass itself is steep and narrow, with little room to pass another vehicle. Take it slowly, in low gear, and make sure your bike is prepared, with good tyres and a spare tube. Rain can turn the track to mud and make dry river crossings dangerous. Heat is intense in summer, so start early, drink plenty of water and avoid riding in the midday sun.

There are no towns anywhere near, so supplies must be brought from outside. Fuel is available at larger towns such as Khorixas and Kamanjab, and it is sensible to fill up there and carry extra, since distances are great and the next pump could be hours away. A lodge on the plateau offers meals and rooms with a view, and it is wise to book ahead. Bring water, food and a good map, and leave word of your route. Sunrise from the rim, with the plains below turning from grey to gold, is one of the nicest sights in the north-west.
t.ravello@40.6,14.6:
Ravello sits about 365 metres above the Amalfi Coast, high enough that the crowds on the shore below sound like a distant radio. Instead of beaches, it offers terraces, gardens and a sense that it has seen all this before. The town perches on a ridge between the Dragone and Reginna valleys, above the sea and the busier resort of Amalfi, and from its balconies you look down on lemon terraces, white villas and the blue curve of the Gulf of Salerno.

Its glory days were in the Middle Ages, when Ravello was a prosperous republic allied with Amalfi, trading with the Eastern Mediterranean, and its rich merchant families built palaces and churches. Villa Rufolo, from the thirteenth century, with its Moorish-looking cloister and gardens, inspired Richard Wagner in 1880, who said he had found the magic garden of Klingsor for his opera Parsifal. Today its terrace hosts concerts in summer. Villa Cimbrone has a long avenue ending in the Terrace of Infinity, lined with marble busts, and the writer Gore Vidal lived in Ravello for years. The cathedral has a fine bronze door from the twelfth century.

The road up from the coast is a classic of southern Italy, a narrow series of hairpins climbing through terraced lemon groves, with drops, walls and blind bends. The surface can be worn, traffic is heavy in summer, and tour buses squeeze through with only inches to spare. Scooters and locals know every corner, so keep right and do not rush. Early morning or late afternoon in spring and autumn is far more pleasant than August, when queues and heat are fierce.

Cars cannot enter the centre, and parking for motorcycles is easier than for cars, though it is limited and signs should be checked. Fuel is not available in Ravello itself: Maiori, about two kilometres away, has stations and shops, as do Amalfi and Salerno. In town, cafes, ice cream stalls and trattorias serve local specialities such as lemon-scented pastries, fresh pasta with seafood, and the sweet limoncello made from the region's lemons. Leave time to walk the lanes and gardens, and look out at the sea from a bench before heading back down.
t.salerno@40.7,14.8:
Salerno is the working city at the eastern end of the Amalfi Coast, and it rarely gets the attention of its prettier neighbours. A busy port with about 125,000 people, it sits on the curve of the Gulf of Salerno, backed by steep hills, and it has an old town of narrow lanes, a long seafront promenade and a distinct, unpretentious character. After the beautiful frenzy of the coast road, many riders find it a relief to be in a place where people just live.

The city's history is richer than it looks. In the Middle Ages, Salerno was home to the Schola Medica Salernitana, one of the first and most famous medical schools in Europe, where scholars studied Greek and Arabic texts and women also practised as physicians. The cathedral, dedicated to St Matthew, was begun in the late eleventh century under the Norman ruler Robert Guiscard and houses the apostle's relics, with a beautiful atrium and bronze doors. In September 1943, Allied troops landed on the beaches nearby, and the fighting around Salerno was among the hardest of the Italian campaign.

The riding in the area is a contrast. To the west, the Amalfi Drive winds along the cliff above the sea, narrow and busy and memorable. To the north and east, the roads cross a broad plain of farms and factories, with fast, straight stretches that are fine for covering distance. In the city itself, traffic is dense, with scooters, buses and impatient drivers, and a quiet focus helps. The seafront, with its palm trees and gardens, is lovely in the early evening, and in winter the old streets are lit with elaborate artistic light displays.

As a stop, Salerno is easy. It has fuel, repair shops, hotels, banks and supermarkets, and the food is excellent and cheaper than on the coast. Buffalo mozzarella from the nearby plain is a local pride, along with fresh seafood, pasta and pastries. Ferries leave from the port for Amalfi and other coastal towns in season, and the central railway station is a good reference point. Park the bike in a secured garage if you can, and take an evening walk along the waterfront.
t.san juan skyway point 7@37.5,-108.5:
Dolores lies where the river of the same name leaves the mountains and starts its long run across the red-rock plateau toward Utah. The town is small, just about nine hundred people, strung along Highway 145 beside the water, with the San Juans visible to the north and the green rampart of the Mesa Verde country to the south. The Spanish explorers who came through in 1776, the Domínguez and Escalante party, gave the river its name, El Río de Nuestra Señora de los Dolores, the River of Our Lady of Sorrows.

The land here is thick with the history of the Ancestral Puebloan people, who farmed these mesas for centuries and left remarkable stone villages and cliff dwellings. The Anasazi Heritage Center, a short drive from town, holds collections of pottery, baskets and tools from dig sites across the region and gives a wonderful background before you see the sites in the open. Canyons of the Ancients National Monument spreads west of here, with thousands of recorded sites, most of them unexcavated and unmarked on the ground.

The riding is relaxed. The highway follows the Dolores River from the foot of Lizard Head Pass, with pine forest on either side and the water flowing clear and green beside the road. South of town it opens into more rolling ranch country toward Cortez, with a long, wide view of the Sleeping Ute Mountain, a ridge shaped like a reclining figure. McPhee Reservoir lies just off the road, a big blue lake in the red desert, popular with anglers and boaters.

Dolores has fuel, a few cafes, a brewery and a handful of motels, and Cortez, about sixteen kilometres away, has everything else. A museum of the Rio Grande Southern railroad sits near the centre of town, a small building with lovely railway relics.

Summer is warm and dry, with temperatures in the nineties on the plateau, while the mountains behind remain cooler. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for riding here, with clear air and soft light. Afternoon thunderstorms can bring flash floods in the washes, so be careful on dirt roads. Mesa Verde lies close, with its famous cliff dwellings, and is a sensible detour.
t.norwegian scenic route rondane point 1@6:
The southern end of the Rondane road is the start of a different kind of mountain country. Gone are the steep fjord walls and dripping waterfalls of the west, and in their place stands a broad, high land of rounded summits, pale slopes and wide valleys, where the sky takes up most of the view. Rondane was Norway's first national park, created in 1962, and the mountains in it include ten peaks over two thousand metres, with Rondeslottet the highest at 2,178 metres. They look smooth from a distance, the product of rock that breaks into blocks and of long ages under ice.

The country feels open and quiet, with birch scrub in the lower valleys giving way to willow and dwarf shrubs, and above the tree line lichen and moss colour the rock in grey and green. Wild reindeer roam the high ground, among the last herds of their kind in Europe, and a lucky rider may see a small group on a ridge, standing quite still against the sky. Mountain birds such as ptarmigan and golden plover are common, and in summer the bogs are bright with cloudberry flowers and cotton grass.

The roads here run high across rolling terrain, with long, gentle bends and few steep sections. The surface is generally good, and in summer the traffic is light, with a few cars and campers. The weather can change quickly, and even in July the temperature can be low, with cold rain and wind from the north, so carry warm layers and waterproofs. In autumn the dwarf birch turns red and gold across the hills, and the air is clear and cold. In winter the road can close in storms, and snow can come as early as September.

There are no big towns near here. Otta, about thirty kilometres to the south-west, and Vinstra, a little farther off, are the closest places with shops and fuel, so it is wise to stock up before heading into the mountains. Bring food and drink for the day. In the stillness at a pull-in, with the engine switched off, the only sound may be the wind in the grass, and the nearest person may be miles away.
t.norwegian scenic route rondane point 2@6:
To understand Rondane, it helps to know what the mountains are made of. The rock here is mostly a hard, pale, layered sandstone called sparagmite, and it weathers in a way that gives the peaks their characteristic rounded forms and their slopes of loose stone. Over millions of years the ice sheets rubbed down the summits, left boulders strewn across the valleys and scooped out hollows that became lakes. The landscape looks old, and it is.

It is also a landscape of subtle colour. In summer the lower slopes are green with grass and birch, the middle slopes are a patchwork of heather, blueberry and willow, and the upper slopes are grey and white with lichen and snow. After rain the rock darkens, and the contrast makes the whole scene glow. In autumn, when the bilberry leaves turn crimson, the whole hillside seems to be on fire. The light is clear and cool, and distances are hard to judge, since there are no trees to give scale.

Walkers love the park for its long, open ridges and its network of huts, and in summer you may see people with big packs on the paths beside the road. The wild reindeer are shy, and they tend to keep to the higher ground, but they are sometimes seen from the road at dawn or dusk. The mountains have also been used by farmers for summer grazing for centuries, and old stone shelters survive among the slopes.

The road across this section is easy and relaxed, a gentle ride with wide views and moderate traffic. The surface is usually good, though frost can break it up in places, and the bends are mostly gentle. Wind is common, and the weather can turn quickly, so be ready. Folldal, about twenty-seven kilometres away, is the nearest settlement of any size, with Otta about thirty-three kilometres in the other direction, so check your fuel and supplies before going on. A quiet pause on a clear morning, with the sun on the peaks, is worth more than a hundred kilometres of road.
t.norwegian scenic route rondane point 3@6:
There is a viewing point on this road that looks across a lake to the peaks of Rondane, named after the painter Harald Sohlberg, who painted these mountains with a stillness that few artists have matched. His best-known picture, Winter Night in the Mountains, shows a snowy peak under a deep blue sky with a single star above it, and it is one of the most loved paintings in Norway. Standing at the viewpoint in the late evening, with the light fading and the water dark, it is not hard to see what drew him.

The lake below is cold and clear, fed by streams from the surrounding slopes, and its surface often holds a perfect reflection of the mountains on a calm day. Birds, including divers and ducks, nest along the shore, and in the evening trout rise in the shallows. The viewing platform and a small paved area have been designed to blend into the hillside, with simple materials and a modest footprint, and the effect is to focus attention on the view rather than on the structure.

For a rider, this is an easy and rewarding stop on a quiet road. The approach is a gentle ride through birch and willow, with the mountains growing larger as you come closer, and the surface is generally good. It is a place for a pause rather than for racing, and the best light comes in the early morning and the evening, when the low sun picks out the shape of the peaks. Wind and cold are common, and snow can fall in any month, so dress warmly.

Services are few in this part of the mountains. Folldal, about twenty-three kilometres away, and Alvdal, about thirty-four, are the nearest villages, with Otta farther south, so plan your fuel and food around them. t.near flisa on the way back@60.5,11.9:
The Solør district lies in the east of Norway, where the land flattens and the forest closes in, and this pin sits in the heart of it, between Kirkenær and the Glomma river. The country is a mosaic of spruce and pine, small farms, bogs and long, slow lakes, running east toward the Swedish border, and it has a quiet, lonely character that suits a rider who has had enough of crowds. Kirkenær, the nearest town, has barely twelve hundred people.

The woods here have a distinctive history. In the seventeenth century, Finnish settlers, drawn by the chance of cheap land and a way of farming that involved burning the forest to grow rye, moved into the area and became known as the forest Finns. They brought their language, their log smoke saunas and their folklore, and their culture survived in the Finnskogen for centuries. At Grue, a church fire in 1822 killed more than a hundred people, one of the worst such disasters in the country, and the present church stands as a memorial.

Riding here is calm, with long, straight roads through the forest, gentle rolls and few bends. The surface is generally good, and traffic is light, though timber lorries use the main routes. The risk is moose, which are common and can cross the road at dawn and dusk, so keep your speed down in the woods and watch the verges. The forest is at its best in September, when the birch leaves turn and the light is low.

The lakes are good for swimming, with soft, brown water and quiet beaches that are often empty. Fuel is available at Kirkenær and Våler, but pumps may be unmanned, and cards are the norm, so carry one that works in Norway. Shops close early, and distances are long, so plan your meals. Bring mosquito repellent in summer, because the forest is full of insects, and a warm layer for the evening. The silence at night is deep.
